title: How to identify Spodoptera armyworms on maize
text: CABI: How to identify Spodoptera armyworms on maize

title: How to identify Spodoptera armyworms on maize
text: *Spodoptera* is a genus of moths which caterpillars cause damage to a variety of crops, including maize. They consume the leaves, creating holes and ragged leaf edges. Feeding through the maize whorl can cause a line of identical “shot” holes, when the leaf unfurls. Caterpillars also burrow into cobs and feed on the tassels and kernels when the plant reaches maturity and the young tender leaves are not available anymore.

title: How to identify Spodoptera armyworms on maize
text:
#### Fall armyworm (Above). African armyworm (Below). ####
Russ Ottens, University of Georgia, Bugwood.org (Above image). Kieser M., via ecoport (Below image)
*Spodoptera* are called armyworms due to their behaviour of feeding in large groups which can quickly devour plants. *Spodoptera* species can look very similar to each other. They also display a variety of colours or patterns within the same species. It is important to identify the species before applying management or control methods. Young <2 cm caterpillars
* *Spodoptera frugiperda* (fall armyworm): Greenish with black heads, soon turning light orange. Feed on young leaves emerging from the whorl causing window-pane damage. * *Spodoptera exempta* (African armyworm): Green or light brown. Also causing window-pane damage when feeding on young leaves, and whorl. * *Spodoptera littoralis* (cotton leafworm): Greyish or dark green body with a brownish head. Feed on lower side of all leaves, and whorl. * *Spodoptera exigua* (beet armworm): Pale green or yellow. Feed on upper surface of all leaves, and whorl. Older up to 3 cm or even 4 cm long caterpillars
* Fall armyworm: Light green to dark brown; backside often has thin white lines, and darker lines on its sides. Inverted light "Y" on front of head. Small black spots on body, and 4 spots in a square at end of body. Feeds on young leaves, whorl, tassels, silk and cob. * African armyworm: Shiny black; thin dark blue lines on the top of the body; several greenish yellow lines at side.

title: How to identify Spodoptera armyworms on maize
text:
Feeds on young leaves, whorl, tassels, silk and cob. * African armyworm: Shiny black; thin dark blue lines on the top of the body; several greenish yellow lines at side. Inverted light "Y" on the front of the head, but doesn’t have the 4 spots on the second-to-last segment like fall armyworm. Feeds on young leaves, and whorl, and cob from the top downwards. * Cotton leafworm: Dark green to reddish-brown or blackish-grey. Dark and light stripes run along the sides of the body, usually a bright yellow stripe along the sides. 2-4 dark semi-circular to triangular spots on the back. Feeds on all leaves, whorl, and cob
* Beet armyworm: Green to dark brown, sometimes almost black, with green and dark brown stripes and spots running along the body. Darker stripe down the back and paler stripe along each side. Pink or yellow underneath. Feeds on all leaves, whorl, and cob.

title: Life cycle of the tomato leaf miner
text: CABI: Life cycle of the tomato leaf miner

title: Life cycle of the tomato leaf miner
text: The tomato leaf miner is a species of moth which causes widespread damage to tomato crops by mining plant tissues, particularly the leaves. These mines are formed by the larva (small caterpillars). Leaf mines are wide, silvery, and gradually become brown and necrotic. Leaf necrosis may result in leaf death or premature leaf drop. Mines in the fruit can also lead to fruit rot. Other hosts of tomato leaf miner include eggplant, *Capsicum* (peppers) and potatoes, as well as solanaceous weeds.

title: Life cycle of the tomato leaf miner
text:
#### Larva of Tuta absoluta (Above). Larva of Tuta absoluta inside a tomato fruit (Below). ####
Dr. Kalleshwara swamy, UAHS, India (Above image) Marja van der Straten/NVWA Plant Protection Service/Bugwood - CC BY-NC 3.0 US (Below image)
Severe infestations can cause 100% yield loss of tomatoes. Knowing the life cycle of the tomato leaf miner can help with selecting and understanding management and control methods. The life cycle of the tomato leaf miner ranges from 24-38 days, depending on the temperature of the environment. It can overwinter as an egg, pupa or adult moth. Females lay creamy white to yellow eggs on host plants, on the underside of leaves, usually singly but sometime in groups of 2-5. Eggs take 4-5 days to hatch. When the larvae hatch they are yellowish in colour and about 0.5 mm long. They soon enter leaf, stem or fruit tissue to feed, creating mines in the process. On leaves, mines appear as silvery streaks which may turn brown and necrotic. Mines may cause leaves to dry out and fall prematurely which can reduce crop yield. Larvae growth involves four developmental stages (instars). Before the next instar a larva must moult. In between moulting, caterpillars can be temporarily found on the leaves, stem or fruit. Exit holes can be seen most easily on the fruits. As a larva matures it develops a distinctive black band on the head and its body becomes greenish to pinkish, reaching up to 9 mm long. It takes about 20 days for a larva to reach the end of the fourth instar. Eventually, the larva forms a light to dark brown hardened pupa around it, about 9 mm long.

title: Life cycle of the tomato leaf miner
text: It takes about 20 days for a larva to reach the end of the fourth instar. Eventually, the larva forms a light to dark brown hardened pupa around it, about 9 mm long. Pupation may take place in the soil, on the surface of a leaf or within a mine. After 10-13 days a brown adult emerges, about 5-7 mm long, with thread-like antennae and forewings with grey scales and black spots. Moths are active during night and hide between leaves during the day.

title: Chilli pepper extract for the management of insect pests
text: CABI: Chilli pepper extract for the management of insect pests

title: Chilli pepper extract for the management of insect pests
text: Capsaicin is the active ingredient in chili peppers. It is used as a bird, animal and insect repellent. Capsaicin also has some insecticidal activity and can be applied to crops with low levels of insect infestation. Chilli pepper extracts have been used to control a wide range of insect pests, both in traditional home preparations and commercial products. Its main target pests are aphids, loopers, armyworms, spider mites, thrips, leaf miners and whiteflies. It does not meet any of the Highly Hazardous Pesticide (HHP) criteria, so it is not a HHP but the signal word "Danger" applies to capsaicin due to its associated hazards. These hazards include toxic if swallowed, harmful if swallowed, skin irritation and serious eye damage. Extracts of chili peppers are prepared by farmers in many countries and commercial products are registered in some countries.

title: Chilli pepper extract for the management of insect pests
text:
#### Capsaicin is extracted from chilli peppers. ####
Public domain CCO
Once applied to the plant surface, the capsaicin induces insects to move from the plant to the soil surface. Treatment with capsaicin-based products may also reduce adult egg-laying. Research indicates that capsaicin disrupts insect metabolism and affects the insect central nervous system. It also damages insect cell membranes, causing holes to form. Some products have capsaicin as the only AI, but can also be used in formulation with other AI, such as azadirachtin, garlic oil and soybean oil. Capsaicin rapidly degrades in the environment, and it is toxic to honeybees.

title: Chilli pepper extract for the management of insect pests
text:
* Some product labels recommend using capsaicin-based products in combination with a sticker
* Capsaicin can be applied in the seedbed and field
* Use this product as a foliar spray to repel and suppress pests
* For best preventive results, this product must be applied at least once a week on a regular and continuous basis
* Use capsaicin at lower rates when pest pressure is low
* When pest pressure is heavy or plant canopy is dense, use higher rates and increase spray frequency. Repeat application if rain occurs within two to three hours of spraying. * This product must come into contact with the target pests to be effective
* Coverage typically requires a minimum of 10 gallons of spray volume per acre. Higher volumes will be required for larger perennial crops. When using capsaicin, wear a long-sleeved shirt and long pants, socks and shoes. Protective eyewear and waterproof or chemical resistant gloves are also advised when using products containing capsaicin.

title: How to make compost manure
text: How to make compost manure

title: How to make compost manure
text: Most soils in Zambia are low in fertility, poor in nutrients retention and have poor drainage. These problems that cannot be solved by application of inorganic chemical fertilizers except by addition of humus through the use of compost or any other organic fertilizers.

title: How to make compost manure
text: Compost is a mixture of decomposed organic materials by microbial activity under warm, moist, and aerobic environment. Compost can be made from a wide range of materials which include vegetative materials, animal manure, wood ash, and kitchen refuse. Well cured compost will always have a fresh smell similar to that of soil. One pile can generate minimum of 600 kg of cured and dry compost. The temperature of the compost is the key determinant of the composting process and a good guide as to when to turn or correct any observed problems.

title: How to make compost manure
text: * Select a location close to where you want to use the compost. Mark out the area for the heap using pegs. It is advisable that the heap is 1 to 1.5 meters wide and 1 to 1.5 meters high. The heap can be of any length above 2 meters. If the heap is smaller than this, it is not large enough to maintain the heat created inside. The heap should not be higher or wider than 1.5m, for if it is too high (above 1.5m), the flow of air into the compost (aeration) will be hindered delaying the composting process and yielding undesired results such as rotting of compost materials. * Loosen the soil in the marked area where layering of materials is going to be done. * During layering, start with the coarse materials consisting of maize stalks, twigs, maize cobs, etc. followed by a layer of dry materials of leaves and/or grass, 20 cm thick after which apply water until moist. It is always a good practice to add water after adding the dry materials. This should be followed by layer of green material, 10 cm thick then about 5 cm manure is added. Repeat the layering until the pile is about 1 to 1.5 meters high. Always remember to add water every after adding dry material. Then cover the whole pile with straw or grass. * Turning is important to attain high quality compost. This is done by bringing the material at the centre outward while the outside material should go towards the centre. The materials will decompose faster if the compost pile is turned regularly, e.g. once every 2 weeks. Spray the heap as you turn with a fine mist of water. The compost should be ready after the fourth turning or approximately eight (8) weeks.

title: 'IPM: Liquid Formulations'
text: CABI: IPM: Liquid Formulations

title: 'IPM: Liquid Formulations'
text: Pesticides are available in many different forms, including liquid, solid and living organisms. Each has advantages and disadvantages.

title: 'IPM: Liquid Formulations'
text: The are a number of types of liquid formulations. Emulsifiable Concentrate (EC or E) - usually contain liquid active ingredients (25-75%) and one or more petroleum solvents and emulsifiers, which allow the formulation to be mixed with water before spraying, forming milky spray mixtures. - Advantages: easy to handle, transport and store; easy to measure and mix with water; little agitation required, does not settle out or separate and sink to bottom of tank; little visible residue on plant treated surfaces; can be used with most types of application equipment. - Disadvantage: usually high concentration of active ingredient so need to measure, mix and calibrate carefully; solvents can cause rubber and plastic sprayer parts to deteriorate rapidly; flammable; easily absorbed through skin; high phytotoxicity.

title: 'IPM: Liquid Formulations'
text:
Flowables (L or F or FL) - a finely ground active ingredient suspended in a liquid, mixed with water prior to application. Similar to ECs but easier to use. - Advantages: easy to handle and apply; rarely clog nozzles
- Disadvantages: require shaking before pouring and mixing; may leave visible residues on sprayed surfaces
Soluble Concentrate (SL) - Liquid formulation with active ingredient dissolved in water. - Advantages: do not plug strainers and filters
- Disadvantages: some that are dissolved salts can be corrosive to skin
Suspension Concentrate (SC) - Non-soluble active ingredient suspended in water to form liquid formulation. Need to be diluted with water before use. Combine benefits of ECs and WPs
- Advantages: easy to transport, handle and store; easy to mix with water; can be used with most types of application equipment; generally less phytotoxic than ECs; dissolve in water, no constant shaking required. - Disadvantages: container must be shaken before use; spray nozzles and filters can be blocked; inert carriers may leave visible residues on sprayed surfaces; require moderate shaking of the spray tank regularly to prevent active ingredient from sinking to bottom
Ultra Low Volume (ULV or LV) - Pesticides in liquid form, used as it is or diluted with small quantities of carrier. Concentration usually close to 100% of active ingredient. - Advantages: Easy to transport, handle and store; don’t need to dilute product with oil or water; little agitation required; don’t plug screens or filters; little agitation required; don't plug screens of filters; little visible residue on sprayed surfaces. - Disadvantages: Specialised equipment required; high drift hazard due to small droplet size; easily absorbed through skin; solvents can cause rubber and plastic sprayer parts to deteriorate rapidly; need to carefully calibrate and apply due to high concentration of active ingredient.

title: 'IPM: What''s in a pesticide?'
text: CABI: IPM: What's in a pesticide?

title: 'IPM: What''s in a pesticide?'
text: Many farmers and field technicians do not have a good understanding of what pesticides are made of nor are they familiar with some of the key terminology which is necessary for making informed decisions when it is time to buy or apply a pesticide. As a consequence, they may inadvertently buy formulations which contain mixtures of active ingredients that are allowed and prohibited, for example.

title: 'IPM: What''s in a pesticide?'
text:
* Pesticides are made up of active and inert ingredients
* An active ingredient (a.i.) is the chemical that is active against the target pest (e.g. kills, repels, limits growth, etc.). There are hundreds of chemicals that are active ingredients. A single a.i. may be sold in many different formulations
* Inert ingredients have no activity against the pest. They allow the chemical to be handled, stored and applied more easily and safely. They are not disclosed (i.e. we don’t know what they are) and in some cases may be more toxic than the active ingredient. However, in most countries they are not regulated.

title: 'IPM: What''s in a pesticide?'
text:
* A pesticide formulation consists of the active ingredient (the chemical that affects the pest) combined the several other chemicals. * Adjuvants are chemicals that are not active against the target pest. They are added to pesticide formulations to improve performance. Sometimes the inert ingredients are part of the formulation, but sometimes they need to be added separately (depending on label instructions). Adjuvants include spreaders (to help the spray mix spread evenly over treated surfaces), stickers (to help the spray mix stick to surfaces), thickeners, pH buffers, plant penetrants (to enhance the adsorption of systemic pesticides), wetting agents (to help wettable powders mix with water and spread on water repellent surfaces), or foaming/defoaming agents. You must follow label instructions for adjuvants. Sometimes they are prohibited for use with a particular pesticide and using one will be risky. * Concentration refers to the amount of the active ingredient in the formulation. * Weight per unit volume: (e.g. 500 g/L)
* Percentage by weight (e.g. 40% WP)
* As with chemical insecticides, the active ingredient in bio-pesticides is the living organism (or component that have been extracted from it) which is combined with other chemicals so it can be applied as a pesticide.

title: 'IPM: How do pesticides work?'
text: CABI: IPM: How do pesticides work?

title: 'IPM: How do pesticides work?'
text: Many farmers and field technicians do not have a good understanding of key terminology which is necessary for making informed decisions when it is time to buy or apply a pesticide. Pesticides can be grouped by the types of pests they control, by the way they work (their mode of action), by their chemical family or by specificity.

title: 'IPM: How do pesticides work?'
text:
#### Monitoring pesticides in the field. ####
CABI
Type of Pesticide - Pesticides are most commonly grouped by the types of pests they control. Common types of pesticides and their targets include: Fungicides (fungi), Insecticides (insects), Herbicides (weeds), Nematicides (nematodes), Rodenticides (rodents), Acaricides/Miticides (spiders, mites), Molluscicides (snails, slugs), Bactericides (bacteria). Bio-pesticides: the type of pest targeted by bio-pesticides varies and is dependent on the active ingredient of the bio-pesticide.

title: 'IPM: How do pesticides work?'
text:
Mode of Action (or site of action) - Mode of action is the way or method in which the pesticide kills or controls the target pest and refers to the biochemical effect on the pest (e.g. neurotoxins)
- Chemicals and biopesticides with the same mode of action attack pests using the same method. (e.g. Organophosphate insecticides attack the nervous system). - Mode of action helps you assess which pesticide you should use, gives clues to which beneficials/non-target organisms might be affected and can help farmers with resistance management. Farmers should not use pesticides with the same mode of action against same pest repeatedly in same season. Chemical Family- a group of pesticides with a similar chemical structure and properties. Pesticides in the same chemical family often have similar modes of action, poisoning symptoms, and persistence in the environment, as well as similar first aid, clean-up and safety guidelines
- Knowing chemical families will help you select the proper pesticide, decide on the personal protective equipment needed and understand the handling precautions for each product. - Common pesticide chemical families include chlorinated hydrocarbons, organophosphates, carbamates and neonicotinoids. Specificity - some pesticides are effective only against a specific pest or disease, and others are toxic to many species and also kill insects, microoganisms, animals and plant species that are not pests. This depends on the pesticide specificity. - Broad Spectrum: Many pesticides are less specific or non-specific. Those can kill a variety of insects, microorganisms, animals and plant species. - Selective: the selective pesticides are more effective against one type of insect. For example, effective against flea beetles but harmless to bees.

title: 'IPM: Insecticides.'
text: CABI: IPM: Insecticides.

title: 'IPM: Insecticides.'
text:
Insecticides are classified by:
- Mechanism of action or exposure routes
- How insecticides move or reach target pest
Some common insecticide chemical families (with their active ingredients) are:
- Carbamates : carbaryl, pirimicarb
- Organophosphates: dimethoate, malathion
- Neonicotinoids: imidacloprid, acetamiprid, thiamethoxam
- Pyrethroids: lambda cyhalothrin, deltamethrin, bifenthrin
- Spynosyn: spinetoram, spinosad
- Avermectins: emamectin benzoate, lepimectin
- Indoxacarb: indoxacarb

title: 'IPM: Insecticides.'
text:
- Direct contact – the pest comes into direct contact with the spray; the insecticide is then absorbed through the ‘skin’ or cuticle of the insect and kills it
- Secondary contact - the pest comes into direct contact with the spray deposit on a leaf ; the insecticide is then absorbed through the ‘skin’ or cuticle of the insect and kills it
- Ingested – the pest feeds on plants that have been sprayed with insecticide; the insecticide travels into the insect’s digestive system and kills it. - Repellency – contact with the spray deposit does not kill the insect, but causes it to move away from the treated area
- Fumigant – the spray deposit emits a ‘gas’ which kills the insect or causes it to move away from the treated area

title: 'IPM: Insecticides.'
text:
How insecticides move or reach target pest:
Contact insecticides:
- Kill the pest upon contact
- The spray only acts where it lands (the insect must move to it)
- Therefore a thorough and even spray coverage on the foliage is necessary
Systemic insecticides:
- Absorbed into the plant tissues from where they land, they are then moved about in the plant. - May be applied to the soil and taken up by roots or applied to leaves (foliage) and transported. - Insects will be killed when they feed anywhere on the plant. - Bigger droplets, smaller in number, can be dispersed over the crop, which makes treatment easier and less costly.

title: 'IPM: What are biopesticides?'
text: CABI: IPM: What are biopesticides?

title: 'IPM: What are biopesticides?'
text:
#### Entomopathogenic fungi can be used to control insects. ####
USDA, released to public domain
There is no legally agreed definition of the term biopesticide, so definitions of what a biopesticide is can vary. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) is one of the few organisations who include macrobials, such as insects, nematodes, along with microbials (bacteria, algae, protozoa viruses), fungi, as well as plant extracts/botanicals, pheromones and semiochemicals. Main Groups of Biopesticide:
- Macrobials (macro-organisms) include insect natural enemies (e.g. Trichogramma) and entomopathogenic nematodes (though often considered under microbials). - Microbial biopesticides consist of a microorganism (e.g. bacteria, fungi, virus, viroid or protozoa) or their products (metabolites e.g. protein toxins) as the active substance. Entomopathogenic nematodes are often classed as microbial pesticides. Biochemical biopesticides, this diverse group could be considered to include naturally derived biochemicals, such as plant extracts/ botanicals, which may have direct effects on the target pest or indirect effects via the host plant. Semiochemicals, which are naturally occurring chemicals emitted by plants, animals and other organisms (or may be synthetically produced) modify insect pest behaviour. They can be used as repellants, or in traps for mating disruption. Biochemical pesticides can also include metabolites derived from the fermentation of living micro-organisms e.g. Spinosad.

title: 'IPM: What are biopesticides?'
text:
They can be used as repellants, or in traps for mating disruption. Biochemical pesticides can also include metabolites derived from the fermentation of living micro-organisms e.g. Spinosad. Some regulatory authorities also include the following as biopesticides:
- Plant strengtheners are substances and micro-organisms that protect plants against harmful organisms by activating the host plant’s defence mechanisms or via competition with harmful organisms for resources. - Plant incorporated protectants are recognised by the EPA as biopesticides. This includes pesticidal substances produced by plants and the genetic material necessary for the plant to produce the substance. Thus genetically modified plants, for example via the introduction of the Bt protein toxin gene, would be included here. Advantages:
- Usually inherently less toxic than conventional pesticides
- Lower potential for residues
- Can be cheaper than chemical pesticides (if locally produced)
- Often effective in small quantities and decompose quickly
- May be more effective in the long-term
- Less prone to development of resistance in target
- Generally more specific, affect target organism and closely related organisms
- Potential for long-term self-dissemination/maintenance (classical biocontrol)
- Lower non-target effects
- Use in IPM system can maintain yield whilst reducing use of conventional pesticides
- Often less onerous registration requirements
Disadvantages:
- Slow speed of action (not always)
- High specificity (not always)
- Can be more expensive commercial products
- Variable efficacy due to biotic & abiotic factors
- Require careful storage and handling

title: 'IPM: Decontamination & disposal of pesticide containers.'
text: CABI: IPM: Decontamination & disposal of pesticide containers.

title: 'IPM: Decontamination & disposal of pesticide containers.'
text: Cleaning pesticide containers sufficiently at the time of use ensures that any potential source of chemical exposure (to the environment, humans and animals) is reduced to a minimum following the correct application of the chemical product. Many disposal requirements are country specific, therefore ensure that you closely read product labels for specific advice on disposing of residual and waste chemicals.

title: 'IPM: Decontamination & disposal of pesticide containers.'
text:
#### Ensure that all product label guidelines are followed. ####
Environmental Protection Agency
Most countries require triple rinsing or pressure washing of empty pesticide containers, with a range of other requirements across different countries. Some countries treat empty pesticide containers as hazardous waste which require special measures for storage, transportation and disposal. Other countries allow for a wider range of options, for example in the USA, once a container has been decontaminated it can be disposed of via recycling, incineration or landfill.

title: 'IPM: Decontamination & disposal of pesticide containers.'
text:
#### Ensure that all product label guidelines are followed. ####
Environmental Protection Agency
Leaf suppliers should apply the following best practices related to empty pesticide container disposal:
- Cleaning the container before final disposal is the responsibility of the person disposing of the container. - When a metal, plastic, or glass pesticide container is empty, it should be immediately rinsed a minimum of three times (or pressure rinsed), with the resulting residue from the pesticide container being added to the spray tank for application on the crop. - After rinsing, the container should be rendered unusable by puncturing, crushing, or breaking down. - Empty pesticide containers should be prohibited. - Burying empty pesticide containers should be prohibited. - Containers must be disposed of in ways that do not cause harm to the environment, including the soil, air, water, flora or fauna. - Other regulations governing the decontamination and disposal of empty pesticide containers should be followed.

title: 'IPM: Empty pesticide container management schemes.'
text: CABI: IPM: Empty pesticide container management schemes.

title: 'IPM: Empty pesticide container management schemes.'
text: Once emptied, pesticide containers must be handled and disposed of appropriately, otherwise, there is a potential risk of chemical contamination and health risks to both the environment and humans.

title: 'IPM: Empty pesticide container management schemes.'
text:
#### Pesticide container management schemes promote approved practices. ####
CABI
In order to promote sufficient and approved use of pesticide containers, it is beneficial to develop a pesticide container management scheme. The scheme contains guidelines on steps that can be taken across the entire pesticide life cycle to ensure safe practices are carried out to reduce the risk of contamination.

title: 'IPM: Empty pesticide container management schemes.'
text:
#### Use of local radio channels to reach rural farmers and stakeholders. ####
CABI
- Engage relevant stakeholders – Successful container management schemes apply a multi-stakeholder approach. Potential partners for the development of container management schemes include national, regional, and local governments, the agro-input industry, other leaf suppliers, waste disposal firms, farmers, and grower organisations. All participants should accept shared responsibility for scheme implementation. Key players that do not engage can limit the impact of such management schemes. - Conduct assessments – Schemes must be adapted to supply chains, geography, and crop calendars across the specific area in which the scheme will be implemented. An assessment should be carried out to understand the current situation regarding the disposal of empty pesticide containers and other variables. Stakeholders should also consider the potential legal and technical considerations as part of the assessment. - Operation planning – To ensure the long-term sustainability of any proposed scheme, a sound business approach (including a business plan, sustainable funding, operating procedures, and personnel) must be implemented. - Communications and training – Develop communications to target stakeholders such as potential partners and end users. These can take the form of direct instructions in the field, posters, training workshops, and media via TV and local radio. - Pilot – Container management schemes are recommended to initiate a pilot project, with reviews and assessments of the results before the expansion of the project on a wider scale. - Monitoring the scheme – Schemes should be actively monitored to improve the likelihood of success. Monitoring activities will vary based on how containers are collected, i.e. if leaf suppliers are responsible for collecting pesticide containers, then data can be collected by the leaf supplier

title: 'IPM: Calculating the amount of biopesticide required per hectare.'
text: CABI: IPM: Calculating the amount of biopesticide required per hectare.

title: 'IPM: Calculating the amount of biopesticide required per hectare.'
text:
To calculate how much of a biopesticide is needed to treat an area, follow these general steps:
Step 1: How large is the area to be treated? Multiply the length of the field by the width. Then divide this number (in m2) by 10,000 (the number of m2 in a hectare). This is the number of hectares (ha). ha = length (m) x width (m) / 10,000 m2/ha
Step 2: How much biopesticide is needed to spray the area? What is the rate of application? It is important to read the label for the application requirement specified per hectare. Labels provide information on the biopesticide rate in metric measures, such as liters per hectare (L/ha), milliliters per hectare (mL/ha), kilograms per hectare (kg/ha) or grams per hectare (g/ha). If the measurement of field size is made in hectares, then the biopesticide rate shown on the label can be used. If the measurement of the field size is made in acres (ac), then it will be necessary to change the rate shown on the label from an amount per hectare to an amount per acre. This can be done by multiplying the rate by 0.4. For example, 2L/hectare x 0.4 = 0.8L/acre. (Amount per hectare x 0.4 = amount per acre). Once the rate of application has been calculated using the method described above, it is now possible to calculate the amount of biopesticide needed. Multiply the area to be sprayed (Step 1 above) by the rate of application. Amount of biopesticide needed = area to spray (ha) x biopesticide rate per hectare, or area to spray (acres) x biopesticide rate per acre. Step 3: How much can be sprayed with one full tank?

title: 'IPM: Calculating the amount of biopesticide required per hectare.'
text:
Step 3: How much can be sprayed with one full tank? Divide the tank size by the sprayer application rate (volume of pesticide used per given area, e.g. per hectare). The sprayer application rate is determined using the following calculation (variables used to calculate this are determined by the specification of the sprayer being used). Nozzle output (L/min) x 600 / forward speed (km/ha) / nozzle spacing (m) = application rate (L/ha)
Tank size (L) = hectares that 1 tank will spray. Area sprayed (ha) = Tank size (L) / sprayer application rate (L/ha)
Step 4: How much biopesticide should be added to one full tank? Multiply the area sprayed by one tank (Step 3 above) by the biopesticide rate being used. Amount of biopesticide to add to a full tank =
area sprayed by one tank (ha) x pesticide rate per hectare OR
area sprayed by one tank (ac) x pesticide rate per acre
Note: It is important to finish the complete tank mix in one spray. Storing the diluted pesticide in the tank can lead to the loss of the efficacy of the active ingredient. The solution should never be stored in the tank.

title: 'IPM: Dry or solid formulations.'
text: CABI: IPM: Dry or solid formulations.

title: 'IPM: Dry or solid formulations.'
text: Pesticides are available in many different forms, including liquid, solid and living organisms. Each has advantages and disadvantages.

title: 'IPM: Dry or solid formulations.'
text: There are a number of types of solid formulations. Dust or Dustable Powders (D) - a powder applied to crops in dry form. Usually low concentration of active ingredient. - Ready to use, usually don’t require mixing; can be applied with simple equipment. Water and spray equipment not needed; effective in water scarce situations and hard to reach indoor areas. - Disadvantages: Dusty, need to wear mask to avoid inhaling when pouring and mixing; can leave visible residues on treated surfaces; drift; usually need to use large quantities due to low concentration; high transport costs; can be washed away by rains.

title: 'IPM: Dry or solid formulations.'
text:
Wettable Powder (WP) - dry finely ground powders that need to be mixed with water before use. WPs do not dissolve in water and so sink quickly. Usually 50% or more a.i. - Easy to transport, handle and store; relatively cheap; easy to measure and mix with water; can be used with most types of application equipment; less phytotoxic than ECs
- Disadvantages: dusty, mask needed to avoid inhaling when pouring/mixing; need to shake the spray tank regularly to prevent active ingredient from sinking to bottom (making the solution less effective); can block spray nozzles and filters; inert carriers may leave visible residues on sprayed surfaces; can cake in storage. Water Soluble Powder (WSP or SP) - active ingredient is a powder that needs to be mixed with water before use. Look similar to WPs, but dissolve easily in water to form solution. Need to be mixed thoroughly initially, but then no additional shaking is required. A.I varies from 15% - 95%. - Easy to transport, handle and store; relatively cheap; easy to measure and mix with water; can be used with most types of application equipment; less phytotoxic than ECs; dissolve in water, no constant shaking required. - Disadvantages: dusty, need to wear mask to avoid inhaling when pouring/mixing
Granules or Grains (G or GR) - similar to dusts, except larger and heavier. Usually applied to the soil. Usually low concentration of a.i. (1-15% by weight)
- Ready to use, usually don’t require mixing; applied to soil, doesn't stick to foliage; lower drift risk compared to dusts; simple application equipment (e.g.

title: 'IPM: Dry or solid formulations.'
text:
(1-15% by weight)
- Ready to use, usually don’t require mixing; applied to soil, doesn't stick to foliage; lower drift risk compared to dusts; simple application equipment (e.g. spreader, seeder); slow release of active ingredient gives extended protection
- Disadvantages: may need to be incorporated into the soil; may need moisture to activate; hard to get even coverage; slow release increases persistence; can be hazardous to non-target animals if they confuse granules with food; do not stick to foliage; more expensive than WPs or ECs
Bait (B) - active ingredients is mixed with food or other substance to attract pest. - Ready to use; little needed as pests move to the bait. - Disadvantages: hazardous to non-target animals/children who mistake it as food

title: 'IPM: What is a pesticide?'
text: CABI: IPM: What is a pesticide?

title: 'IPM: What is a pesticide?'
text: Recognize the problem Many farmers and field technicians do not have a good understanding of what pesticides are made of nor are they familiar with some of the key terminology which is necessary for making informed decisions when it is time to buy or apply a pesticide. As a consequence, they may inadvertently buy formulations which contain mixtures of active ingredients that are allowed and prohibited, for example.

title: 'IPM: What is a pesticide?'
text:
- Pesticides are made up of active and inert ingredients
- An active ingredient (a.i.) is the chemical that is active against the target pest (e.g. kills, repels, limits growth, etc.). There are hundreds of chemicals that are active ingredients. A single a.i. may be sold in many different formulations
- Inert ingredients have no activity against the pest. They allow the chemical to be handled, stored and applied more easily and safely. They are not disclosed (i.e. we don’t know what they are) and in some cases may be more toxic than the active ingredient. However, in most countries they are not regulated.

title: 'IPM: What is a pesticide?'
text:
- A pesticide formulation consists of the active ingredient (the chemical that affects the pest) combined with several other chemicals. - Adjuvants are chemicals that are not active against the target pest. They are added to pesticide formulations to improve performance. Sometimes the inert ingredients are part of the formulation, but sometimes they need to be added separately (depending on label instructions). - Adjuvants include spreaders (to help the spray mix spread evenly over treated surfaces), stickers (to help the spray mix stick to surfaces), thickeners, pH buffers, plant penetrants (to enhance the adsorption of systemic pesticides), wetting agents (to help wettable powders mix with water and spread on water repellent surfaces), or foaming/defoaming agents. - You must follow label instructions for adjuvants. - Sometimes they are probihited for use with a particular pesticide and using one will be risky. - Concentration refers to the amount of the active ingredient in the formulation. - Weight per unit volume: (e.g. 500 g/L)
- Percentage by weight (e.g. 40% WP)
- As with chemical insecticides, the active ingredient in bio-pesticides is the living organism (or component that have been extracted from it) which is combined with other chemicals so it can be applied as a pesticide.

title: 'IPM: Other types of formulations.'
text: CABI: IPM: Other types of formulations.

title: 'IPM: Other types of formulations.'
text: Pesticides are available in many different forms, including liquid, solid and living organisms.

title: 'IPM: Other types of formulations.'
text: Each has advantages and disadvantage. As well as solid and liquid formulations, there are a number of other formulations which are given below.

title: 'IPM: Other types of formulations.'
text:
Seed Dressings (DS, ES, FS, LS, PS, SS, WS) - can be liquid or solid formulations. Often contains dye. Dry formulations don’t require dilution (except SS). Liquid formulations require dilution with water. Advantages: easier to identify treated seed due to dye; can be applied on-farm using simple equipment; some types are similar to EC, WP and SC formulations. Disadvantages: Protective gloves must be used when applying; treated seed may be eaten by domestic animals, wildlife or humans; some types are similar to EC, WP and SC formulations. Fumigants (F) - pesticides that form a gas when applied. Generally used for soil pests, or in food storage facilities. Advantages: highly effective against a wide range of pests; usually only one application needed; can easily move through soil or cracks in walls, wood or grains. Disadvantages: usually extremely toxic to humans and all other organisms; need special training to use. Special equipment and protective clothing required; site where applied (e.g. soil or building) must be covered to prevent to prevent gas from escaping
Attractants - Include pheromones, sugar and protein syrups, yeasts, and rotting meat used in various types of traps. Can be combined with pesticides and sprayed onto foliage or other things in area to be treated.

title: 'IPM: Fungicides.'
text: CABI: IPM: Fungicides.

title: 'IPM: Fungicides.'
text:
Fungicides can be grouped based on different characteristics: mobility in plant, role in protection, breadth of activity. Some common fungicide chemical families (with their active ingredients) are:
Dithiocarbamates: maneb, mancozeb, metiram. Carbamates: iodocarb, propamocarb, prothiocarb. Methoxy-acrylates: azoxystrobin, flufenoxystrobin. Acylalanines: metalaxyl, metalaxyl-M, benalaxyl, benalaxyl, benalaxyl-M.

title: 'IPM: Fungicides.'
text:
Mobility in plant:
Contact fungicides are not absorbed by the plant, they remain on surface of plant. They prevent fungal spores from germinating on the leaves where they land and must therefore be applied evenly and thoroughly to the foliage before disease attack in order to be effective. Systemic fungicides are absorbed and moved about in the plant. They protect the plant by killing the germinating fungal spores when they start to grow into the leaf. Not as susceptible to weather as surface protectants but more susceptible to resistance.

title: 'IPM: Fungicides.'
text:
Role in protection. Fungicides are described as preventive or curative. Preventive:
- Not absorbed by the plant. - Prevent fungal spores from germinating on the leaves where they land. - Must therefore be applied evenly and thoroughly to the foliage before disease attack in order to be effective. - Generally contact. - Repeated applications are needed to protect new growth of the plant and to replace material that has been washed off by rain or irrigation, or degraded by sunlight. - Sometimes referred to as ‘residuals’ because residues remain on plant surface. Curative (or Eradicants):
- Directly attack pathogens after they have invaded plant tissue. - Protect plant by killing the germinating fungal spores when they start to grow into the leaf. - Mainly systemic - these are absorbed and moved about in the plant. Breadth of activity:
- Single-site action. - Hilghtly specific in their toxicity (only attack one site in pathogen). - More prone to resistance. - Usually systemic. - Multi-site action. - Affect many fungi. - Mostly contact.

title: 'IPM: Herbicides.'
text: CABI: IPM: Herbicides.

title: 'IPM: Herbicides.'
text:
Herbicides differ by their mode of action, pest or crop selectiveness (Selectivity), timing of application. Some common herbicide chemical families (with their active ingredients) are:
- Thiocarbamates: triallate, EPTAC, butylate
- Glycines: glyphosate, sulfosate
- Acetamide: napropamide
- Isoxazolidinone: clomazone

title: 'IPM: Herbicides.'
text:
Herbicide mode of action
Contact herbicides:
- Only kill plant parts that make contact with the product. Have little or no  movement (translocation) within the plant. - Most effective when applied to small young weeds
- Usually unsuitable for the control of perennial weeds. The chemical only “burns off" the tops of the plant. Roots can still produce new top growth. Systemic herbicides:
- Enter the plant via roots or leaves. Move through the plant by translocation. This kills the whole plant. - May not show control effects for a week or more after treatment. - Do not work as well if too much product is applied to the leaves. Leaf cells can die too quickly and prevent translocation. - Can be used to treat annual, perennial, and biennial weeds.

title: 'IPM: Herbicides.'
text:
Herbicide Selectivity - all herbicides are either:
- Selective - Kill certain types of plants (e.g. broadleaf or grass weeds). The weed plants are controlled, but the crop plants among which they are growing, are left unharmed
- Non-selective – Kill all plants which they land on
Herbicide Timing of Application - herbicides can be grouped by the timing of their application for best effect. Herbicides are usually foliar applied or soil applied. Some herbicides can be applied as pre-plant, pre-emergence, or post-emergence treatments. Pre-plant
- Applied and mechanically mixed into the soil before seeding or transplanting the crop. Mostly non-selective herbicides. Pre-emergence
- Applied to the soil or via irrigation after planting but before weeds emerge though soil surface
- Absorbed by the roots and/or shoots of the weeds as they germinate or begin to grow
- Mostly all systemic (absorbed by the plant and translocated)
Post-emergence
- Sprayed directly onto weeds (foliar applied) after they appear (have broken soil surface)
- Can be applied soon after emergence, or when a given plant height or leaf number is reached
- Mostly contact (kill plant issue upon contact), but can also be systemic

title: 'IPM: What are highly hazardous pesticides.'
text: CABI: IPM: What are highly hazardous pesticides.

title: 'IPM: What are highly hazardous pesticides.'
text: There are many different ways in which pesticides can potentially cause harm to human health or to the environment. For example, substances which are acutely toxic can knock someone down rather rapidly, with symptoms felt within a short space of time. Chronic toxicity, on the other hand, can lead to effects which develop slowly following long and continuous exposure to low concentrations of a hazardous pesticide. Potential consequences of chronic exposure include health problems such as birth defects, developmental issues, cancers, etc. pesticides can also impact non-target organisms such predators, pollinators, soil biota and aquatic organisms. Of course, pesticides are not all the same. The degree to which a product is hazardous differs from formulation to formulation. Some products are generally not harmful whereas certain pesticides are highly hazardous. A relatively small group of highly hazardous pesticides are often the cause of the majority of poisoning cases.

title: 'IPM: What are highly hazardous pesticides.'
text:
#### The symbol for chemicals which are health hazards such as carcinogen, mutagens and reproductive toxins. ####
GHS
Highly Hazardous Pesticides (FAO, 2016) are defined as pesticides that are acknowledged to present particularly high levels of acute or chronic hazards to health or the environment according to internationally accepted classification systems. Pesticides that cause severe or irreversible harm to health or the environment under the conditions of use in a country may also be considered highly hazardous. Esposure to the HHPs should be mitigated. Whenever possible, use of highly hazardous pesticides should be avoided and other lower risk pest management options should be used instead. Highly hazardous pesticides are pesticide active ingredients or formulations which meet one or more of the following criteria:
1. Pesticides which are extremely or highly acutely toxic (classes Ia or Ib of the WHO Recommended Classification of Pesticides by Hazard)
2. Carcinogens (carcinogenicity Categories 1A and 1B of the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals - GHS)
3. Mutagens (mutagenicity Categories 1A and 1B of the GHS)
4. Reproductive toxins (reproductive toxicity Categories 1A and 1B of the GHS)
5. Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs listed in the the Stockholm Convention in its Annexes A and B)
6. Pesticide active ingredients and formulations for which are listed in the Rotterdam Convention because they have been banned or are severely restricted for health or environmental reasons
7. Ozone depleting substances (listed by the Montreal Protocol)
8. Pesticide active ingredients and formulations that have shown a high incidence of severe or irreversible adverse effects on human health or the environment.

text:
#### The skull and crossbones symbol indicates that a chemical is acutely toxic. ####
