title: 'IPM: Conserving pollinators.'
text: CABI: IPM: Conserving pollinators.

title: 'IPM: Conserving pollinators.'
text:
#### Growers using pesticides should minimise impact on pollinators. ####
CABI
More than 80% of plants either require or benefit from pollinators, such as bees and butterflies, to be able to produce seeds and fruit. Approximately one third of agriculture production is at least somewhat dependent on pollinators. Crop protection agents (pesticides) which are used to manage pests can have serious negative impacts on pollinators. For example, most pesticides are at least somewhat toxic to honeybees and some are deadly to bees. In order to ensure that we continue to receive the benefits that pollinators provide, steps must be taken when applying pesticides to avoid causing harm to pollinators. The degree of toxicity of pesticides to pollinators varies from product to product. Insecticides are generally more toxic to bees than herbicides and fungicides. Some insecticides are highly toxic to pollinators like bees, whereas others are not. There are many different ways in which pollinators can be exposed to pesticides. Residues of pesticides can be present in the flowers, foliage, pollen and nectar of treated crops or in neighboring plants through drift. Pollinators can also come into contact with pesticide residues in the soil, e.g. some bees make nests on the ground or collect mud. Likewise, pollinators can be exposed to pesticides through contaminated water. In order to conserve pollinators, their biology, the hazards posed by pesticides and the pathways for exposure should be taken into consideration.

title: 'IPM: Conserving pollinators.'
text:
Follow these guidelines in order to reduce risks to pollinators:
- Always read the product labels and follow any warning statements regarding bees or other pollinators. - Preferentially use products with the lowest levels of toxicity to pollinators. Products containing Bacillus thuringiensis, Heliothis virus, neem (azadirachtin) and some Lepidopteran pheromones are relatively non-toxic to bees. Systemic pesticides tend to be more highly toxic to bees, and residues of systemic insecticides can be present in plant parts such as pollen and leaves for many months after treatment. - Protect pollinator habitats such as bee nests and flowers from pesticides
- Avoid applying pesticides to flowering plants. - If you must use a product which is toxic to pollinators, apply the pesticide late in the day to avoid the flight hours of honey bees. - Choose the available formulation which is least likely to drift. Dusts drift more than other formulations. Spray formulations drift less than dusts. Granular formulations are the least likely to drift. - Do not apply pesticides when it is windy. - If present, inform neighbour beekeepers about the pesticide application.

title: 'IPM: Pesticide resistance management.'
text: CABI: IPM: Pesticide resistance management.

title: 'IPM: Pesticide resistance management.'
text: Resistance to certain pesticides is observed to be a problem (e.g. pigweed resistance to glyphosate or insect resistance to indoxacarb). In some countries, most of the interviewed farmers said that they do not apply a resistance management strategy. In many instances, farmers were not even aware that pests can become resistant to pesticides.

title: 'IPM: Pesticide resistance management.'
text:
#### Avoid applying pesticides with the same mode of action to reduce the chance of resistance build-up. ####
CABI
Resistance may be defined "as a heritable change in the sensitivity of a pest population that is reflected in the repeated failure of a product to achieve the expected level of control when used according to the label recommendation for that pest species". Natural selection by a pesticide allows some initially very rare, naturally occurring, pre-adapted insects with resistance genes to survive and pass the resistance trait on to their offspring. Through continued application of pesticides with the same mode of action, selection for the resistant individuals continues so the proportion of resistant insects in the population increases, while susceptible individuals are eliminated by the pesticide. Under permanent selection pressure, resistant insects outnumber susceptible ones and the pesticide is no longer effective. The speed with which resistance develops depends on several factors, including how fast the insects reproduce, the migration and host range of the pest, the availability of nearby susceptible populations, the persistence and specificity of the crop protection product, and the rate, timing, and number of applications made. Cross-resistance occurs when resistance to one pesticide confers resistance to another pesticide, even where the pest has not been exposed to the latter product. Misuse and overuse of pesticides will select resistant pests, increasing the risk that pesticide resistance may evolve.

title: 'IPM: Pesticide resistance management.'
text:
A resistance management strategy should include the following:
- Avoid repetitive and sole use of pesticides with the same modes of action
- Mix or alternate pesticides with an appropriate partner fungicide
- Limit the number and timing of treatments
- Avoid eradicant use
- Maintain recommended dose rate
- Integrate with (give preference to) non-chemical methods
Wherever feasible, several strategies should be used together. To learn about modes of action, visit the following websites:
- Insecticide Resistance Action Committee: http://www.irac-online.org/modes-of-action/
- Fungicide Resistance Action Committee: http://www.frac.info/
- Herbicide Resistance Action Committee: http://hracglobal.com/pages/classificationofherbicidesiteofaction.aspx

title: 'IPM: Label interpretation.'
text: CABI: IPM: Label interpretation.

title: 'IPM: Label interpretation.'
text: Many farmers do not always refer to and follow label recommendations. The label is to provide the user with all the essential information about the product and how to use it safely and effectively.

title: 'IPM: Label interpretation.'
text:
#### Primary Display Panel ####
CABI
A pesticide label has two parts:
The primary display panel must be fixed to the container and provides information on:
- Product name, formulation and the chemical name, common name and amount of product ingredients (including the active ingredient)
- Registration number and precautionary symbols / words
The secondary display panel is often a booklet attached to the container and provides information on:
- Directions for use, e.g. pests controlled, crops, dosage, how to mix and apply, equipment required, PPE, maximum number of applications, preharvest interval (PHI)
- Safety information, e.g. Health hazards, environmental toxicity, re-entry interval (REI), instructions about storage and disposal of the product and the product container, and the notice to buyer (limitation of warranty statement) to state that the buyer accepts all risks of product use.

title: 'IPM: Label interpretation.'
text:
#### NEVER decant products into other containers ####
Stewardship Community
It is important that farmers ALWAYS read and follow label recommendations:
- Always read the label, or have the label read to you, to be sure the pesticide is safe for your intended use
- Do not buy pesticides if the container is missing a label or the information is illegible/unreadable
- Check manufacturing date and expiration date. - Look for the PHI, REI, and the maximum number of applications permitted for that crop. - Read the directions to understand how much of the pesticide to use, when and how to apply. - Always follow the label recommended Dosage Rate
- Too low - not effective. Risk of resistance increases. - Too high - waste and increase in cost. Risk of resistance increases. - Phytotoxicity to plants increases. Human health risks increases.

title: 'IPM: Purchasing pesticides.'
text: CABI: IPM: Purchasing pesticides.

title: 'IPM: Purchasing pesticides.'
text: In some countries, farmers’ purchase of pesticides from largely unregulated retailers has been highlighted as an urgent issue. Generally, national and regional governments are responsible for fighting problems like counterfeit and poor quality pesticides, but government enforcement is often weak and inadequate. Where this is an issue, farmers need to be aware of potential issues and able to recognise counterfeit, adulterated or low quality pesticides so that their choices when in retail shops are informed ones that are not just based on price.

title: 'IPM: Purchasing pesticides.'
text:
#### Ensure the pesticides you purchase have not been adulterated. ####
CABI
There are a number of issues that can be associated with illegal, fake or low quality pesticides which may be available in market places or some agro-dealer shops. These include:
- Pesticides that have been re-packaged may be missing a label, so the instructions for use are missing
- Pesticides that have been re-packaged may be adulterated or may not be genuine, so they may not work against the target pest
- Adulterated products may contain substances which are harmful to crops, human health or the environment
- Adulterated or mislabelled products may contain pesticides which are not allowed, potentially leading to residue problems
- Products may contain the correct a.i. but at lower concentrations leading to low effectiveness and increased resistance problems

title: 'IPM: Purchasing pesticides.'
text:
To avoid buying illegal or counterfeit pesticides:
- Buy products from preferred source (e.g. leaf supplier or cooperative) or reputable stores or dealers. - Avoid deals that seem to be "too good to be true". - Never buy pesticides that do not have instructions written in the language required by law. - Ensure the product has a proper label that includes a registration number (in countries where applicable) or any other legally required identifiers. - Make sure the label clearly identifies the active ingredient names. Never buy pesticides that are not in their original container. Check that the container is in good shape with the seal intact. - Check that the product has not expired.

title: 'IPM: Routes of pesticide contamination.'
text: CABI: IPM: Routes of pesticide contamination.

title: 'IPM: Routes of pesticide contamination.'
text: Pesticides are toxic substances which can potentially impact on human health. This can be direct to the pesticide spray operators or indirectly to other people coming into contact with the pesticide prior, during or post-application. The effects of pesticide contamination maybe acute or chronic. It is therefore important to recognise the potential routes of contamination with pesticides to enable appropriate preventive measures to be employed to reduce the health risks to farmers, farm workers and the wider community.

title: 'IPM: Routes of pesticide contamination.'
text:
#### Applicators should avoid exposure to pesticides. ####
CABI
The use of pesticides poses a number of acute and chronic risks to humans. The ways by which the pesticides may contaminate people are referred to as routes of contamination. These routes of contamination are primarily grouped into three types, dermal (through skin, may also include eyes), oral (through the mouth), inhalation (through nose).

title: 'IPM: Routes of pesticide contamination.'
text:
It is necessary to be aware of the potential mechanisms and routes of exposure/contamination with pesticides, to reduce immediate or long-term effects of pesticides. Avoid the following to reduce the risk of exposure:
Dermal exposure:
- Not washing hands after handling pesticides or containers
- Splashing or spilling pesticide on skin
- Wearing pesticide contaminated clothing
- Applying pesticides in windy weather, drift exposure
- Touching treated plants or soil
Oral exposure:
- Not washing hands before eating, smoking or chewing
- Splashing pesticide into mouth
- Accidentally applying pesticide to food
- Storing pesticides in drink containers
- Getting drift on lip or mouth
Inhalation exposure:
- Spraying in confined or poorly ventilated areas
- Being exposed to drift
- Mixing/loading dusts, powders or other dry formulations
- Using an inadequate or poorly fitting respirator
Eye exposure:
- Rubbing eyes or forehead with contaminated gloves or hands
- Splashing pesticides in eyes
- Applying pesticides in windy weather, drift exposure
- Mixing/loading dry formulations without wearing goggles

title: 'IPM: Personal hygiene when handling pesticides.'
text: CABI: IPM: Personal hygiene when handling pesticides.

title: 'IPM: Personal hygiene when handling pesticides.'
text: Pesticides are toxic substances which can potentially impact the health of operators and people getting in contact with. Precautions should be taken to reduce health risks to farmers and farm workers. Those handling pesticides should be able to minimise the risk of contamination because it is easier to prevent pesticide poisoning than treat it.

title: 'IPM: Personal hygiene when handling pesticides.'
text: Pesticides can cause both short-term and long-term effects in humans. It is therefore necessary to take care whenever handling or applying pesticides to prevent immediate contamination as well as the build-up of the toxic effects over time.

title: 'IPM: Personal hygiene when handling pesticides.'
text: - Ensure that all the safety precautions on the pesticide label are observed. - Do not eat, drink, or smoke while mixing or applying pesticides (to avoid contamination of food and drinks, limit contact with mouth, eyes, and other sensitive areas). - Always wash hands and face thoroughly after handling or using pesticides, especially before eating. - Do not store pesticides in drinks bottles or food containers – they MUST be kept in their original containers. - Wash thoroughly after work. Waiting until the end of the day to clean up can allow additional absorption of the pesticide through the skin. - Clean work clothes separately from family washing. Keep contaminated clothing separate from other laundry and tell the person who washes the clothes of the possible hazards. Encourage him/her to wear protective gloves while doing the laundry. - Dispose of contaminated clothing if it cannot be cleaned properly. - Never wear contaminated clothing under any circumstances. - Also, do not touch your face or other bare skin with contaminated gloves or hands (even if they look clean, hands and gloves can be contaminated).

title: 'IPM: Personal Protection Equipment (PPE).'
text: CABI: IPM: Personal Protection Equipment (PPE).

title: 'IPM: Personal Protection Equipment (PPE).'
text: Pesticides are toxic substances which can potentially impact the health of operators and people getting in contact with them, farmers and farm workers need to protect themselves and wear personal protective equipment. Conditions related to the use of PPE may vary but a minimal PPE is needed.

title: 'IPM: Personal Protection Equipment (PPE).'
text:
#### Wear face musk, hat and overall. ####
CABI
PPE must always be worn whenever handling and applying pesticides as well as when cleaning and maintaining sprayers. The minimum requirement for all types of pesticide operations is clothing covering most of the body i.e. Long sleeved shirt, trousers covering the legs pulled over the outside of boots, rubber gloves, waterproof boots, a hat, eye protection (glasses) or face shield, face mask (mouth and nose protection such as handkerchief/bandana) and an apron. Overalls may be one piece suit or two piece garments. A two piece garment offer greater flexibility and comfort. Level of protection depends on weight, weave and thickness of the fabric.

title: 'IPM: Personal Protection Equipment (PPE).'
text:
#### Use gloves, gumboots and apron. ####
CABI
- Read the pesticide label to select the recommended PPE
- Use cotton or polyester/cotton blended overall
- Protect the coverall from becoming wet e.g by not walking through wet field. Use aprons and rain suit to provide extra protection in wet conditions
- Use gloves made of nitrile, rubber or neoprene because natural rubber gloves can be damaged by some solvents such as those in emulsifiable concentrates (ECs)
- Gloves should reach the elbows, fit comfortably and be flexible enough to grip containers and other equipment firmly
- Short gloves should at least cover the wrists and be worn outside the sleeves of the shirt/overall, Leather, or any other absorbent, gloves are not suitable
- Rubber boots offer good protection, Leather boots are unsuitable because they absorb some pesticides and cannot be decontaminated
- Clean plastic sheets or sacks cut to form an apron can be worn as a temporary measure and destroyed after use in case an apron is unavailable.

title: 'IPM: Problems associated with pesticides.'
text: CABI: IPM: Problems associated with pesticides.

title: 'IPM: Problems associated with pesticides.'
text: Pesticides are toxic substances which can potentially have an adverse impact on farmers, farm workers and consumers health as well as on the environment. Awareness of and knowledge about these risks is the basis for adapting the behaviour in such a way that these risks can be minimised. The WHO classification system is an important tool in this context to assess the potential effects of a pesticide that is chosen for application. Awareness of possible negative effects of pesticides, especially if connected with personal experience, often proves to be an important driving force for adopting recommended practices in RPU as well as for further farmers’ efforts to implement IPM.

title: 'IPM: Problems associated with pesticides.'
text:
#### Make sure you understand the hazard warning on the label. ####
Stewardship Community
There are several problems associated with the use of pesticides:
- Pesticides are potentially dangerous/harmful to sprayer operators. Often farmers do not wear protective gear due to a lack of awareness to toxicity. - Pesticides are harmful to the environment (rivers and lakes, soil) and non-target organisms (fish, birds, pollinators, natural enemies, worms etc.) - Pesticide residues can be harmful to consumers if PHI is not obeyed
- Improper disposal poses risk to children, environment, farm animals etc.

title: 'IPM: Problems associated with pesticides.'
text:
- Avoid using Class Ia (Extremely hazardous) and Ib (Highly hazardous) chemicals. Some biological pesticides, e.g. nicotine can also be very toxic and their use is as hazardous as many inorganic pesticides. Less toxic biopesticides include Pyrethrum flowers, root extract of Derris elliptica (Rotenone) and Neem leaves/flowers. The same precautions must be taken whether using chemical or biological pesticides
- Be vigilant for signs of acute (severe poisoning after exposure to a single dose) and chronic health effects (poisoning as a result of repeated non-lethal doses over time.) - Consider how the pesticide may affect the environment, e.g. where will the pesticide go in the environment after it it applied? What effects can this pesticide have on those non-target sites it may reach in the environment? - Movement in air, aka drift- Occurs during mixing and application of pesticides which may be carried as spray droplets, vapour, or solid particles, and can even be carried away on soil particles. - Movement in water - Usually by surface movement out of the treated field (runoff) or by downward movement through the soil (leaching) either when too much pesticide is applied or too much rainwater or irrigation water moves the pesticide through the soil into groundwater, and on to drainage systems, streams, ponds, drinking water. - Movement on or in objects, plants or animals, e.g. when sprayer operators bring home contaminated PPE or work clothes residues can rub off on furniture, clothing, pets and people.

title: 'IPM: Calculating dosage.'
text: CABI: IPM: Calculating dosage.

title: 'IPM: Calculating dosage.'
text: Many farmers do not know how to calculate dosages and some turn to unreliable sources for information on what dosage to use. As a consequence, farmers may inadvertently be applying the wrong dosage – this can result in wasted product, poor pest control, resistance, high levels of pesticide residues and potentially even dead plants.

title: 'IPM: Calculating dosage.'
text:
Farmers must calculate the correct dosage for every application and for each individual field. There are 4 basic ways dosages are stated on a label:
1. Amount of active ingredient (pure chemical) needed per hectare or acre. 2. Amount of actual formulation needed per hectare or acre. 3. Amount of actual formulation needed per litre or gallon of water. 4. As a percentage concentration in the spray water (i.e. solution).

title: 'IPM: Calculating dosage.'
text:
To convert the dosage from an active ingredient basis to an actual formulation:
For solid formulations (e.g. WP, EC, G):
Actual formulation needed = Amount of a.i. / % active ingredient in formulation
e.g. To calculate the dose of Malathion 40% WP needed to apply 2 kg active ingredient/hectare : 2kg / 40 % = 2kg / 0.4 = 5kg of Malathion 40%
For liquid formulations (EC's):
Litres/ha of EC = kg/ha of a.i. / % a.i. in EC
e.g. To calculate the dose of Perfekthion 20% EC needed per hectare for a recommendation of 0.2 kg a.i. Perfekthion per hectare: 0.2 kg /20% = 0.2 / 0.2 = 1 litre of Perfekthion 20% EC
Once you know how much actual formulation is needed per hectare (or acre), you can easily calculate how much is needed for a farmer's field. - Hectares: Amount of formulation needed for a farmer's field = [Amount of formulation needed per ha x Field area (m2)] / 10,000
- Acres: Amount of formulation needed for a farmer's field = [Amount of formulation needed per acre x Field area (ft2)] / 44,000 e.g. How much Volaton 2.5% strength granules are needed to apply 120 kg/ha on a field measuring 35 x 40 meters? 35x40 = 1400m2. [120x1400m2] / 10,000 = 16.8 kg Volatin 2.5% granules needed for field.

title: 'IPM: Calculating dosage.'
text:
35x40 = 1400m2. [120x1400m2] / 10,000 = 16.8 kg Volatin 2.5% granules needed for field. To calculate a percentage spray dosage recommendation for:
Wettable powders (WP):
- Grams of WP needed per litre of water = [% strength spray desired x 1000] / % a.i. in wettable powder
- Grams of WP needed per litre or water = % strength spray desired x 1000
Liquids (ECs):
- cc (ml) of EC needed per litre of water = [% spray desired x 1000] / % a.i. in the EC

title: 'IPM: Environmental and wildlife considerations while spraying.'
text: CABI: IPM: Environmental and wildlife considerations while spraying.

title: 'IPM: Environmental and wildlife considerations while spraying.'
text: Farmers need to be aware of special risk areas and practices that can be employed to minimise environmental impacts.

title: 'IPM: Environmental and wildlife considerations while spraying.'
text:
#### It is important that pesticides are properly applied and disposed of to minimise damage to the environment. ####
CABI
Whenever a pesticide is used, there is a possibility that some of it will end up outside of the field being treated. The resulting contamination of the environment can be a hazard to wildlife and people. Special risk areas include:
- Open water - rivers, water reservoirs, ditches and streams
- Cultivated land - where existing or subsequent crops may be contaminated
- Uncultivated land - where wild plants and animals may be contaminated

title: 'IPM: Environmental and wildlife considerations while spraying.'
text:
- Do not spray in strong winds - check the weather forecast and the actual weather conditions for wind speed and direction before you start
- Do not treat an area closest to the downwind border of the field being treated e.g. leave a row of plants untreated
- Do not spray close to special risk areas if they appear to be at risk from spray drift
- The safest conditions in which to spray are when it is cool and humid with a light breeze blowing away from any sensitive areas
- Do not spray when temperature is above 30°C - as rising air currents may spray droplets and vapour in an unexpected way
- If using a tractor mounted sprayer, do not drive too fast
- Avoid spillages and leaks of pesticides
- Minimise the area of pesticide application (e.g. by only treating affected plants)
- Ensure correct disposal of empty containers, waste pesticides and sprayer tank washings
- If farmers store large quantities of pesticides, they could set up an environmental monitoring system. Under a monitoring system, samples are periodically taken from water, wildlife, and plants near the storage area. The samples are assessed to be sure that no pesticides are getting out into the environment.

title: 'IPM: General precautions while spraying.'
text: CABI: IPM: General precautions while spraying.

title: 'IPM: General precautions while spraying.'
text: In order to ensure the applicator is doing the right thing during the whole preparation and application process, it is necessary to remember important precautions that should be taken.

title: 'IPM: General precautions while spraying.'
text:
#### Avoid exposure to pesticide. ####
CABI
It is important to plan the spray application so that you do not have to walk or drive through the newly treated crop or area, you leave an area untreated for disposing of sprayer washings and to ensure that there is no risk of spray drifting outside of the orchard, taking wind speed and direction into account. Many states require that all persons in the intended treatment areas, or even in adjacent areas, be informed about pesticide applications before the pesticides are applied. This warning is referred to as "pre-notification" and is intended to protect others from exposure to pesticides.

title: 'IPM: General precautions while spraying.'
text:
Take general precautions while spraying:
- Do not work in strong winds and ensure any wind blows the pesticide away from the operator
- Avoid spraying into orchard margins, watercourses and wildlife areas
- Maintain a constant speed
- Do not spray while the vehicle is turning
- Never suck or blow out clogged nozzles or pipe connections by mouth, clean them with water and a soft stick, e.g. a grass stem, or nylon bristle brush. Do not use any tool that is used for this kind of job for anything else. Never leave pesticides or machinery unattended. Wash your hands and face thoroughly after you use pesticides and before you do any other activity. - Never eat, drink, or smoke when handling pesticides, or in recently treated areas. - Wash your hands carefully before eating, drinking, smoking, or using the toilet. Wash them as soon as you are finished handling the pesticides. - Pesticide applicators are required by law to prevent direct or indirect exposure of workers and other persons. Keep children, unauthorized persons, and pets out of the area to be sprayed and at a safe distance from sprayers, dusters, filler tanks, storage areas, and/or old pesticide containers. - Avoid spraying near houses, schools, playgrounds, hospitals, bee hives, lakes, streams, pastures, or sensitive crops. If you must spray there, never spray or dust outside on windy days and always apply downwind from any sensitive area. Notify residents and beekeepers when you plan to spray in their areas and urge them to take appropriate precautions. - Avoid exposure to toxic pesticides. Do not work in drift, spray, or run-off unless you are properly protected. If pesticides spill on your gloves, be careful not to wipe your hands on your clothing.

title: 'IPM: General precautions while spraying.'
text: - Avoid exposure to toxic pesticides. Do not work in drift, spray, or run-off unless you are properly protected. If pesticides spill on your gloves, be careful not to wipe your hands on your clothing. - Choose weather conditions, pesticides, application equipment, pressure, droplet size, formulations, and adjuvants that minimize drift and run-off.

title: 'IPM: Method of application.'
text: CABI: IPM: Method of application.

title: 'IPM: Method of application.'
text: It is important to match the product to the available equipment for application. Certain formulations cannot be used with knapsack or other hydraulic sprayers.

title: 'IPM: Method of application.'
text:
#### Fungicide application ####
Howard F. Schwartz, Colorado State University, Bugwood.org
Insecticides and fungicides are usually applied as foliar sprays, and herbicides are mostly sprayed either onto the foliage or the soil. Thus spraying of liquid and wettable powder formulations is the most common method of application and consequently a wide variety of hand-operated and powerdriven spray apparatus has been developed over the years. Other formulations such as granules, dusts and fumigants require different equipment for their application or none at all. For example, granules can either be applied by mechanical spreaders or broadcast by hand.

title: 'IPM: Method of application.'
text:
#### Pesticide application. ####
Keith Weller, USDA Agricultural Research Service, Bugwood.org
To get the best result using the least amount of pesticide, applicators need to think through the application process carefully. Different application methods are appropriate for different crop and pest types, but the method of application should always be consistent with the label directions. Application methods include:
- Band application, applying a pesticide in parallel strips or bands, such as between rows of crops rather than uniformly over the entire field. - Basal application directs herbicides to the lower portions of brush or small trees to control vegetation. - Broadcast application is the uniform application of a pesticide to an entire area or field. - Crack and crevice application is the placement of small amounts of pesticide into cracks and crevices in buildings, such as along baseboards and in cabinets, where insects or other pests commonly hide or enter a structure. - Directed-spray application specifically targets the pests to minimize pesticide contact with non-target plants and animals. - Foliar application directs pesticide to the leafy portions of a plant. - Rope-wick or wiper treatments release pesticides onto a device that is wiped onto weeds taller than the crop, or wiped selectively onto individual weeds in an ornamental planting bed. - Soil application places pesticide directly on or in the soil rather than on a growing plant. - Soil incorporation is the use of tillage, rainfall, or irrigation equipment to move the pesticide into the soil. - Soil injection is the application of a pesticide under pressure beneath the soil surface. - Space treatment is the application of a pesticide in an enclosed area. - Spot treatment is the application of a pesticide to small, distinct areas.

title: 'IPM: Mixing products - Homogenization & Incompatibility.'
text: CABI: IPM: Mixing products - Homogenization & Incompatibility.

title: 'IPM: Mixing products - Homogenization & Incompatibility.'
text: Incompatibility is a condition that prevents pesticides from mixing together properly to form a uniform solution or suspension. Pesticides are not always compatible with each other or with the water or liquid fertilizer carrier. Lack of compatibility may result in the formation of a gel, precipitate, or sludge that plugs up screens and nozzles. But extreme incompatibility may produce a settling out of material that can harden like concrete in the bottom of the tank and in hoses, pumps, and other internal parts of the sprayer. The result may be total loss of the pesticide and use of the sprayer.

title: 'IPM: Mixing products - Homogenization & Incompatibility.'
text:
#### Always stir with a stick, never by hand. ####
Stewardship Community
Some manufacturers’ pesticide labels will expressly state that the applicator assumes all liability if tank-mixing. Some labels will provide precautions regarding potential physical or chemical compatibility problems when combining the contents with certain substances. Physical incompatibilities refer to mixtures that form flakes, gels, layers, crystals, or other precipitates that are not suitable for application through spraying equipment. Chemical incompatibility occurs where the effectiveness of a pesticide’s active ingredient is reduced or rendered ineffective by another chemical in the mixture.

title: 'IPM: Mixing products - Homogenization & Incompatibility.'
text: All pesticides must be mixed thoroughly and agitated in the tank to ensure uniform coverage. Some products (such as wettable powders) tend to settle, others (like emulsifiable concentrates) tend to separate. When you are using these products, jostle or agitate the tank with a brisk sidestep to keep the solutions well mixed. Insufficients agitation may be a problem with large or irregularly shaped tanks. This problem is most serious when applying wettable powder-type pesticides. If there are dead spots or sharp corners in the tank, and if the agitation is not sufficient for a given tank, wettable powders may settle to the bottom. In other cases, dry pesticides may float on the surface a long time before a uniform concentration of pesticide in the tank is achieved. As a result, the mixture sprayed may have varying amounts of active ingredient at different times during the spray operation. Many formulations have very specific mixing requirements in terms of the particular constituents required in the solution, the order of their addition into the solution, and especially the agitation required to dissolve or maintain a uniform pesticide concentration in the spray solution. Though it may be only a general term, such as moderate or heavy agitation, it is critical to thoroughly mix the solution. This will increase pump flow requirements if hydraulic agitation is used. Mixing the chemical in a small container first, then pouring it into the sprayer tank helps achieve uniform mixing.

title: 'IPM: Nozzle selection and maintenance.'
text: CABI: IPM: Nozzle selection and maintenance.

title: 'IPM: Nozzle selection and maintenance.'
text: Many farmers are unaware that the nozzle they use matters (or even that there are differences in nozzles). Likewise, many farmers do not maintain nozzles.

title: 'IPM: Nozzle selection and maintenance.'
text:
#### Top to Bottom: Hollow cone, flat fan and deflector nozzles. ####
Stewardship Community
Nozzles are used to regulate the amount of spray delivered (nozzle output), break liquid into droplets and spread droplets in a given pattern. There are different shapes of nozzle, including hollow cone, flat fan, deflector, flood jet and air inducing (bubble jet). Nozzles of the same colour at the same pressure will deliver the same flow rate.

title: 'IPM: Nozzle selection and maintenance.'
text:
#### More droplets from the same volume of water are produced if drop size is decreased. ####
Stewardship Community
- Water volume rates are usually stated on product labels to ensure adequate coverage of target surfaces. Too low a volume rate results in poor coverage and poor penetration. Too high volume rate results in product run off from the target, over dilution of product and surfactants, and more time taken to spray the crop
- Patterns and droplet size- too small of droplet size can cause drift, too large droplets can cause runoff. More droplets available means more coverage on the target. The general rule in the field for any product is to aim for an average 20 drops/cm2 but higher rates may be better for contact acting pesticides. Nozzle Maintenance and Safety
DO NOT:
- Clean a nozzle with an abrasive implement
- Clean a nozzle by blowing through it with your mouth
- Use damaged or worn nozzles
- Use fine spray drop sizes on a windy day
DO:
- Wear gloves when handling nozzles
- Clean a nozzle with water and a light brush
- Protect nozzles from blockages with use of recommended filters
- Frequently clean nozzles
- Replace the nozzle if damaged
- Change nozzles as necessary depending on the crop, growth stage and product mode of action

title: 'IPM: Precautions when mixing.'
text: CABI: IPM: Precautions when mixing.

title: 'IPM: Precautions when mixing.'
text: In order to correctly mix pesticides, farmers must read the label and follow instructions, but they also must know to follow and be able to apply certain good practices to safeguard their own health.

title: 'IPM: Precautions when mixing.'
text:
#### Minimum PPE ####
Stewardship Community
It is important that farmers know the general precautions that should be observed when measuring and mixing pesticides.

title: 'IPM: Precautions when mixing.'
text:
#### Pour pesticides with care. ####
Stewardship Community
The general precautions are:
- Always wear PPE (follow label recommendation)
- Minimum PPE: rubber gloves, non-absorbent boots, pants, long sleeved shirt, eye protection and mask (for powders)
- Always read the label
- Never mix or fill sprayer next to rivers, wells or other water ways. - Have clean water available for washing and mixing
- Use measuring device supplied with product or graduated cylinder. Never use old food containers or spoons
- Pour liquids carefully to avoid splashing
- Handle dry powders with extra care to avoid raising a dust cloud
- Never leave pesticide containers open or unattended - return them to the pesticide storage facility immediately
- Never allow children to mix or apply pesticides. They should not even be around when these activities are taking place, as they are more likely to be harmed by exposure to pesticides than adults. - After spraying, clean out the sprayer thoroughly first with water and then use a small amount of soap. - Don't forget to wash yourself and your clothes thoroughly. It is also very important that the farmer:
- Do not smoke, eat or drink during the clean-up operation
- Keeps people and animals away

title: 'IPM: Correct preparation of mixtures.'
text: CABI: IPM: Correct preparation of mixtures.

title: 'IPM: Correct preparation of mixtures.'
text: To correctly mix pesticides, farmers must read the label and follow instructions, but they also must know to follow and be able to apply certain good practices. They must also understand why correct preparation of mixtures is important, both to ensure that the product is effective and for safeguarding their health.

title: 'IPM: Correct preparation of mixtures.'
text:
#### Always pour pesticides carefully. ####
S.K. McDonald
Good practices when mixing and applying pesticides include:
- Select your target, what are you trying to control? Where does the spray deposit need to go? - Select the right nozzle for the job. For a sprayer fitted with a variable hollow cone nozzle, decide what setting should be selected. Squirting high targets with a jet is usually wasteful. Remember, the high flow rate leads to bigger droplets, causing a greater risk of run-off (dripping from leaves). When there is run-off, most of the pesticide will end up on the soil surface, rather than on the leaves or stems where you need it! - Calibrate the right amount of water (volume rate) and pesticide. How many plants per tank load? How many tank loads (thus litres) are required to spray the whole farm? - Use proper application techniques. Be systematic about treating rows and plants. Are all the plants being sprayed effectively? - Watch for dripping from the leaves. This means you are wasting pesticide.

title: 'IPM: Correct preparation of mixtures.'
text:
To correctly fill up the sprayer tank:
- Read labels to ensure products are compatible and can be mixed safely. - Half-fill the sprayer tank with clean water. - Measure out the correct dosage of pesticide and add it to the spray tank. - Remember that wettable powders may need creaming (made into a paste with a small amount of water) before being added to the sprayer tank. General rule: first solids, then liquids. - Stir with a stick, never with a hand. - Rinse out empty pesticide containers and measuring devices three times. Put all washings into the sprayer tank. - Top up the sprayer tank with water to the required level
- Place caps on empty containers, pierce with a sharp tool to prevent re-use and store safely inside plastic bags in a pesticide storage facility before safe disposal
- Return part-empty containers to the pesticide storage facility (see Factsheet on storage for more information on how pesticides should be stored)

title: 'IPM: Transporting pesticides.'
text: CABI: IPM: Transporting pesticides.

title: 'IPM: Transporting pesticides.'
text: If procedures for minimising risks are not observed during pesticide transport, then accidents can happen. If these accidents happen on a public road then the wider community is placed in jeopardy.

title: 'IPM: Transporting pesticides.'
text: It is important that anyone transporting pesticides is aware of hazards and knows how to minimise them. - Pesticides can catch fire. - Pesticides can give off fumes, so keeping them in closed spaces is a health risk and could cause accidents. - If there is an accident, the pesticide could spill on the road. - If the pesticide is being transported in the back of a truck and is not secured, it could bounce out and spill. - Spills can be difficult to clean up inside a vehicle.

title: 'IPM: Transporting pesticides.'
text:
#### Never leave products unattended during transport. ####
Stewardship Community
Some measures to reduce risks include:
- Making sure the vehicle is well-maintained and roadworthy. - Check to see that the containers being transported are closed and intact. Do not transport leaking containers. - Keep pesticides separate from drivers, passengers, and animals. Avoid carrying pesticides in the passenger compartment of a vehicle because of the potential for spills and fumes. If this is not possible to avoid, make sure the vehicle is ventilated (e.g. windows are open) during transport. - Do not transport pesticides with food, animals, or animal feed. - Make sure the load is safe and secure. The cargo area must be able to securely hold containers so that they do not bounce out of the vehicle and are protected from tears, punctures, or impacts. Enclosed cargo boxes offer the best protection. - Organise the load to maximise stability. - In pick-up trucks, never stack pesticide containers higher than the side of the vehicle. - For flat-bed trucks, secure the load using tarpaulins which are tied down using cleats. - Steel beds are preferable over wooden beds as they are more easily cleaned. Pesticides can soak into wood. - Protect the pesticides from temperature extremes. - Keep herbicides separate from other pesticides and fertilisers to reduce the risk of cross-contamination. - Never leave pesticides unattended or unsupervised. When transporting pesticides, make sure to carry the Master Safety Data sheets for the pesticides being transported, a spill kit, and PPE.

title: 'IPM: Influence of weather on effective pesticide application.'
text: CABI: IPM: Influence of weather on effective pesticide application.

title: 'IPM: Influence of weather on effective pesticide application.'
text: Weather conditions can significantly affect the efficiency of the application of pesticides and requires special attention.

title: 'IPM: Influence of weather on effective pesticide application.'
text: Weather conditions can both help and hinder the applicator. Weather-wise application can reduce pesticide hazard to the environment. A good applicator carefully checks the weather conditions before beginning spray procedures. Not only do a few simple precautions protect the environment, but also save money. Pesticides which do not reach or remain on the target areas are wasted. More pesticide, time, and money must be used to control the pests in the target area.

title: 'IPM: Influence of weather on effective pesticide application.'
text: Temperature and humidity affect pesticide drift. High temperature and low humidity increase the rate of evaporation of the pesticide. Small droplets that completely evaporate leave pesticide particles in the air that may be carried several miles away from the treatment area (vapour drift). High winds increase drift and result in the loss of pesticide from treated areas. Drifting pesticides increase the possibility of injury to wildlife, pollinators, and domestic animals. They may settle on forage, pasture or wildlife areas or contaminate water. Pesticide application on quiet days reduces the inhalation and contact hazard to the applicator and the bystander. Drift onto sensitive crop areas can also be avoided in this way. The applicator is legally responsible for any injury or money loss due to pesticide drift onto non-target areas. Don't take a chance by spraying in the wind.

title: 'IPM: Sprayer calibration and dosage calculation.'
text: CABI: IPM: Sprayer calibration and dosage calculation.

title: 'IPM: Sprayer calibration and dosage calculation.'
text: Many farmers do not calibrate their backpack sprayers. As a consequence, farmers can inadvertently be applying the wrong dosage - this can result in wasted product, poor pest control, high levels of pesticide residues and potentially even dead plants.

title: 'IPM: Sprayer calibration and dosage calculation.'
text:
#### Measure how much water comes out of the sprayer in the same time required to spray 100 square meters. ####
CABI
Spray equipment must be correctly calibrated. Calibration ensures the output of the sprayer is known and accurate and therefore ensures that pesticide can be applied at the rate specified on the label. It is important to remember that application of more than the recommended dose is probihited.

title: 'IPM: Sprayer calibration and dosage calculation.'
text:
To calibrate a sprayer and calculate dosage, follow these steps:
- Backpack Volume: Record the total volume of your backpack sprayer
- Calibration time: Mark out a square area measuring 10 meters (= 10 large paces) wide by 10 meters long. This will be about 100 square meters. Fill one third of the sprayer with clean water and have a participant from each group spray the marked area as if they would normally spray pesticide. Record how many seconds it took. - Calibration Volume: Measure how much water comes out of the sprayer in the same time required to spray 100 square meters: Spray water into a clean water bucket for the same number of seconds recorded in the calibration time box. Measure and record the volume of water in the bucket. - Water rate per hectare: This is how much water-pesticide solution is needed for one hectare at the sprayer operator's walking speed and the pressure that they are using: Multiply the Calibration Volume by 100 and record the result. - Chemical rate per hectare: This is how much chemical concentrate must be applied per hectare. This can be determined by the manufacturer or an agronomist. - Number of backpack refills per hectare: Divide the water rate by the backpack sprayer volume and record the result. - Amount of chemical concentrate per refill: Divide the chemical rate per hectare by the number of backpack refills per hectare and record the result. - Number of backpack sprayer refills: Calculate the number of backpack refills needed for your field: Multiply the number of backpack refills per hectare with the number of hectares of your field and record the result.

title: 'IPM: Disposal of waste pesticides.'
text: CABI: IPM: Disposal of waste pesticides.

title: 'IPM: Disposal of waste pesticides.'
text: Excess pesticides - both from left over material after application as well as from the storage facility - can cause problems if not correctly dealt with and are a common cause of environmental contamination.

title: 'IPM: Disposal of waste pesticides.'
text:
#### It is important to dispose of  pesticides properly. ####
CABI
A number of reasons are may exist leading to waste pesticides at a farm operation and below is a non-comprehensive list of those:
- Registration of the pesticide is cancelled and use is no longer permitted
- Newer, better pesticides are available so an older one is no longer recommended and used. - The expiry date has passed or the product has been rendered ineffective (e g. due to poor storage conditions). - A pesticide was purchased but then pests never reached threshold levels so the pesticide was not applied. - The farmer bought more pesticide than they needed for another reason, e.g. pressure from retailers. - Excess pesticide was mixed. Either calibration or field application was not carried out correctly or the dosage was calculated wrong.

title: 'IPM: Disposal of waste pesticides.'
text:
Some guidance on how to avoid having excess pesticides and what to do with pesticide waste is provided below:
- Only buy pesticides when needed and in the quantity needed. - Avoid storing pesticides for long periods (e.g. don't carry over pesticides from one season to the next. Practice stock control, i.e. first in, first out. - Estimate needs and only buy what is needed accordingly. - Resist temptation - don't let unscrupulous retailers to convince them to buy more than they need. - Always check the size of the job before mixing. - Make sure sprayer is calibrated and the dosage is calculated correctly. - Follow local laws and best practices. - If the pesticide is still factory-sealed, possibly it could be returned to the point of sale and / or the manufacturer. - If there is another site where the target pest is a problem, then excess tank mixture could be applied there. - Be careful with herbicide contaminated rinse water - it can potentially damage plants. - Spray remaining pesticides in another 1:10 H2O dilution over crop,
- Create a biobed and dispose waste there
- Never dispose of pesticide contaminated rinse water or excess tank solution where it can contaminate water sources.

title: 'IPM: Empty pesticide container disposal.'
text: CABI: IPM: Empty pesticide container disposal.

title: 'IPM: Empty pesticide container disposal.'
text: In some countries, systems for disposal of empty pesticide containers are not in place whereas in other countries systems have recently been introduced or may even have been in place for some time but are being under-utilised. Where container disposal systems exist, a goal is to see that they are being used.

title: 'IPM: Empty pesticide container disposal.'
text:
#### Empty container disposal. ####
J. Grunder and L. Heeb
In locations where systems do reach or systems have not been established, the aim is for empty containers to be disposed safely according to established best practices. The list of best practices will depend on local circumstances.

title: 'IPM: Empty pesticide container disposal.'
text:
#### Bins for pesticide disposal. ####
J. Grunder and L. Heeb
General guidelines for disposal of empty pesticide containers are as follows:
- Triple rinse and drain all containers immediately upon use. Regardless of the disposal method (recycling, incineration, burning on the farm, burying on the farm), triple rinse first. - Do not reuse containers
- Damage (e.g. puncture or cut up) empty containers. - If empty pesticide containers must be stored before disposal, make sure to store them in a secure location
- Regulations should be followed. Also, follow company policies. - Only bury or burn containers in areas where collection systems do not exist. - Guidelines for burning empty pesticide containers:
- Prior to burning, check that the container can be burned. Do not burn glass or metal containers. If possible, avoid burning plastic/PVC containers. Do not burn containers which held herbicides. - During burning, avoid coming into contact with smoke and especially do not inhale smoke – stay upwind
- Bury ash in a deep pit (>0.5 m). The bottom of the burial pit must be at least 2 m above the water table
- For burial of empty containers and ash from burned empty containers
- Only bury containers in locations where permitted by law and where alternate disposal systems are not available. - In most instances, containers should first be burned. For containers which cannot be burned (e.g. glass or metal), compress them as much as possible prior to burial. - Burial pits should be located so as to reduce the risk of water contamination. Do not locate them near water sources such as wells and surface water or in flood prone areas. - Use biodegradable waste such as food scraps to cover buried materials and to promote their biological degradation. - Cover filled burials pits with soil then plant bushes to limit drainage of rain water.

title: 'IPM: Re-entry intervals, safeguarding areas after spraying.'
text: CABI: IPM: Re-entry intervals, safeguarding areas after spraying.

title: 'IPM: Re-entry intervals, safeguarding areas after spraying.'
text: Re-entry intervals (REI) need to be considered after application of pesticides because the farmer, farm people and other people in the community, including children, may face getting health problems from uptake of or contact with pesticides of the sprayed fields.

title: 'IPM: Re-entry intervals, safeguarding areas after spraying.'
text:
#### It is important to wait for the full REI before entering the field again. ####
E. Chernoh
REI refers to the time after the end of a pesticide application during which entry into the treated area is restricted. When treated plants are touched during work activities such as weeding, thinning, or brushing against plants, some pesticide material may be transferred to skin. People in treated areas may also breathe fumes from a recent pesticide application. REIs have been established to prevent people from being exposed to pesticides immediately after application. Following REI allows residues to disperse so that they do not pose a risk. Re-entry times are established by a number of factors including the toxicity of the active ingredient, the formulation, the rate and method of application, characteristics of the crop and crop stage being sprayed.

title: 'IPM: Re-entry intervals, safeguarding areas after spraying.'
text:
Some guidance for this topic is shown below:
- Post warning signs that state when treated areas can be re-entered. Warning signs should also incorporate symbols, e.g. a stop sign or skull and cross bones, so that it is clear to everyone that the area is restricted. - Signs should be posted on all likely entry corners of the field. - REIs can be found by reading the pesticide labels (or the information provided by the leaf supplier). The pesticide label will also say what protective equipment is needed if someone enters an area that has been sprayed before the REI has elapsed. - If the REI is not on the label, a general rule of thumb is to establish an REI of 24 hours for a slightly toxic pesticide and 48 hours for moderately or very toxic pesticides. - For more intense work in the field (e.g. for weeding), it is strongly suggested to extend the minimum REI
- If a person got exposed in a freshly sprayed field, wash affected skin parts immediately. Have them get out of the area, change clothes, and see a doctor if necessary.

title: 'IPM: Sprayer decontamination and maintenance.'
text: CABI: IPM: Sprayer decontamination and maintenance.

title: 'IPM: Sprayer decontamination and maintenance.'
text: To take care for good maintenance of the spraying equipment is necessary to ensure its function which in turn is a prerequisite guaranteeing a high quality of the distribution of the pesticide on the crop and high effectiveness. Furthermore, it is important to minimise exposure of the spray operator and other on-farm people as well as the environment. Decontamination is particularly important because pesticide residues in the sprayer tank can do damage to the crop during the following treatment, to the sprayer itself or to the environment.

title: 'IPM: Sprayer decontamination and maintenance.'
text:
#### Sprayer should undergo mechanical service on a regular basis. ####
CABI
Even though you emptied your knapsack sprayer/tank after use (see Factsheet on waste pesticide disposal), always wash your equipment carefully before you store it. This will avoid damage to crops from harmful spray residues (e.g. by remains of herbicides) and damage to the sprayer from corrosion or abrasion, thus ensuring its sound functionality and a prolonged life. If maintenance is not strongly considered, several functions may be constricted, e.g. damaged or worn nozzles can lead to over application. In addition, drips or leaks can cause contamination of the spray operator as well as having environmental implications.

title: 'IPM: Sprayer decontamination and maintenance.'
text:
#### Sprayer should undergo mechanical service on a regular basis. ####
CABI
Some guidance on how to ensure good maintenance of your sprayer and on how to ensure sound decontamination is provided below:
- Thoroughly rinse off inside and outside of your spraying equipment while it is placed in the special wash area. - Start washing as soon as possible after the pesticide application because it has been shown that pesticides that were allowed to dry onto a surface were more difficult to remove than when they remained wet. - Do not allow rinse water to get on the ground and into streams, ponds, or other sensitive areas. Collect it and hold for proper disposal. - For maintenance make sure that your spraying equipment is carefully checked for proper functionality of all important parts once per year by a qualified specialist. - A certificate for sprayers would be advantageous as well as a system established where farmers must prove spraying equipment has undergone mechanical service on a regular basis.

title: 'IPM: Dealing with spills in the pesticide storage area.'
text: CABI: IPM: Dealing with spills in the pesticide storage area.

title: 'IPM: Dealing with spills in the pesticide storage area.'
text: Even if safety precautions for pesticide storage specified on product labels and any accompanying label information are followed, accidents can still happen. If a pesticide spills in the storage area, quick action must be taken so anyone with access to the pesticide store needs to know what to do in case of an emergency.

title: 'IPM: Dealing with spills in the pesticide storage area.'
text:
#### Always clean up any spills immediately, using absorbent material such as sawdust. ####
Stewardship Community
Preparations must be in place to be ready in case an accident occurs. A list of safety procedures should be posted it in the storage area. Safety equipment should also be available including hazard warning signs, outside and inside the store; telephone numbers for emergency contacts; fire extinguisher; first aid kit; absorbent material to soak up any spills (e.g. activated charcoal, absorptive clay, vermiculite, pet litter, or sawdust); shovel, broom, dust pan and sprinkler can for decontamination and clean-up; waste bin for contaminated waste; soap/high pH commercial detergent and clean water; personal protective equipment in separate store close to product store.

title: 'IPM: Dealing with spills in the pesticide storage area.'
text:
#### After the spill has been soaked up, the area is cleaned with detergent. ####
Stewardship Community
- Some guidelines for cleaning up after a store are as follows:
- If the pesticide gets on anyone, wash it off immediately. Have them get out of the area, wash thoroughly, change dothes, and see a doctor if necessary. - Clear the storage area except for a small clean-up crew. Be sure the crew wears the proper personal protective equipment. - For spills and leaks of liquid pesticides, cover the entire spill with absorbent material. Use enough to soak up most of the liquid. Then sweep or shovel the material and put the waste in the bin for contaminated materials. - If the spill is a dust, granular, or powder, sweep or shovel it directly into a large drum. Sweeping compound can be useful when picking up spills of dry pesticides. - Once the spilled pesticides have been cleared away, next cover the spill area with a decontamination agent recommended for that particular pesticide. The manufacturer or supplier may have to be consulted. Hydrated lime and high pH commercial detergents are often recommended as they can neutralise many pesticides. Repeat procedure several times. - Rinse the whole area with plenty of water to wash away any remaining poison. Collect the rinse water and hold it for proper disposal. - Check the storage area carefully to see if any other pesticides were contaminated by the spill. If so, do not take a chance on using them dispose of them as well. - When finished, seal the bin for contaminated waste tightly and dispose of properly.

title: 'IPM: Safe and secure storage of pesticides.'
text: CABI: IPM: Safe and secure storage of pesticides.

title: 'IPM: Safe and secure storage of pesticides.'
text: A number of farmers do not store pesticides appropriately and as result the likelihood of accidents and product deterioration increases. Farmers and farm workers should know the basic safety rules for pesticide storage and follow them.

title: 'IPM: Safe and secure storage of pesticides.'
text:
#### Pesticides should be stored securely. ####
S. Sastroutomo
Pesticides are valuable products, which may deteriorate and become useless if they are not stored under proper conditions. Likewise, since they are hazardous substances accidents can happen if precautionary measures are not put in place. Correct and safe storage of crop protection products is essential to protect human health, safeguard the environment, reduce the risk of theft and maintain product integrity and effectiveness. Correct storage of pesticides is an important part of GAP.

title: 'IPM: Safe and secure storage of pesticides.'
text:
#### Do not smoke or eat in store rooms. ####
J. Grunder and L. Heeb
- There are some general rules that apply regardless of the type of pesticide storage area. The key dos and don'ts of pesticide storage are as follows:
- Product Storage - **Do not:**
- Buy pesticides in excessive of what is needed immediately. - Store pesticides for long periods. - Leave products unlocked and unattended at any time. - Store products or keys to stores within reach of children. - Store liquids above powders. - Store close to foodstuffs, animal feed, seed, fertiliser, gasoline or medical supplies. - Smoke, eat or drink in the store room. - Do not store pesticides in direct sunlight, where exposed to rain or to extreme temperatures. - Product Storage - **Do**:
- Only purchase as much as needed. - Use older products before new. - Follow specific requirements for storage as listed on the label. - Store products in their original containers with intact labels. - Keep the store under lock and key. - Have absorbant material available to soak up any spills. - Clean up any leaks or spills immediately. - Remove waste and dispose of it safely and legally. - Deal with damaged or deteriorating containers. - Post warning signs on outside and inside of pesticide storage area. Keep pesticides in a cool, shaded, well-ventilated location.)

title: 'IPM: Guidelines for pesticide stock management.'
text: CABI: IPM: Guidelines for pesticide stock management.

title: 'IPM: Guidelines for pesticide stock management.'
text:
#### Pesticides should only be stored if they are properly labeled. ####
J. Grunder and L. Heeb
Poor stock management can lead to problems. Farmers and farm workers should know the basic rules for pesticide stock management and follow them.

title: 'IPM: Guidelines for pesticide stock management.'
text:
Some guidelines for pesticide stock management are as follows:
- Check the condition of products at delivery. - After use, partly empty pesticide containers should be resealed and returned to storage. Seal caps should be securely closed. - Pesticides should only be stored in properly labeled containers with the label in plain sight. Original packaging should be used. Pesticides should never be stored in soda bottles, fruit jars, milk cartons, etc. Storing pesticides in improper containers such as these is a common cause of pesticide poisoning. Never put tank mix in a jar and give it to someone in an unlabelled container. Unlabelled pesticides are dangerous since their contents and instructions for use are not known. - All pesticide containers in the storage should be checked regularly for signs of corrosion, leaks, loose caps, or dents. Inspect containers before handling. Correct any problems immediately when detected. If containers are damaged and the contents are still in good condition, the pesticide should be re-packed in a sound and suitable larger container that can be sealed and labeled. Never use empty food or drink containers to re-pack pesticides. Firmly fasten the label from the damaged container to the new container. - Avoid storing pesticides for a long time because they may become ineffective or start leaking. It is important to plan purchases carefully to reduce storage time and avoid surpluses. Only buy sufficient for the area of crop you will treat. Containers should be dated when purchased. Stock control must allow older pesticides to be used first. Put the oldest products in front and use the oldest pesticide first. Expired pesticides should be discarded. (See Factsheet on disposal of unwanted pesticides for more information.) - Avoid storing pesticides that have been mixed with another substance (such as a diluent, carrier, marker, or adjuvant). Do not mix more than what you need for that day.

title: 'IPM: Guidelines for storage areas for larger quantities of pesticides.'
text: CABI: IPM: Guidelines for storage areas for larger quantities of pesticides.

title: 'IPM: Guidelines for storage areas for larger quantities of pesticides.'
text: Care must be taken when storing pesticides; precautions are even more necessary when large amounts of pesticides are stored. Farmers and farm workers should know the basic safety rules for pesticide storage and follow them.

title: 'IPM: Guidelines for storage areas for larger quantities of pesticides.'
text:
#### Large pesticide store. ####
J. Grunder and L. Heeb
The type and size of the pesticide storage area will depend on the amount of product to store and any local regulations. A simple locked box may be appropriate for the safe storage of small product volumes (<200 litres or kgs of pesticides). Larger amounts of pesticides (>200 litres or kgs) should be kept in dedicated buildings or rooms.

title: 'IPM: Guidelines for storage areas for larger quantities of pesticides.'
text:
Guidelines for proper storage of large quantities of pesticides are as follows:
- If farmers use large amounts of pesticides and/or equipment, they should have a dedicated storage fadlity just for their pesticides. If it is not possible to have a separate building, they should choose a room or corner on the first floor of a building. - The storage area should be fenced in or at least able to be locked tightly to prevent unauthorised access. - Weatherproof warning signs should be hung over every door and window. The area in which they are stored should be marked with appropriate warning signs, e.g. "danger", "no entry" and "no smoking" signs. - The floor of a pestidde storage building should have a solid floor, preferably made of non-porous material like sealed cement or ceramic tile. - Good lighting is important in that it allows handlers to read pesticide labels, monitor the condition of the stored materials, detect and clean up leaks. - The building should be well-ventilated. Fans are an important feature of any pestidde storage building. A properly installed ventilation system should have a switch outside, so that the fan can be turned on before anyone enters the fadlity. Exhaust fans should be directed to the outside of the building. - Large pesticide warehouses should also be bunded, fire- and flood-proof, and temperature controlled. Avoid locations which are prone to fires or flooding. - The pesticide storage area should only be used for pesticides and pesticide equipment. Never store or use food, drinks, medicine, silverware, PPE or any other farm materials (e.g. oil, fertilisers, fuel, tools, etc.) in the pesticide storage area. Livestock feed, living plants, and seeds should never be stored with or near pesticides. - Do not keep unapproved or unwanted pesticides in pesticide store.

title: 'IPM: Guidelines for storage of small quantities of pesticides.'
text: CABI: IPM: Guidelines for storage of small quantities of pesticides.

title: 'IPM: Guidelines for storage of small quantities of pesticides.'
text: Care must be taken when storing pesticides, even if only a limited quantity of pesticides is stored for short periods of time. Some farmers do not store pesticides appropriately. For example, they store pesticides in the home, in harsh conditions such as extremely hot places, etc. As a result the likelihood of accidents or product deterioration increases. Farmers and farm workers should know the basic safety rules for pesticide storage and follow them.

title: 'IPM: Guidelines for storage of small quantities of pesticides.'
text:
#### Pesticide stores should be kept off the ground and clearly state that the box contains pesticides. ####
Irshad Ali
The type and size of the pesticide storage area will depend on the amount of product to store and any local legislation relating to that storage. A simple locked box, cabinet or cupboard - mounted on the wall away from the reach of children when not in use - may be appropriate for the safe storage of small product volumes (<200 litres or kgs of pesticides). Larger amounts of pesticides (>200 litres or kgs) should be kept in dedicated building or rooms.

title: 'IPM: Guidelines for storage of small quantities of pesticides.'
text:
Guidelines for proper storage of small quantities of pesticides are as follows:
- Small quantities of pesticides kept in cupboards (preferably metal) or boxes must be kept outside the house and away from where animals live. - The box should be kept locked at all times to avoid unauthorised access and keep out of reach of children. Keys and access to the pesticide store muse be controlled by someone who has been trained. - A fixed warning sign, e.g. entitled "Pesticide Storage", should be on the front of the cupboard or box. - The pesticide storage lock box should be placed on supports that lift it off the ground or mounted on the wall. - The box should have adequate space to enable products to be stored neatly and safely. The box should be large enough to store products on trays or within secondary containers that would retain contents in case 01 leaks. - The pesticide storage area should only be used for pesticides and pesticide equipment. Never store or use food, drinks, medicine, silverware, PPE or any other farm materials (e.g. oil, fertilisers, fuel, tools, etc.) in the pesticide storage area. Livestock feed, living plants, and seeds should never be stored with or near pesticides. - Do not have unapproved or unwanted pesticides in pesticide store. - Pesticide cabinets should be kept in a cool, shaded, well-ventilated location. Do not store pesticide cabinets in direct sunlight, where exposed to rain or to extreme temperatures.

title: 'IPM: Optimal environmental conditions for pesticide storage.'
text: CABI: IPM: Optimal environmental conditions for pesticide storage.

title: 'IPM: Optimal environmental conditions for pesticide storage.'
text: Some farmers store pesticides haphazardly, with little regard to the environmental conditions of storage. This can result in problems like water contamination, deterioration of the pesticide containers or the products inside of them, human exposure to pesticide fumes or splashes, or even fire. Pesticides should be stored in locations where the risk of environmental hazards like floods or fires are minimal. Likewise, pesticides should not be stored under extreme temperatures, either hot or cold.

title: 'IPM: Optimal environmental conditions for pesticide storage.'
text:
#### Pesticides should be stored in a cool, dry, airy place. ####
Keith Holmes
Flooding or percolation in the pesticide storage can result in contamination of surface or groundwater. Moisture can cause metal containers to rust, cardboard containers to deteriorate, labels to peel or smear, and dry formulations to clump or dissolve. Heat is also an issue: it may cause liquid pesticides to expand putting contents under pressure and causing the pesticide to splash out when opened. When some formulations get too hot they vaporize, becoming a health hazard. Some formulations lose their strength and break down when exposed to heat. Certain pesticides will catch fire if they are too hot or are exposed to flame. Freezing will destroy the usefulness of some pesticides, and it may also cause liquid pesticides to break their containers and leak.

title: 'IPM: Optimal environmental conditions for pesticide storage.'
text: - Pesticides should be protected from the rain and should not be stored in damp, humid locations. - Avoid locating the storage facility near streams which are prone to flooding, sites where run-off can be a problem and sites which are close to wells or other water sources . - Consult pesticide labels for specific information on the temperature limits for storing a particular pesticide. In general, avoid storing pesticides under extreme temperatures (below 4°C or above 38°C). - Pesticides should be stored in a cool, dry, airy place which is fireproof. - Never store pesticides under direct sunlight, as this can lead to overheating. - Beware of fire hazard resulting from cigarette smoking, use of open fire or direct sunlight coming in through glass windows. - Avoid storing pesticides in hot places. Glass and metal containers of liquid pesticides should not be stored near heat sources such as steam pipes, furnaces, etc. or in direct sunlight. - Opened containers of chlorates (used as weed killers) should not be stored as they are highly flammable.

title: 'IPM: Organisation of pesticide storage areas.'
text: CABI: IPM: Organisation of pesticide storage areas.

title: 'IPM: Organisation of pesticide storage areas.'
text: If pesticides are stored on the farm, they must all be stored together in one location in a storage facility. Correct and secure storage of crop protection products is essential to protect human health, safeguard the environment, reduce the risk of theft, and maintain product integrity and effectiveness. Correct storage of pesticides is an important part of GAP.

title: 'IPM: Organisation of pesticide storage areas.'
text: The pesticide storage area should be kept clean and organised. Some guidelines are given below.

title: 'IPM: Organisation of pesticide storage areas.'
text: - Pesticide storage areas should have adequate space for pesticides to be stored in orderly rows with the pesticide labels plainly visible. - Stores must contain shelving so that pesticides can be kept off the floor. This helps to contain spills, prevent damage from dampness, and prevent people from tripping or knocking over containers. - Containers should always be set in an upright position so they cannot spill. - Liquid pesticides must be stored below dry pesticides. - Pesticide dosage and application recommendations (e.g. Pest Management Decision Guides) should be displayed in the pesticide storage facility or on the cupboard or box. - Dosage measuring devices must be available inside the pesticide storage facility. - Follow storage instructions on pesticide labels. Some products require separation from other products. For example, some herbicides can vaporize and get into other pesticides nearby. When the contaminated pesticide is used, the herbicide vapours in it could injure or kill crops and sensitive plants. Hence, herbicides that can vaporize should be stored in a special place apart from other pesticides, fertilizers, and seeds or bulbs.

title: Trichogramma as a biocontrol agent
text: CABI: Trichogramma as a biocontrol agent

title: Trichogramma as a biocontrol agent
text: Trichogramma egg parasitoids can be released in crop fields to control various moth and butterfly pests. Typical target pests are fall armyworm, tomato fruit borer or corn borers. Trichogramma can be mass produced and made available for farmers via egg cards.

title: Trichogramma as a biocontrol agent
text:
#### Trichogramma female on Ephestia egg ####
Gabi Brändle, Agroscope
Trichogramma are tiny wasps of about 0.5 mm. They attack and develop inside the egg stage of the pest, meaning that instead of the pest larvae hatching, another Trichogramma adult will emerge from the host egg. Development from egg to adult may take 7-12 days, depending on temperature. Generally Trichogramma are released as parasitized host eggs. They may be applied as egg cards or inside capsules. The capsules can be released by drone technology, but egg cards are usually applied manually to the crop.

title: Trichogramma as a biocontrol agent
text:
#### Trichogramma egg card in the tomato crop ####
Dirk Babendreier, CABI
* It is generally recommended to release Trichogramma several times during the relevant cropping stages, i.e. during those times where adults and eggs of the pest are present. It depends on the crop and the pest pressure but typical release intervals are about 14 days. * When releasing egg cards, make sure that the printed side, without the parasitized eggs, shows upright as this will protect the Trichogramma on the back side from rain and direct sun light. * For each hectare of crop fields, 100 Trichogramma egg‐cards may be applied with release points being about 10 m apart from each other. * For maize and similar crops, use egg cards containing 1,000 Trichogramma wasps each, resulting in 100,000 wasps per hectare. For tomato, the commonly recommended release rate is 150,000 wasps per hectare (1,500 Trichogramma per card)
* Avoid release during hot times of the day and during or before heavy rain. * Avoid spraying pesticides to your crop, in particular broad-spectrum insecticides, one week before and after release of Trichogramma as these chemicals may kill the Trichogramma wasps that emerge from the cards
* Newly emerged wasps will be look for more eggs of pest insects to parasitise and kill. * The efficacy of Trichogramma is improved if they are released on a larger area, i.e. if farmers from a village agree to combine their efforts. If only released on a single field, some Trichogramma might leave the field. * With Trichogramma releases, insecticide applications are often made unnecessary, resulting in healthy products and improved marketing.
