### Overview ###
Red palm weevil *Rhynchophorus ferrugineus* is an invasive insect pest of date palm and causes damage in most date-producing areas of the world, particularly in the Middle East and North Africa. This case study describes current management strategies with an example from the Al-Ahsa Oasis of Saudi Arabia. It also suggests new areas of research underway that might improve red palm weevil control in the future.

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text: 1. To become familiar with the life cycle of RPW, and methods of spread both locally and globally. 2. To obtain a good understanding of available control options for RPW, and the reasons why some are more effective than others. 3. To inspire the study of new technologies to detect and bait RPW, and develop biological control agents, and molecular techniques to modify the genome of either date palm or RPW.

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text: The genus *Rhynchophorus* contains many weevil species, but the most important globally is *R. ferrugineus* commonly known as the red palm weevil (RPW) or Asiatic palm weevil, coconut weevil, palm weevil, and red stripe weevil (EPPO Global Database, 2022). The RPW is a cosmopolitan invasive insect pest attacking a range of different palm species including date palm (*Phoenix dactylifera*), Canary Island date palm (*Phoenix canariensis*), and coconut palm (*Cocos nucifera*). The weevil was first discovered in India in 1891 and was later described as a serious pest on coconut in 1906 and on date palm in 1917. Since then, the transport of infested trees and offshoots (seedlings) whether for fruit production or landscaping has facilitated its spread.

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text: RPW has been found in countries of the Middle East and most parts of North Africa, from where it has invaded Southern Europe, particularly Spain, Italy, Portugal, Turkey, France, and Greece (EPPO Global Database, 2022). The RPW was introduced into the Arabia Peninsula in the 1980s and has since become a major pest of date palm. Recently RPW was detected on date palms in Djibouti in East Africa and the Canary Island date palm in Abkhazia in the Republic of Georgia. In 2019, the weevil established itself in Bulgaria in the Black Sea Basin region and Bosnia-Herzegovina in South Eastern Europe. RPW also reached Aruba and Curacao islands in the Caribbean region and the Netherlands Antilles. The weevil has invaded a total of 49 countries over the last 30 years, and the host range has expanded from only four species in the mid-1950s to 40 species in 2020. It is difficult to eradicate RPW once established in an area, which has only been achieved in the Canary Islands. RPW can kill a date palm within 6–12 months, depending on its age, physiological condition, cultivar type, and environmental conditions. For these reasons, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations considers RPW a category-1 pest of date palm.

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
section: Distribution and Economic Impact in Saudi Arabia
text:
In Saudi Arabia, RPW was first detected in Al-Qatif in 1987 (Fig. 1), and specimens were presumably imported on infested ornamental palms from East Asia. Two years later in 1989, the weevil was reported in northern Riyadh and Tabuk. These areas are both separated from Al-Qatif by large bodies of sand and arid land, which indicates that the weevil was likely transported on infested palm offshoots and/or adult palms. In the period from 1987 to 2016, RPW spread to eleven provinces of Saudi Arabia (Fig. 1). Only two provinces, the Northern Borders and Jazan in the South remain pest free. RPW damage affects the income of around 123,000 small farms in Saudi Arabia. Annual losses in date production range between US$ 6 and 17 million and the cost of removal of infested palms in the Gulf region is estimated to be between US$ 5 and 25 million at an infestation rate of 1% and 5% palm tree, respectively. These losses reduce the contribution of the date palm sector to Saudi Arabia’s GDP. Moreover, farmers are often spiritually connected to their palms, which makes it difficult to accept the need to remove infested individuals, and this type of stress is impossible to measure in monetary value. Although RPW has been under rigorous management in Saudi Arabia for the past 35 years, there are still outbreaks in different regions of the country. This plant health case highlights aspects of RPW concerning its biology and current management practices as well as prospects for control in the future. ##### Fig. 1 #####
Red palm weevil (RPW), *Rhynchophorus ferrugineus*, invasion history in Saudi Arabia.

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text: The RPW belongs to the order Coleoptera and the family Curculionidae. The insect undergoes four developmental stages to complete its life cycle, namely egg, larva, pupa, and adult (Fig. 2). The egg is elongated (2.5 × 1 mm) with a shiny creamy-white colour. A newly hatched larva measures only 5 × 2 mm and weighs about 1 mg, while the final larval instar can reach 5 × 2 cm and weigh between 4 and 7 g before pupation. The final larval instar forms a barrel-shaped cocoon made from palm tree fibres measuring 7 × 4 cm, while the pupa inside is 3.5 × 1.5 cm (El-Shafie and Faleiro, 2020; Abdel-Banat and El-Shafie, 2021). The RPW has a great capacity for flying and can travel 10–50 km per day, which helps to explain its successful dispersal over large palm-growing regions (Hoddle *et al*., 2015). Organic volatiles released from fresh wounds on the palm attract and stimulate adult females to lay their eggs. They usually prefer date and coconut palms under 20 years old and lay the eggs in cracks and crevices of soft or wounded tissues. A single female weevil can lay over 200 eggs during its life. The eggs hatch after 3–6 days and the larvae feed during 7–16 instars inside the palm tree tissues, where they gain weight over 35–100 days and therefore cause a high degree of plant damage (Fig. 2). The final larval instars pupate in cocoons, and after 13–17 days adult winged weevils emerge. The male weevil is distinguishable from the female by the presence of soft reddish-brown hairs on the dorsal side of its elongated snout (Fig. 2).

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text:
The male weevil is distinguishable from the female by the presence of soft reddish-brown hairs on the dorsal side of its elongated snout (Fig. 2). The female snout has no hairs and is longer, slender, and with a little downward curvature relative to the male snout. The adult weevils leave the palm seeking new food sources and suitable mates and can live for up to four months. An infested palm tree may contain several overlapping generations of weevils. Oviposition is strongly affected by temperature. Under laboratory conditions (25–27°C) the RPW develops from egg to weevil in 3 to 4 months. However, in the Mediterranean region, the larval stage can span a prolonged period of up to 5 months during the cooler winter season and early spring (Dembilio and Jacas, 2011). ##### Fig. 2 #####
The life cycle of the red palm weevil (RPW), *Rhynchophorus ferrugineus*.

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text: Some date palm cultivars have a hard trunk that is difficult for the RPW to penetrate, and in such cases, the weevil will attack the softer apical growing point. The cultivar ‘Sagae’ shows apical infestation more than other cultivars because the fronds (leaves) bend downwards, thereby exposing the soft parts of the frond base, where the weevil can more easily dig and lay its eggs. Similarly, the heavy weight of fruit bunches of some cultivars pushes the fronds downward thus exposing the tender tissues to weevil attack (Faleiro *et al*., 2014).

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text:
The main symptoms of RPW infestation usually appear up to one meter above soil level on palm trees less than five years old. If tissue damage is extensive it can result in the toppling of the trunk (Fig. 3A). For palms between 5 and 12 years, which usually have a trunk more than two meters in circumference, the infestation takes place 1–1.5 m above the ground. In palms older than 25 years, infestation occurs mostly in the crown (apical infestation) of both female and male individuals (Fig. 3B and inset), and on aerial offshoots when the weevil population is high. An indication of an early infestation is frass (larvae excrement) at the base of fronds (Fig. 3C), followed by drying and wilting of the outer and older fronds (Fig. 3D). Fruit bunches and offshoots are also affected. Infested trunks may show oozing of a brownish viscous fluid, which together with frass has a fermented odour (Fig. 3E). Sometimes both adults and pupae can be found at the base of the fronds and on the ground near infested palms. ##### Fig. 3 #####
Damage incurred by red palm weevil (RPW) on date palm. (A) Trunk collapse of a young date palm tree caused by feeding of RPW larvae. (B) Wilt of outer fronds (leaves) in the crown of a date palm tree. Inset showing a close-up of the remains of plant tissues and frass (excrement) of larvae and adult weevils. (C) Palm tissues and frass are excreted by feeding larvae on the top of infested aerial offshoots (seedlings).

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text: The RPW in Saudi Arabia is managed through the inspection of palms for early detection of infestation, mass trapping of adults, insecticide treatments, and removal of infested palms. Quarantine measures have been used to prevent the entry of the weevil into uninfested areas. Due to the high value of date palm as a cash crop, and the damage caused by RPW, it is recommended to control the pest at 1% infested palm trees. It is of utmost importance to adopt the best possible method concerning trap design and colour, trap placement and density, as well as quality and quantity of a pheromone lure. Equally important is servicing the traps at regular intervals to renew food bait, water, and lure. A four-window bucket trap is popular in the Middle East and Gulf countries, while a dome-shaped conical PicusanTM trap, is used in several European countries. The standard RPW trap, commonly used in Saudi Arabia, consists of a plastic bucket (5 l capacity), inserted into a hollowed date palm trunk 0.5 m above ground, with four round windows in the upper one-third of the bucket (Fig. 4). The bucket holds about 200 g fermented dates in about 1 l water. The lid is fitted with a pheromone lure (700 mg FerrolureTM) which is a mixture of ferrugineol and ferrugineone (9:1) emitting 3–10 mg of the pheromone per day. The same pheromones are produced naturally by the RPW males and attract both male and female weevils for feeding and mating. One to four traps per hectare is suitable depending on the pest intensity. Since water and dates keep the insects inside the trap, it is recommended to provide trap service every two weeks to replace both water and bait.

One to four traps per hectare is suitable depending on the pest intensity. Since water and dates keep the insects inside the trap, it is recommended to provide trap service every two weeks to replace both water and bait. Co-attractants such as ethyl acetate/ethyl alcohol are known to enhance capture, but they significantly increase the cost particularly if the control area is large. Despite the food-baited pheromone traps being the most popular, the requirement of frequent service increases the cost and makes these traps unsuitable over a large area. For this reason, service-less traps such as the ElectrapTM have been tested whereby the efficiency of insect attraction is increased by more than 300% (ELECTRAP®, 2013). The ElectrapTM is principally based on food-baited pheromone in addition to an electromagnetic device that generates vibrational frequencies to both amplify and quench the smell. Other trap designs under development are capable of recording and transmitting data of captured weevils in real-time. ##### Fig. 4 #####
(A) Four-window bucket trap with date bait in water inserted into a cut palm trunk 0.5 m above ground with a pheromone lure mounted in the lid. (B) Boxes containing adult weevils captured in these traps. The decision on whether to implement an area-wide RPW management programme usually follows a sequential sampling plan over a defined time period (Etikan *et al*., 2016). In sequential sampling, one measurement is taken at the time of either number of infested palm trees or the number of RPWs in pheromone traps.

text: In sequential sampling, one measurement is taken at the time of either number of infested palm trees or the number of RPWs in pheromone traps. There are three possible outcomes: if there is a large number of infested trees or trapped insects then control action is initiated; if the numbers are low then no action is taken, but if the number is close to a predetermined threshold a new measurement is taken until a decision can be based on either high or low numbers. In practice 100 young date or coconut palms (or all trees on 1 ha) are inspected followed by inspection of another group if necessary, and so on until a decision can be made. The number of samples cannot be determined in advance, since sampling continues until a conclusion can be reached. Sometimes mathematic models are used for both experimental design and data analysis. Due to the high value of date and coconut palm, the damage caused by RPW, and the ease of insect spread, it is recommended to control the RPW at 1% infested palms. This strategy can also be used to assess the effectiveness of an ongoing control programme.

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text: Experience has shown that sole dependence on pheromone trapping of adult weevils without additional control methods often leads to outbreaks. Preventive and curative insecticidal treatments are therefore essential for efficient RPW management. Treatment of palms in the early stage of infestation is an integral part of a management plan as the infested palms often recover after application. Early detection is difficult because the weevil resides inside the palm trunk and canopy. Currently, the most common way to detect RPW infestation is done by well-trained personnel using visual inspection of individual palm trees and sampling with hand-screw probes. Insecticides can be applied using different methods such as spray application, soil drench, or using a trunk microinjection technique. However, insecticides are expensive, and excessive application of insecticides can harm the environment, and may also lead to the development of chemical resistance in weevil populations (Abdel-Banat and El-Shafie, 2021).

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text: A study of RPW management was conducted in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia between 2007 and 2012 in the district of Al Ghowaybah (Hoddle *et al*., 2013). This district is part of the Al-Ahsa oasis, which is the world’s largest oasis consisting of 3 million palm trees grown on 530,000 km2 of fertile land. The Al Ghowaybah district has around 185,000 palm trees grown on 1104 ha with about 222 individual date palm farms ranging from 5 to 20 ha. The area produces date fruits worth US$ 14.8 million annually, primarily from cultivar ‘Khalas’ that grown on 70% of the acreage. Three years after the initial identification of the RPW in Al-Qatif, the weevil invaded the Al-Ahsa Oasis in 1991. For many years the RPW was managed through palm tree inspection, pheromone trapping of adults, insecticide application, and removal of highly infested palms that could not recover. Management practices in Al Ghowaybah specifically between 2006 and 2009 comprised bait traps placed at relatively low density (0.08 trap per ha), an inspection of trees in areas with the highest weevil catches, insecticide treatment of 6% of the palm trees (e.g. 11,000 palms in 2008), and removal of infested palms. However, the infestation rate was 3.7% of palm trees, which is relatively high and necessitated a change in management strategy. Consequently, RPW monitoring, pesticide control, and tree removal were intensified the following year. The number of insecticide-treated palms increased dramatically to 2.9 applications per year using nine different insecticide products (four organophosphates, three pyrethroids, one neonicotinoid, and one carbamate). Palm tree removal in 2009 was three times higher compared to 2007 and 2008 (Fig.

Palm tree removal in 2009 was three times higher compared to 2007 and 2008 (Fig. 5C), and by 2011, the rate of trap deployment was ~0.9 trap per ha (91% increase). The combination of these control measures resulted in a reduced RPW population and less use of insecticides in the following years. By 2012, insecticide use decreased by 91% compared to 2009 (Fig. 5C), palm removal was 89% of the 2009 level (Fig. 5A), and RPW captures decreased by 86% relative to 2010 (Fig. 5B). The overall impact of the intensified RPW management in Al Ghowaybah was a reduction in infestation rate from 3.7% to 0.36% palm trees over three years. Similar management methods in Al Qatif reduced the rate of RPW infestation from 6.6% to 2.5% palms. Deployment of pheromone-baited traps integrated with other tactics was also effective in the Sultanate of Oman, where the RPW infestation dropped from 24% in 1998 to 3% in 2003. ##### Fig. 5 #####

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text:
In 2011, 393 date palm growers in Al-Ahsa oasis participated in a survey to determine relationships between RPW infestation and different agronomic practices used by the farmers (Sallam *et al. * 2012). A total of 39,330 palm trees were visually inspected, and 167 (0.4%) RPW infestations were detected. The farmers used three watering methods namely flood, basin, and drip irrigation systems. Basin irrigation is a type of surface irrigation practiced at a field level in all directions. The land is surrounded by embankments to prevent runoff and provides an undirected flow of water onto the field. The survey of watering methods resulted in obvious differences since 88% of RPW infestation occurred under flood irrigation compared to only 9.6% and 2.4% with basin and drip irrigation, respectively (Fig. 6). Furthermore, 79% of palms where offshoots had been removed had weevil infestation. The survey also showed that 6 and 10 years old palms were highly susceptible and that the date palm cultivar was of some importance. As a result, these factors should be taken into consideration in future RPW management programmes. Importantly, any control programme needs to be implemented over a wide area, since management on individual farms is less effective because weevils readily immigrate from neighbouring fields. ##### Fig. 6 #####

section: Future Research Areas to Improve RPW Management
text: 1. One future challenge is to provide farmers with low-cost devices for the accurate detection of RPW. Several laboratories around the world have researched different techniques to detect the larvae inside the palm, including chemical signatures detected by an ‘electronic nose’ combined with machine learning. Acoustic devices and thermal imaging using infrared cameras have also been tested (Pugliese *et al*., 2018). 2. A geographic information system (GIS) could be used to map the location of a large number of traps. However, trap maintenance and manual recording of weevil catches would still be a demanding task, although dry trapping (ElectrapTM) as well as other ‘attract and kill’ traps has addressed the problem to some extent. A prospect for the future would be dry traps that automatically record and transmit the number of weevils captured. This method would allow the estimation of population densities and changes in graphical distribution over time. The RPW data could be used to forecast the risk of spread into new areas, and also provide input for risk assessment models. In addition, real-time information on weevil catches and information on integrated pest management methods could be transferred to farmers via smartphone applications. 3. Date palm cultivars vary somewhat in susceptibility to RPW as described above, but the genetics of resistance is poorly understood. The genome of the date palm cultivar ‘Khalas’ has been sequenced and annotated, which in the future could facilitate genetic engineering of desirable traits such as resistance to insect pests. However, the lack of consumer acceptance at this point hampers the development of genetically modified date palm cultivars. 4. A so-called precision-guided sterile insect technique (pgSIT) was demonstrated in the model insect *Drosophila* (fruit fly).

section: Future Research Areas to Improve RPW Management
text: 4. A so-called precision-guided sterile insect technique (pgSIT) was demonstrated in the model insect *Drosophila* (fruit fly). In brief, genes were knocked out using a molecular technique (CRISPR) that resulted in the survival of only sterile males among F1 eggs (Kandul *et al*., 2019). Future utilization of pgSIT in RPW requires a method for mass rearing of RPW in the lab, efficient genetic modification of sex determination genes, followed by cost-effective and logistics distribution of the sterile males. The cumulative effect of the continued release of sterile males would likely reduce the overall RPW population. 5. Laboratory experiments have shown that genes in RPW can be silenced through an RNA interference (RNAi) technique. Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) targeting -amylase, vacuolar-type ATPase (V-ATPase), catalase, and ecdysone receptors were administered to RPW larvae through diet, topical application, or microinjection resulting in inhibition of growth and varying degree of mortality (Laudani *et al*., 2017). This method warrants further investigation for RPW control. 6. A wide range of natural enemies and parasites of RPW has been reported in the literature from several countries. Around 50 potential biological control agents have been described such as other insects, bacteria, fungi, viruses, yeasts, entomopathogenic nematodes (EPN), and birds (Dembilio *et al*., 2010; Mazza *et al*., 2014). Their effect on RPW and adaptability to Arabian environmental conditions needs to be examined. Subsequently, questions about mass production, distribution, shelf-life, delivery, and effect on off-target organisms must be addressed one by one.

title: Management of the Red Palm Weevil in Date Palm Plantations in Al-Ahsa Oasis
text: There are several gaps concerning nearly all components of the current management strategies for RPW in Saudi Arabia, which makes control unsustainable and prevents eradication of the pest. The components include shortcomings in early detection, limitation of pheromone trapping over large areas, overreliance on insecticide application, difficulties with the implementation of phytosanitary measures, and low farmer participation in proposed control programmes. Clear national and regional phytosanitary requirements and quarantine regulations along with trained staff to implement these regulations would help to reduce the spread of RPW into uninfected areas. The current overdependence on chemical insecticides for both preventive and curative treatments of RPW, emphasizes the need for the development of new control methods that are less harmful to the environment.

title: Citrus Huanglongbing (Greening) Disease
text: Huanglongbing disease (HLB) is one of the best-known yet also unrecognized diseases of a global crop. Accounts from the 1700s in India describe a serious condition on citrus that reduced fruit production and quality on a wide scale, later interpreted to be HLB. Visual or field diagnosis of HLB can be unreliable. The key symptoms of HLB (leaf loss, damaged fruit, death of branches and trees) are associated with other pests and diseases and abiotic factors, such as low soil fertility and adverse weather events. It was not until the 1970s that scientific advances and new laboratory methods allowed researchers to confirm that *Liberibacter* bacteria are the cause of HLB. Modern diagnostic methods for *Liberibacter*, based on molecular and genetic characteristics, are accurate and reliable yet require sophisticated equipment and skilled scientists. Progress in confirming HLB is, however, hampered by the availability of diagnostic services, while large-scale testing and routine monitoring of citrus orchards is only feasible using simpler approaches. Training in the accurate visual diagnosis of HLB is still an important part of surveillance, while new methods based on detecting distinctive volatile organic compounds produced by infected trees show promise. This includes the use of ‘sniffer’ dogs. The discovery of HLB in Brazil in 2004 and, particularly, in Florida in 2005 led to a huge boost in HLB research. Oranges are a key crop for Florida farmers and a key source of income for the state. State and federal funds were quickly made available to tackle the complex challenge of HLB to citrus production. HLB is now endemic to the USA and Brazil and while valuable progress has been made in understanding *Liberibacter*, the vector and their interaction with citrus host plants, there has yet to be a major breakthrough in effective control methods.

title: Citrus Huanglongbing (Greening) Disease
text: HLB is now endemic to the USA and Brazil and while valuable progress has been made in understanding *Liberibacter*, the vector and their interaction with citrus host plants, there has yet to be a major breakthrough in effective control methods. Despite the unrelenting challenge posed by HLB to citrus production worldwide, there are positive signs that the disease is, at the very least, being kept in check. The use of insecticides to control the vectors of HLB is effective in some instances. Better monitoring, improved regulation of healthy planting material and timely removal of infected trees have also contributed to keeping HLB at bay. HLB remains a major risk to citrus production worldwide and a worrying threat to growers in Europe, where the disease is still absent. The disease poses a constant threat to one of the world’s most important groups of fruits and emphasises the need for research to work closely with extension and advisory services and growers in making the best use of existing knowledge about how to mitigate losses. Support from governments, the citrus industry and international donors targeting low and middle income countries is essential.

title: Citrus Huanglongbing (Greening) Disease
text:
The disease was first reported with certainty, in 1919, in southern China. Reports soon followed from a broad region stretching from China to Pakistan, where the disease was described in 1927. In 1928, the disease was found in South Africa. The origin of HLB appears to go back much further, with accounts of widespread damage to citrus fruits caused by a ‘dieback’ in India in the 1700s. Until relatively recently, no one was certain about the cause of the symptoms we now know to be HLB. There was much speculation about the role of different microorganisms as well as soil conditions and climate. In 1956, a Chinese scientist, Professor Lin Kong-Hsiang, was the first person to transmit the disease by grafting, the first indication that an infectious agent was involved in the disease. Shortly after this work, studies in South Africa, India and the Philippines showed that the disease could be transmitted by insects. The elegant studies carried out by Lin remained unknown for many years. His dedication to understanding HLB and persistence and dedication in the face of professional challenges and personal hardships has only recently been appreciated (see Williams *et al*., 2020 for more details of Lin’s work). The disease spread throughout Asia, the Middle East and Africa (Table 2) up to the 1990s. Until then the disease was absent from the Americas. But the growing movement of people, goods and citrus material during the 20th century made it inevitable that HLB would eventually arrive in the Americas. The disease was discovered in Brazil in 2004 and the following year in Florida, USA. These new outbreaks were significant not only because of the subsequent major losses that occurred but because fresh impetus was given to research on all aspects of HLB. ##### Table 2. #####

title: Citrus Huanglongbing (Greening) Disease
text: HLB has travelled far and wide and has been confirmed from over 60 countries (Table 2). There are two important things to know when discussing the distribution of the disease. First, HLB is caused by two main species of closely related bacteria: *Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus* (CLas) and *Ca*. *Liberibacter africanus* (CLaf). CLaf is only found in Africa. CLas has spread much more widely, from Asia to the Americas, and even a few countries in Africa. Second, HLB is spread by two sap-sucking insects, known as psyllids. *Diaphorina citri* is the vector for CLas and *Trioza erytreae* is the vector for CLaf. HLB has not been recorded from Europe or from nearby citrus producers in North Africa, such as Morocco and Egypt (Table 1). Other countries have also avoided the disease, such as Nigeria and other countries of West Africa, Bolivia, Peru and Ecuador in South America, South Korea, Turkey, Egypt and Israel. Some are important producers of citrus, but even countries who are minor producers still have substantial numbers of farmers who grow oranges, lemons, tangerines, pomelos and other citrus fruits. The absence of HLB does not mean the absence of vectors (Table 3). Some of the countries noted in Table 3 are bordered by neighbours who have HLB, including Afghanistan (Pakistan and Iran) and Bolivia (Brazil and Argentina). There are many possible reasons why countries with the vectors are still free of HLB, ranging from effective phytosanitary controls to chance. It is also clear, however, that such countries need to be most vigilant in preventing HLB incursions and maintaining strong surveillance programmes. text:
CLas is more damaging than CLaf. However, citrus production in Africa is dominated by smallholders in many countries and information and estimations of losses are limited, compared to those from commercial producers. Smallholders will commonly have a few citrus trees on their land, often close to houses, and fruits are for domestic consumption. Sales in local markets are limited. The best data on losses due to CLaf are from South Africa, a major global producer of citrus fruits. Around four million citrus trees were estimated to have been infected with HLB in the mid-1970s. Annual losses of around ZAR 35 million in the 1980s were reported, equivalent then to approximately US$13.5 million. The most startling evidence of how CLas affects citrus production comes from Florida. Note the dramatic decline in citrus production (excluding tangerines, mandarins and tangelos) in Florida up to 2017, which has now steadied (Fig. 2). It appears that a combination of effective control, better coordination between farmers and the replacement of diseased trees with fresh, healthy stock has helped stabilise production. Figures vary on HLB cumulative economic losses to date from one to several billion dollars. Whichever way you look at, Florida is no longer the major producer of citrus fruits it once was and is unlikely to recover from the impact of HLB. ##### Fig. 2. #####
The decline in the importance of Florida as a citrus producer, following the discovery of HLB in 2005.

title: Citrus Huanglongbing (Greening) Disease
text: HLB is a bacterial disease. It took much longer than other bacterial pathogens to confirm because the HLB bacteria cannot be cultured outside the host. This also means that they cannot be inoculated into a healthy host under the controlled conditions required to confirm Koch’s postulates, the standard method for establishing that a microorganism is the cause of a disease. Advances in microscopy enabled scientists in the 1970s to visualise the bacteria within the host for the first time. New diagnostic tools based on molecular methods have expanded knowledge on the nature of the bacteria, and the conclusion that there were two main species responsible for HLB: *Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus* (CLas) and *Ca. Liberibacter africanus* (CLaf). Research on HLB and the characterization of *Liberibacter* helped scientists to confirm the role of these specialised bacteria in other plant diseases, such as zebra chip of potato, caused by *Ca*. *Liberibacter solanacearum*. Another HLB bacterium, *Ca*. *Liberibacter americanus*, was found in Brazil but this is of minor importance. Although the inability to culture the HLB bacteria has hindered research, molecular and genetic studies over the last 50 years have greatly expanded knowledge of the pathogens and suggested potential vulnerabilities that could be exploited in managing the disease. One of the most important discoveries is that temperature plays a vital part in the infection process. CLas is heat tolerant while CLaf is heat sensitive. Prolonged temperatures above 20–24°C suppress symptom expression by CLaf. The behaviour of the two bacterial species in response to different temperature regimes is matched by that of their corresponding vectors. *Diaphorina citri*, the African citrus psyllid (ACP), and the natural vector of CLas, is also heat tolerant.

title: Citrus Huanglongbing (Greening) Disease
text: *Diaphorina citri*, the African citrus psyllid (ACP), and the natural vector of CLas, is also heat tolerant. *Trioza erytreae*, the African citrus psyllid (AfCP), the natural vector of CLaf, is also heat sensitive. Both psyllids can transmit both bacterial species, though there is no evidence that this is of any practical relevance in the field. The temperature profiles of the bacteria and their vectors help to explain the current distribution of the two different forms of HLB. More importantly, information on tolerances and preferences allows scientists to model future spread and estimate the risks of new incursions (Narouei-Khandan *et al*., 2015). Australia is at major risk from HLB, for example, and has already recorded the ACP vector – which was eradicated 4 years later. Much effort has gone into defining risks and responses to HLB in Europe (EFSA *et al*., 2019; EFSA Panel on Plant Health, 2021b) and national and regional bodies, such as the European Plant Protection Organization, are on high alert.

title: Citrus Huanglongbing (Greening) Disease
text: Citrus is a perennial crop and both the insect vectors and the causal agent can be carried over from one growing season to the next. Once the disease has become established, consistent efforts by farmers are needed to keep the disease in check. Farmer efforts required careful coordination for maximum effect, hence the importance of what is known as area-wide management. Current control methods and management strategies are described by Alquézar *et al*. (2022). This review discusses advances in research as well practical experiences with both CLas and the Asian citrus psyllid and CLaf and the African citrus psyllid. The overall message is that avoidance and prevention is the only successful management strategy. Achieving this requires effective surveillance, rapid and decisive responses to incursions of the HLB bacteria, plus strict phytosanitary controls. All these actions are costly and only feasible where commercial interests and local and national governments are willing to fund staff, field operations and diagnostic services. Consider the discovery of HLB in California, where it was first detected in 2012, 7 years after its discovery in Florida. Ten years on, HLB is still restricted to citrus trees in domestic and suburban areas. Impressive human and financial resources in California are available to maintain ‘find and destroy’ programmes in citrus areas and to regulate vector populations (see the ‘California Citrus Threat’ website for more details). There are, however, persistent fears that the disease will eventually be detected in commercial groves and there has been a steady rise in the detection of infected trees in recent years. Many of the suggested control methods (Alquézar *et al*., 2022), particularly from most recent research studies, are still ‘in development’ and lack clear evidence that they work in the field, or that farmers are willing or able to use them. Biological control using parasitoids which attack the insect vectors of HLB showed early promise in helping to limit disease impact.

title: Citrus Huanglongbing (Greening) Disease
text:
Biological control using parasitoids which attack the insect vectors of HLB showed early promise in helping to limit disease impact. In one spectacular case, the release of *Tamarix radiata*, a parasitic wasp which attacks the Asian citrus psyllid, in Réunion in 1978, almost completely eradicated this vector and greatly reduced the impact of HLB. Sadly, this level of control no longer exists and HLB is causing major damage to citrus production (see Williams *et al*. (2020) for more details of this fascinating story). Further details of control methods and area-wide management efforts are covered in other publications, including Parnell *et al*. (2019), Bragard *et al*. (2021) and EPPO (2020a, b). They describe the use of different insecticides, the importance of producing disease-free planting material and the early detection of HLB infections. There are particular challenges in diagnosing and confirming the presence of the bacteria. They include the uneven distribution of bacteria within plants and over time, resulting in false negatives: the bacteria are present but sampling is unable to detect them. When bacteria are introduced into plants by the psyllids, trees do not show symptoms for at least 6 months. Yet these symptomless trees remain a source of new infections and vector insects can acquire and transmit the disease rapidly. Surveillance depends on the rapid detection of new infections. Those monitoring citrus groves are at several disadvantages: distinguishing HLB leaf (Fig. 3) symptoms from common mineral deficiencies (Fig. 4) is a skilled task while detecting the HLB bacteria relies on successful sampling and the availability of advanced diagnostic techniques and scientific expertise. ##### Fig. 3. #####

section: Future Research Areas to Improve HLB Management
text:
The search for resistance and improved ways to attack the HLB bacteria and its vectors continues. New breeding techniques such as rapid gene editing using CRISPR show promise, yet any likely success in the field is many years away. HLB is not, however, an intractable problem. A consistent combination of effective monitoring, regular surveillance, destruction of infected material and replacement with healthy plants may not always be easy to achieve but it has in some countries, such as Brazil, reduced the impact of HLB. Doing the ordinary things well is not a long-term solution to HLB but it offers hope to farmers and citrus production everywhere that things can get better (Fig. 5). ##### Fig. 5. #####

### Overview ###
Coffee is susceptible to a wide range of pests and diseases. The disease most dreaded amongst growers is coffee leaf rust caused by the fungus *Hemileia vastatrix*. title: 'Coffee Leaf Rust: Wreaking Havoc in Coffee Production Areas Across the Tropics'
text:
“Civilisation has produced only three important non-alcoholic beverages—the extract of the tea plant, the cocoa bean, and the coffee bean.” – William Ukers, 1921
The appropriately titled book *All about Coffee* (Ukers, 1922) proposed that the lure and universal appeal of coffee can be explained by a so-called twofold effect. First, the enjoyable, aromatic sensations of drinking coffee and second, the increased efficiency which provides its recipient via caffeine stimulation. It is no wonder that coffee is virtually ubiquitous in kitchens, cafes and in the hands of pedestrians on just about every street corner. Ethiopia may be the widely accepted origin of the oldest known species of coffee, *Coffea arabica*, but Yemen is thought to be the birthplace of consuming coffee in the beverage form we know today (Friis, 2015). Early observations from Ethiopia described the invigorating effects of chewing roasted coffee beans as “better than a loaf of bread or a meal of meat” (Friis, 2015). In Yemen, coffee as a hot drink went by at least three Arabic names: “bunna”, “gahve” and “geschr” and was said to be drunk by people at any time of day (Friis, 2015). Nowadays, most coffee drinkers could not imagine going a day without their cup of “liquid gold”. This means that coffee is a big business; annual global earnings exceed US$200 billion. Consequently, any pest and disease which impact coffee yield are of keen interest to the farmer and the scientific community at large. ##### Fig. 1. #####

Coffee leaf rust (CLR) is one of the most significant diseases to strike coffee production. Due to its widespread prevalence across all global coffee-growing regions and the calamity it brings in terms of yield reduction, CLR is by far the most studied coffee disease. CLR damages coffee plants by causing heavy leaf defoliation, leading to dramatic yield losses (up to 75%) and in some cases plant death (Fig. 1). Countries plagued by CLR suffer financial losses at the national level, which have trickle-down effects on poor farmers and, in extreme circumstances, has led to the mass abandonment of coffee farms. In fact, estimates suggest that the most recent epidemic of CLR cost up to US$1 billion in losses and cut 250,000 jobs, mainly on farms. CLR was first officially discovered on uncultivated, wild coffee off the shores of Lake Victoria (Kenya) in 1861 by a British explorer (Koutouleas *et al*., 2019). Yet it was not until 1869 that the disease reached the public eye after it reaped havoc across several colonial coffee plantations in Sri Lanka (then called Ceylon).

title: 'Coffee Leaf Rust: Wreaking Havoc in Coffee Production Areas Across the Tropics'
text: Yet it was not until 1869 that the disease reached the public eye after it reaped havoc across several colonial coffee plantations in Sri Lanka (then called Ceylon). The British colonialists were so taken aback by CLR in their fields that they resorted to tearing out the coffee plants and replacing them with tea bushes instead. Through this case study, the longstanding history of CLR will be considered and linked to key colonial trade activities (Fig. 2). The relevance of the disease will be highlighted briefly in terms of modern coffee farming practices using testimonies and data from Central American and East African coffee farms. Future prospects of coffee farming in new ways to combat disease pressure by *H. vastatrix* will also be explored.

text:
*Hemileia vastatrix* Berk. & Broome is an obligate parasitic fungus in family Pucciniaceae (Koutouleas *et al*., 2019). This means that the fungus cannot survive in the absence of its plant host. Optimal environmental conditions for the development of *H. vastatrix* are 21–25°C air temperature with 100% relative humidity. CLR infection peaks, therefore, tend to occur immediately after the peak of the rainy season across tropical and sub-tropical regions. Under optimal environmental conditions, a fungal germ tube of *H. vastatrix* penetrates via stomatal openings on the underside of the coffee leaf. Upon entry, *H. vastatrix* grows nutrient-absorbing mycelium within the leaf mesophyll cells using haustoria to invaginate the mesophyll cells to obtain nutrients. Vibrant bouquet-shaped, orange uredinia and telia sporulate from the stomata (Figs 3 and 4). ##### Fig. 3. #####
Uredinium of *H. vastatrix* budding orange rust-coloured urediniopores (bar = 20 μm). Courtesy of Carvalho *et al*. (2011), CC BY 2.5 via Wikimedia Commons. <https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hemileia_vastatrix_Uredinium_02.png>

Uredinia give rise to urediniospores, dikaryotic cells (containing two unfused nuclei), which can survive up to six weeks on detached coffee leaf tissue. Under cool, dry conditions, the telia give rise to two more spore types: teliospores and subsequently basidiospores. Teliospores are two-celled, thick-walled and produce basidia; which then develop four haploid basidiospores – the sexual spores of *H. vastatrix*. By producing both asexual and sexual spore types, rust fungi such as *H. vastatrix* increase their chances of transmission via multiple hosts and across the seasons. For this reason, many rusts are observed to have complex disease cycles with different spore types or reproductive structures (Koutouleas *et al*., 2019). The covert and complex nature of the fungal attack lies in the fact that urediniospores adhere to and enter via the underside of the leaf (where stomata are most numerous). This means that the early onset of the disease can go largely undetected to the naked eye. When traversing a coffee field infected by CLR, yellow pin spots on the upper leaf surface can be seen as a sign of disease. However, by the time this visual indicator catches the attention of a coffee worker, the fungus has already established its nutrient supply from the leaf tissues via penetration of the epidermal cells through the stomata.

title: 'Coffee Leaf Rust: Wreaking Havoc in Coffee Production Areas Across the Tropics'
text: During the 15th century, coffee plants were transported from their centre of origin in Africa, across the Red Sea to southern Arabia (Yemen) and meticulously cultivated along sloped terraces. Until the end of the 17th century, the world’s limited supply of coffee was almost exclusively distributed by Yemeni merchants and traders (Friis, 2015). Ethnobotanists mark this time as the great Yemen coffee monopoly era, given that there was a careful watch on the export of any green coffee beans by Arabians (Ukers, 1922). In fact, any precious coffee beans leaving Yemen at the time were ordered to be steeped in boiling water or parched, in order to destroy any possibility of foreign germination of the cash crop. Yemen’s coffee supply monopoly came to its end by the early 17th century, at which point the Dutch drove the Portuguese out of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) and began coffee cultivation. The British then entered the coffee scene through their occupation of this tropical island in 1796. However, they only began formally cultivating coffee in 1825. In the 50 years thereafter, coffee was one of the island’s leading export products. *H. vastatrix* first appeared in coffee fields in 1869*. * At first, the disease was dubbed by coffee planters and field workers as “Devastating Emily” due to the destruction it brought to the coffee fields. Little did they know that this plant disease would single-handedly ruin the coffee industry in Ceylon. For more than three centuries coffee was cultivated by both the Arabian and Dutch colonialists without any reports of CLR. The onset of extensive cultivation methods (introduced by the British) provided the perfect substrate for the fungal pathogen *H. vastatrix* to manifest a serious epidemic, destroying coffee productivity and profitability. Enter the British tea industry.

title: 'Coffee Leaf Rust: Wreaking Havoc in Coffee Production Areas Across the Tropics'
text: The onset of extensive cultivation methods (introduced by the British) provided the perfect substrate for the fungal pathogen *H. vastatrix* to manifest a serious epidemic, destroying coffee productivity and profitability. Enter the British tea industry. At the time of the first major CLR outbreak, exporters and researchers, under secondment by the British government to Ceylon, were trying to figure out what was causing the coffee yield losses and plant death. Coffee planters and field staff surmised the onset of “Devastating Emily” was due to poor plant growth and humid environments. Cultural practices with the aim of bolstering plant vigour and growth were used as a result of these evaluations. When these efforts failed, a simple experiment by a tea planter James Taylor to helped re-write the history books of early coffee production. Taylor demonstrated that tea plants were completely “resistant” to the foliar disease and henceforth, the majority of coffee plants were ripped out of the ground and replaced with tea plants. These days, it is widely known that *H. vastatrix* only infects coffee (as its primary plant host) and no alternate plant host has been discovered – yet. Given this, Taylor’s findings were somewhat simplistic, as just about any plant (other than coffee) would have been deemed “resistant” to CLR at that time. It is often said that this piece of history explains why the British drinks more tea than coffee, even today. Although this is considered to be more of a fable than a fact, since any drop in coffee supply could have easily been recouped from other British colonial territories growing coffee during the same period (i.e. Jamaica, Tanzania, northeastern Australia, etc.). Scholars are still uncertain why “Devastating Emily” became so severe in Ceylon during the first major outbreak.

One explanation could be that other outbreaks may have occurred but either went undetected or unreported by local plantation managers at the time. In fact, British colonial activities represent some of the most detailed records that we have today concerning trade and agriculture in the period of the first outbreak. Another explanation could be a change in wind patterns which helped to spread fungal spores across long distances. However, this explanation does not explain why CLR outbreaks were not detected across other Asian coffee-producing countries at the time. Intensive monoculture farming of the coffee crop in the Ceylon region no doubt led to a concentration in coffee plant substrate for *H. vastatrix*, further increasing the likelihood of such a significant outbreak (compared to coffee gardens and small-scale production employed in other regions). The increase in transportation routes of people and goods during the late 19th century is another likely entry mechanism for the primary inoculum of rust spores into coffee plantations.

title: 'Coffee Leaf Rust: Wreaking Havoc in Coffee Production Areas Across the Tropics'
text: After the debut of CLR in Ceylon, the fungus made its way across Asian and Oceania coffee-producing countries such as Australia, Fiji, India, Indonesia, Mauritius, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines and Vietnam. The coffee disease was then reported to have made a return to the mother continent of Africa with widespread outbreaks first in the East (e.g. Uganda, Kenya and Mozambique) and then in the West (e.g. Ivory Coast). Latin American coffee production was free from CLR until the 1970s when the first report was made in Brazil. The disease was coined the “big rust” after the significant outbreak period starting in 2008 in Colombia (McCook and Vandermeer, 2015). The epidemic spread north to Central America and Mexico by 2012–2013 and since 2014 has begun impacting coffee farms in Ecuador and Peru. In 2020, *H. vastatrix* reached Hawaii, the only country growing coffee that avoided CLR for more than a century. Today, CLR plagues all coffee-producing countries, albeit to varying degrees depending on climatic conditions, on-farm resources, de-forestation activities (in which trees acted as buffer zones between farms) and general coffee plant health. A group of smallholder coffee farmers in Nicaragua has recently declared that CLR continues to cause heavy disease pressure in the major coffee-growing region of Matagalpa. Irregular rainfall patterns coupled with unusually high average air temperatures could be leading to more sporadic and localized outbreaks, which are being largely controlled through chemical fungicide application (when accessible to the farmer). Recent studies from Ethiopia, the motherland of coffee, have shown that the fungal disease is increasing in severity over time across major coffee-growing areas of the Southern districts. A surge in CLR has been reported across Ethiopia, with an average incidence rate of 35.3%. Moreover, the disease has shown to be spread upward from lowland to mid and highland coffee-growing areas.

These are just a few developing countries that rely on coffee as a key export commodity and are therefore at the mercy of this devastating pathogen.

section: Current Best Management Practices for *Hemileia vastatrix*
text:
Carbohydrate production by photosynthesis in leaves ensures the maintenance, growth and reproduction of the coffee plant. When *H. vastatrix* sporulates heavily, coffee leaves are damaged by both the intracellular growth and the nutrient leaching of the fungus. In order to protect coffee leaves from CLR, some form of disease control should be considered. This is especially relevant during the fruit development phase which demands the presence of healthy plant foliage for carbohydrate supply (De Filho and Domian, 2019). Both chemical and cultural practices are recommended for the control and containment of CLR (De Filho and Domian, 2019). These include:
* Protective and systemic fungicides
* Coffee plant and shade tree pruning
* Use of resistant cultivars
* Renovation of old coffee farms with new plants
* Biological control agents
The use of multiple lines of defence against plant pests or pathogens is called an Integrated Pest-Disease Management system (IPDM) and coffee farmers benefit from employing such an approach when faced with CLR. Today, the primary mode of control recommended is a mixture of fungicides (triazoles and strobilurin) to control and prevent the disease (Table 1). Resistant and/more tolerant coffee varieties and hybrids have been identified and selectively bred, based on nine known resistance genes (called SH genes). Resistance genes SH1, SH2, SH4 and SH5 were discovered in the *C. arabica* species; SH6, SH7, SH8 and SH9 come from the *C. canephora* species and the SH3 gene originates from the less cultivated *C. liberica* species (De Filho and Domian, 2019). Combined use of resistant coffee varieties or hybrids, with these SH genes, along with fungicide application can provide even better protection from severe CLR outbreaks.

text: By pruning both the coffee plant and the shade trees which surround them, the coffee field benefits from better air circulation, lowering the inter-canopy relative humidity levels, which can hinder the sporulation of *H. vastatrix* urediniospores. The mere act of pruning also removes the possible build-up of primary spore inoculum on the coffee plant itself. Selection of locally adapted and/or improved varieties, cultivars, or coffee hybrids which exhibit known resistance to CLR is considered as frontline protection from the pathogen. Locally adapted coffee types can exhibit better plant vigour, which, in turn, bolsters their overall defence when encountered with a disease such as CLR. Complete farm renovation or rehabilitation of old coffee plants with these vigorous and/or resistant varieties is a decision that coffee farmers can make only a few times in the long production cycles of the coffee crop. Therefore, the choice of the coffee variety grown is a critical decision to make and requires a cost-benefit analysis weighing up the suitability of the variety to the local environment, yield potential, niche market value of the beans, and pest and disease resistance. Coffee plants that have high production of fruits tend to be more severely attacked in the subsequent year by CLR. This has been attributed to the transport of protective phenolic compounds from the leaves to the beans, leaving the evergreen leaves vulnerable to pathogen attack (De Filho and Domian, 2019). Given these findings, a holistic approach to developing an IPDM against CLR involves the fine balance of the coffee plant yielding capacity with the age of the plant (i.e. older plants will be less vigorous and therefore more prone to attack) along with the planting density in the field (i.e. high-density planting will lead to higher in-field relative humidity thereby promoting disease outbreaks).

### Can natural enemies control *H. vastatrix? * ###
Habitat complexity in farming coffee can lead to enhanced ecological pest-disease control and overall better plant health (compared to monoculture farming). By farming coffee together with different plant and tree species, a higher number of predators and natural enemies may be present in the coffee field. Control of certain pests or pathogens can also be achieved through the timely introduction of microorganisms or insects which act as BCAs in the coffee field (Koutouleas *et al*., 2022). BCAs may act through various mechanisms to control a pest or disease. These mechanisms include competition, antibiosis, hyperparasitism, or induced resistance. Table 2 highlights some of the BCAs which are known to target *H. vastatrix*. These organisms range from other fungi, bacteria and insects which can have an inhibitory effect on the growth, survival and/ or reproduction of *H. vastatrix. * However, there are challenges associated with disease control with BCAs such as off-target effects on other organisms in the coffee field or a lack of efficacy due to the presence of other enemies which may feed on or compete with the BCA (Fig. 5). ##### Fig. 5. #####
The hyperparasite *Lecanicilium lecanii* (white spores) attacking *H. vastatrix* (orange spores) on a coffee leaf. Courtesy of Dr Melanie Bordeaux, director of NICAFRANCE Foundation’s research centre, Nicaragua. ### An alternate host or secret sex life? ###
*H. vastatrix* is considered a macrocyclic rust, which means it produces different spore types. Thus far, the role of the sexual basidiospores in the fungal life cycle remains unknown.

text:
###
*H. vastatrix* is considered a macrocyclic rust, which means it produces different spore types. Thus far, the role of the sexual basidiospores in the fungal life cycle remains unknown. Basidiospores are very small (around 5 microns). The baffling thing is, no one knows the target host these spores are intended for. It is hypothesised that *H. vastatrix* uses basidiospores to alternate from its primary host (the coffee plant) to an alternate plant host (unknown) (Fig. 6). This lifestyle pattern allows the fungus to “overwinter” and complete its sexual cycle on an alternate plant host when the season changes. However, in tropical coffee-growing regions, there is no real winter season, and since the first outbreak of coffee leaf rust in 1869, no alternate host has ever been detected in or around coffee plantations. With no known host to complete its sexual cycle, it is a mystery how the fungus can possibly create new, more virulent versions of itself, which are today plaguing our coffee production and therefore causing huge economic losses. A similar situation is known for stripe (yellow) rust of cereal crops and grasses (caused by *Puccinia striiformis). * The rust fungus was discovered in the mid-18th century, yet the alternate host plant (*Berberis* spp.) was not detected until 2010. Some researchers postulate the basidiospores of *H. vastatrix* are remnants of an earlier rust ancestor and no longer utilised by the fungus. Others argue that the preservation of the basidiospores in the observed disease cycle is enough evidence for the possibility of a viable, alternate host.

Others argue that the preservation of the basidiospores in the observed disease cycle is enough evidence for the possibility of a viable, alternate host. Recent scholars have uncovered a so-called “crypto-sexuality”, in which *H. vastatrix* can asexually produce new versions of itself without the need for an alternate host (Carvalho *et al*., 2011). Despite apparently not completing its sexual cycle, the fungus is capable of producing new virulent variants. These new “races” hinder plant-breeding efforts. In addition, the fungus can develop resistance to fungicides. ##### Fig. 6. #####
Disease cycle of *Hemileia vastatrix*. The asexual cycle has been well documented, while the sexual cycle has been hypothesised to take place on an unknown alternate plant host. Courtesy of Koutouleas and Collinge (2022). ### Future coffee farming under agroforestry systems ###
Simply put, agroforestry means “farming with trees”. However, this farming system is far from simple and the ecological interactions which lie within are largely unknown both from an agronomical and ecological point of view. A coffee agroforestry system is a farming approach that incorporates the growth of the coffee crop along with other shade trees and/or shrub species. The shade tree species are often fast-growing timber, fuel and/or fruit trees which can provide an alternate means of income for coffee farmers. Since *C. arabica* has its evolutionary origins in the Afromontane forest understorey, many coffee scientists share the opinion that the plant is shade-loving (or shade-tolerant to say the least). With global reforestation being a top priority, the use of agroforestry systems in coffee production has recently gained increased traction.

text:
With global reforestation being a top priority, the use of agroforestry systems in coffee production has recently gained increased traction. Some would argue that traditional African farmers intuitively practiced different forms of agroforestry together with small-scale coffee production. However, since the expansion of coffee production across sub-tropical growing regions (e.g. Vietnam, Bolivia, etc. ), coffee agroforestry systems have decreased in popularity. Monoculture coffee farming in open fields with full sun exposure has been shown to increase short-term yields and easily scale-up production (compatible with modern agricultural technologies). But how does infection by “Devastating Emily” compare between a monoculture versus agroforestry coffee production system? Researchers have been elucidating the interactions between shade and CLR. Figure 7 illustrates the key dynamics that have been identified to play a role in disease development in shaded coffee. Under the shade, coffee tends to produce a lower fruit load which in turn reduces the likelihood of rust infection. However, dense shade trees promote a higher overall relative humidity which allows for more leaf moisture and the potential for optimal water conditions for the sporulation of *H. vastatrix* urediniospores. The habitats under the shaded coffee system can also play a role in the disease development of CLR. More diverse plant species can support the presence of natural enemies of *H. vastatrix* such as the hyperparasitic fungus *Lecanicillium lecanii. * Given these dynamics, it is easy to see how the use of shade is a contentious issue for coffee farming. ##### Fig. 7. #####

### Coffee leaf rust and climate change ###
Interactions between *H. vastatrix* and weather patterns have been linked to different stages of the disease cycle. However, predictions concerning future climate changes and disease pressure are difficult to unravel. Like most fungal pathogens, the disease cycle of *H. vastatrix* is tightly regulated to the atmospheric temperature and humidity. Provided that the coffee plant leaf is moist for 6–24 hours and air temperatures are maintained between the optimal of 21 and 25°C, then *H. vastatrix* can germinate in most coffee-growing environments. If future coffee-growing climates are warmer and drier then CLR prevalence may be reduced. On the other hand, if excessive rainfall occurs in the dry seasons then there could be more opportunity for additional CLR outbreaks to occur. Nevertheless, recent modelling efforts in coffee-growing areas of Brazil have failed to predict connections between CLR outbreaks and climate forecasting.

text: There are many plant diseases that can impact our daily lives; CLR impacts the reliability of our future coffee supply. To some, this is a serious threat to a daily habit, natural stimulant and source of culinary pleasure. To smallholder coffee farmers, this disease poses a danger to farm productivity and in turn the livelihoods of those who depend on coffee beans as a main source of household income. By understanding the causal fungal pathogen and the best methods to prevent and control CLR, we can ensure the health of coffee plants across the tropics which supply the nearly 10 billion kg of beans needed annually for our cups of “liquid gold”.

Alfalfa weevil, *Hypera postica* Gyllenhal, is an invasive insect pest of alfalfa in North America causing economic damage throughout the continent. title: 'Alfalfa Weevil: A Challenging Insect Pest of Forage Alfalfa in the Western
text: The genus *Hypera* contains a minimum of 280 described species of weevil, many of which are agricultural pests. One species, the alfalfa weevil, *Hypera postica* Gyllenhal (Coleoptera: Curculionidae), is one of the most economically damaging agricultural pests of alfalfa in North America. Alfalfa weevil is native to Eurasia and North Africa and has become an invasive insect pest in North America as well as Japan and South Korea where it infests forage and seed alfalfa production systems (Sanaei *et al*., 2019). The alfalfa weevil was first discovered in the United States in 1904 in Salt Lake City, Utah, then in 1939 in Yuma, Arizona, and finally, in 1952 in Maryland. Each of these discoveries represents a new strain in the United States, the western (Utah), Egyptian (Arizona), and eastern (Maryland) (Pellissier *et al*., 2017). Since then, the alfalfa weevil has become one of the primary economically damaging insect pests of alfalfa in the United States and has become resistant to the primary mechanism of managing their populations, pyrethroid insecticides.

title: 'Alfalfa Weevil: A Challenging Insect Pest of Forage Alfalfa in the Western
text: Half a century after the alfalfa weevil was discovered in the United States, the first reports of alfalfa weevil in Canada were recorded in south-eastern Alberta and south-western Saskatchewan in 1954. Additional reports of alfalfa weevils in parts of Canada occurred between 1950 and 1960 in southern Ontario and south-western Québec. It is thought that these insects moved into Canada from the eastern United States. Today, alfalfa weevils are found across the United States and parts of Canada and Mexico (Soroka *et al*., 2020).

section: Economic Impact in the United States and Canada
text:
Alfalfa weevil larvae feed on alfalfa terminals, foliage, and crown shoots. When infestation and feeding damage is high, larvae skeletonize the leaves resulting in dry leaves that are grey or white in color (Fig. 1). In extreme cases, larval feeding damage can result in decreased growth and maturity of the alfalfa stand (Pellissier *et al*., 2017). Yield loss is no exception, as the alfalfa weevil reduces yield on average by 10–15% annually. Furthermore, alfalfa weevil larvae feed predominantly on alfalfa leaves, where most of the plant’s protein can be found. This negatively impacts forage protein content, which reduces forage quality. Thus, both forage yield and quality are negatively associated with larval feeding (Hintz *et al*., 1976). ##### Fig. 1. #####

text: Alfalfa weevil eggs are yellow in color and oval, approximately 0.5 mm in length. The egg color alters as it develops, as the dark head capsule of the developing larvae is notable through the casing, especially in the later stages of this life stage. Alfalfa weevil larvae are light green in color with a dorsal white strip along the length of their abdomen and have a black head capsule that increases in width as they develop. Pupating alfalfa weevils are encased in small white silken cocoons for the duration of this life stage. Adults are brown in color with a dark brown stripe along the middle of their oval abdomen and are approximately 1.6–3 cm in length. Like all members of the Curculionidae family, alfalfa weevil adults possess a very noticeable rostrum or snout protruding from their head containing their chewing mouthparts. The seasonal phenology of the alfalfa weevil life cycle is dependent on the climate conditions that vary across North America. However, all alfalfa weevils have one generation per year (Fig. 2). In general, female alfalfa weevils oviposit clusters of 5–20 eggs (800–2000 eggs total) within alfalfa stems, generally 15 cm (6-inches) above the soil surface. Generally, the egg stage of the alfalfa weevil lasts approximately 7–21 days after oviposition, depending on temperature (Pellissier *et al*., 2017). Larvae develop through four instar stages before entering pupation (Fig.3.). Larval development lasts from 2 to 4 weeks, during which the early instars feed within the stem of the plant and the terminal buds, and the larger 3rd and 4th instars feed openly on leaves, causing the majority of the economic damage.

title: 'Alfalfa Weevil: A Challenging Insect Pest of Forage Alfalfa in the Western
text:
Pinholes in the developing leaves are an indication of early instar feeding within the buds. During pupation, mature 4th instar larvae encapsulate themselves in cocoons on the foliage or near the soil surface (Fig. 2). After 1–2 weeks the next generation of adult alfalfa weevils emerge and feed prior to a summer estivation period where they shelter in the leaf litter of the alfalfa fields or within the edge habitat of the field, to avoid desiccation due to high summer temperatures and alfalfa harvests, and then disperse to overwintering sites (Prokopy and Gyrisco, 1965). After their dormancy, the adults will reemerge and return to alfalfa fields in the fall, however, depending on location (e.g., Arizona versus Montana) adults may overwinter and return to the fields in the spring (Pellissier *et al*., 2017). ##### Fig. 2. #####

Third and fourth instar larvae are much larger and openly feed on open alfalfa leaves and can easily be seen while scouting.

text: The best way to make informed decisions about when to apply control tactics is through monitoring or scouting alfalfa fields for adult emergence in the early season and a few weeks later for larval emergence. One method to determine when scouting should occur is based on degree day (DD) models. In general, scouting should begin once the accumulated DDs reach between 350 and 400, with a base of 48°F (180–204 DD with a base of 8.89°C), coinciding with pique 1st and 2nd instar larval stages, generally occurring prior to economic thresholds are reached (MSU, 2023). There are three main scouting methods for alfalfa weevil. The first scouting method is sweep-net sampling using a 38-cm diameter sweep net swung in a 180° arc, with one swing per step. 10–20 sweeps are taken at 3–5 locations within the field to calculate an average number of larvae per sweep. Using this method, the economic threshold is 20 larvae per sweep (Pellissier *et al*., 2017). The second, the shake-bucket method, where stems are randomly and gently collected from various locations within the field, placed into a bucket, and then shaken vigorously to dislodge the larvae from the plant. The number of larvae in the bucket is counted, and the number per stem calculated (e.g., divide the number of larvae by the number of stems collected). Using the shake bucket method, the economic threshold is 1.5–3 larvae per stem. This average value represents the number of alfalfa weevil larvae per stem, representing the alfalfa weevil density for that field site. The third method is looking at alfalfa weevil damage on the plant terminals.

text: This average value represents the number of alfalfa weevil larvae per stem, representing the alfalfa weevil density for that field site. The third method is looking at alfalfa weevil damage on the plant terminals. Randomly selected terminals, 50 in total, are evaluated for pinholes and defoliation, close monitoring efforts are recommended if 30–50% of terminals exhibit damage (Blodgett, 1996). However, each method has limitations and specific thresholds are being updated for different production systems (local sources should be consulted). Sweep netting is the most efficient method but is biased toward sampling larger 3rd and 4th instar larvae, compared to the shake-bucket method that dislodges more of the 1st and 2nd instars.

text: The general economic threshold for the alfalfa weevil is 1.5–3 weevils per stem or 20 larvae per sweep. However, economic thresholds are meant to be updated and adjusted depending on the overall cost of treatment and the value of the product (seed or hay). Thus, the true economic threshold for an individual production system may be greater than or lower than the described values. For example, Harrington *et al*. (2021) updated the economic threshold for alfalfa weevil in irrigated alfalfa systems in the low desert of Arizona. They adjusted the threshold to 1–3 third and fourth instar larvae per sweep compared to the 20 larvae per sweep standard. Highlighting the importance of evaluating the economic threshold for each system, and making management decisions based on that specific value. Note that this value should be updated every time a value within the equation changes (e.g., fuel or hay value). The first step is to identify the cost of management per acre.

text: Alfalfa weevil can be managed through biological, cultural, chemical, and mechanical control tactics. Biological control tactics can be a serious source of mortality, with the alfalfa weevil larval life stage being the most vulnerable to disease, parasitism, and predation. However, when alfalfa weevils were first established in North America, there was a lack of native obligate parasitoid species, allowing for unfettered population growth. Key predators of larvae are lady beetles (Coleoptera: Coccinellidae), damsel bugs (Hemiptera: Nabidae), and Lacewings (Neuroptera: Chrysopidae) (Table 1; Fig. 4; Pellissier *et al*., 2017). However, one of the most successful sources of biological control of alfalfa weevil is eight *Ichneumonidae* parasitoid wasps, which were released by the United States Department of Agriculture – Agricultural Research Service (USDA-ARS) and Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) at the end of the 20th century (Pellissier *et al*., 2017). The most successful of these are of the *Bathyplectes* genus (Hymenoptera: Ichneumonidae) like *Bathyplectes curculionis* (Thomson), *B. anurus* (Thomson), and *B. stenostigma* (Thomson). Although parasitism rates are generally lower in the western United States than in other parts of the country, parasitism rates in MT and ND ranged from 4.1 to 85.1% by *Bathyplectes curculionis*, with parasitism greatly influence by irrigation status and location (Rand, 2013). ##### Table 1.
