##### Fig. 4. #####
Common natural enemies of alfalfa weevils. In general, natural enemy predation on alfalfa weevil is most effective during the first and second larval instars. (A) features a collection of adult lady beetles (Coleoptera: Coccinellidae), (B) features an adult assassin bug (Hemiptera: Reduviidae), (C) features an adult green lacewing (Neuroptera: Chrysopidae), (D) features an adult brown lacewing (Neuroptera: Hemerobiidae). The larval stages for all of these insects are also highly predacious, and (E) features an Ichneumonidae parasitoid wasp with (F) representing a parasitized alfalfa weevil larvae often referred to as a mummy. Chemical control is commonly used by alfalfa producers for alfalfa weevil management. The most common active ingredient used are pyrethroids (Mode of Action Group (MoA) 3A) and an oxadiazine insecticide (i.e., Indoxacarb, MoA 22A) (Rodbell *et al*., 2022). Insecticides should only be applied when the alfalfa weevil densities reach the economic threshold. Pyrethroids and indoxacarb negatively impact beneficial insects, therefore, adjusting the timing of the insecticide application to reduce non-target insect exposure is important (e.g., do not apply if there is floral bloom). Spinosad, a biopesticide, is the only organic chemical control tactic available for alfalfa weevil, however, it only suppresses alfalfa weevil populations (Vardiman *et al*., 2022; ARBICO Organics, 2023).

title: 'Alfalfa Weevil: A Challenging Insect Pest of Forage Alfalfa in the Western
text: Cultural control and its efficacy can differ by geography and production system. Grazing of livestock (sheep or cattle) on alfalfa fields can effectively remove eggs, but the timing of grazing needs to correspond with insect phenology. In warmer climates with fall egg laying winter grazing can be effective, while in northerly climates grazing must occur after egg oviposition in the spring. Early harvest, 7–10 days before normal harvest can salvage yield when economic levels of alfalfa weevil are present. This tactic is effective in areas where the larval population peaks at harvest time, typically first harvest in northerly latitudes. Early harvest can result in significant larval mortality, particularly during hot dry weather that desiccates the larvae (Prasad, 1993; Pellissier *et al*., 2017). However, larvae can survive and continue to feed under the windrow, especially when the hay takes longer to dry (raking the windrows can speed drying and increase larval mortality), stunting the growth of the next stand. Additional cultural control tactics have been suggested but their effectiveness needs further research, including intercropping, flaming during alfalfa dormancy, and rolling with weighted rollers (Pellissier *et al*., 2017). Using weighted rollers is an additional source of alfalfa weevil mortality in the fall (more southern latitudes) or early spring (more northern latitudes) by squashing eggs within the stems.

title: 'Alfalfa Weevil: A Challenging Insect Pest of Forage Alfalfa in the Western
text: During the 1950s and 1960s the insecticides used to control alfalfa weevil in the United States were primarily organochlorines (MoA 3B), heptachlor, and dieldrin (Bishop, 1964). In 1962, however, reports of resistance to either heptachlor or dieldrin occurred in Virginia and Utah and indicated poor control of adults and larvae, with repeated applications of heptachlor failing to kill resistant adults in laboratory bioassays (Bishop, 1964). Cross-resistance to dieldrin was noted for populations never exposed to the insecticide, indicating cross-resistance to multiple active ingredients of the same MoA (Bishop, 1964). Today, the main source of alfalfa weevil control is pyrethroid (MoA 3A) insecticides, however, reports of insecticide failures from concerned producers indicate an emerging issue in the United States and Canada (Glen, 2015; Orloff *et al*., 2016). Thirteen active ingredients are registered for the control of alfalfa weevil in forage alfalfa systems in the United States (Vardiman *et al*., 2022). These active ingredients vary in their efficacy (e.g., suppression), with only two highly efficacious MoA registered for alfalfa weevil in forage alfalfa systems (i.e., Pyrethroids (MoA 3A) and Indoxacarb (MoA 22A)). Pyrethroids are classified as type I and type II, based on the presence of a cyano-group (type II) or absence (type I). In general, type II pyrethroids are more toxic than type I pyrethroids because of this structural distinction, as type II pyrethroids modify the sodium ion channel for a longer period (Davies *et al*., 2007).

title: 'Alfalfa Weevil: A Challenging Insect Pest of Forage Alfalfa in the Western
text:
Currently, there is 1 type I and 6 type II pyrethroid active ingredients registered for forage alfalfa in the United States (Vardiman *et al*., 2022). However, the efficacy of pyrethroids in North America is in question. The first reports of control failure in the field began in 2015, in Alberta, Canada, and California (Glen, 2015; Orloff *et al*., 2016). In 2021, reports of control failure in Montana were confirmed as resistance was identified using laboratory bioassays and field trials (Rodbell and Wanner, 2021). This research was expanded to several western US states and lambda-cyhalothrin (i.e., active ingredient of Warrior®) resistance has now been confirmed in Arizona, California, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming (Rodbell *et al*., 2022) (Fig. 5). Additionally, data from Rodbell *et al*. (2022) suggests multiple resistance between lambda-cyhalothrin and zeta-cypermethrin (both type II pyrethroids), highlighting the risk of multiple resistances to other type II pyrethroids. Field trials in Big Horn County, Montana corroborate this pattern of resistance (Wanner *et al*., 2022a). These studies indicate resistance to pyrethroids is well established across the western region of the United States. However, susceptible populations remain, highlighting the importance of conserving them in the landscape (Wanner *et al*., 2022b). ##### Fig. 5. #####

section: Integrated Resistance Management for Pyrethroid Resistant Alfalfa Weevil
text: Data indicates the loss in efficacy of all type II pyrethroids, like Baythroid® (a.i. Beta-cyfluthrin), Grizzly Too® (a.i. lambda-cyhalothrin), and Mustang-Maxx® (a.i. zeta-cypermethrin). The continued reliance on type II pyrethroids will reinforce resistance to these insecticides. Outbreak levels of alfalfa weevil larvae in resistant fields are challenging and expensive to control, threatening forage production and its economic feasibility (Wanner *et al*., 2022b). Thus, IRM recommendations are urgently needed to mitigate production losses in these systems. What alternative MoA groups are available for the control of alfalfa weevil larvae? Indoxacarb (MoA 22A, active ingredient of Steward EC®) is generally efficacious against pyrethroid-resistant populations. One concern is that indoxacarb will be used routinely in place of pyrethroids, raising the risk of resistance developing to this MoA. Three recommendations that can help limit the impact of pyrethroid-resistant alfalfa weevil on forage alfalfa production systems. First, watch for slipping field efficacy of pyrethroid insecticide products and conduct in-field small plot treatments to compare the effectiveness (Wanner *et al*., 2022b). Second, rotate the insecticide MoA group so that the same MoA group is not applied more than once every 3 years. Given the lack of MoA choices, IPM tactics such as spraying only when economic thresholds have been met or employing early harvest will be necessary to maintain a 3 or more year MoA rotation.

title: 'Alfalfa Weevil: A Challenging Insect Pest of Forage Alfalfa in the Western
section: Integrated Resistance Management for Pyrethroid Resistant Alfalfa Weevil
text: Given the lack of MoA choices, IPM tactics such as spraying only when economic thresholds have been met or employing early harvest will be necessary to maintain a 3 or more year MoA rotation. In doing so, producers limit the selection pressure placed on their alfalfa weevil population, thus conserving the efficacy of pyrethroids and indoxacarb in areas with low to moderate resistance. In these instances, it is recommended that producers should: (1) Survey their fields and apply insecticides at the economic threshold; (2) Rotate control tactics, especially the MoA group; (3) Ensure the optimum efficacy of the insecticide is being realized. This can be done by ensuring optimum insecticide application timing, applying higher label rates, and including adjuvants that optimize coverage and precision (Wanner *et al*., 2022b). Third, if a producer’s production system is in an area with high pyrethroid resistance, it is highly unlikely that pyrethroids will still be effective. In these areas, producers will have to rely on indoxacarb (i.e., Steward, MoA 22A) and IPM strategies in rotation. After 3 or more years, test the efficacy of pyrethroids to determine whether they can return to the 3 or more year rotation that includes pyrethroids.

section: How to Monitor Fields for Pyrethroid Resistant Alfalfa Weevil
text: The first step in integrated resistance management is monitoring for resistance within the field early in resistance development. The easiest way to identify a loss in the efficacy of an insecticide is through insecticide spray trials and glass vials. Strips of an alfalfa field can be treated on a small section of a commercial field. The commercial pyrethroid formulation(s) can be applied using an ATV sprayer with a 4m boom or a pressurized backpack sprayer, and applied at the maximum label rate, compared to an untreated strip (i.e., control strip). These strips should be replicated four times and organized in a randomized complete block design; the replicates help account for variation in the field. Before insecticide application, collect 10–20 sweep samples from each strip, and again 1e-week after insecticide application, place collected material from each strip in its own labeled paper bag. The contents of each bag should be counted to identify the number of larvae collected from each strip which allows for the efficacy of each insecticide to be determined and management decisions to be made accordingly. Typically, strips treated with a pyrethroid active ingredient should have >90% fewer larvae compared to the untreated control plots 7-days after application. The same degree of efficacy (90% fewer larvae) should also be observed in strips treated with indoxacarb (MoA 22A). If pyrethroids fail to reduce the alfalfa weevil population in these trials, indoxacarb should still provide 90% control. If these trials are repeated annually over the years, any loss in efficacy should be apparent, allowing for quick management decisions to better mitigate economic losses from resistance. Alternatively, glass vials treated with an insecticide provide a method that does not require alfalfa acreage and can be done at any point of the season, barring that there are enough weevil larvae to collect.

Following the methodology outlined in Rodbell and Wanner (2021) and Rodbell *et al*. (2022), for each pyrethroid active ingredient tested, ten-glass vials (Discount Vials, 27 mm diameter × 95 mm length) would be required. Five vials as a control (1mL of acetone) and five vials each treated with 1 mL of the insecticide at a concentration of 18.9 μg/mL for type II pyrethroids and 189.0 μg/mL for type I pyrethroids. These concentrations represent concentrations closest to the maximum label rate for the associated insecticides. Identifying alive and dead/moribund individuals can be done by following the Rodbell and Wanner (2021) and Rodbell *et al*. (2022) methods using a hotplate. If at these conservative diagnostic concentrations 50% mortality is not achieved, it is likely that the location sample is resistant to the insecticide, and intensive IRM and IPM tactics should be employed.

section: Future Research Areas to Improve Alfalfa Weevil Management
text: * Evaluating current economic thresholds: Since Harrington *et al*. (2021) published an updated economic threshold specific to the low desert region of the United States, it is important to test and update economic thresholds in other irrigated and non-irrigated alfalfa production zones in Canada, Mexico, and the United States. * Evaluating pyrethroid efficacy in North America: Researchers in Canada are exploring the efficacy of pyrethroids in Canada. The results of this effort will greatly inform management decisions and integrated resistance management strategies in the country. Furthermore, other researchers are identifying pyrethroid-resistant alfalfa weevils in Utah and Oklahoma, states not addressed by previous studies (i.e., Rodbell *et al*., 2022). * Identifying molecular markers for resistance: A large collection of alfalfa weevils preserved in ethanol is currently being used for population genomics studies in the western United States and Canada. This collaborative study benefits from knowledge of the pyrethroid resistance status of each population and a first draft of the *Hypera postica* whole genome sequence generated recently by USDA-APHIS. The goal is to find molecular markers that associate with resistance, confirm their predictive value, and develop highly sensitive molecular tests for early detection of resistance. * Identify optimum timing of insecticide application: An academic and industry collaboration is underway to research the precise timing of insecticide applications for optimal control of alfalfa weevil in Montana, Washington, and Oklahoma states. Typically, insecticide applications are recommended when threshold levels of 2nd and 3rd instar larvae are reached. However, recent field trials suggest earlier applications of indoxacarb may be more effective in some production systems, possibly through toxicity to ovipositing females and hatching first instars when this phenology occurs in a more narrow time window.

title: 'Alfalfa Weevil: A Challenging Insect Pest of Forage Alfalfa in the Western
text: Alfalfa weevil is an invasive pest that was first reported in North America in 1904 (Salt Lake City, UT) and is now established throughout the continental United States and parts of Canada and Mexico as a primary pest of forage alfalfa. Alfalfa weevil management has predominantly relied on chemical control tactics, resulting in insecticide resistance. Over the last half-century, pyrethroids have been widely used to control their populations, and recently, pyrethroid resistance has developed in the western United States. Integrated resistance management strategies provide an avenue to limit or avoid pyrethroid resistance. Further research and outreach are required to implement an effective IRM program to mitigate further economic losses. Together, these efforts will provide desperately needed information to ensure sustainable control of this key pest of forage alfalfa.

### Overview ###
The fall armyworm has recently spread to many countries in Africa, where more than 300 million people in sub-Saharan Africa depend on its preferred host plant, maize, as a staple crop. This case assesses the current state of knowledge on biopesticides for the fall armyworm in Africa, including information gaps and compatibility with other recommended management practices.

text: 1. Provide an overview of the biopesticide options for the fall armyworm (FAW) in Africa, including their relative advantages and disadvantages. 2. Detail information gaps in current knowledge of biopesticide potential against FAW. 3. Describe the biopesticides prioritized for research, development and promotion against FAW in Africa. 4. Understand how the biopesticide field has developed in recent years.

title: Assessing Biopesticides for Managing Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
text:
The fall armyworm (FAW, *Spodoptera frugiperda* (J.E. Smith), Lepidoptera: Noctuidae) is native to the Americas, where its larvae are one of the most important pests of maize. The last two instars – four and five – require 50 times more food than earlier stages so an infestation of these larvae can easily destroy an entire crop overnight (CABI PlantwisePlus Knowledge Bank). The adult moths themselves feed on nectar (Figs 1–3). ##### Fig. 1. #####

The FAW has recently spread to much of Africa, the Near East, Asia and the Pacific (FAO, 2020), reaching central and Western Africa in 2016 (Goergen *et al*., 2016) and dispersing rapidly (De Groote *et al*., 2020). FAW is a particular pest of cereals. As maize is a staple food crop for more than 300 million people in sub-Saharan Africa, FAW poses a major threat to livelihoods and food security in this region (Fig. 4). ##### Fig. 4. #####

Many farmers have increased their use of synthetic pesticides to combat FAW (Kansiime *et al*., 2019) but this use may not be safe or effective (Rwomushana *et al*., 2018). It could potentially put farmers’ health at risk (Tambo *et al*., 2020), especially as they often do not use personal protective equipment (Rwomushana *et al*., 2018). Additionally, broad-spectrum pesticides harm natural enemies that could help to manage FAW. There is a clear need for alternative management options suitable for smallholder farmers – biopesticides could offer effective, sustainable, accessible, practical and affordable outcomes with lower risks to human health and the environment. Biopesticides – pesticides derived from natural materials – can be divided into three main substance groups: biochemical pesticides, microbial pesticides and macrobials.

title: Assessing Biopesticides for Managing Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
text: Biopesticides – pesticides derived from natural materials – can be divided into three main substance groups: biochemical pesticides, microbial pesticides and macrobials. Biochemical pesticides can be further divided into sub-groups of plant extracts/botanicals, synthetic pheromones/semiochemicals, microbial extracts/fermentation products, insect growth regulators, compounds synthesized by other organisms, and inorganic compounds. Microbial biopesticides can be split into bacteria, fungi, protozoa, viruses, oomycetes, yeasts and algae, while macrobials can be subdivided into insect predators, parasitoids and entomopathogenic nematodes. This case considers all these types of biopesticides, with the caveat that most countries do not include macrobials in their lists of registered pesticides so macrobials are likely to be under-represented. It looks at the state of play in 2018 and 2020 for biopesticides for FAW management based on two previous assessments (Bateman *et al*., 2018; Bateman *et al*., 2021), commenting on both progress and remaining information gaps.

title: Assessing Biopesticides for Managing Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
text: In order to make information on biopesticides for FAW management readily available, in 2018 the authors of this case identified and assessed some 50 biopesticides that had been registered for management of FAW, *Spodoptera* species or Lepidoptera in general, in one or more of 30 countries in FAW’s native region and Africa (Bateman *et al*., 2018). The countries included were Argentina, Benin, Bolivia, Brazil, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Chile, Colombia, DR Congo, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Malawi, Mali, Mexico, Mozambique, Nigeria, Panama, Peru, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, South Africa, Tanzania, Togo, Tunisia, Uganda, USA and Zambia. The team assembled a detailed profile on each of 54 commercially available biopesticide active ingredients (AIs), providing information on its efficacy against FAW, hazard to human health and the environment, agronomic sustainability, and practicality for use by smallholder farmers, including its availability and cost-effectiveness. Based on these profiles, the team determined whether using each biopesticide would put farmers and the wider community and environment at risk, as well as whether the active ingredient would be practical for smallholder farmers. Using this information, the researchers then developed a decision matrix for designing interventions that would make biopesticides for FAW control more widely available in Africa. Several of the active ingredients had been shown to be effective in field trials in FAW’s native range but there was minimal data from the field in Africa. Few biopesticide active ingredients had been registered for most countries in Africa, and almost none of the active ingredients had been specifically registered for use against FAW. In addition, little information about cost-effectiveness was available.

text: Few biopesticide active ingredients had been registered for most countries in Africa, and almost none of the active ingredients had been specifically registered for use against FAW. In addition, little information about cost-effectiveness was available. As a result of this assessment, the team recommended 23 biopesticides for follow-up actions such as field trials, participatory trials or laboratory studies (Fig. 1) (Bateman *et al*., 2018).

title: Assessing Biopesticides for Managing Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
text:
### Overview ###
In 2020, the case authors assessed how the state of knowledge in this field has changed. They provided updated information on the biopesticide active ingredients registered and commercialized that could be used for the management of FAW in the same 30 countries as before. Completing this update involved accessing lists of registered pesticides and biopesticides for the 30 countries between April and August of 2020 and looking for biopesticides already registered and allowed for use against FAW, *Spodoptera* or Lepidoptera in general. A total of 12 countries specifically identified biopesticide active ingredients in their list of registered pesticides, and 19 countries included information about the specific pests for which products are registered. The team updated the profiles of previously identified biopesticide active ingredients and created additional profiles for newly identified active ingredients. In total, team members identified 41 biopesticide active ingredients registered and allowed for use for FAW management in at least one of the 30 countries. Four of these were not identified in the previous assessment – *Aspergillus oryzae*, *Autographa californica* multiple nucleopolyhedrovirus (AcMNPV), *Spodoptera littoralis* nucleopolyhedrovirus (SpliNPV) and thyme oil. As a result of the exclusion of active ingredients that are no longer categorized as biopesticides or are not registered for Lepidoptera, this study identified fewer biopesticide active ingredients than the 54 assessed in 2018. Three inorganic compounds (borax, cryolite and silicon dioxide), two microbial fermentation products (emamectin benzoate and spinetoram) and two insect growth regulators (lufenuron and methoxyfenozide) are no longer categorized as biochemical biopesticides by national authorities in any of the assessed countries.

title: Assessing Biopesticides for Managing Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
text: Two other inorganic compounds (kaolin and sulfur), one other microbial fermentation product (spinosad) and one other insect growth regulator (s-methoprene) are still designated as biochemical biopesticides by one or more countries although many definitions would not class them as biopesticides. No products were registered for use against FAW or its relatives for three active ingredients that were identified through the previous study – 2-phenylethyl propionate, octanoate d-glucitol and sucrose octanoate. In total in 2020, biopesticide active ingredients were represented by more than 1500 products in 30 countries. These products included 852 botanicals, 419 microbials, 85 microbial extracts or fermentation products, 125 inorganic compounds and 7 insect growth regulators. Some macrobials were also identified, namely, eight products containing parasitoids (*Trichogramma pretiosum* Riley) and six products containing entomopathogenic nematodes (*Steinernema carpocapsae* Weiser) were registered for FAW. Most countries do not include macrobials in their lists of registered pesticides so macrobials are likely to be under-represented. Of the 30 countries in this study, only Brazil, Kenya and Uganda include macrobials. The team also identified one product containing spider venom peptide. In 2018, 18 of the biopesticide active ingredients were registered in three or more countries; by 2020, this figure had increased to 30. Azadirachtin, *Bacillus thuringiensis* Berliner (*Bt*), pyrethrins, soybean oil and sulfur were present in the highest numbers of products (Fig. 5). ##### Fig. 5.

The number of biopesticides demonstrated to be effective against FAW, *Spodoptera* spp. or Lepidoptera increased between 2018 and 2020, rising from 26 to 34. A total of 23 active ingredients in 2020 showed efficacy against FAW versus 15 in 2018. There was also more evidence of efficacy from the field in Africa – 13 active ingredients in 2020 compared to 4 in 2018 (Fig. 5). Only five studies concluded that any of the active ingredients were ineffective against FAW (Fig. 6). ##### Fig. 6. #####
Comparison of the findings of the assessment of the efficacy of the biopesticide active ingredients (AIs) in 2018 (left, pale) versus 2020 (right, dark). ### Hazard profiles ###
A total of 26 of the hazard profiles for the identified biopesticide active ingredients were unchanged from the 2018 assessment. Five active ingredients had data gaps filled, three were assigned higher toxicity categories and three were assigned to lower categories. All 41 active ingredients have relatively low levels of hazard. Only kaolin clay met any of the criteria for highly hazardous pesticides (HHP) but US regulators have categorized it as ‘Generally Recognized as Safe’. ### Agronomic sustainability ###
The team concluded that 28 of the biopesticide active ingredients would be agronomically sustainable, offering low risks to non-target organisms, low risks of pests developing resistance, and low risks of becoming invasive. Eleven of the active ingredients would need mitigation measures.

title: Assessing Biopesticides for Managing Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
text:
Eleven of the active ingredients would need mitigation measures. Four active ingredients – allyl isothiocyanate, pyrethrins, S-methoprene and spinosad – are highly or very highly toxic to non-target organisms. There are examples in the literature of FAW developing resistance to spinosad and to genetically-modified maize incorporating genes of *Bt*, while another Lepidoptera species showed resistance to products containing *Bt* in the field (Mota-Sanchez and Wise, 2020). Neem trees (*Azadirachta indica* A. Juss.) and *Dysphania ambrosioides* (L.) Mosyakin and Clemants both have the potential to be invasive weeds in Africa (CABI, 2017) so local production should only take place after risk assessments have been conducted. Data on agronomic sustainability were not available for matrine and oxymatrine. ### Practicality of use by farmers ###
According to the literature and their product labels, 27 of the biopesticides would be suitable for smallholder farmers to use, whereas six would be difficult for such use in the short term – allyl isothiocyanate, soybean oil, *Steinernema carpocapsae, Steinernema feltiae* and *Trichogramma* spp. Reasons for this impracticality included requirements for application equipment, high frequency of application, storage needs, shelf life and the need for an area-wide management approach. The assessment of practicality of use in 2020 was virtually unchanged from the 2018 findings. ### Registration status and availability of biopesticide active ingredients in Africa ###
The national lists of registered biopesticides for the 19 African countries in the study included products containing 32 of the 41 biopesticide active ingredients under assessment.

title: Assessing Biopesticides for Managing Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
text:
Many, but not all, countries had more products registered for 2020 than 2018. In 2018, only South Africa had biopesticide products specifically registered for use against FAW. By 2020, Ghana, Kenya and Tanzania had joined South Africa in this respect. These four and most other countries had products that were broadly registered for Lepidoptera and that would potentially be effective against FAW. Ghana has registered products containing *Bt*, maltodextrin, and the combination of *Metarhizium anisopliae* and *Beauveria bassiana* for use against FAW in maize while some other products, such as ones containing ethyl palmitate, have registrations that broadly cover all caterpillars. Many biopesticides are registered in Kenya but only one product containing *Bt* is specifically registered for use against FAW. Kenya had the highest number of registered biopesticide active ingredients and products that could potentially be used against FAW, with 22 active ingredients and 125 products while South Africa listed 14 such active ingredients and 37 products, Ghana had 14 active ingredients and 26 products, and Tanzania registered 13 active ingredients and 117 products (Fig. 7). ##### Fig. 7. #####

Little information on cost or cost-effectiveness was available for most of the biopesticide active ingredients. Field trials and farmer surveys in Africa indicate that azadirachtin is cost-effective and relatively affordable for smallholder farmers (Babendreier *et al*., 2020) whereas ethyl palmitate (Rwomushana *et al*., 2018) and maltodextrin (Babendreier *et al*., 2020) are less cost-effective and not as affordable.

title: Assessing Biopesticides for Managing Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
text: Assessments for other pests or in other countries indicated that a number of active ingredients were cost-effective, including capsaicin, *Chromobacterium subtsugae,* garlic extracts, *Isaria fumosorosea, Metarhizium anisopliae,* spinosad and *Trichogramma* spp. (Kivett *et al*., 2015; Dougoud *et al*., 2019; Nayak *et al*., 2019; Manisha *et al*., 2020).

title: Assessing Biopesticides for Managing Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
text: It is encouraging that the number of biopesticide active ingredients registered per country that could potentially be used to manage FAW had more than doubled and that increases in the number of products registered were similar. There is also more evidence of efficacy for many of the active ingredients, particularly for FAW itself, and from the field in Africa. However, the findings are not always clear-cut, for example it is uncertain whether several of the botanical extracts are effective on their own or must be combined with other active ingredients. Some of the case authors participated in field trials that showed efficacy in Africa for eight active ingredients – *A. oryzae,* azadirachtin*, B. thuringiensis subsp. Aizaiwai,* maltodextrin, FAW sex pheromones, spinosad, *Spodoptera frugiperda* multiple nucleopolyhedrovirus and *Spodoptera littoralis* nucleopolyhedrovirus*. * As a result, products have been registered across some countries in Africa. While some of these biopesticide active ingredients have already been incorporated into integrated pest management (IPM) schemes or are being provided to farmers, most still have IPM information gaps that need to be filled. For example, most biopesticide active ingredients, including many that have been registered and are being recommended to farmers, lack data on cost-effectiveness. Findings from the literature on other cropping systems are not transferable as they will be out of date and inaccurate for other locations. Costs need to be in the form of prices sold to farmers by in-country distributors and calculated per hectare per season. Most maize in Africa is grown by smallholder farmers for subsistence (Hruska, 2019), making most pesticides – whether synthetic or biopesticides – too expensive for use.

title: Assessing Biopesticides for Managing Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
text: Most maize in Africa is grown by smallholder farmers for subsistence (Hruska, 2019), making most pesticides – whether synthetic or biopesticides – too expensive for use. In addition, many governments and other initiatives are scaling back the distribution of pesticides, making cost likely to become a bigger issue (Hruska, 2019). Conducting further field work that establishes the most cost-effective methods for using many of these active ingredients would be beneficial. Since most countries do not include macro-organisms in their lists of registered pesticides, it would be helpful to conduct a separate review on natural enemies. There is currently much research in progress on parasitoids, including field trials on *Telenomus remus* and *Trichogramma* in Kenya. So far, *T. remus* seems more promising than *T. pretiosum* but is more difficult to mass-produce and not yet available as a commercial product. The increase in the number of biopesticide active ingredients that have been registered in Africa is lower than in FAW’s native countries, and registrations for some active ingredients have moved more quickly in countries in Asia. This disparity could be due to registration costs, regulatory hurdles or lack of manufacturer action due to their perception of the size of the pesticide market (Constantine *et al*., 2020; Nyangau *et al*., 2020). What’s more, registration of an active ingredient does not make it locally available to or affordable for a farmer. Awareness and confidence can also limit uptake by smallholders. Surveys show that farmers in some countries are using biopesticides but it would be useful to examine biopesticides’ availability and affordability to farmers, as well as farmers’ perceptions of their efficacy, in more detail.

title: Assessing Biopesticides for Managing Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
text:
A decision matrix has been created to make recommendations for field trials in Africa for eight active ingredients that were registered in at least one country and had been reported effective against FAW either in field trials in FAW’s native range or in lab bioassays – *B. thuringiensis* subsp. *kurstaki, B. beauveria, D. ambrosioides,* ethyl palmitate, eugenol, garlic extract, *M. anisopliae* and *Steinernema* spp (Bateman *et al*., 2021)*. * Some of these field trials are underway. We also recommended bioassays to determine the effectiveness of four active ingredients against FAW, namely GS-omega/kappa-Hx-tx-Hv1a, canola oil, capsaicin and D-limonene. If the ingredients prove effective, field trials could follow. We do not recommend the follow-up of 18 active ingredients. This group is similar to the group receiving the same evaluation in the 2018 study, with the addition of some active ingredients such as sucrose octanoate that are no longer registered for FAW in any of the 30 countries, other ingredients that the hazard data now indicate are an HHP (for example, kaolin), or in the case of matrine and pyrethrins because studies do not indicate they are effective (Table 1). ##### Table 1. #####

### Overview ###
This case study provides information on plant pathogenic *Phytopythium vexans*, host range, symptoms, identification methods, and management options. The pathogen causes damping off and root rot diseases in hosts from 19 families resulting in diverse economic losses. Innovative and sustainable management methods have been identified through case studies.

title: 'Impact of Phytopythium vexans on Plant Health: Hosts, Symptoms, Detection,
text: In December 2016, the rooted cuttings of flowering cherry (*Prunus serrulata* L.) grown in propagation beds (containing 40% coarse sand and 60% ground pine bark) at a commercial propagation nursery in Warren County, Tennessee were exhibiting root and crown rot symptoms. The appearance of dark brown to soft black lesions symptoms on the roots as well as the crown regions of the plants made the rooted cuttings non-marketable. Upon isolation of the causal organism, it was confirmed to be *Phytopythium vexans* (previously called *Pythium vexans*) causing the disease symptoms which was verified by fulfillment of Koch’s postulates. Later in 2020, the pathogen was also found to be causing root and crown rot symptoms in ginkgo (*Ginkgo biloba* L.) and red maple (*Acer rubrum* L.) in other nurseries in Tennessee (Baysal-Gurel *et al*., 2021; Panth *et al*., 2021). It is reported to be a cause of plant root and crown rot disease in Australia, Brazil, China, India, Iran, Italy, Japan, Morocco, Panama, Rwanda, South Africa, Spain, Taiwan, Thailand, Tunisia, Turkey, USA, and Vietnam. Root and crown rots in plants from Actinidiaceae, Anacardiaceae, Araceae, Araliaceae, Euphorbiaceae, Fabaceae, Ginkgoaceae, Lauraceae, Malvaceae, Myrtaceae, Orchidaceae, Pinaceae, Rosaceae, Rutaceae, Salicaceae, Sapindaceae, Solanaceae, Urticaceae, and Zingiberaceae families are documented to be caused by *P. vexans*. The ability of the pathogen to move with water and survive in the soil makes it even harder to manage. title: 'Impact of Phytopythium vexans on Plant Health: Hosts, Symptoms, Detection,
text:
### Causal agent ###
*Phytopythium vexans* Abad, De Cock, Bala, Robideau, Lodhi & Levesque, a member of the oomycete group commonly known as water molds, inhabits both soil and water. It falls in the Kingdom Chromista, phylum Oomycota, order Pythiales, family Pythiaceae, and genus *Phytopythium*. It causes damage to young plants, seedlings, or cuttings of ornamental plants by creating necrotic lesions in the root system, leading to yellowing of leaves, wilting of stems and leaves, and decay in the top part of the seedlings. As the disease progresses, the affected roots, stems, and collar regions exhibit symptoms such as discoloration and necrotic brown lesions, with the occurrence of tissue rotting (Fig. 1c–f). Furthermore, infected roots experience root rot and sloughing of the cortex when exposed to gentle pull, leaving the inner stele behind. ### Pathogen biology, life cycle, and epidemiology ###
*P. vexans* produces a unique mycelial growth pattern resembling a white radiating chrysanthemum flower and spherical zoospores on V8-PARPH medium (Fig. 1a). Antheridia are elongated and cylindrical with constrictions (Baysal-Gurel *et al*., 2021). The pathogen grows quickly on Potato Dextrose Agar (PDA), forming white, cottony colonies that can cover a 9 cm petri dish in just 4 days. It can survive as a saprophyte on dead plant material or as a pathogen on the fibrous roots of perennial plants.

title: 'Impact of Phytopythium vexans on Plant Health: Hosts, Symptoms, Detection,
text: It can survive as a saprophyte on dead plant material or as a pathogen on the fibrous roots of perennial plants. It requires free water to infect a host, and heavily infested soil can pose a risk to young seedlings or seeds in the soil. It can tolerate temperatures ranging from 5 to 30°C, with the best growth occurring at 25–30°C. Moreover, the pathogen can grow at soil moisture potential of −0.67 Mpa at 25°C and 30°C temperature (Jabiri *et al*., 2022). The rapidly growing white mycelia produce infective sporangia. These sporangia can germinate directly by producing one to several germ tubes or can produce a secondary sporangium called a vesicle. Within the vesicle, zoospores are produced, which are released and swim before rounding off to form a cyst and germinate. The germ tube typically penetrates the host tissue and initiates a new infection, but sometimes it produces another vesicle in which more secondary zoospores are formed, and this process may be repeated. The mycelium also produces spherical oogonia, which, once fertilized, become thick-walled oospores. The movement of actively swimming zoospores accounts for the active dispersal of the pathogen. Passive dispersal of the pathogen inoculum could occur by movement of encysted zoospores, oospores, or mycelia via above land and subsurface flow of the water. The plant-to-plant spread of the pathogen could take place by root-to-root contact when an infected root of a plant encounters roots of adjacent plants. The life cycle of *P. vexans* is demonstrated in Fig. 2. ##### Fig. 2.

text:
The life cycle of *P. vexans* is demonstrated in Fig. 2. ##### Fig. 2. #####
Diagram depicting the life cycle and pathogenesis of *Phytopythium vexans*. ### Diagnosis ###
Diagnosis of diseased plant tissues involves multiple steps such as visual observation of signs and symptoms, pathogen isolation, and molecular identification. The necrotic brown lesions and discoloration symptoms in the root (Fig. 1c), stem, and collar regions (Fig. 1e-f) of young plants and occasionally apical part of the seedlings, yellowing of leaves, and generalized leaf and stem wilt are typical symptoms of infection by this pathogen. In roots infected by *P. vexans* displaying rotting symptoms, the outer layer of the root easily separates and comes off when pulled, leaving behind the inner core. In addition to this, the roots become too fragile and hence can easily be separated. Isolation of *P. vexans* may be conducted by first washing the infected crown region and roots of the plants under running water to remove any external debris. Then, small sections (1–2 mm) may be cut from the crown, primary, and secondary roots that show signs of browning and necrosis. Surface sterilization can be conducted with 70% ethanol (dipping for 30 s or longer) and washing twice with sterilized water or dipping in 1% bleach and 70% ethanol for 30 s each, rinsing with sterilized distilled water three times and blot drying in filter paper/absorbent paper. The sterilized infected root and crown part can be plated either on V8-PARPH or P10ARPH or Corn Meal Agar (CMA) or PDA media.

title: 'Impact of Phytopythium vexans on Plant Health: Hosts, Symptoms, Detection,
text: The sterilized infected root and crown part can be plated either on V8-PARPH or P10ARPH or Corn Meal Agar (CMA) or PDA media. The isolation plates (that contain the plated tissues) should then be kept at 25°C for 72 h to 7 days. Diagnostic kits or techniques that employ biochemical methods such as *Phytophthora* (Phyt) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays test (ELISA) and *Phytophthora* ImmunoStrip test (Agdia Inc., Elkhart, IN) which rely on antibody–antigen reactions, can be useful for winding down the causal agent of the disease as an oomycete since those tests cross react with *Phytopythium* species. More precise identification of the pathogen can be done by employing molecular methods of detection. Molecular detection of *P. vexans* from infected plant tissues and water could be done by utilizing polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and sequencing, loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay, and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assay (Spies *et al*., 2011; Ghimire and Baysal-Gurel, 2023; Ghimire *et al*., 2023).

title: 'Impact of Phytopythium vexans on Plant Health: Hosts, Symptoms, Detection,
text: To effectively manage *Phytopythium* disease, it is advisable to adopt the principle of minimizing initial inoculum, preventing introductions, and controlling the growth rates of pathogens. Various practices such as using pathogen-free cuttings, seedlings, using clean or disinfected irrigation water, and avoiding standing water in production areas could limit the introduction and reduce the primary inoculum. Disinfection of irrigation water using various approaches such as chlorination, ozonation, and UV-C radiation is possible depending upon their availability and feasibility. UV-C irradiation could be utilized to inactivate *P. vexans*, but it is important to note that the assessment of the pathogen load in irrigation water must be monitored. Based on the evaluated pathogen load, the water must be exposed to corresponding doses to achieve complete inactivation of the target organism. The decimal reduction dose (D10 value) of UV-C which is the dose that causes 90% mortality of *P. vexans* is determined to be 8 mJ.cm−2 (Ghimire *et al*., 2022). Additionally, it is advisable to ensure general sanitation in the propagation area, maintain consistent use of clean containers, remove leaf debris, eliminate diseased plants, and regularly monitor plants for potential disease symptoms. It is essential that the propagation area remains as clean as possible within the nursery and immediate elimination of weeds, diseased or dead plants, and leaf debris that could serve as potential hosts for pathogens is recommended. Disinfection of propagation beds and area among the crops is advised. Proper sanitation of containers or trays before reuse is recommended, which can be achieved through methods such as heat treatment by soaking pots in hot water or exposing containers to aerated steam.

text:
Proper sanitation of containers or trays before reuse is recommended, which can be achieved through methods such as heat treatment by soaking pots in hot water or exposing containers to aerated steam. Furthermore, it is advised to prevent placing pots containing plants directly on bare soil, as it can lead to the splashing of *Phytopythium* onto plants or the potential movement of zoospores into the pot soil through water films. A layer of gravel or rocks can be placed as a barrier between the soil and the containers since the soil in the nurseries could have a risk of being a source of *Phytoptyhium*. ### Chemical control ###
An integrated approach is recommended to manage this pathogen in woody ornamental production. It is advisable to implement a rotation strategy involving fungicides and biofungicides, considering their efficacy in managing resistance. By adopting a rotation program that includes fungicides with different modes of action, biofungicides, and host plant defense inducers, the *Phytopythium* root rot disease can be managed while reducing the chances of resistance emergence. Panth *et al. * (2021) verified that drench applications of fungicides Pyraclostrobin (Empress), Pyraclostrobin and Boscalid (Pageant), Oxathiapiprolin (Segovis), and Mefenoxam (Subdue Max) were able to significantly suppress the root rot disease caused by *P. vexans* on infected ornamental plants (maple and ginkgo).

title: 'Impact of Phytopythium vexans on Plant Health: Hosts, Symptoms, Detection,
text:
Moreover, biofungicides such as Stargus containing *Bacillus amyloliquefaciens*, and host plant-defense inducers such as Fosetyl-aluminum (Aliette), and Mon and Di potassium salts of phosphorus acid (Agri-fos) have also been confirmed to be effective suppressing *Phytopythium* root rot disease on rooted cuttings of ginkgo and maple potted in 1-gallon pots and grown for a year in greenhouses. ### Effect of cultural practices ###
Cover crops such as annual rye grass, triticale, Japanese millet, Austrian winter pea, cowpea have been generally used as cover crops to suppress soilborne pathogens. Parajuli *et al. * (2022) demonstrated that cover cropping of Triticale (x *Triticosecale* W.) and crimson clover (*Trifolium incarnatum* L.) suppressed *P. vexans* disease in red maple plants in the field and are hence recommended to be planted in fields with susceptible woody ornamental crops for the management of *Phytopythium* root and crown rot. The utilization of cover crops suppresses not only the pathogen in soil but also enhances soil organic carbon, total nitrogen, and improves plant growth by enhancing positive changes in soil chemistry and increasing microbial activities in the soil (Parajuli *et al*., 2022).

title: 'Impact of Phytopythium vexans on Plant Health: Hosts, Symptoms, Detection,
text: *P. vexans* is an emerging oomycete pathogen associated with disease in the root and crown regions of various plants. The demonstrated multi-host pathogenicity of the pathogen indicates the need for future anticipation and preparedness of additional crop genera being infected by this pathogen. Management studies have been conducted on only a few hosts and a range of aggressiveness of isolates of *P. vexans* on different kinds of plants and cultivars are asserted. It is advised to adopt the recommended general management practices for managing this disease along with the chemical and cultural measures explained. Use of clean and pathogen-free irrigation water in specialty crop production is recommended. Various approaches to ensure the use of pathogen-free water such as treating the irrigation water using germicidal ultraviolet light, ozone, heat, etc. solitarily or in combination with various filtration methods could be utilized. There are no documented *P. vexans* resistant cultivars of crops including woody ornamentals, hence it is recommended to develop *P. vexans* resistant cultivar evaluation and breeding programs.

### Overview ###
Cassava brown streak disease (CBSD is an invasive disease of cassava. It causes substantial yield losses by damaging the most edible portions of the cassava plant resulting in food insecurity. This case study presents the problem of CBSD, its exacerbating factors, management efforts and the need for a coordinated response in its effective management in Zambia and similar agro-ecologies.

Recognise the impact of CBSD at household, community and national levels and why it is regarded as a transboundary pest of regional significance. 3. title: 'Cassava Brown Streak Disease in Zambia: An Integrated Approach to Managing
text: Cassava (*Manihot esculenta* Crantz family Euphorbiaceae) is Zambia’s second most important crop after maize. It is traditionally grown in four of Zambia’s 10 provinces and provides dietary caloric needs for an estimated 30% of the country’s population (Chikoti *et al*., 2019). Unfortunately, since 2018, the arrival of the cassava brown streak disease (CBSD), an invasive pest threatens the production of cassava in the country. CBSD is a viral disease of cassava, which is currently considered the most threatening constraint to cassava production in Africa (Muhindo *et al*., 2020; Ano *et al*., 2021). It manifests as hard rots in cassava roots that are often accompanied by brown streaks on stems and discolouration of leaves. CBSD has caused substantial yield losses in East, Central and Southern Africa, where over 200 million people depend on the crop for their livelihoods (Elegba *et al*., 2020). In the wake of climate change, characterized by recurring crop failures, cassava is regarded as a drought insurance crop because of its capacity to withstand sub-optimal agronomic practices including a limited supply of irrigation. Additionally, modelling studies have shown the resilience of cassava over other crops like maize making it ideal for climate adaptation. However, CBSD poses a major challenge to harnessing the potential of the cassava subsector in enhancing food security in Africa.

title: 'Cassava Brown Streak Disease in Zambia: An Integrated Approach to Managing
text:
The first report of CBSD was in the early 1930s in the low-altitude regions of Tanzania (Chikoti and Tembo, 2022). It remained latent and restricted to the coastal areas of East Africa for many decades until early 2000 when it emerged more aggressively in the higher altitude inland regions of Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania (Alicai *et al*., 2007; Legg *et al*., 2011; Masinde *et al*., 2016). It has since spread further in East Africa and has extended to several countries in Central and southern Africa. Presently, the countries with confirmed CBSD presence in Africa include Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, Congo, Madagascar, Gabon, South Sudan, Burundi, Angola, Mozambique, Democratic Republic of Congo, Zimbabwe, Malawi and Zambia (Legg *et al*., 2011; Masinde *et al*., 2016; Mulenga *et al*., 2018; Munguti *et al*., 2023). In West Africa, various pre-emptive measures including screening for resistance to CBSD in order to prevent its entry and subsequent spread in the world’s largest-producing cassava region are ongoing (Elegba *et al*., 2020; Ano *et al*., 2021). In Zambia, CBSD was first reported in 2018 in Kaputa and Chienge districts located in Northern and Luapula provinces, respectively (Mulenga *et al*., 2018) (Fig. 1). In 5 years, the disease has spread to further districts within the two provinces. There are also unconfirmed reports of CBSD-like symptoms in some selected districts of north-western province such as Kapombo. ##### Fig. 1. #####

The typical symptoms of CBSD on cassava can be identified in three main plant parts namely; the leaves, stems and roots (Fig. 2). In some cases, CBSD symptoms have been observed on cassava fruits as well as the insect vector *Bemisa tabaci* on cassava leaves (Fig. 3). ##### Fig. 2. #####
Symptoms of cassava brown streak disease of varying severity on cassava leaves, stem and root. ##### Fig. 3. #####
(a) Cassava brown streak disease symptoms on cassava fruits, (b) *Bemisia tabaci* on cassava leaves. CBSD infection on cassava leaves manifests as chlorotic patches or blotches sometimes referred to as mottling. The patches form a characteristic viral mosaic that runs along the primary and secondary leaf veins culminating in a feathery chlorotic pattern. As the name of the disease suggests, CBSD is marked by the appearance of brown streaks on the plant and these typically occur on the stem. The brown streaks resemble lesions that can be more prominently seen on younger cassava stems because of the contrast between the green colour of the stems and that of the brown streaks (Muhindo *et al*., 2020). Cassava roots are the major edible portion although the leaves are also consumed as a vegetable in selected parts of Africa including Zambia, Malawi and the Democratic Republic of Congo (Achidi *et al*., 2005).

title: 'Cassava Brown Streak Disease in Zambia: An Integrated Approach to Managing
text: Cassava roots are the major edible portion although the leaves are also consumed as a vegetable in selected parts of Africa including Zambia, Malawi and the Democratic Republic of Congo (Achidi *et al*., 2005). CBSD causes hard, odourless rots in cassava roots known as necrotic rots that render the roots inedible by both humans and animals. This damage can translate into significant losses in yield and quality of produce, which may threaten food security, especially in traditional cassava-growing regions where the crop is the main staple food. CBSD is capable of causing 100% yield losses when susceptible cassava varieties are used coupled with poor agronomic practices. Presently, the average global yield is 11 t/ha (Ritchie *et al*., 2022). In Zambia, the average yield for the crop is even lower at 6t/ha (Kaluba *et al*., 2022). With the arrival of CBSD, cassava yields are further threatened as both the incidence and severity of the disease continue to increase in the country. As the second most important staple crop after maize in Zambia, cassava production is being promoted for crop diversification and climate change mitigation. Particularly in the past 10 years, there have been marked developments within the cassava subsector of Zambia in an effort to promote production and diverse utilization of the crop to enhance the agricultural sector and drive economic growth. These developments and other sectoral plans are documented in the country’s National Cassava Sector Development Strategy of 2020–2024 (Bundi *et al*., 2022). The presence of CBSD offsets some of the progress made to promote cassava and its utilization as a crop of strategic importance for the country.

section: Biological and Ecological Factors Influencing the Invasiveness of CBSD
text: The causal viruses of CBSD known as cassava brown streak viruse (CBSV) and Ugandan cassava brown streak virus (UCBSV) belong to the family Potyviridae and the genus Ipomovirus. Both viruses are transmitted through the vector *Bemisia tabaci* Gennadius (Hemiptera: Aleyrodidae), over short distances such as within a cassava field or across fields that are in close proximity with each other (Maruthi *et al*., 2005). Transmission of both CBSV and UCBSV through *B. tabaci* is in a semi-persistent manner unlike the persistent transmission of the CMD causative virus by the same vector (Legg *et al*., 2011). Across longer distances, CBSD spread happens when cassava cuttings that are infected with either or both causal viruses are used to propagate new fields of the crop, thereby transferring viral inoculum from one field to the next (Patil *et al*., 2015). Within field transmission of CBSV through aphids is also reported (Ateka *et al*., 2017). Studies suggest that UCBSV is more prevalent than CBSV in Africa, although the two viruses cause the same characteristic symptoms in cassava. CBSV is also more genetically diverse and is believed to generally cause more conspicuous foliar symptoms on cassava than UCBSV (Mulenga *et al*., 2018). Further studies are required to characterize the nature of damage caused by the two CBSVs to inform improved management methods. Efficient and cost-effective methods of inoculation for the transmission of CBSD causal viruses using chip bud grafting have been demonstrated (Wagaba *et al*., 2013). This will enable improved methods of laboratory and greenhouse studies on CBSD aetiology and biology.

title: 'Cassava Brown Streak Disease in Zambia: An Integrated Approach to Managing
section: Current Efforts to Manage CBSD in Zambia
text: In Zambia, CBSD is fairly new compared to some of her neighbouring countries that have had the disease for much longer such as Malawi, Tanzania and the Democratic Republic of Congo. For most farmers that have experienced the disease on their crop, CBSD has elicited uncertainty of what is damaging their cassava crop and how to manage it. Consequently, efforts to manage the disease at the farmer level have been limited. Additionally, some methods for managing CBSD in Zambia are either not yet available or are unfamiliar to farmers in the current CBSD-affected regions of the country. However, in the 5 years that CBSD has been present in Zambia, there have been efforts to mitigate the spread of the disease that have also considered lessons from other countries grappling with the problem. Following the first report of CBSD presence in Zambia by Mulenga *et al*. (2018), pre-breeding efforts to identify suitable cassava varieties with appreciable levels of CBSD tolerance were among the first national responses to the disease. The Zambia Agricultural Research Institute (ZARI) in collaboration with the International Institute for Tropical Agriculture (IITA) embarked on germplasm screening aimed at identifying genotypes with tolerance to the disease. Owing to the complex nature of the genetics that govern resistance to CBSD in cassava and the sole reliance on conventional breeding techniques, these efforts are still ongoing, although with slow progress. Learning from the experience of Uganda, breeding for resistance to CBSD can take many years before a fairly acceptable variety can be achieved. It took over a decade to develop the first variety with appreciable levels of CBSD tolerance in Uganda (Kawuki *et al*., 2016). Besides the ongoing pre-breeding and breeding efforts, the need for additional approaches to curb the spread of CBSD in Zambia became more apparent as the disease began to spread rapidly to new districts.

title: 'Cassava Brown Streak Disease in Zambia: An Integrated Approach to Managing
section: Current Efforts to Manage CBSD in Zambia
text: Besides the ongoing pre-breeding and breeding efforts, the need for additional approaches to curb the spread of CBSD in Zambia became more apparent as the disease began to spread rapidly to new districts. In 2021, when nearly half of the farming camps in Kaputa and Chienge, the districts in which the disease was first detected had reported the presence of CBSD, CABI embarked on a CBSD awareness campaign. The campaign aimed to stimulate a nation-wide response to mitigate the spread of CBSD and its impacts in the country. Prior to the implementation of the campaign, a survey targeting the most affected districts and one with reported CBSD-like symptoms was conducted to determine the prevalence of CBSD and farmers’ levels of awareness about the disease. The survey provided valuable baseline information on CBSD, cassava production practices and farmers’ circumstances in these areas (Bundi *et al*., 2022). A focus group discussion component was also incorporated in the survey and this provided gender-responsive insights into farmers’ cassava production and resources management profiles in Kaputa, Chienge and Kabombo districts. Notably, women and youth in these communities were more involved in field-level cassava production activities. For the activities related to the management of resources, men’s participation was found to increase compared to their participation in production-level activities (Figs. 4 and 5). These factors were important when designing the awareness campaign on CBSD to make it gender-inclusive by soliciting the participation of women in gatherings on CBSD awareness. This follows from a low participation of women in community gatherings and meetings in general. These factors are also important considerations in the design of a gender-responsive and certified propagule system for cassava. ##### Fig. 4.

Stakeholder consultation was also conducted and it provided insights on the design and implementation of the awareness campaign, which was actively launched in November 2021 and is currently ongoing. Outputs of the stakeholder meeting helped to prioritize the target recipients of important messages on mitigating CBSD spread and to identify the appropriate modes of communication to recipients (Fig. 6). So far, the awareness campaign has covered some of the most affected districts in Zambia’s traditional cassava-growing provinces including northern, western, north-western and western provinces. Key messages on methods to mitigate the spread and impact of CBSD have been shared with farmers, extensionists, policy makers, regulators, media and the general public. Modes of information sharing included meetings, radio programmes, plant health rallies, trainings, short messaging system (SMS), short videos, jingles, television adverts and distribution of various information, education and communication (IEC) materials such as posters and flyers. The content in the key messages was prepared in English and translated into four local languages commonly used in the four target provinces including Tabwa, Kaonde, Lozi, and Luvale. Additionally, local radio stations were used to host the radio programmes and phone in sessions in the target provinces. ##### Fig. 6.

Sharing of key messages through the awareness campaign on CBSD revealed the need for the provision of disease-free cassava cuttings to farmers in the CBSD-affected regions. This arose when farmers provided feedback following the key messages shared with them on curbing CBSD spread. Particularly, the key message on ensuring the use of disease-free cassava planting material in new cassava fields was met with questions on where to source such planting material. Consequently, CABI embarked on a collaborative intervention involving the Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit (DMMU) under the Office of the Vice President of the Republic of Zambia and other private and public sector organizations to procure and distribute disease-free cuttings to farmers in five of the most affected northern districts. In addition, CABI enrolled 16 lead farmers in an official cassava propagule production training to initiate local production of disease-free cassava cuttings and promote local access by other farmers in the CBSD-affected areas. ### Prospects for sustainable management of CBSD ###
Considering that CBSD has been present for a long time in several eastern and southern African countries, Zambia can learn valuable lessons and build on the efforts of these countries in the management of CBSD. In east Africa for instance, there are notable efforts in the area of breeding for tolerance against CBSD involving diverse sources of germplasm. Extensive screening to identify CBSD-resistant germplasm and development of CBSD breeding populations derived from exotic and local sources has been conducted (Kawuki *et al*., 2016).

title: 'Cassava Brown Streak Disease in Zambia: An Integrated Approach to Managing
section: Current Efforts to Manage CBSD in Zambia
text: Extensive screening to identify CBSD-resistant germplasm and development of CBSD breeding populations derived from exotic and local sources has been conducted (Kawuki *et al*., 2016). This has enabled the identification of promising breeding material that countries like Zambia with a limited spread can exploit to develop their own local breeding programmes. Currently in Zambia, there is no cassava variety that has been validated as resistant or tolerant to CBSD that farmers can readily use (Chikoti and Tembo, 2022). Conventional breeding often can take a long time for appreciable gains to manifest and therefore building on the breeding efforts in Uganda of more than 17 years suggests a logical approach to breeding against a new disease. Further notable breeding efforts have assessed the response of advanced cassava genetics to field infection by CBSD (Mukiibi *et al*., 2019). This led to the identification of promising superior cassava clones for downstream breeding against CBSD, which can be combined with locally adapted cassava germplasm and integrated into ongoing CBSD-breeding efforts in Zambia. Another promising approach to alleviate the spread of CBSD in Zambia is community phytosanitation, which was used to eradicate the presence of the disease in Uganda when it first appeared in the country (Jameson, 1964). Under localized and varying levels of disease incidence, phytosanaitation can be applied effectively to protect disease-free regions, prevent a spike in low disease incidence areas and reduce incidence in the medium- to high-CSBD affected areas. Out of four traditional cassava-growing provinces in Zambia, CBSD’s presence is officially confirmed in the Northern and Luapula provinces. It is suspected that the disease is present in selected areas of north-western and western provinces.

title: 'Cassava Brown Streak Disease in Zambia: An Integrated Approach to Managing
section: Current Efforts to Manage CBSD in Zambia
text: Out of four traditional cassava-growing provinces in Zambia, CBSD’s presence is officially confirmed in the Northern and Luapula provinces. It is suspected that the disease is present in selected areas of north-western and western provinces. This localized and sporadic prevalence of CBSD within the affected provinces creates an opportunity to design a tailored community phytosanitation response for mitigating disease impacts. Success of community phytosanitation, however, requires multi-stakeholder awareness that should enhance coordinated action. Presently in Zambia, there is still a general paucity of information on CBSD despite the awareness efforts so far implemented. This is because of the limited span of time within which the awareness campaign has been implemented as well the targeted nature of most activities, which focussed primarily on the most affected districts and value-chain actors. Thus, CBSD awareness-raising campaigns are still required both to reach a wider audience and to reinforce key messages that will elicit meaningful action from stakeholders. An assessment is underway to determine the level of impact of the CBSD awareness campaign and inform the next steps that should ensure increased impact. The absence of a formal, functional, accessible and certified propagule system for cassava was foreseen as one of the major impediments to the use of disease-free planting materials by farmers. This implies that prospects exist for mitigating CBSD impacts through a regulated cassava propagule system such as the one in operation for seed maize in Zambia. A reliable propagule system would provide a credible source for recommended cassava planting material for farmers. Establishing a certified propagule system involves various activities and the participation of various multi-sectoral partners including farmers, extensionists, researchers, government regulatory institutions and private sector institutions.

title: 'Cassava Brown Streak Disease in Zambia: An Integrated Approach to Managing
section: Current Efforts to Manage CBSD in Zambia
text: Establishing a certified propagule system involves various activities and the participation of various multi-sectoral partners including farmers, extensionists, researchers, government regulatory institutions and private sector institutions. Collaborative action from identified stakeholders is possible when there is a unified purpose underlined by a good understanding of the devastating nature of CBSD to the cassava subsector as evidenced by the experience in many affected countries. The application of advanced molecular tools in agriculture presents future prospects for dealing with CBSD, although biotechnology is still a subject of considerable contention in Zambia and other countries in Africa. Among the promising transgenic approaches, host-induced gene silencing (HIGS), is favoured because the resulting plants do not produce a new protein but resistance is specific to the targeted pathogen (Collinge and Sarrocco, 2021). In the particular case of CBSD, post-translational gene silencing (PTGS) has been demonstrated to successfully enhance disease resistance in cassava grown in field and greenhouse trials (Ogwok *et al*., 2012; Vanderschuren *et al*., 2012). Unfortunately, biotechnology techniques in their entirety have limited application in Zambia as regulated by the Biosafety Act No. 10 of 2007 (UNEP-LEAP, 2007). Currently, this Act prohibits the application of transgenesis for crops of strategic importance and this includes cassava, which is Zambia’s second most important staple (Chikoti *et al*., 2019). However, aspects of biotechnology that are permissible by the act, such as viral strain diagnosis, marker-assisted selection in breeding and investigations into the nature of disease resistance that do not result in genetically modified crops can still be applied to fast-track progress in research. Overall, more successful management of CBSD in Zambia and similar agro-ecologies entails a multi-faceted, multi-sectoral, collaborative and well-coordinated approach.

title: 'Cassava Brown Streak Disease in Zambia: An Integrated Approach to Managing
section: Current Efforts to Manage CBSD in Zambia
text: Overall, more successful management of CBSD in Zambia and similar agro-ecologies entails a multi-faceted, multi-sectoral, collaborative and well-coordinated approach. This should integrate various methods of disease control preferably in the order of cultural, host-resistance and biocontrol as suggested by Collinge and Sarrocco (2021). This should enable an effective, sustainable, inclusive and nature positive response to the CBSD challenge and the growth of the cassava subsector for improved food security.

title: 'Cassava Brown Streak Disease in Zambia: An Integrated Approach to Managing
text: The invasive CBSD is among the most serious biotic challenges faced by cassava farmers in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). In Zambia, the spread of the disease is exacerbated by many factors. Notably, the traditional farming systems that promote the exchange of planting material and limited application of recommended agronomic practices by farmers owing to the informal status of the cassava value chain. There are prospects for effective management of CBSD to mitigate spread and offset substantial yield losses. However, there are prerequisites to be met for the identified management options to effectively address the management of the disease. Key among them is the need to develop suitable tolerant cassava cultivars for use by farmers and to implement a collaborative and coordinated community phytosanitation plan that is anchored on adequate information dissemination to stakeholders. Overall, CBSD presents an opportunity to establish a functional, inclusive, sustainable and certified propagule system for cassava that will integrate modern technology in agriculture to ensure the viability of the cassava sub-sector.

### Overview ###
The desert locust outbreak in 2019/2020 put 42.3 million people across East, West and South-west Africa in ‘crisis or worse’ for food security. Biopesticides can be highly effective against locusts and do not have detrimental environmental impacts. Despite this, their use is relatively limited compared to chemical pesticides – only Somalia employed chiefly biopesticides during the 2019/2020 outbreak. This case examines strategies to improve the uptake of sustainable biocontrol measures.

text: 1. Describe the advantages and challenges of using biopesticides for locust control. 2. Detail how biopesticides based on *Metarhizium acridum* work. 3. Explain how and why biopesticides were deployed in the 2019/2020 locust outbreak.

title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
text:
The desert locust, *Schistocerca gregaria* Forsskål (Orthoptera: Acrididae), usually lives in a solitary form across a band of nations from Mauritania in the west of Africa across the Sahelian countries to Sudan, through Middle Eastern nations such as Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Oman and United Arab Emirates, to southern parts of Iran and Pakistan and the north-western part of India (Showler, 2009) (Fig. 1). Solitary desert locusts live as scattered individuals across 25 countries, in an area of around 16 million km2 of desert (WMO-No. 1175, 2016). ##### Fig. 1. #####
The range of the desert locust, *Schistocerca gregaria* in solitary (dark green) and gregarious (light green) forms. Desert locusts lay their eggs in pods around 10–15 cm below the soil surface. The eggs hatch in 10–65 days. When heavy rains follow a period of drought, many eggs may hatch simultaneously and the insect may become extremely numerous and shift to its gregarious form (Fig. 2). ##### Fig. 2. #####
A gregarious phase adult desert locust. Source: Wikimedia Commons. The locust can change from one form to another at any stage of its life cycle. The hatchlings, called hoppers, go through five nymphal stages in the gregarious form and six nymphal stages in the solitary form. The locusts cannot fly until they become adults. Immature adults take around 3–4 weeks to mature into mating adults and the female lays, on average, 3 egg pods – with around 80 eggs per pod – in her lifetime (3–5 weeks).

title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
text:
Immature adults take around 3–4 weeks to mature into mating adults and the female lays, on average, 3 egg pods – with around 80 eggs per pod – in her lifetime (3–5 weeks). The duration of the life cycle is highly dependent on environmental conditions such as rainfall, moist sandy soils and vegetation and so can range from 3 to 5 months. Hopper bands of gregarious nymphs can march long distances – 4th instar bands have been measured to travel from 200 to 1700 m in one day (Symmons and Cressman, 2001). Gregarious adults form locust swarms that can travel 100 km or more in one day, primarily following the wind direction. Swarms can contain 40–80 million locusts in less than half a square mile (National Geographic, 2020). These locusts have longer wings than the solitary form and tend to migrate in huge swarms outside the insect’s normal solitary range, potentially heading south to Tanzania and as far east as China (Fig. 1). The area the locusts live in, and the number of countries affected, may double, representing about 20% of the Earth’s land mass (WMO-No. 1175, 2016). The solitary and gregarious phases look as if they are different species – gregarious adults are bright pink when immature and bright yellow when mature whereas immature solitary adults are a pale grey or beige, and the males turn pale yellow on maturity (Fig. 3). ##### Fig. 3. #####
Immature solitary adult desert locust. Source: Wikimedia Commons. In 2018, heavy rains due to cyclones led to favourable breeding conditions for the desert locust (Fig. 4). This went unnoticed until the first locust swarms appeared in January 2019. The FAO Locust Watch reports (FAO, 2020b) give a good summary of the 2018/2020 outbreak.

In the 2020 outbreak, locust swarms across the Horn of Africa consumed as much as 1.76 MT per day (FAO, 2020b). Locusts will eat crops including sugarcane, other root crops, maize, sorghum, wheat and vegetables (Retkute *et al*., 2021). The swarms resulted in over 42 million people facing severe acute food insecurity in 2020 in ten targeted countries (Food Security Information Network, 2020), with over 1.7 million hectares targeted for control of the desert locust.
