title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
text: Traditionally, chemical pesticides have been used to manage locusts, particularly during outbreaks. However, these can be detrimental to natural predators of the locust, other wildlife, humans, livestock and the environment. Chemical pesticides were used heavily during the 1986–1989 locust plagues. In 1989, as a result of concerns over this use, a project to develop biopesticides against locusts was set up. The LUBILOSA (LUtte BIologique contre les LOcustes et SAuteriaux – biological control of locusts and grasshoppers) project was funded by the governments of Canada (CIDA), the Netherlands (DGIS), Switzerland (SDC), UK (DFID, now FCDO) and the USA (USAID). The project was executed by CAB International, the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture, INSAH (part of CILSS), AGRHYMET/DFPV (part of CILSS) and GTZ (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Technische Zusammenarbeit). LUBILOSA cost US$13.5 million (£10.2 million) (Bateman *et al*., 2017). During the 13 years it ran, LUBILOSA developed a bioprotection product based on fungal spores of *Metarhizium acridum*  (formerly *Metarhizium flavoviride* Gams & Rozsypal (Deuteromycotina: Hyphomycetes))*. * Fungi were seen as the obvious choice as they can be produced in artificial culture in large quantities and applied using standard spray equipment. That said, fungi have always been perceived as rather unreliable and needing humid conditions to work well. One of the principal successes of the LUBILOSA project was overcoming the requirement for high environmental humidity by spraying fungal spores in oil, making the treatment suitable for desert conditions.

title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
text:
One of the principal successes of the LUBILOSA project was overcoming the requirement for high environmental humidity by spraying fungal spores in oil, making the treatment suitable for desert conditions. The use of oil brings its own environmental considerations (Müller *et al*., 2021). Once they come into contact with a locust, spores of *Metarhizium acridum* attach to its body and extend a penetration peg that, through a combination of protease action and mechanical pressure, penetrates the insect cuticle and grows down into the haemolymph (Fig. 5). There the fungus grows profusely. After 3–4 days the locusts have severely reduced feeding and movement. Depending on the environmental conditions, they die within ca. 7–14 days. If the temperature is between 20 and 30°C, the fungus will grow faster and the locust will die sooner. Once dead, the locust turns pink and if there is high humidity, spores may emerge between its segments (Fig. 6) in a process known as external sporulation (mycosis). The dead locusts are very brittle and easily break apart, releasing more spores into the environment that can infect and kill other locusts through ‘secondary pick-up’. ##### Fig. 5. #####
How a *Metarhizium acridum-based* bioprotection product (Green Muscle®) kills locusts and grasshoppers. Here an adult locust is shown, however, the product works equally well on nymphs and juveniles. ##### Fig. 6. #####
A dead locust infected by *Metarhizium acridum*. The green spores exit the body in between the segments on the locust and the body becomes very fragile. Note the slight pink tinge to the abdomen. This is a common sign of fungal infection. © CABI.

The green spores exit the body in between the segments on the locust and the body becomes very fragile. Note the slight pink tinge to the abdomen. This is a common sign of fungal infection. © CABI. The biopesticide product survives for around 1 month on vegetation in the field (Milner and Hunter, 2001); new locusts entering the area pick up fungal spores and die in turn. They also become infected with spores from dead locusts via secondary pick-up. Together these two factors mean that one application per agricultural season is normally enough to control locusts. Modern synthetic chemical pesticides, in contrast, often need repeated treatments; although *Metarhizium* does not have the ‘knock down’ effect of a chemical pesticide and takes longer to kill locusts initially, it is longer-lasting. By the end of one trial, 22 weeks after application, the Senegalese grasshopper (*Oedaleus senegalensis* Krauss (Orthoptera: Acrididae)) population treated with chemicals was back up to ten insects per square metre (Fig. 7), the same level as before spraying, whereas the population treated with *Metarhizium* still only had one locust per square metre (Langewald *et al*., 1999). ##### Fig. 7. #####

(1999). *Metarhizium acridum* spores only grow if they touch locusts and grasshoppers.

title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
text: Adapted from Langewald *et al*. (1999). *Metarhizium acridum* spores only grow if they touch locusts and grasshoppers. Under field conditions eco-toxicological studies demonstrated no negative effects on non-target organisms such as ring-necked pheasant chicks (Smits *et al*., 1999) and the fringed toed lizard (Peveling and Demba, 2009). Tests carried out by LOCUSTOX, Senegal, by Agriculture Canada, and by LUBILOSA, found that neither birds nor fish were affected by the fungus. Similarly, there were no infections in beetles (Coleoptera) or bugs (Heteroptera) and normal field rates constitute a very low risk to honey bees. No strains caused infections in mammals, and the strains recommended for use gave no adverse reactions. However, normal precautions should be taken to avoid inhalation and contact with the eyes to avoid allergic reactions. The product is now available commercially as Green Muscle®. It has been recommended for use in environmentally sensitive areas and near water courses by the Pesticide Referee Group since 1996 (Anon, 1997).

title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
text: Green Muscle is supplied as a dry powder (technical concentrate [TC] formulation) and is suspended in oil in the field. The resultant suspension is applied using conventional ultra low volume (ULV) spinning disk spray equipment either hand-held, vehicle-mounted or aerially, in a similar manner to the way that chemical pesticides would be applied. It is imperative that spray tanks are cleaned well before use, especially if they have been used for spraying a chemical pesticide, the residue of which may damage the fungal spores of the mycoinsecticide. Green Muscle is delivered at a rate of 1–2 l/ha, with a spore application rate of 50g/ha. A 5 kg bag of fungal spores is, therefore, enough to treat 100 ha. Green Muscle was used against locusts in a large field operation for the first time in 2009, to treat 10,000 ha of wetlands in Tanzania where red locusts (*Nomadacris septemfasciata* (Orthoptera: Acrididae)) threatened an outbreak. This averted the risk to the food crops of around 15 million people in Eastern and Southern Africa, while still protecting wildlife and the environment (FAO, 2009). Following this success, in 2013 mycoinsecticides were applied in response to a desert locust upsurge in Israel. The upsurge was largely controlled within the first week (FAO, 2013). A large-scale trial of mycoinsecticides has also taken place over 60,000 ha in Madagascar.

section: Use of Biopesticides during the 2019/2020 Outbreak
text: Éléphant Vert acquired the licence and right to produce and sell mycoinsecticides in April 2019. Éléphant Vert also produces and sells Novacrid, a mycoinsecticide based on a different isolate of *Metarhzium acridum* that controls locusts and grasshoppers. Due to delays in obtaining a licence to import *Metarhzium acridum* isolate into Morocco, production of the biopesticide did not start until the end of 2019/beginning of 2020. This coincided with the 2019/2020 desert locust outbreak and delayed bioprotection products from reaching the market. The 10th session of the Pesticide Referee Group (PRG) recommended that *Metarhizium acridum* should be considered the most appropriate control option for desert locust (Anon, 2015). However, despite this recommendation, only 1.2% of control during the 2019/2020 desert locust outbreak used bioprotection products. Insecticide operations began in March 2020 and by March 2021 officials in Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Uganda and Yemen had sprayed 1.8 million litres of pesticides (Müller *et al*., 2021). Most of these insecticides were synthetic and from the organophosphate class including chlorpyrifos, fenitrothion and malathion, and the pyrethroid, deltamethrin (Müller *et al*., 2021). This raises concerns about impacts on health and the environment. Almost 96% of the pesticides delivered by the time Müller *et al*. section: Use of Biopesticides during the 2019/2020 Outbreak
text: Adapted from the FAO dashboard on locust control. Available at: <http://www.fao.org/locusts/response-overview-dashboard/en/> (accessed 9 November 2023). During the first part of the 2019/2020 outbreak, bioprotection products were not applied, partly due to lack of availability and partly because governments chose conventional chemical pesticides instead. Later in the outbreak, *Metarhizium acridum*-based products were available and were used as the main method of control in Somalia with good effect (Owuor and McRae, 2022), where they were applied to over 155,000 ha. In Somalia, *Metarhizium* was used in at least 76.5% of the controlled area (Retkute *et al*., 2021). Somalia also used the insect growth regulator Teflubenzuron, which is toxic to bees and other beneficial insects as well as other invertebrates and aquatic organisms (Müller *et al*., 2021). The Somali government is said to have chosen *Metarhizium* to protect the nomadic pastoralists who occupy about two-third of the country (Owuor and McRae, 2022). It appears that the environment may not have been Somalia’s sole consideration in avoiding conventional pesticides. Those such as chlorpyrifos contain neuro-toxins and are related to chemical warfare nerve agents. As such, they are banned in Somalia due to the ongoing conflict there (Müller *et al*., 2021). Somalia does not require registration of *Metarhizium acridum*-based bioprotection products before use but getting an import licence for such products to Somalia was a challenge in 2020, due in part to COVID-19.

title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
section: Use of Biopesticides during the 2019/2020 Outbreak
text: Somalia does not require registration of *Metarhizium acridum*-based bioprotection products before use but getting an import licence for such products to Somalia was a challenge in 2020, due in part to COVID-19. Following the use of an early warning and modelling system, Somalia had agreed on a delivery schedule with the manufacturers for a 12-month period in advance, ensuring sufficient supply (Owuor and McRae, 2022). As a result of this use of biopesticides in Somalia, the FAO recommends applying *Metarhizium acridum* in the morning and evening when desert locusts are more subdued (and when the temperatures are below 30°C so that the ULV spray droplets hit the ground rather than being lifted upwards by heat convection), as well as earlier in the breeding season for easier targeting before larger and more mobile swarms form (Owuor and McRae, 2022). The technique can be particularly effective against hopper bands. Kenya obtained a provisional permit for *Metarhizium acridum*-based bioprotection for the 2019/2020 outbreak. Again Covid-19 delayed this process.

title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
section: Challenges and Opportunities of Applying Biopesticides
text:
### Costs ###
At the time, Green Muscle was sold at US$272/kg product plus transport costs. Transport costs varied depending on the country. For example, to get *Metarhizium acridum*-based bioprotection product to Somalia, which was challenging, cost $30/kg product in July 2020. However, for Kenya the transport costs were $13/kg product in the same month. Green Muscle is applied at a recommended rate of 50 g/ha. Hence cost per ha of applying GM is $13.60 plus transport costs (making Kenya $14.25/ha and Somalia $15.10/ha). The cost of disposal of the Green Muscle containers is very little as the empty sachets can be burned. Somalia procured 4000 l of *Metarhizium acridum*-based bioprotection product, enough to treat 80,000 ha (Cressman, 2020, personal communication). Some chemical pesticides would require 80,000 l to treat that same area (Available at: <https://www.soci.org/chemistry-and-industry/cni-data/2020/11/plague-of-locusts>, accessed 9 November 2023). Comparing the direct costs of obtaining and applying biopesticides to those of obtaining and applying chemical pesticides does not provide a full picture, however. According to Müller *et al*. (2021), it is an imperative to understand the ‘true cost’ of controlling the 2019/2021 outbreak – not just the fiscal costs but also the expected prohibitive costs to the environment and to human health caused by such toxic pesticides. Once the true cost is considered, the researchers say a compelling case can be made to the multilateral system for creating better global governance and investing in the underpinning early warning and control systems to eventually relegate harmful pesticides to redundancy.

title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
section: Challenges and Opportunities of Applying Biopesticides
text:
The true cost includes the indirect costs that are generally external to the individual decision maker as they are absorbed by society. Leach *et al*. (2015) used true cost accounting to analyse the locust outbreak from 2003 to 2005 in Senegal. The researchers split these costs into four categories: *environment* (soil and drinking water contamination, wildlife losses, obsolete stock disposal, loss of beneficial arthropods), *human health* (intoxications), *production losses* (domestic mammal and poultry losses, honey and wax losses, pollinator losses, fish losses, and crop losses due to heavy contamination), and *damage prevention costs* (communication, human health monitoring, environment monitoring and development of alternatives). When Leach *et al*. (2015) assessed the external costs of bioprotection products they concluded that the cost was predicted to be $0.16 (€0.12 quoted in Leach *et al*., 2015 work) per hectare in comparison to the chemical average of $33.74 (€28.17 quoted in Leach *et al*., 2015 work) per hectare of the active ingredient. So even though bioprotection products may be more expensive to buy than some chemical pesticide treatments, when the external costs are added this can, in most cases, make bioprotection products cheaper. It is important for Governments to take these external costs into consideration by reviewing the longer-term effects of chemical pesticide application in a similar manner to Leach *et al*. (2015). ### Funding ###
There is sometimes hesitancy to use biopesticides due to the perceived slow kill rate and efficacy, and a general lack of knowledge about using bioprotection products. In order to avoid such extensive use of chemical pesticides and to achieve better control of the desert locust, preventative application should be encouraged.

title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
section: Challenges and Opportunities of Applying Biopesticides
text:
In order to avoid such extensive use of chemical pesticides and to achieve better control of the desert locust, preventative application should be encouraged. It is important to support governments in understanding the importance of surveillance of the desert locust (using tools such as eLocust3 (FAO, 2016)) and potentially of yearly applications of biopesticide to small hopper bands in known breeding sites, and using the product after ‘favourable’ rains, so that earlier control can take place. Donors are very generous in funding locust control in times of emergency: for the 2019/2020 outbreak, the donor community (including country donations and organisations) donated US$200.5 million (Available at: <http://www.fao.org/locusts/response-overview-dashboard/en/>, accessed 9 November 2023) to control the desert locust outbreaks in 22 countries. However, during recessions, when desert locust numbers are low, it is difficult to obtain funding that could potentially be used to stop desert locust outbreaks from occurring. Providing funds to deliver preventative desert locust control, such as spraying small emerging hopper bands before they have a chance to migrate, breed and form larger bands, could greatly reduce damage by the desert locust. ### Availability ###
The availability of bioprotection products is a significant hurdle. On average it takes 6 weeks to produce fungal bioprotection products, which is a real challenge when the product is needed urgently to deal with a locust outbreak. It is not financially viable for any commercial company to keep large stocks of products available just in case there is an outbreak of desert locusts, especially when these only happen every 7–10 years. One possible solution is for donors or the FAO to purchase bioprotection products during recession years. This would give producers time to make bioprotection products that could be stored for future use.

title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
section: Challenges and Opportunities of Applying Biopesticides
text:
One possible solution is for donors or the FAO to purchase bioprotection products during recession years. This would give producers time to make bioprotection products that could be stored for future use. Bioprotection products are living organisms and have a shelf-life; they can be stored for at least 1 year at 5 °C and often longer, depending on the isolate. As a result, they would need to be used on a rolling stock basis, with any purchaser receiving the oldest product first and replacing the donor/FAO stock – in most years there are locust or grasshopper bands that need to be controlled even if there is not an outbreak. This would enable bioprotection products to be readily available for any potential desert locust outbreak and permit early spraying of hopper bands. ### Monitoring and early detection ###
Bioprotection products and chemical pesticides are most effective when applied to hoppers as a preventative control treatment before locusts become mature adults and can swarm. Monitoring and early detection is particularly important for bioprotection products as they take longer to kill the locust nymphs compared to chemical pesticides. In the past, monitoring has mainly been carried out by human scouts. However, as breeding grounds are often in remote places it is not always possible to spot newly hatched locusts. The locusts can then develop and breed undisturbed – as they did in 2018 – and eventually form swarms and outbreaks as seen in 2020. Modelling can help overcome this problem.

title: Improving Uptake of Biopesticides for Desert Locust Control
text: Biopesticides can provide highly effective, long-lasting control of the desert locust without detriment to the environment. However, their uptake has been slow and governments need additional persuasion to apply them while consumers need extra information and training. The use of biopesticides as a preventative measure before locust outbreaks occur would be most effective. Donors require encouragement to provide funding for the production and storage of biopesticides during recession years so that they are readily available when outbreaks do occur.

### Overview ###
Having arrived on the African continent in 2008, the tomato leafminer (TLM), *Tuta* (*Phthorimaea*) *absoluta* is now officially present in at least 37 African countries and has become the most important tomato pest on the continent. This case looks at the crop loss and pesticide use and cost findings from a household survey held in Zambia and Kenya in 2018 and the implications for the sustainable management of TLM.

1. Describe the impact of TLM on tomatoes. 2. Compare smallholder farmer responses to TLM in Zambia and Kenya*. *

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text: Worldwide production of the tomato (*Solanum lycopersicum* L) was 182 million tonnes in 2017. The tomato is the most consumed fruit in Africa, both in its raw and processed forms. Tomato production is particularly significant to women as they contribute to over 60% of the tomato production labour force (Villareal, 1980). Africa produces 37.8 million tonnes of tomatoes each year (FAOSTAT, 2017); Egypt, Nigeria, Tunisia and Morocco are the biggest producers. The African continent does not produce enough tomatoes to meet its own needs and spends US$ 645 million each year on imports of tomatoes and related products (FAOSTAT, 2017). The tomato leafminer (TLM), *Tuta (Phthorimaea*) *absoluta* (Meyrick), also known as the South American tomato pinworm, is currently the most important tomato pest in North and sub-Saharan Africa. The pest has spread and established in many countries mainly because of its high dispersal ability and reproductive rate, short life cycle, and ability to withstand a wide range of environmental conditions. Its primary host is tomato but the insect can also feed on other members of the Solanaceae family. TLM first arrived on the African continent in 2008, in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia (Brévault *et al*., 2014). The species (Figs. 1 and 2) probably travelled from South America, where it is native to Peru (Meyrick, 1917), via Spain, where it was reported in 2006 (Desneux *et al*., 2011).

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text:
The species (Figs. 1 and 2) probably travelled from South America, where it is native to Peru (Meyrick, 1917), via Spain, where it was reported in 2006 (Desneux *et al*., 2011). It is now present in at least 37 of the 54 African countries (Mansour *et al*., 2018) as well as throughout Europe and the Middle East, South America outside Peru (Campos *et al*., 2017) and China and parts of Asia (Zhang *et al*., 2020), with the latest invasion reported in Togo (Fiaboe *et al*., 2021). TLM has been reported in Costa Rica and may further spread into North America. Ecological niche models have projected large suitable areas for TLM establishment in the Southern Hemisphere under current and future climatic scenarios, and the risk is expected to increase in Europe, the USA, greater parts of Southern Africa, and some parts of Asia in the future (Azrag *et al*., 2023). Indeed, given the rapid spread across Asia and Africa, increased incidences of human-aided movements of pests accidentally or through trade observed with other pests, geographic proximity to invaded countries, and absence of geographic barriers, countries such as New Zealand, the United States, and Australia could eventually be invaded. Large areas with large monocultures of tomatoes and other host plants could then abet the establishment. ##### Fig. 1. #####
Adult tomato leafminer (TLM). Courtesy of CABI. It is hard to detect infestations of TLM early as the larvae are internal feeders and develop inside the plants’ leaves, stems or fruits (Karadjova *et al*., 2013) (Fig. 3).

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text:
It is hard to detect infestations of TLM early as the larvae are internal feeders and develop inside the plants’ leaves, stems or fruits (Karadjova *et al*., 2013) (Fig. 3). In leaves, larvae feed on the mesophyll layer, creating irregular mines on the surface of the leaf and harming the plant’s capacity for photosynthesis. The damaged leaves shrivel, further harming photosynthetic capacity. In severe attacks, the leaves can even look burnt. Other common signs of TLM damage include: puncture marks, abnormal shape, exit holes (Fig. 4), rot due to secondary inective agents (the mines and galleries in the stems and fruits can be entry routes for pathogens, further increasing the damage and cost of control, and lowering the market value of the fruits (EPPO, 2005; Garzia *et al*., 2012; Campos *et al*., 2017), and frass (fine powdery material that insects pass as waste after they digest plant parts). Mature larvae (third to fourth instar) can feed on all parts of the plant, resulting in significant damage. At high densities, TLM larvae will bore into the plant stem and fruits. The pest, a Lepidopteran, also feeds directly on the growing bud of the plant which kills or halts the development of the plant, directly compromising crop yield (Desneux *et al*., 2010; Campos *et al*., 2017). ##### Fig. 2. #####

Overall, TLM can lead to severe damage to young plants and significant yield losses of tomatoes and other crops, including reductions in crop quality. Yield losses normally range from 11 to 43% but in some places, the entire crop may be lost. Farmers lose income both directly because the moth reduces their marketable yield and indirectly as they must spend money on pest management. Consumers, meanwhile, will see increased tomato prices and perhaps even long-term effects from the misuse of pesticides. Countries exporting produce to the European Union (EU) may be required to apply mandatory phytosanitary procedures since TLM is recommended for regulation as a quarantine pest in the EU. Such procedures add extra costs for exporters and the National Plant Protection Organization. ##### Fig. 4. #####

section: Survey of Farmers in Kenya and Zambia
text: CABI, in partnership with Kenya Agricultural Research Organization (KARLO), county governments, and the Zambia Agricultural Research Institute (ZARI), conducted household surveys of farmers in Kenya and Zambia during August and September 2018 to understand their knowledge, attitudes and practices towards TLM. The survey reached 400 farm households in Kenya and 426 in Zambia that had grown tomato crops in 2017 and 2018. Between 97.9 and 99% of farmers reported TLM as a problem in their tomato fields. They also mentioned tomato blight, whiteflies and bacterial wilt. Farmers in Kenya said they had lived with TLM longer than the farmers in Zambia, which tallies with the dates the pest was first reported in each country. The survey indicated that infestation rates were lower in Kenya than in Zambia; 53% of farmers in Kenya reported a minor part of the crop to be infested, while in Zambia about 50% of farmers reported that a major part or the entire area of their tomato crop was affected. On average, 57% of farmers in Zambia indicated they had lost a big proportion of their crop to TLM, compared to 41% of farmers in Kenya. Based on farmers’ own estimates, the mean seasonal production loss due to TLM was at least 114,000 tonnes for Kenya and 10,700 tonnes for Zambia. This translates to economic losses of US$ 59.3 million and US$ 8.7 million for Kenya and Zambia, respectively. Estimates for 12 selected countries – Kenya, Zambia, Nigeria, Tanzania, Mozambique, Benin, Senegal, Rwanda, Niger, Mali, Ethiopia, Malawi – taken together suggest that TLM results in losses for sub-Saharan Africa tomato production of at least 1.05 million tonnes annually out of an expected production of 3.64 million tonnes. That equates to losses of at least US$ 791.5 million annually, of the total expected value of US$ 2,737 million.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
section: Survey of Farmers in Kenya and Zambia
text: That equates to losses of at least US$ 791.5 million annually, of the total expected value of US$ 2,737 million. These figures are based on farmer responses and could be an overestimate. More specific field research studies are recommended to fully understand the economic repercussion of TLM using specific yield loss experiments and modelling, taking into cognizance other factors such as climate change. To control TLM, 96.5% of farmers surveyed in Kenya used pesticides, as did 97.6% of farmers in Zambia. However, only 27.2 and 17.2% of farmers in Kenya and Zambia, respectively, indicated that these pesticide treatments were efficient. About 6.4% of farmers used highly hazardous pesticides, with up to three such products recorded in Zambia and one product in Kenya. The common molecules are Chlorantraniliprole, Flubendiamide and Alphacypermethrin in Kenya, while in Zambia, products with the molecules Emamectin benzoate, Flubendiamide and Abamectin are the most widely used. In the Mediterranean region, the common pesticides are diamides (chlorantraniliprole, cyantraniliprole), avermectins (abamectin, and emamectin benzoate), spinosyns (spinosad), oxadiazines (indoxacarb) and semicarbazones (metaflumizone) (Roditakis *et al*., 2018). In Kenya, most farmers (73.1%) applied between one and five insecticide sprays per season, while in Zambia, 33.9% of farmers applied between six and ten insecticide sprays.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
section: Survey of Farmers in Kenya and Zambia
text: In Kenya, most farmers (73.1%) applied between one and five insecticide sprays per season, while in Zambia, 33.9% of farmers applied between six and ten insecticide sprays. Kenyan households spent an average of Kenyan Shillings (KES) 4864 (US$ 47.2), which is approximately US$ 33.7/ha, against TLM. In Zambia, the average amount spent on pesticides per household was Zambia Kwacha (ZMW) 504 (US$ 42.1), approximately US$ 9.4/ha – more than three times less than Kenya. In terms of cost per spray, the average farmer in Kenya spent KES 1250 (US$ 12.3), whereas in Zambia each spray cost ZMW 43 (US$ 4.2). Regarding pesticide safety, 34.8% of farmers in Kenya and 38.3% in Zambia did not use any personal protective equipment. Skin itching was one of the most frequently reported side effects of pesticide use; it was experienced by 30.6% of farmers in Kenya and 24.8% in Zambia. Using broad-spectrum insecticides against pests is unsustainable and likely to lead to widespread development of resistance, contamination of fruits with pesticide residues, and human and environmental health hazards. In South America, extensive use of synthetic insecticides led TLM to develop resistance to all classes of insecticides (Guedes *et al*., 2019). This is likely to be the case in Africa too unless a sound integrated pest management (IPM) approach is implemented. Households reported using pesticides, pheromone traps, destroying infected plants, staking, organic pesticide and crushing larvae as methods to monitor and control the moth and its larvae.

text:
Courtesy of CABI (Available at: [https://www.cabi.org/Uploads/CABI/about-us/Scientists%20output/WP12\_tuta\_evidence\_note.pdf, accessed 7 December 2023](https://www.cabi.org/Uploads/CABI/about-us/Scientists%20output/WP12_tuta_evidence_note.pdf)). ### Pheromone lures ###
#### Monitoring using pheromones ####
Female TLMs release pheromones that attract males for mating purposes. Sex pheromones are in wide use to detect and monitor insect pests, including TLM (Witzgall *et al*., 2010). Pheromone traps can provide an early warning of an infestation and indicate TLM densities at low-population to medium-level infestation levels. Captures show the presence of the pest and when its seasonal flight period starts, which is important in determining the threshold levels either for the timing of control procedures or for deciding whether or not to take remedial action (Witzgall *et al*., 2010). For heavy infestations, pheromone traps tend to give high levels of capture, which makes data collection difficult, and alternative products with a lower capture rate may be more suitable. Cost: A smallholder grower will require one pheromone trap; this includes a paper sticker for catching the moths (US$ 0.5), a pheromone (US$ 3) and a trap at US$ 3 (total: US$ 6.5).

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text:
#### Mass trapping using pheromones ####
Pheromones can also be employed to control the insect, mainly through mass trapping (attracting one or both sexes to a lure inside a large-capacity trap), or through the attract-and-kill option, which uses an insecticide-impregnated target. Pheromones have the benefit of not requiring a pre-harvest interval if this is the only method used. Mass trapping involves placing about 45–50 pheromone traps per hectare of the crop field, in strategic positions to remove a high proportion of male insects from the population and so reduce mating and the number of viable eggs. This can eventually cause the population to reduce significantly. The trap may be a simple bucket trap, containing water at the bottom that drowns any moths that enter. This method is useful in greenhouses, particularly in combination with insect exclusion nets and tight doors. It also has potential for use in open fields. Mass trapping is often used in combination with other control measures to control TLM at a low cost and in an environmentally safe way. So far, light traps for mass trapping of low-medium infestations of TLM have been tried experimentally but are unlikely to suit open-field production by smallholders. A solar-powered trap that combines light and pheromones, in order to maximize trap catch, may also be used. The trap catches female moths as well as males, using a base filled with water and a thin layer of oil. The device should switch on 3–4 h before sunrise in order to maximize its moth catches. Cost: The paper sticker for catching the moths costs about US$ 0.5, pheromones at US$ 3 and the device that holds the whole system at US$ 3 (total: US$ 6.5). Based on 40 traps for 1 ha of open field, the initial cost would reach US$ 260.

text:
Based on 40 traps for 1 ha of open field, the initial cost would reach US$ 260. While modern pheromones are designed to last the cropping cycle, the paper sticker would need to be replaced almost weekly, which would drive the cost of this method far above what a smallholder farmer could afford. However, if farmers were to recycle old plastic bottles and use cheaper water basins and buckets rather than the commercial trap, for instance, the cost is likely to be a little lower. ### Mating disruption using pheromones ###
Although still under development, mating disruption can reduce the number of insecticide sprays needed (Cocco *et al*., 2012). The technique uses synthetic sex pheromones to disorient and disrupt communication between the sexes. As a result, male TLM moths cannot find females to mate with, which delays, reduces, or prevents fertilization of females. The method reportedly confers complete population control with no visible crop damage during the first 4 months of the crop; however, it does not prevent economic losses when applied in the open field or unscreened greenhouses (Vacas *et al*., 2011). Trials revealed that the flight of TLM was satisfactorily disrupted with an initial pheromone dose of 30 g/ha, and levels of damage did not significantly differ from those in reference plots with insecticide treatments (Vacas *et al*., 2011). What’s more, release studies showed that control of damage and flight disruption occurred when releasing at least 85 mg pheromone/ha/day. Cocco *et al*. (2012) showed that mating disruption pheromone dispensers applied at a density of 1000/ha reduced the percentage of damaged fruits by 62–89%.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text:
Cocco *et al*. (2012) showed that mating disruption pheromone dispensers applied at a density of 1000/ha reduced the percentage of damaged fruits by 62–89%. Cost: Mating disruption could be most suited to greenhouse tomato production, where it can saturate the atmosphere in a short time. However, Isonet-T dispensers are still undergoing tests. ### Chemical control ###
Chemical control, using synthetic pesticides, has been the go-to option in the management of TLM (Guedes and Picanço, 2012). Initially, this technique relied on organophosphates, pyrethroids, cartap and abamectin but the focus has shifted to insect growth regulators and, more recently, novel insecticides. Farmers may apply insecticide to control TLM multiple times within one cropping season (Campos *et al*., 2015). However, insecticides have the potential to harm not only the environment but also beneficial organisms (Desneux *et al*., 2007). Chemical residues in fruits are also a concern. Effectiveness: Since larvae live in the mesophyll of tomato plant leaves, it may be hard for insecticides to reach them (Retta and Berhe, 2015), limiting effectiveness. TLM can also develop resistance rapidly; resistant populations have already been recorded in Italy, Greece and Israel (Roditakis *et al*., 2018).

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text:
TLM can also develop resistance rapidly; resistant populations have already been recorded in Italy, Greece and Israel (Roditakis *et al*., 2018). Resistance of TLM has been reported to cartap, abamectin and pyrethroids (Siqueira *et al*., 2000; Siqueira *et al*., 2001; Siqueira *et al*., 2005), organophosphates, spinosad, Emamectin benzoate and abamectin (Guedes and Picanço, 2012), chloride channel activators, benzoylureas (Campos *et al*., 2014) and diamides (Khalid, 2011; Roditakis *et al*., 2015; Silva *et al*., 2016). It is generally prudent to rotate different active pesticide ingredients to avoid build-up of resistance. The suggested active ingredients for rotation in the management of TLM include imidacloprid, indoxacarb, spinosad, deltamethrine (against adult moths) and rynaxypyr. Cost: Small packets and bottles tend to work out more expensive, which ups the effective cost for small-scale farmers. Using synthetic chemicals is likely to reduce profit margins due to the number of sprays required. Less toxic products are usually expensive and are likely to be out of reach of small-scale farmers. Usually, between six and ten insecticide sprays are used per tomato season and applied based on a spray regime rather than TLM infestation levels. The cost could be variable depending on the molecules used, and ranges between US$ 40 and 50 per season, which excludes the labour for spraying that would drive this cost even higher. ### Microbial pesticides ###

text:
### Microbial pesticides ###
Microbial pesticides contain a microorganism (e.g. a bacterium, fungus, virus or protozoan) as the active ingredient. Different microbial pesticides have been found to be effective against TLM (Abd El-Ghany *et al*., 2016), with *Bacillus thuringiensis* var. *kurstaki* (Btk), *Beauveria bassiana* and *Heterorhabditis bacteriophora* (an entomopathogenic nematode) effective against the larvae. Entomopathogenic fungi *Metarhizium anisopliae* and *Beauveria bassiana* can infect all stages of the pest (Moussa *et al*., 2018), causing female mortality of 37 and 68% for *M. anisopliae* and *B. bassiana*, respectively. A baculovirus has also been developed for TLM and registered in countries such as Brazil, Germany, Greece and Cyprus. The product, Tutavir, contains a *Phthorimaea operculella* granulovirus (PhopGV) for selective control of the TLM with up to 81% effectiveness at a rate of 100 ml/ha reported in trials in Italy. Effectiveness: Biopesticides often act more slowly than chemical pesticides, which can reduce their attractiveness to farmers, who like to see dead insects immediately after application to show that the method is working. Since TLM has multiple overlapping generations, multiple sprays/applications are required to control the vulnerable stages. Because they contain a living organism, microbial pesticides are affected by unfavourable conditions (Moussa *et al*., 2018) and may become less effective during storage.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text:
Because they contain a living organism, microbial pesticides are affected by unfavourable conditions (Moussa *et al*., 2018) and may become less effective during storage. Batta (2003) showed that after 4.6 months, the viability of spores of *M. anisopliae* was reduced by 50%. Cost: In Kenya, South Africa, Ethiopia and Ghana, a commercial isolate Met69 is registered for use against TLM. It is available as a total fermented product and a pure spores-in-oil product (Real IPM). A 500ml pack of the spores-in-oil formulation costs about US$ 25 and with an application rate of 200ml/ha at every spray, this cost is likely to be steep for a smallholder. ### Botanicals ###
Plant extracts used in the management of pests may be contact or systemic. Several have been used to control TLM, including azadirachtin, an extract from neem (*Azadirachta indica*) seeds used as a contact insecticide. Effectiveness: Neem extract has been shown to result in a 24.5% egg and 86.7–100% larval mortality of the pest at different concentrations in laboratory studies (Kona *et al*., 2014). In the same study, petroleum ether extract from Jatropha, achieved 18–25% egg and 87%–100% larval death. It is worth noting that the remaining eggs hatched post-4 days’ exposure. In another study in Bulgaria, Neem Azal T/S 0.3% showed very good effectiveness (84.10 and 86.61% respectively) in the greenhouse, both in twofold and threefold treatment in intervals of 7 days against mixed population of larvae 1–4 instars of TLM (Yankova *et al*., 2014).

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text:
Neem oil applied to the adaxial side of the leaves or directly on the larvae has also shown efficacy against TLM. Under greenhouse conditions, neem-corticated seed extracts reduced the percentage infestation of tomato fruits and yield loss to less than 10% (Mahmoud *et al*., 2020). Garlic, basil, thyme, castor bean, eucalyptus, chinaberry, geranium and onion have also been found to exhibit insecticidal activity with different efficacies against TLM larvae (Abd El-Ghany *et al*., 2016; Birhan, 2018). A challenge with extensive use of neem extract is the photosensitivity of azadirachtin, which breaks down or isomerizes under sunlight. As a result, neem has a low residual effect under field conditions (Ahmed, 2007; Madaki, 2015). Also, homemade and other formulations can vary in efficacy due to poor standardization and quality control. For neem and other pesticidal plants, the main cost involved is labour, which on small farms can be provided by family members. Cost: Neem-based products are the most widely available botanical. They cost US$12–15 for 1 l and require repeat applications. The higher cost of botanicals makes it very unlikely that smallholder farmers will purchase such products, particularly if they feel that pesticides work better. Many stockists do not stock botanicals, due to low demand. There is a general lack of awareness about the benefits of the use of botanicals in IPM of insect crops. ### Biological control ###
Several studies have assessed which natural enemies attack TLM and can potentially be used in biological control (see Mansour *et al*. (2018)). Such natural enemies include parasitoids and mirid predators. Mansour *et al*.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text: (2018)). Such natural enemies include parasitoids and mirid predators. Mansour *et al*. (2018) proposed the following strategies: (1) mass-production of natural enemies for regular releases in fields affected by the pest (augmentative biological control); (2) adaptation of specific cultural practices (conservation biological control) and (3) exotic natural enemies from the pest’s native ranges could be introduced in Africa for permanent establishment (classical biological control). Currently, augmentative biological control is being applied exclusively in Northern Africa, where it is exploiting egg parasitoids and predatory bugs such *as Macrolophus pygmaeus*, *Nesidiocoris tenuis*, *Trichogramma pretiosum*, *T. acheae* and *T. euproctidis*. Classical biological control for TLM is also being employed in Africa using an imported larval parasitoid *Dolichogenidea gelechiidivoris*. This parasitoid controls TLM by laying its eggs inside the pest’s caterpillars. The eggs eventually emerge as adult wasps thereby killing the larvae of the pest. Studies of this parasitoid in quarantine suggest that it prefers the early TLM larval instars, with an average parasitism rate of over 60% (the parasitoid has the potential to achieve a parasitism rate of up to 86%). This makes *D. gelichiidivoris* a promising candidate for classical biological control against TLM in Africa. The agent has already been released in Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania (Mohamed *et al*., 2022) and is known to be established in Algeria (Krache *et al*., 2021). Effectiveness: The field parasitism of TLM is generally low in Africa, although in the laboratory parasitism levels can reach 55%.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text: Effectiveness: The field parasitism of TLM is generally low in Africa, although in the laboratory parasitism levels can reach 55%. In Kenya, naturalized parasitoids such as *Stenomesius* sp. near *japonicus* and *Bracon nigricans*, can cause up to 17 and 21% parasitism, respectively (Mama Sambo *et al*., 2022b). Tunisia has reported some successes with biological control, where after releasing a total of 25,000 adults of either parasitoid *Trichogramma cacoeciae* or *T. bourarachae*, a reduction of 87 and 78% in leaf damage, respectively, was observed in greenhouse tomato (Zouba *et al*., 2013). Additionally, the predatory mirid *Nesidiocoris tenuis* significantly reduced the density of TLM eggs in Tunisian greenhouses (Ettaib *et al*., 2016). Importantly, this species can persist on tomato crops even when the density of TLM is low, as it can feed on other insect pests, such as aphids, leaf miners (e.g. *Liriomyza* spp. ), noctuid eggs and young larvae, herbivorous mites (e.g. *Tetranychus* spp.) and (to a lesser extent) thrips (Giorgini *et al*., 2019). Cost: A single inundative release of *Nesidiocoris tenuis* is estimated to cost around US$ 68 for a 100 ml bottle containing 500 adults and nymphs. This probably makes it unattractive for smallholder growers of open-field tomatoes, whose yield is much lower than that of large-scale commercial farms. It is likely that some macrobials could be produced in local rearing units, reducing the cost for the farmer.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text:
It is likely that some macrobials could be produced in local rearing units, reducing the cost for the farmer. Classical biological control, on the other hand, is a one-off investment, and high cost: benefit ratios have been reported for a number of successful programmes. ### Resistant varieties ###
Breeding programmes for tomato cultivars that are resistant to damage by TLM have been active globally since the early 1990s, especially in Brazil (Guedes and Picanço, 2012). Initial research focused on the role of leaf glandular trichomes, with Ecole *et al*. (1999) showing that trichomes produce insecticidal compounds effective against TLM larvae. Recently, research is ongoing into the role of allelochemicals and possible incorporation into commercial varieties of resistant genes from wild types of tomato lost during domestication (De Oliveira *et al*., 2012). Allelochemicals (acyl sugars, zingiberene, and 2-tridecanone) and trichome density have been associated in tomatoes with conferring resistance against TLM and other insect pests (Resende *et al*., 2006; Maluf *et al*., 2010). The presence of acyl sugars, zingiberene, and 2-tridecanone reduced the oviposition rate, plant damage severity, injuries to the leaflets and percentage of leaflets attacked in studies of the resistance of different tomato strains to TLM (De Oliveira *et al*., 2012). Recently, Bt tomato caused high mortality of TLM larvae and a reduced formation of leaf mines (Selale *et al*., 2017). Effectiveness: Pest-resistant tomato may have a role to play in managing TLM but is unlikely to be a sole solution.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text:
Effectiveness: Pest-resistant tomato may have a role to play in managing TLM but is unlikely to be a sole solution. Even after extensive research into breeding resistant varieties, especially in South America, there is little information as to their actual success, especially for commercial use (Zekeya *et al*., 2017). Much less information is available for the African continent and so we do not anticipate this being a suitable approach in the short to medium term. Cost: Bt crops are generally considered to be cost-effective although, depending on how many genes are stacked in the product, resistance could occur after several years. Traditional breeding is likely to cost the farmer less but appears to be a distant technology. ### Netting technology ###
Nets ensure insect pest exclusion. They are able to reduce or eliminate chemical pesticide applications; produce quality and marketable fruits; contain/retain beneficial biocontrol agents; improve seedling germination, survival and transplant quality; and result in microclimate modifications that are important for the tomato crop. Effectiveness: Netting technology can lead to a 70% decrease in chemical sprays by farmers and a 35–70% increase in marketable yield of the tomato. Cost: Tanzanian company A to Z Textile Mills Ltd produces nets locally. A single net can be used for 3–5 years. The growers’ gross margins and return on investment are not yet known; a project in Kenya is currently assessing the scalability of the technology. ### Sterile insect technique (SIT) ###
This environmentally-friendly method is based on the release of sterile irradiated insects to control individuals of the same species (Lachance, 1985). However, the approach is less widely used for moths (Bloem and Carpenter, 2001). Effectiveness: Lepidopteran species are more resistant to the sterilizing effects of radiation than insects of any other order (Lachance, 1985).

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text:
Effectiveness: Lepidopteran species are more resistant to the sterilizing effects of radiation than insects of any other order (Lachance, 1985). That said, Cagnotti *et al*. (2016) achieved a certain level of suppression of a wild TLM population by releasing irradiated insects at an overflooding ratio of 15:1. Cost: SIT is only economically viable if large numbers of sterile insects can be produced cheaply. SIT also requires a special facility. Currently, the only known programme on the African continent for crop pests is in South Africa, where SIT is used for the control of false codling moths in fruit orchards. We believe that control of TLM using SIT in Africa is not likely to be feasible for many years. ### Genetic control ###
A company called Oxitec has developed a proprietary technology, known as RIDL (Release of Insects with Dominant Lethal), that is meant to overcome the limiting constraints of SIT by releasing genetically engineered, male-selecting, self-limiting strains of pest insects. When these self-limiting males mate with wild females, their offspring inherit a copy of a self-limiting gene, resulting in the mortality of female offspring; with sustained releases the target pest population is suppressed. Effectiveness: Further research is still needed for efficient and large-scale insect production and application. Understanding of the field performance of males in dispersing, finding and mating with females, immigration and insect fitness of the self-limiting strains is still needed. Cost: While this technology has been developed for fall armyworm, pink bollworm and diamondback moth, it is still under development for TLM and is unlikely to be feasible for many years, as it will also need to navigate the regulatory requirements of countries with regard to genetic modification of insects. All these factors may have cost implications.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text:
All these factors may have cost implications. ### Integrated pest management ###
Integrated pest management (IPM) involves the careful consideration of all available pest control techniques and the subsequent integration of appropriate measures that discourage the development of pest populations and keep pesticide and other interventions to levels that are economically justified and reduce or minimize risks to human health and the environment. IPM emphasizes the growth of a healthy crop with the least possible disruption to agroecosystems and encourages natural pest control mechanisms (FAO and WHO, 2014). It comprises a combination of all available control measures and strategies: cultural, physical, biological and the judicious use of registered pesticides. For instance, high mortality (~80%) of TLM was achieved when *D. gelechiidivoris* and the fungus *M. anisopliae* ICIPE 20 were used in combination, indicating an additive impact on the target pest (Mama Sambo *et al*., 2022a). Effectiveness: TLM requires an integrated approach as it can develop resistance to any control measure used alone (Mohamadi *et al*., 2017). Several IPM successes have been reported for TLM early-invaded areas (i.e., first report between 2006 and 2012) and newly invaded areas (i.e., first report after 2012) where control programmes have evolved along with the areas and time since invasion with a more rapid shift from chemical control to biological control (Desneux *et al*., 2022). For instance, Giorgini *et al*. (2019) considered that the integration of biological control agents (e.g. mirid predators and egg parasitoids), microbial insecticides (i.e. *Bacillus thuringiensis*), selective chemical insecticides, and sex pheromone-based control proved adequate, especially in tomato greenhouses.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text: *Bacillus thuringiensis*), selective chemical insecticides, and sex pheromone-based control proved adequate, especially in tomato greenhouses. In Egypt, an IPM component involving mass trapping TLM males in red plastic basin traps at a density of eight traps/feddan (4200 sq. m), bi-weekly application of voliam flexi 40% WG (20% Thiamethoxam+ 20% chlorantaniliprole) and Dan top 50% WG (Clothianidin) in sequence during the vegetative stage, and weekly application of Dipel DF 6.4% WG (Bacillus thuringiensis) during the fruiting stage, was found to be more effective in reducing the damage (to between 1 and 5% of fruits) than the use of pheromones only or farmers’ practices (Taha *et al*., 2013). It also emphasized the importance of sex pheromones in an IPM programme. In this same study, the spray/chemical application frequency in the IPM programme was lower than the conventional farmers’ practice, with 11 sprays rather than 16. Crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops helps to breaks the life cycle of TLM. This is a low-cost management strategy, but issues of long seasons and the need for food and income always limit adoption, especially for smallholder farmers. Removing wild relatives from the vicinity of tomatoes will eliminate alternative hosts for TLM, limiting the chances of the pest developing and moving to the next generation. Cultural practices like early scouting and/or monitoring are important in finding the pest early and for decision making. Meanwhile, destroying infested plants and plant parts helps stop the pest from developing to the next life stage.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text: Cultural practices like early scouting and/or monitoring are important in finding the pest early and for decision making. Meanwhile, destroying infested plants and plant parts helps stop the pest from developing to the next life stage. It is also important to inspect packaging equipment to ensure there are no eggs, larvae or pupae that might develop and spread; fruits from foreign countries should hold a phytosanitary certificate. Proper fertilization gives the plant a competitive ability to tolerate pest damage; studies show that TLM develops more slowly in fertilized soils (Mohamadi *et al*., 2017). Irrigation not only provides an optimum environment for plant growth but also drowns the pests. Cost: IPM offers good promise for managing TLM, particularly in the African context, given the production systems that exist. The costs largely depend on the individual combinations of control strategies. Before deciding on the number of combinations, it is important to consider labour, especially where IPM involves multiple sprays, introduction of agents or even cultural practices. Overall, based on its effectiveness, IPM might be the solution for the sustainable management of TLM.

title: Strategies for Sustainable Management of the Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
text: Pesticides remain the key strategy used by farmers for managing TLM in Africa. This widespread use is based on the premise that pesticides offer better control than other management methods, and they are usually easily accessible, largely due to aggressive marketing. However, pesticides should not be considered the main approach for judicious management of TLM. The continuous use of some products may result in insecticide-resistant populations, with farmers coping by using a cocktail of products and in some cases highly hazardous chemicals, in a bid to find what works for them. This could cause acute and chronic human health burdens. Pesticides also harm pollinators and the natural enemies of the TLM, and there is a need to document these negative impacts. Harder to quantify are the health and societal costs of pesticides for TLM control, and hidden impacts such as the economic cost to the country of treatment for pesticide exposure. Pesticide recommendations for TLM should include selecting those materials that may be used with minimal protective clothing (PPE), and that allow re-entry to the field one day or less after application. More effort is needed to promote alternatives that are affordable, readily available, safe, effective, practical to use and combined with training on responsible use, especially pheromones and mass trapping, insect-proof nets, conservation and augmentation of natural enemies, and use of lower-risk products such as biorationals and biopesticides, all within a genuinely balanced IPM strategy.

### Overview ###
Apple snail (*Pomacea canaliculata*) is a freshwater snail indigenous to South America that has spread to become an invasive pest. This case presents the results of a survey of smallholder rice farmers in Mwea Irrigation System in Kenya, with the intention to assess the awareness of the problem, the socio-economic impact that apple snail is having, and the current control methods.

title: Assessment of the Socio-Economic Impacts Associated with the Arrival of Apple
text: Apple snail (*Pomacea canaliculata* (Lamarck, 1819)) is native to South America and was deliberately introduced into East and South-east Asia during the 1980s as a food source for both domestic consumption and export (Constantine *et al*., 2023). Some snails escaped or were released into waterways and irrigation systems, especially when their demand in the market declined. Since then, apple snails have become a serious agricultural pest in rice paddy systems with consequences for yield, livelihoods, biodiversity, ecosystems, and human health. *P. canaliculata* feed on young and emerging rice plants, typically cutting the rice stem at the base and destroying the whole plant (IRRI, 2023). In 2020, *P. canaliculata* was identified in Mwea Irrigation Scheme (MIS) located in Kirinyaga County, Kenya. The pest constitutes a serious economic threat to farmers in Kenya and other rice-growing countries in Africa if it continues to spread (Djeddour *et al*., 2021). This case study is a timely assessment of the current situation among smallholder farmers throughout MIS.

title: Assessment of the Socio-Economic Impacts Associated with the Arrival of Apple
text:
*Pomacea canaliculata* is a yellow-brown to greenish-brown or dark chestnut freshwater snail species, 35–60 mm in height. Adults are sexually dimorphic with females being larger than males. The eggs are spherical, 3 mm in diameter, calcareous, and deep pink-red to orange-pink becoming paler as the calcium hardens (Fig. 1). They are whitish pink just before hatching. Eggs are laid in clutches of 12–1000 (260 average) from a few cm to 2 m above water, on vegetation or other firm substrates. When the eggs hatch, 7–14 days after being laid, the 2.6 mm wide × 2.8 mm tall hatchlings drop into the water below where they feed on algae and organic detritus (Cowie, 2013). ##### Fig. 1. #####
Apple snail laying eggs. Courtesy of CABI. Two weeks after hatching, snails develop into juveniles, and once the shell reaches approximately 15 mm in diameter, the snail will start to feed on rice seedlings and other aquatic plants. They attack the base of the seedling first and then eat the aerial parts. An adult snail can eat a blade of rice in 3–5 minutes (Cowie, 2013). After 45 days, when the snails are about 25 mm in diameter, they reach the adult stage (Fig. 2), and they can then mate and reproduce sexually (Fig. 3) (Cowie, 2013). ##### Fig. 2. #####
Adult apple snails and eggs at Mwea Irrigation Scheme. (a) adult snail; (b) snail eggs (c) snail egg mass on stalk (d) and (e) snail specimens. All images courtesy of CABI. ##### Fig. 3. #####

title: Assessment of the Socio-Economic Impacts Associated with the Arrival of Apple
text:
The study was conducted in MIS, Kirinyaga County, Kenya between November and December 2021 (Fig. 4). Initiated in 1954, MIS originally covered approximately 26 ha. Currently, it covers approximately 12,141 ha. Of these, 8903 ha have been developed for paddy rice production. MIS is the leading rice production scheme in the country, known for its aromatic basmati rice. It is also the first place where apple snail was reported in Kenya (Buddie *et al*., 2021). ##### Fig. 4. #####
Survey locations in Mwea Irrigation Scheme (MIS). ### Surveys ###
Surveys were conducted using both qualitative and quantitative data collection to understand smallholder knowledge and practices at the community level, including challenges and management methods. In addition to structured interviews with smallholder farmers, focus group discussions were also conducted. Key stakeholder interviews were undertaken with agricultural extension service providers and agro-dealers to assess their levels of apple snail awareness and the management advice they provide to farmers. The household survey engaged with 706 smallholder rice farmers. It targeted rice farmers in the core MIS and in out-grower sections (not managed by MIS). It used a structured questionnaire, which was coded on the Open Data Kit (ODK). Household heads, spouses, or family members responsible for making farming decisions, such as choice of crops, inputs, and when to sell, were interviewed. A pre-tested tablet-based questionnaire was used to collect information on household demographics, farm information, farm decision making, rice cultivation, productivity and inputs, apple snail presence and management measures, and information sources. Focus group discussions (FGDs) were held with farmers and community members to gain further insight into their knowledge, attitudes, and practices in rice farming including the management of apple snail.

title: Assessment of the Socio-Economic Impacts Associated with the Arrival of Apple
text:
Focus group discussions (FGDs) were held with farmers and community members to gain further insight into their knowledge, attitudes, and practices in rice farming including the management of apple snail. Open-ended survey questions were used to promote discussion and provide the opportunity to elaborate on the topics discussed. In total nine FGDs were held with separate men, women, and youth groups. Qualitative data were analysed using content analysis. Quantitative data were analysed by comparing means using *t*-tests. ### Sampling ###
Rice farmers were identified with assistance from Mwea Irrigation Agricultural Development (MIAD) centre staff and sub-county agricultural officers through unit/block leaders and lead farmers who assisted in identifying the survey areas. For spread and to reduce bias, random sampling of farmers occurred at the Unit level from where the questionnaires were administered. Interviews were concentrated around major themes associated with rice cultivation, productivity and inputs, management measures, good agricultural practice, water management/irrigation water supply, household assets, food security, cooperation, training, extension, and information sources. Key informant interviews were held with extension agents and agro-dealers who were identified by referral. Questions were asked about the history of apple snail infestation, management practices promoted, and the extent of spread of the pest. To assess the economic effects of apple snail, ordinary least squares regression technique was used. ### Household survey ###

### Apple snail presence ###
In most households, 85% reported observing apple snail attacks on their crops in the past year. Many reported that they first saw apple snail in the last 2 years, with the pests mainly seen on rice. In terms of the level of infestation, 68, 15, and 2% of the households reported minor, moderate, and major apple snail infestation, respectively. On average, the proportion of rice-cultivated areas affected by apple snail was about 11%, indicating that the level of infestation was generally minor. ### Effect on rice yield and income ###
Apple snail infestation (irrespective of the extent of infestation) had a negative effect on rice yield and net rice income, although the coefficients were not statistically significant. The percentage of cultivated area affected by apple snail had a negative impact on rice yield/income (Table 3). Specifically, a 10% increase in the cultivated area affected by apple snail is significantly associated with a 0.5 and 3.4% reduction in rice yield and net rice income, respectively. ##### Table 3. #####

When the effects of different levels of apple snail infestation were compared between households, those with a minor area of apple snail infestation did not experience significant declines in rice yield and net rice income compared to those unaffected by the pest (Table 3). title: Assessment of the Socio-Economic Impacts Associated with the Arrival of Apple
text:
A small proportion reported using chemical pesticides just for apple snail (16%), with lambda-cyhalothrin being the most frequently used. An increase in the use of chemical pesticides has been reported since the arrival of apple snail (Fig. 6). ##### Fig. 6. #####
The perception by farmers of the change in the level of chemical pesticide used to control apple snail (sample size = 197, these were the farmers that reported an increase in chemical pesticide use). The main advice given by agro-dealers was to use various chemical pesticides at the recommended dose, but if it did not work, they advised farmers to increase the dosage. Farmers reported that since there is no legally recommended chemical for apple snail control, they resorted to other chemical pesticides, some of which are illegal and detrimental to human health and the environment. In some rice-growing areas in Asia, where apple snail has been a problem for some decades, and where education programmes are attenuating, farmers may be relying on molluscicides that are toxic to other freshwater organisms (Schneiker *et al*., 2016). Farmers used a range of non-chemical management options to control apple snail with the most frequently used method being physical/mechanical, e.g., hand-picking egg masses and snails followed by water management, e.g., draining and water spraying (Table 6). Water spraying involves the frequent spraying of eggs with pure water to dislodge eggs and can also reduce hatching rates provided water spraying occurs at regular intervals soon after the eggs are laid. Other less commonly adopted methods include cultural control and the use of plant extracts such as neem and tobacco. Extension agents recommended physical removal of eggs and snails, water management including alternative wetting/drying and draining paddy fields, as well as cultural methods, erecting barrier feeder lines, screening inlets, and cleaning canals.

title: Assessment of the Socio-Economic Impacts Associated with the Arrival of Apple
text: A relatively small proportion of farmers had a screen at water supply inlets (23%) and even fewer had screens at water outlets (6%), with limited frequency of cleaning (16% reported daily or weekly cleaning through to 6% rarely or never cleaning screens). On average, over 50% of farmers removed and destroyed snail and egg masses from their fields by hand with this task generally occurring at random times. The most frequently used method of destroying snails was by leaving them in a dry area to desiccate (55%) or a combination of crushing and leaving to desiccate (6%). Only 2% reported placing bamboo stakes around their fields, a method that provides snails with good egg-laying sites, the stakes can then be pulled up and the eggs are easily knocked off. Most farmers (70%) constructed small canals/trenches along the edge of their rice plots. Snails are concentrated in these deeper parts when the water is drained, allowing for ease of collection. Most farmers weeded the canals (removing plant substrates used by snails for egg-laying) to minimize snail habitats/hiding places; however, very few (6%) used attractants or baits to attract snails. Most farmers (87%) reported cleaning tools and equipment after every use, but 5% reported rarely or never doing so. Most farmers mentioned birds as snail natural enemies (86%) followed by snakes (10%) and water bugs (3%). Rats, ants, cats, and fish were also mentioned by a small proportion of farmers (<1% each). Few farmers wore protective clothing such as gloves and rubber boots (19%). For physical and water management, the main cost was the labour associated with the activities.

section: Awareness of area-wide management of apple snail
text: The variable household head age significantly (negatively) influenced respondents’ level of awareness on area-wide management of apple snail. For each additional year of age, farmers are 0.2% less likely to be aware of any area-wide apple snail management – the older the farmer, the less likely they are to be aware of any area-wide management of apple snail. For each additional increase in the area of land owned, respondents were 1.5% more likely to be aware of area-wide management of apple snail. Farmers that had received extension advice were 13.7% more likely to be aware of the area-wide apple snail management where each additional contact with extension increased the likelihood of farmers’ apple snail awareness. Similarly, farmers who were members of a farmer organisation were 4.5% more likely to be aware of apple snail management and each increase in years of membership increased the likelihood of farmers’ apple snail awareness, suggesting the farmer organisation has a positive effect on member farmers’ awareness. Farmers who had received general training (in the last 3 years) were less likely (5.8%) to be aware of area-wide apple snail management, probably because of the training covering general topics unrelated to apple snail management.

title: Assessment of the Socio-Economic Impacts Associated with the Arrival of Apple
text:
*Pomacea canaliculata* is beginning to impact yield and income for smallholder rice farmers in Kenya. Based on data from South-east Asia where apple snail is a problem, and Kenyan rice yield data, the potential annual economic costs of *P. canaliculata* in Kenya could be between US$ 5.33 M and US$ 9.21 M approximately 10 years after introduction, even with snail management in place (Djeddour *et al*., 2021). Its presence in Kenya therefore poses a serious economic threat, and urgent action is now required if it is to be contained. Awareness of the problem varies according to various factors such as: the size of smallholding; farmer age; access to extension advice; belonging to farming organisations; and training. Farmers who use agro-chemicals to control pests, reported weeds, stem borers, African armyworm, leaf miners, and rice caseworm as a problem more frequently than *P. canaliculata. *
Physical, mechanical, and water management practices that could control *P. canaliculata* are varied among the smallholders. For instance, over 50% remove eggs and snails by hand, while only 23% have screens at water inlets and only 6% have screens at water outlets. If the snails are allowed to spread from MIS in Kenya, towards the edge of Lake Victoria, they could reach Tanzania and Uganda and severely affect rice production in those two countries. Therefore, this potential spread poses a food security risk in Kenya and beyond.

### Overview ###
Reports in the early 1990s of a widespread decline of neem across the Sahel, of unknown origin, were followed by intensive but short-term investigations. Vigorous debate on the dependability of neem petered out in the mid-1990s when trees appeared to recover. This report revisits what happened during the investigations and whether neem decline can be considered a threat to an invaluable tree.

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
text: 1. Highlight the occurrence of neem decline in the 1990s in Niger and Nigeria and what is known about its cause and impact. 2. Recognise that although the research on genetic improvement of neem was prompted by neem decline, subsequent international provenance trials (mostly in Asia) often failed to mention the problem or take it into account when analysing results of the trials. 3. Understand that organizations that promote and rely on a valuable tree for projects and other initiatives need practical and clear guidance on the significance of known risks and potential threats, regardless of how well they are known scientifically. 4. Know that planting and promoting trees is the easy part of increasing forest cover. Long-term strategies are essential for sustaining healthy and productive trees through monitoring, management and research.

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
text: The neem tree (*Azadirachta indica*) has proved to be hugely popular in dry, sub-tropical and tropical regions. It is robust and resilient in harsh conditions, keeps its leaves throughout the year and has multiple benefits, ranging from much-vaunted insecticidal properties, to fuelwood and timber. The reputation of neem as an invaluable species for agroforestry and other non-plantation settings (for example residential areas and roadsides) was burnished by a widely-circulated publication announcing that it was ‘a tree for solving global problems’ (National Research Council, 1992). This short and attractive handbook highlighted the many reasons why neem was ideal for areas where few realistic options were available for planting trees, bolstered by neem’s multiple benefits. Prominence was given to seed preparations as a reliable alternative to synthetic insecticides as well as general medicinal properties of neem products. The book assessed neem’s potential, promising to ‘… marshal the various facts about this little-known species (and) to help illuminate its future promise’. These prescient words were published at the same time as reports emerged of a widespread decline of neem trees in the Sahel (Figs. 1 and 2). Few details were available in initial news items published in 1992 by organizations with a broad interest in agriculture, forestry and human development. Perhaps the most notable fact was that a hugely successful agroforestry project in Niger led by CARE, an international non-governmental organization, was under threat. CARE had promoted neem as a windbreak and used the species exclusively to establish shelterbelts, protecting crops from the scouring of soil by winds and thus enhancing agriculture outputs for many poor farmers.

text:
CARE had promoted neem as a windbreak and used the species exclusively to establish shelterbelts, protecting crops from the scouring of soil by winds and thus enhancing agriculture outputs for many poor farmers. The US Agency for International Development had a major presence in Niger and was to the fore in organizing technical assistance to investigate *le dépérissement du neem* or neem decline. ##### Fig. 1. #####
Neem is planted in many countries in Africa but is particularly prevalent (and prized) in the semi-arid zone known as the Sahel.
