title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
text:
Further surveys of scale insects (Fig. 3), prompted in part by the emergence of neem decline, showed that while the scale caused significant damage to the crowns of neem trees in towns and on roadsides it was a distinct and separate problem (Boa, 1995). ##### Fig. 3. #####
Neem scale (*Aonidiella orientalis*) in northern Nigeria. Heavy infestations of the insect weakened leaves, causing them to dry up. Progressive damage resulted in browning of leaves, beginning the lower crown (above right) but did not result in giraffe necks or other features associated with neem decline. Scale attacks were restricted to towns and urban areas. The discovery of neem decline and heightened interest in scale insect infestations suggested a lack of awareness about the general risks posed by pests and diseases of neem. An implicit assumption was that a tree lauded for its insecticidal properties was unlikely to be troubled by infestations and infections. The FAO book on neem pests and diseases (Boa, 1995), which includes a detailed account of neem decline and neem scale, suggested that more attention was needed to the now fashionable concept of tree health, where all influences, both abiotic and biotic, should be considered. In subsequent years more reports have been published on neem pests and diseases, including a number of ‘fungal trunk pathogens associated with declining of neem’ in Iran (Ghasemi-Sardareh and Mohammadi, 2020). This report and another from Brazil describing the involvement of scolitid beetles on a neem decline (*declinio do nim*) are unrelated to the neem decline found in the Sahel. Following the flurry of activity and short-term investigations on neem decline in Niger and Nigeria from 1992 to 1996, no further reports have been found of neem decline.

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
text: Following the flurry of activity and short-term investigations on neem decline in Niger and Nigeria from 1992 to 1996, no further reports have been found of neem decline. The problem has ostensibly disappeared, either because trees have fully recovered following a temporary blip related, as suggested, to extended dry periods in the Sahel, or because the decline has diminished to a degree that it is no longer considered a problem. These and other explanations why neem declines no longer appears to be threat are discussed later on. First, it is important to describe the symptoms of neem decline and the results of investigations into its possible cause(s) (Section 1: What is Neem Decline?) and to discuss what actions were taken in the 1990s to minimize damage and reduce future risks to neem trees (Section 2: Managing Neem Decline in the Short and Long Term). The case study concludes with a discussion of whether neem’s reputation as ‘a tree for solving global problems’ is warranted and why a more measured assessment of its value is needed.

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
text:
A full account of neem decline was published in the FAO guide to neem diseases and pests (Boa, 1995). Further details were obtained from a detailed report written by two experienced forest health specialists contracted by USAID to carry out a preliminary assessment of neem decline (Hodges and Beatty, 1992). Despite the high priority given to the study of neem decline from 1992 to 1996, investigations took place in short bursts of a few weeks at a time. No longer-term studies were established in Nigeria or Niger. This partly explains why no peer-reviewed papers were ever published on neem decline and why anecdotal evidence is important in understanding neem decline. The Hodges and Beatty report includes observations and comments on the action of national institutes and organizations based in Niger and Nigeria, as well as agencies funding work. The interaction between donors, local and international scientists and NGOs was a crucial part of how neem decline was perceived and therefore investigated. The attention span of donors to tree research in the 1990s was at best short to medium term, inevitably limiting what research could be done. No significant local funds were made available in Niger to study neem decline. ### Symptoms and cause ###
Neem decline is characterized by excessive loss of leaves, resulting in sparse crowns, preceded by yellowing and premature senescence (Fig. 4). In severe cases branches die, though there is no underlying sign of a progressive necrosis, suggesting fungal infection, for example. The most distinctive feature used to identify neem decline is a pronounced terminal tufting of leaves on branches, aptly named ‘giraffe necks’ because of the loss of leaves immediately below the terminal tuft (Fig. 5). Giraffe necks are present throughout the year in severely affected trees, suggesting a permanent rather than temporary reduction of growth that might be reversed.

Reddening in the bark and gummy exudates from young shoots were initially thought to be a symptom of neem decline, but both features occur in trees without any loss of leaves (Fig. 6). No evidence of root damage was seen or trunk rots indicative of fungal attack or waterlogging (flooding is not uncommon in the Sahel, though of limited intensity and unlikely to cause long-term damage to neem). ##### Fig. 4. #####
Different stages in thinning of crowns and development of giraffe necks (rows 1 and 2). Some trees showed a more pronounced lateral progression. Compare with healthy trees (row three). ##### Fig. 5. #####
Giraffe necks, a characteristic feature of neem decline (above left). A close-up of the tufts (above right) shows compressed internodes, much reduced growth and limited leaf development. ##### Fig. 6. #####
Reddening in the bark and gummy exudations were widely observed but thought to be more general signs of stress rather than specific indicators of neem decline. A short investigation prior to the first joint visit by Hodges, Beatty and Boa in 1992 described neem decline as a vascular disease associated with *Verticillium*, a common wilt pathogen of woody hosts. There was no supporting evidence, however, and all the available information suggested that neem decline (known as *le dépérissement du neem* in French) was an abiotic disorder. Other theories that the decline was associated with fungal infections were also dismissed because of a lack of evidence (see Hodges and Beatty, 1992).

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
text: Other theories that the decline was associated with fungal infections were also dismissed because of a lack of evidence (see Hodges and Beatty, 1992). A global overview of tree declines and diebacks provided a useful comparison with other conditions that had abiotic causes and mimicked neem decline: general loss of leaves and no evidence of infections by pathogens or infestations by insects (Ciesla and Donaubauer, 1994). Testing of leave samples for phytoplasmas, specialized bacteria that interfere with the growth of plants (including trees), gave negative results. In the early 1990s, diagnostic testing for phytoplasmas was a specialized and difficult procedure, and although a close relative of neem, *Melia azedarach*, is widely attacked by phytoplasmas (see Harrison *et al*., 2003), often severely, the two trees rarely occur in close proximity. The symptoms of Melia yellows are also different from those of neem decline and can include shoot proliferation and highly distinctive patterns of altered growth. The failure to find a clear fungal or other microbial cause of neem decline added fuel to an alternative theory; the loss of leaves and poor appearance and growth of neem was simply part of the long-term fluctuation in the growth of neem in a harsh climate and general poor growing conditions. The debate about climate change and the wider impact on tree health was already active in the 1990s but was hampered by the difficulty of making clear links between extended drought and general decline of trees. Leaf fall and yellowing have many causes and even though intensive and extended symptoms may occur, it is also possible that trees can recover when growing conditions improve. A preliminary attempt was made to examine the possible links between neem decline and historical rainfall in Niger but no definitive conclusions were reached and no longer-term investigations were carried out (Hodges and Beatty, 1992).

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
text:
A preliminary attempt was made to examine the possible links between neem decline and historical rainfall in Niger but no definitive conclusions were reached and no longer-term investigations were carried out (Hodges and Beatty, 1992). There was an attempt to establish monitoring plots of neem trees, so that the pattern of growth and health of trees could be tracked over longer periods. A scheme for recording leaf cover and other features indicative of decline was set up in Niger in 1994 by Abdul Maisharou, a local scientist who showed a keen interest in neem decline. He carried out two sets of observations of 115 plots, 6 months apart starting in late 1994, divided among neem planted along roads, in villages, the green belt of Niamey, plantations and in shelterbelts. Although inconclusive, the results showed that some trees had recovered while others continued to decline. As this author noted at the time in personal notes: ‘An inexpensive and carefully thought out monitoring (scheme) was used only twice to monitor the health of the most important agroforestry tree in Niger.’ Despite contacts made with foresters and plant health specialists in Nigeria and Niger, the principal countries considered suitable for doing research on neem decline and attempts to establish collaborations with institutes in the global north (i.e. the US and UK), the investigations into neem decline relied exclusively on short-term inputs funded by donors. Researchers in Nigeria, which unlike Niger had a dedicated Forest Research Institute, appeared unconvinced that neem decline was a serious problem. They had other priorities to consider, mostly concerning plantation tree species. ### Distribution and severity of attack ###
The first officially recorded occurrence of neem decline was in 1990, close to Niamey, the capital of Niger. Further observations of neem decline from northern Nigeria, Chad and northern Cameroon were made in 1992.

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
text: Further observations of neem decline from northern Nigeria, Chad and northern Cameroon were made in 1992. Unconfirmed records from Mali and Burkina Faso lack detail but appear credible given the similar conditions to other regions in the Sahel where neem decline has been described. Neem trees were also reported to be declining in Senegal in 1992 but again details are scanty. The present author remembers seeing huge swathes of trees planted close to the main road from Niamey to Zinder in southern Niger and noting the widespread presence of declining neem. Differences were observed between plantations of neem and those growing in villages, where neem decline was present but less intensely (Ciesla, 1993). CARE staff reported that all mature, pollarded trees in the shelterbelts plants in the Maggia valley in Niger were affected, as were 15% of ‘the younger neem’, information published in a short article from another NGO. The same article also noted that ‘100% of 1991 planting stock and private woodlands are affected, as well as seedlings in the Tahoua nursery’. The lack of detail on how the assessments were made makes it difficult to interpret these observations. The decline of tree seedlings is unlikely to be the same problem as seen on mature neem. Yet CARE was sufficiently worried in Niger to stop ‘planting of neem until further notice’. As the short-term missions by international scientists attempted to work out what was happening with neem so others were making critical decisions on the future of neem in agroforestry. This highlighted a clear difference between scientists, development practitioners and myriad farmers and others who had planted neem and wanted to know what to do. Scientists were reluctant to be prescriptive yet such was the alarm about declining neem that those promoting and using the tree wanted practical advice on what to do. Waiting for recommendations from scientists who were struggling to understand what was happening created tensions that were difficult to resolve.

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
section: Section 2: Managing Neem Decline in the Short and Long Term
text:
Actions were taken quickly following the brouhaha in Niger about neem decline to address the needs of those growing and planting neem. The main initiative was to set up an International Neem Network, with the main aim of improving the genetic stock of neem and to make available more resilient and productive types for future plantings. ### Managing short term ###
The stark reality in making recommendations about neem decline, or indeed any abiotic-related problem, is that there are few if any practical steps to halt the decline or restore trees to a healthier state. The absence of any evidence supporting the involvement of a pathogen or pest in neem decline immediately eliminated actions such as selective pruning to remove infected branches, the use of chemicals or removal of trees to limit the spread of the problem to new areas. Although widely planted and highly regarded by farmers throughout southern Niger and northern Nigeria, neem was a low-value tree. Even if neem decline was associated with a pathogen, the cost of treating trees could not be justified, even before considering the major practical difficulties in carrying out actions. The challenge remained for scientists to explain that ‘wait and see’ was the best way to proceed in managing neem decline. There was still substantial resistance to convincing some that this was a real problem that needed addressing in some way, either with immediate actions or in a more measured approach over the long term. Abiotic disorders can be reversed and trees recover or at least show improved growth, but this is only likely to happen over a number of years. One season of good rains, for example, is unlikely to restore healthy growth in trees that are showing the cumulative effect of prolonged drought. The recommendation to stop planting neem was never officially espoused. This had some merit yet it also exposed a lack of suitable alternatives.

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
section: Section 2: Managing Neem Decline in the Short and Long Term
text:
The recommendation to stop planting neem was never officially espoused. This had some merit yet it also exposed a lack of suitable alternatives. There are many local trees that are hardy and valued by farmers in the Sahel, such as *Parkia biglobosa* and *Balanites aegyptiaca*, but they do not necessarily have the same features that farmers value in neem. *B. aegyptiaca* is slow growing by comparison to neem. *P. biglobosa* is not suited to shelterbelts because it is deciduous. Neem keeps its leaves throughout the year. ### Managing long term ###
The debate about neem decline revived interest in the lack of genetic diversity in trees growing in the Sahel. Like many introduced trees, limited sources of planting material had been used to establish neem. The relative ease of planting neem from seed had been a major factor in enabling the spread of trees across the Sahel. Genetic improvement and the possibilities of breeding for composite traits such as disease and drought resistance and higher limonoid content in seeds were major motivation in establishing international provenance trials (Kundu *et al*., 1998). Limonoids are chemical compounds associated with medicinal properties of neem preparations, exhibiting antimalarial and antibacterial activity, for example. A breeding programme was initiated by FAO in 1993 (Thomsen and Souvannong, 1994) under the auspices of The International Neem Network (INN). This brought together 14 collaborators in 10 countries who received agreed protocols on how to establish trials. Seeds were collected from 23 sources (provenances) in India, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Thailand. Neem’s native range is India and Myanmar. The coordination role of the INN changed over the following years, with new organizations taking over responsibility for sharing information and results.

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
section: Section 2: Managing Neem Decline in the Short and Long Term
text: Neem’s native range is India and Myanmar. The coordination role of the INN changed over the following years, with new organizations taking over responsibility for sharing information and results. INN was successful in stimulating the establishment of the trials and results continued to be published in peer-reviewed journals up to the late 2000s (Himmapan *et al*., 2009) and possibly later. There was a clear link to neem decline in the early work of the INN. The World Bank Second Forestry Project states in a 1997 report that neem provenance trials were set up in most AP states ‘in response to the Neem Decline Disease observed in many parts of Northern Nigeria in the early nineties’. Neem decline was a major motivation for setting up trials yet as results were published this appears to have been forgotten in a broader genetic improvement. Neem decline is discussed in a UK-funded project (Chamberlain *et al*., 2000) but this is an exception. It is difficult to discern what the provenance trials achieved across INN participants in terms of reducing the risk of neem decline. It is also unclear how new genetic stock has been made available beyond the geographic boundaries of provenance trials. In India, the Central Agroforestry Research Institute (ICAR-CAFRI) has the largest germplasm collection of neem held in the Neem Field Gene Bank in Jhansi and has 170 accessions. No details of their phenological or other growth characteristics are readily available on CAFRI’s website.

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
section: Section 3: Current Update on Neem Decline
text: A simple conclusion is that neem decline came and went in the Sahel and that it was a temporary blip in the steady growth of enthusiasm for an immensely versatile and useful tree. In the 1980s, around 50,000 neem trees were planted in the Plains of Arafat near Mecca, said to be the world’s largest single stand of the species (Ahmed *et al*., 1989). An assessment of the scheme published 25 years later (Marihda and Al-Suhaibani, 2014) raised doubts about its success. Large numbers of trees had died and the authors said that this could be due to ‘physiological and/or pathological’ reasons. This brief study considered the role of insect pests and fungal diseases in the deaths without reaching any definitive conclusion. The authors (who are not plant pathologists) wondered why a tree that produces a medley of antimicrobial compounds could be susceptible to pathogens and pests. Yet pathogens adapted to a particular tree are able to detoxify antimicrobial compounds and overcome other barriers to establishing infections (Westrick *et al*., 2021). Marihad and Al-Suhaibani appeared to be unaware of the debate concerning neem decline in the Sahel in the 1990s (Boa, 1995). A risk assessment of neem as an invasive species in Queensland, vigorously promoted because of the economic potential of azadirachtin, a natural insecticide, said that many plantations had failed (Queensland Government, 2016). The report also says that ‘neem trees are generally pest-free’ and does not refer to neem decline. There is no detailed description of symptoms associated with the death of neem trees in Saudi Arabia and there is no indication that these align with those of neem decline. It is clear, however, that planting neem in pure stands is not a good idea and that trees do not thrive.

title: What Ever Happened to Neem Decline in the Sahel?
section: Section 3: Current Update on Neem Decline
text: It is clear, however, that planting neem in pure stands is not a good idea and that trees do not thrive. Neem remains a popular tree in 2023, widely planted and widely admired. The dramatic decline of neem in Niger and Nigeria was a concrete event, not to be dismissed as readily as some foresters did in the early 1990s. But it was also a temporary event, albeit over a limited number of years. Neem appears to have recovered in Niger and Nigeria, or to put it another way, there was no mass death of trees. It is perhaps more worrying that 30 years on few are aware of what took place when emergency assistance was urgently called for to cope with a potential catastrophe. The main motivation for this report is to highlight the discussion, studies and findings concerning neem decline and for these to be considered in the light of neem’s dominance in agroforestry and greening of marginal lands characterized by harsh growing conditions. The clamour to plant more trees grows in such places grows louder as the debate about the climate emergency becomes more urgent. Neem is a useful tree with many valuable features and benefits but like any species, it has weaknesses that need to be fully appreciated. In retrospect suggesting that neem was ‘a tree for solving global problems’ (National Research Council, 1992) appears hubristic and over-optimistic.

Agroforestry has been enthusiastically promoted by supporters for many decades and is now and well-established land management option in low, middle and high-income countries. How does neem decline or indeed any similar major problem undermine this enthusiasm? ### Conflict of interest ###

### Overview ###
Phoma stem canker (blackleg) of Brassicas is caused by *Plenodomus lingam* or *P. biglobosus* (formerly *Leptosphaeria maculans* and *L. biglobosa*), which are important pathogens of Brassicas in temperate areas, surviving on crop debris, spreading by airborne and rain-splashed spores and infected seeds, to cause phoma leaf spots and stem canker, which is the main cause of yield loss.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text: 1. Provide methods for identification of the pathogens by molecular diagnostics and visual symptoms. 2. Provide an understanding of the transmission and dispersal of the pathogens. 3. Explain the disease cycle and provide information on management and control methods.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text: This article explains the current taxonomy, identification methods, disease symptoms, epidemiology and control of phoma stem canker or blackleg of Brassicas, which is caused by two species, *Plenodomus lingam* or *P. biglobosus* (formerly known as *Leptosphaeria maculans* and *L. biglobosa* and they may be known by the asexual stage, *Phoma lingam*). These are important plant pathogens of oilseed rape (canola; *Brassica napus*), vegetable Brassicas (e.g. *B. oleracea*: cabbage, broccoli and kale; *B. rapa*: turnip and pak choi) and some other herbaceous plants, mainly in temperate areas, but *P. lingam* has not been found in China, nor in most parts of both South America and Africa. In addition, *P. dezfulensis* (a close relative of *P. biglobosus*) causes phoma leaf spot in Iran. Phoma stem canker can cause yield losses exceeding 50% in some individual fields, but usually losses are 0–15%. The fungi survive saprophytically on crop debris and spread by two types of spores – ascospores, which are wind dispersed and can travel hundreds of metres and potentially longer, and conidia, which are rain-splashed short distances (e.g. <2m) but occasionally a few hundred metres as a fine spray of splashed rain in strong wind. Spread to new locations can also occur through infected seed or crop debris. Infection of leaves requires high humidity and is via stomata or wounds, and the fungi grow down the leaf vascular tissue to infect the stem, where they cause stem canker, a type of dry stem rot.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text: Infection of leaves requires high humidity and is via stomata or wounds, and the fungi grow down the leaf vascular tissue to infect the stem, where they cause stem canker, a type of dry stem rot. Fungicides are not effective once the fungus has reached the stem, so prevention of leaf spots is the best control strategy, aided by good crop rotation and cultivar resistance. Identification methods by PCR and DNA sequencing are also described.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text: Phoma stem canker is caused by two closely related species, *Plenodomus lingam* (Tode) Höhnel and *P. biglobosus* (formerly *Leptosphaeria maculans* and *L. biglobosa*), which are ascomycetes in the class Dothideomycetes and family Leptosphaeriaceae. The asexual stage of *P. lingam* is *Phoma lingam*. Many sources of literature refer to them as *L. maculans* and *L. biglobosa*, and before 2001, *P. biglobosus* (*L. biglobosa*) was known as the weakly aggressive, B type or Tox0 type of *L. maculans*. Currently, there are subclades of both species, which are *P. lingam* subclades ‘brassicae’ and ‘lepidii’ and *P. biglobosus* subclades ‘americensis’, ‘australensis’, ‘brassicae’, ‘canadensis’, ‘erysimii’, ‘occiaustralensis’ and ‘thlaspii’, see Mendes-Pereira *et al*. (2003). In addition, a very close relative of *P. biglobosus* has been named from samples in Iran and is termed *Plenodomus dezfulensis*.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text: Ascospores of both species are identical physically although the pattern of initial hyphae produced by germinating ascospores is different. *P. lingam* hyphae emerge initially from central cells of the ascospore and branch profusely with side branches angled almost perpendicularly from the initial hypha, while *P. biglobosus* produces germ tubes initially from the terminal cells at each end of the ascospore, and these grow relatively long and straight hyphae, branching by dichotomising at relatively shallow angles (Huang *et al*., 2001). Other physical differences between the two species are the production of a dark yellow pigment in culture by *P. biglobosus* and production of pink to violet conidial ooze (cirri) by *P. biglobosus* compared to pale cream coloured cirri in *P. lingam,* but there can be some overlapping characteristics in some isolates, so molecular diagnostics are needed for complete identification (see later). Ascomata (pseudothecia) are flattened black spheres 200–250 μm high × 300–500 μm in diameter with a single pore on the top surface. The ascomata occur alone or clustered in groups initially immersed or partly immersed in crop debris but becoming raised above lignified material as softer dead plant tissues degrade away. The mature ascocarp can be hydrated in water and squashed or sectioned to show the outer dark pigmented thick-walled cells of the outer layer, an inner subhyaline or light brown layer of angular cells and the internal contents of sterile hairs (periphyses) and sacs (asci) containing eight ascospores. The asci are 90–110 × 10–12 μm hyaline, bitunicate (double-walled) structures sausage-shaped apart from tapering towards the base.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text: The asci are 90–110 × 10–12 μm hyaline, bitunicate (double-walled) structures sausage-shaped apart from tapering towards the base. The ascospores are 35–70 × 5–8 μm, pale tan coloured, ellipsoids, sometimes slightly curved and comprising six cells divided by five septae, and sometimes slightly constricted at the central-most septum. Each cell may contain one or more guttules (vesicles) (Fig. 2). The asexual stage is produced in pycnidia, which are embedded in leaf lesions and are 150–350 μm in diameter, dark-brown to black flattened spheres with a small pore at the apex of a raised neck or spout in the centre of the upper surface. The pycnidia occur singly or more normally in groups within the leaf lesion. Alternatively, larger pycnidia occur on the surface of crop debris and are 300–700 μm in diameter and slightly more spherical that the type of pycnidia occurring in leaf lesions. In both cases, the pycnidium comprises several layers of pseudoparenchymatous cells pigmented dark brown. Conidia produced in the pycnidia are 3–5 × 1–2 μm, hyaline, aseptate, elongated spheres, occasionally with two small guttules near each end. The mass of conidia produced from the ostiole or pore of the pycnidium appear as a pale white, cream or pink-coloured ooze (cirrus), which readily disperses into water.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text:
The mass of conidia produced from the ostiole or pore of the pycnidium appear as a pale white, cream or pink-coloured ooze (cirrus), which readily disperses into water. In culture, both *P. lingam* and *P. biglobosus* grow on common media like PDA or V8-agar at 15–25°C in the dark, producing a mat of mycelium ranging from white to pale grey in colour, sometimes with other pigments and particularly most isolates of *P. biglobosus* produce a dull yellow-orange pigment, which is easily seen on PDA (Fig. 1). Both also produce pycnidia in culture. *P. biglobosus* tends to stale in culture and loses viability if kept for a long time. ##### Fig. 1. #####
Cultures of *P. lingam* (left) and *P. biglobosus* (right) growing on potato dextrose agar and showing yellow pigment production by *P. biglobosus. *

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text: The fungus survives on stem and root debris for a few years or more unless the debris is immersed by flood water, which tends to cause it to be replaced by other microbes (Peluola *et al*., 2013). Both pycnidia and ascocarps can be produced on the surface of crop debris. Pycnidia tend to survive on crop debris only short periods, and as they empty, further fruiting body production tends to be ascocarps. In temperate locations, these mature and release wind-dispersed ascospores in the autumn and to a lesser extent into the winter and spring. In Canada, due to longer, cold winters, ascospores are released from the previous season’s crop debris the following spring, while in Australia, they can be released to infect autumn-winter-sown crops of spring type canola crops and can continue to be released the following year. Factors affecting maturation and timing of ascospore release are discussed in a later section. Ascospores infect leaves in wetness films by producing hyphae that penetrate stoma, hydathodes or wounds. Leaf spots develop about 7–20 days after infection but vary in appearance according to host resistance and leaf age. *P. lingam* causes pale lesions approximately 5–20 mm in diameter which develop multiple small dark specks in them (Fig.2a). These are pycnidia, which produce a type of asexually produced spores called conidia (described earlier). Conidia can cause secondary infections by splashing short distances to other leaves and nearby plants. In contrast, *P. biglobosus* tends to cause small dark brown spots which may be surrounded by chlorotic tissue (Fig. 2b). The centre of some spots may degrade or drop out completely.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text:
In contrast, *P. biglobosus* tends to cause small dark brown spots which may be surrounded by chlorotic tissue (Fig. 2b). The centre of some spots may degrade or drop out completely. In humid conditions, aerial mycelium may be produced, particularly at the margin of lesions. ##### Fig. 2. #####
Disease cycle of phoma stem canker, showing air dispersed ascospores approximately 50 μm long (top left), Phoma leaf spots of both types (top right), stem cankers (bottom right) and ascocarps on the surface of dead stem debris. All photos by Jon West except ascocarps which was by Rothamsted’s photography group. Stem cankers and stem lesions result from the fungus growing down vascular tissue of the petiole to reach the stem. Cankers appear from flowering onwards in oilseed rape at stem positions where the infected leaf had been attached. Green stem tissue darkens to almost black immediately around the edge of cankers leading to the alternative name, blackleg, but the centre of cankers appear as a dry pale brown lesion, which with maturation towards harvest, may crack open and also develops pycnidia and later still ascocarps. The severity of canker is a product of the extent of girdling and internal stem infection and may result from several cankers coalescing. In severe cases, upper parts of the plant become drought-stressed due to insufficient water transport, leading to reduced yield and premature senescence. This is exacerbated by hot and windy weather due to increased water demand. In very severe cases, the plant may lodge. Infections of later leaves (after the rosette leaves) and bracts can lead to stem lesions, whereas stem cankers occur at the stem base or crown of the plant.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text: In very severe cases, the plant may lodge. Infections of later leaves (after the rosette leaves) and bracts can lead to stem lesions, whereas stem cankers occur at the stem base or crown of the plant. Upper stem lesions tend to spread up and down the softer stem tissues more readily, so the black or dark discolouration becomes more apparent. Pod lesions can occur from late spore releases after flowering and are similar to leaf spots but occurring on the pods [siliques] and peduncles, causing some constriction and reduced development of the affected pod. These can be important by infecting seed in the pods, which is one of the main ways for the disease to be introduced to completely new locations. Root infection also occurs either by growth of the fungus down the stem from basal stem cankers or directly from the soil where spores may have been washed or where the fungus may have survived on crop debris. Tap roots and the root collar persist longest after harvest due to their lignified, woody composition and on affected plants, these may appear to have blackened areas encrusted with melanised ascocarps or their empty shells.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text: Morphological discrimination of *P. lingam* and *P. biglobosus*, for instance by growing the isolated fungus on artificial agar media such as potato dextrose agar (PDA) and examining cultures for the production of pigment (see *Description*), can be a cost-effective method for species identification, particularly in resource-poor laboratories, but can also be time-consuming and not always reliable (King and West, 2021). Identification of the pathogens can also be attempted via isolation from infected seeds using the blotter test described by Andreoli and Maguire (1995), although again this approach can be time-consuming and give inconclusive results. Thus molecular PCR-based diagnostic approaches are often used, including species-specific quantitative PCR (qPCR) assays that can determine amounts of DNA of each pathogen species in environmental samples. These can be simple SYBR-green qPCR assays that are relatively cheap but rely on a non-specific fluorescent dye binding to amplified DNA, and thus, results might be affected by any spurious non-target PCR amplification. Alternatively, Taqman qPCR diagnostics are available for *Plenodomus* spp. (Jacques *et al*., 2021) that are considered more reliable given the inclusion of an additional but expensive internal target-sequence specific probe, with fluorescence only detectable upon successful probe binding to the target DNA sequence. For all molecular-based diagnostics, however, a good understanding of *Plenodomus* population biology and genetics is essential to ensure the required target is being correctly amplified and identified. For example, in Europe, both *P. biglobosus* ‘brassicae’ and the rare ‘canadensis’ subclades are present (King and West, 2021), but the SYBR green assay of Liu *et al*.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
text: (2006) does not detect the ‘canadensis’ subclade (Kaczmarek *et al*., 2023). Other molecular diagnostics, such as loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), utilising six primers for each target species and operating at a single constant temperature, have also been developed for detection and discrimination of *P. lingam*/*P. biglobosus* (Omer and Wallenhammar, 2020). LAMP offers some advantages over PCR-based approaches, including purportedly improved speed, specificity and sensitivity and the potential for applied use of this technology by end-users such as growers in the field using a portable device. Last, genomic approaches are now being used for monitoring and quantifying *Plenodomus* spp. in field populations. For example, a work at Rothamsted Research (UK) is currently utilising minION third-generation nanopore sequencing to investigate ratios of *P. lingam*/*P. biglobosus* in air and plant samples to explore how pathogen populations might be influenced by agronomic practices (e.g. application of fungicides).

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
section: Discussion Points on Epidemiology and Control
text: Ascospores can be dispersed many kilometres but tend to decline to the regional background level within a few hundred metres of a source. Conidia have been shown to cause secondary infections on new leaves and adjacent plants, and in some cases in Canada, they were shown to blow in a fine spray combined with wind to infect plants in adjacent fields. Management of crop debris and separation of subsequent crops to avoid close proximity to debris of the previous crop are important cultural control options to reduce disease pressure. Plant breeders working with plant pathologists in pre-breeding schemes have developed a number of varieties of oilseed rape with resistance to *P. lingam* in recent years. Less is known about host resistance in vegetable brassicas, and little is known about host resistance to *P. biglobosus*. About 20 different host resistance genes are now known in oilseed rape against *P. lingam* (*L. maculans*) (Borhan *et al*., 2022). At the time of writing (2024), all are named according to the former pathogen name of *Leptosphaeria maculans*, e.g. Rlm1 or LepR3. In 2024, UK commercially available oilseed rape varieties have resistance ratings of 4 to 9 on a 1–9 scale. Current varieties that have excellent resistance to the disease include Vegas (Hybrid variety rated 9) and Murray (rating 8), and others are Dolphin (7), Tennyson (7), Matrix CL (7) and Miraculix CL (7). In many cases, the most durable resistance comes from a good background level of quantitative (polygenic or partial) resistance which does not stop infection but reduces the severity of disease. Cold weather slows down disease development resulting in reduced canker severity by harvest and a delay in release of ascospores the following autumn.

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
section: Discussion Points on Epidemiology and Control
text: Cold weather slows down disease development resulting in reduced canker severity by harvest and a delay in release of ascospores the following autumn. This is why the disease is generally not a problem in cooler locations (e.g. in the UK north of Lincolnshire). However, climate change predictions suggest that warmer weather will exacerbate this disease. Fungicides are often used in combination with host resistance, particularly in locations where the yield potential of oilseed rape is high. Fungicides should be targeted at preventing leaf infections in initial growth stages as this prevents early infection of the stem. Although some fungicides can have a negative growth regulatory effect if applied to very young plants, in parts of Australia, where leaf infections can often occur on very young plants, growers sometimes coat fertiliser pellets with fungicide, and this is drilled below the seed to boost any short-term fungicide effect from seed coatings. In Europe, it is more normal to apply one or two autumn fungicides to oilseed rape, and this is done because the yield potential is relatively high due to the temperate conditions. Indeed, one or two fungicide applications, by controlling this disease, were found to reduce the greenhouse gas emissions per ton of grain produced by 15%. Fungicides have very little effect once the fungus has reached the stem. The best timing of fungicide application is after the first significant release of ascospores in the autumn, ideally before more than 10% of plants have phoma leaf spots. The timing of spore release varies each year due to the weather – in Europe, wet summers promote an early release of spores to infect autumn-sown crops (Huang *et al*., 2007).

title: Phoma Stem Canker (Blackleg) of Oilseed Rape (Canola) and Other Brassica Crops
section: Discussion Points on Epidemiology and Control
text:
The timing of spore release varies each year due to the weather – in Europe, wet summers promote an early release of spores to infect autumn-sown crops (Huang *et al*., 2007). Ascospores in Europe are mainly from the previous season’s debris, while in North America, spring-sown plants are infected from spores produced on debris of the previous or preceding crop while in Australia, autumn-sown varieties are infected by ascospores released from debris 6–18 months old. In the UK, a weather-based forecasting tool is available, which forecasts the date when 10% of plants will have phoma leaf spot – see Evans *et al*. (2007) and <https://ahdb.org.uk/provision-of-oilseed-rape-decision-support-systems-to-the-uk-arable-industry> (accessed 29 May 2024). Due to improvements in host resistance, locations that routinely used two autumn fungicides have now reduced applications to a single autumn spray unless phoma leaf spotting is very early or if the variety grown is known to be very susceptible. On more resistant varieties of oilseed rape, fungicide applications can even be omitted completely (against phoma stem canker) and particularly if phoma leaf spotting is late. Fungicide options are to use at least two modes of actions such as a DMI (FRAC code 3, e.g. mefentrifluconazole) plus an SDHI (FRAC code 7, e.g. bixafen) or a QoI (FRAC code 3, e.g. pyraclostrobin). ### Conflict of interest ###

### Overview ###
*Prosopis juliflora* is a spiny tree or shrub that has become invasive in savanna and grassland areas of Eastern Africa. It has spread rapidly and has transformed socio-ecological systems, negatively impacting livelihoods in pastoralist-dominated regions. This case presents the results of a three-year-long study testing methods to control *P. juliflora* in warm arid areas of Ethiopia, Kenya, and Tanzania.

title: Experimental Prosopis juliflora Management Practices and Grassland Restoration
text: 1. Understand how invasive species such as *P. juliflora* are affecting socio-economic systems in pastoralist areas of East Africa. 2. Outline methods for testing, collecting data, and analysing the effects of control treatments on woody species such as *P. juliflora*. 3. Describe effective control methods for *P. juliflora*.

title: Experimental Prosopis juliflora Management Practices and Grassland Restoration
text: Woody alien species have been introduced in places to provide economic benefits, however, some of them cause widespread economic and environmental damage. The environmental changes they cause can affect the livelihoods of local people, especially in regions where the dominant livelihood is (agro-) pastoralism. As invasive alien species (IAS) spread and displace native vegetation, the more they negatively affect natural resources that people depend on, as well as traditional sources of income and cultural goods (Bekele *et al*., 2018). Invasion of arid and semi-arid lands by woody IAS such as *P. juliflora* is associated with reductions in biodiversity, water availability, and grazing capacity for both wildlife and livestock. Controlling invasions and restoring degraded areas is important to ensure the sustainability of these ecosystem services. Therefore, there is an urgent need for management of IAS and for subsequent restoration or rehabilitation of the cleared land to safeguard livelihoods and ecosystem services. These interventions can reduce the impact on livelihoods by increasing fodder and water availability to livestock and may also provide environmental benefits such as reduced erosion or enhanced soil carbon sequestration (Eschen *et al*., 2021). Although people are willing to invest in the management of IAS (Bekele *et al*., 2018), the lack of tested options affects informed decision making in the affected communities. To manage woody IAS in a sustainable way, the trees must be killed and, if the land is subsequently used for agriculture, the rootstocks removed. Bulldozers and chain-pullers may be used for large areas. Manual and chemical methods may be more suitable for treating small, localized invasions. Local eradication at the start of an invasion should target individual young trees that are uprooted by pulling or digging.

title: Experimental Prosopis juliflora Management Practices and Grassland Restoration
text: Manual and chemical methods may be more suitable for treating small, localized invasions. Local eradication at the start of an invasion should target individual young trees that are uprooted by pulling or digging. Small stands of trees too large to be uprooted may be treated by spraying herbicide on the lower trunk (basal bark treatment, BB) or on the stump immediately after the trunk has been cut (cut stump treatment, CS). Restoration of grassland ecosystems involves accelerated vegetation development through methods that promote the establishment of species such as native perennial bunch grasses that are good fodder species, particularly in semi-arid and arid grasslands. The establishment of perennial vegetation would provide ecological and livelihood benefits, such as carbon sequestration, fodder, protection against erosion, and reduced weed establishment. The creation of ridges or divots, that collect rainwater and seeds, could increase the establishment of species already present in the seed bank by creating good conditions for seedling emergence. A mulch of hay on the soil surface may create a shade that helps maintain soil moisture, suppresses weeds, and moderates soil temperatures that can promote seed germination and establishment. Finally, sowing seeds of desired species can reintroduce or increase the density of these species. On restored pastures, grazing management such as rotational grazing and temporary grazing bans, may be needed to reduce overgrazing and allow permanent establishment and regrowth of fodder. Removal of *P. juliflora* from invaded land would mitigate some of its negative impacts, while restoration of grassland would strengthen pastoralist livelihoods and finally contribute to climate change mitigation (Mbaabu *et al*., 2020; Eschen *et al*., 2021). In Eastern Africa, the Kenyan government promotes management through utilization, including harvesting above-ground biomass for charcoal or using the pods as animal feed.

title: Experimental Prosopis juliflora Management Practices and Grassland Restoration
text: In Eastern Africa, the Kenyan government promotes management through utilization, including harvesting above-ground biomass for charcoal or using the pods as animal feed. Several NGOs promote the utilization for charcoal to manage *P. juliflora* in Eastern Africa, while also supporting livelihoods. There is no evidence that the utilization results in lasting reductions in abundance or spread (Mbaabu *et al*., 2019), and removing biomass for charcoal does not kill the trees, instead, they coppice profusely and produce flowers and seeds within a few months. The most successful and cost-effective way of permanent removal of *P. juliflora* is not known, and this case study describes a 3-year-long study that tested proposed management methods and grassland restoration interventions in three Eastern African countries. Four hypotheses were tested: (1) all three management methods are equally effective, but basal bark (BB) takes the least time and manual removal the most time to implement; (2) management without removal of above-ground biomass (BB treatment) results in the more rapid establishment of herbaceous species than interventions that remove the above-ground biomass (manual uprooting (MR) and cut stump (CS) treatments); (3) combining management with restoration interventions accelerates vegetation establishment and leads to a higher vegetation cover and species number; and (4) sowing grasses promotes the establishment of desired indigenous grass species (through mulching and sowing), as opposed to divots that promote the establishment of all species.

section: Description and Life Cycle of *Prosopis juliflora*
text:
*Prosopis juliflora*, known commonly as mesquite or algarrobo in its native neotropical region, is a tough, resilient and spiny tree, providing fuelwood in arid lands worldwide (Fig. 1). As a tree, it can grow up to about 13 m in height, with a twisted sinuous stem, sometimes shrubby in habit, and it can produce robust, hard, and strong timber suitable for construction purposes and fine furniture production. However, this is a best-case scenario and in practice this does not happen often. The trees rarely grow to this height and once the tree has been cut once, the coppices are of inferior quality. It can grow on any type of soil, including highly alkaline and saline soils. It requires very little rainfall (it can survive on 70 mm per year) (Pasiecznik, 2017; Tropical Forages, 2020). ##### Fig. 1. #####
*P. juliflora* tree. Available at: <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/>. *Prosopis juliflora* produces greenish-white turning light yellow florets on long cylindrical racemes of 7–15 cm length (Fig. 2), and these are pollinated by a wide range of insects (Tropical Forages, 2020). Depending on environmental conditions, flowering may start as early as in 1-year-old plants to as late as 12-year-old plants. *P. juliflora* produces nutritious and palatable straw-coloured pods that mature in the dry season and provide valuable fodder and human food crops. Seeds are broadly ovoid, 6 × 4 mm and brownish (Tropical Forages, 2020) (Fig. 3).

text:
Seeds are broadly ovoid, 6 × 4 mm and brownish (Tropical Forages, 2020) (Fig. 3). The leaves are 3–11 cm long and along with other foliage is good fodder, especially as emergency fodder during droughts, but only in small quantities (Fig. 4). *P. juliflora* seeds are primarily spread by animals that ingested pods containing mature seeds. The species is suitable for use in hedges and live fences. It has been used in reclamation reforestation of mining spoil, wastelands, and sand dunes (Pasiecznik, 2017). ##### Fig. 2. #####

Within the context of this case study, the key point is that the trees coppice when aboveground parts are cut. This is the rationale for the cut stump treatment and why the mechanical removal treatment was designed as it was. Given this, as an invasive species with animals as the major vector of spread and causing *P. juliflora* to spread far and wide, this is a problem due to the numerous negative impacts that outweigh the benefits of its use for fodder and wood. ##### Fig. 4. #####

title: Experimental Prosopis juliflora Management Practices and Grassland Restoration
text:
### Study areas ###
The study was conducted in three countries to assess the applicability of the tested methods in different regions and habitat types affected by *P. juliflora* in Eastern Africa (Fig. 5). The climate of the three sites was comparable (arid and warm), but the history of invasion, land use, and disturbance varied across the sites. All three countries have adopted national strategies for dealing with invasive species or *P. juliflora* specifically, although no herbicides have been approved or tested for control of *P. juliflora*. The results of this study were, therefore, expected to support decision making concerning *P. juliflora* management. ##### Fig. 5. #####
Map of Eastern Africa showing the approximate locations of the study areas in Ethiopia (Awash Town), Kenya (Baringo County), and Tanzania (Moshi District) (Eschen *et al*., 2023). ### Characteristics of the study areas ###
#### Ethiopia ####
Location: Awash
Characteristics: Arid and semi-arid dryland
Occupation of the population: Almost 90% of the population are pastoralists
Natural vegetation cover: Patches of scattered dry shrubs, acacia woodland, bushland, grassland, and wooded grassland
Situation: Awash River floodplains, the main dry season source of grazing, are invaded or under risk of invasion by *P. juliflora*. *P. juliflora* is replacing the original vegetation and other land use types (grassland, bare land, bush-shrub-woodland, and natural forests). Effects of the invasion: Biodiversity loss, reduced water availability and mobility loss and ultimately resulted in significant negative impact of local livelihoods, mainly pastoralism (Bekele *et al*., 2018; Shiferaw *et al*., 2019).

title: Experimental Prosopis juliflora Management Practices and Grassland Restoration
text:
#### Kenya ####
Location: Njemps flats of Baringo. Occupation of the population: Largely (agro-) pastoralists keeping cattle, sheep, and goats and engaging in small-scale cultivation. Natural vegetation cover: Historically classic savanna vegetation such as Acacia trees (mainly *Vachellia tortilis*) in association with *Boscia* spp, *Balanites aegyptiaca,* and bushes of *Salvadora persica*. Generally, the understory lacked permanent herbaceous cover but ephemeral herbs appeared during the wet season. Situation and effects: *P. juliflora* was introduced in 1983 to an area of 250 ha (2.5 km2), to mitigate problems such as lack of firewood and decreasing vegetation cover. Effects of the invasion: The *P. juliflora* invasion now covers an area of 1276 km2, with significant impacts on water resources, land use, and livelihoods. #### Tanzania ####
Location: Kahe Ward in Moshi District. Occupation of the population: The main economic activities are crop cultivation (maize, beans, and tomatoes) which rely on irrigation from existing canals, rivers and wells, and livestock keeping dominated by cattle, sheep, and goats. Natural vegetation: Characterized by scattered Baobab (*Adansonia digitata*), *Faidherbia albida* (apple-ring acacia), *Vachellia xanthophloea* (Yellow-bark acacia), and the two shrubs *Suaeda monoica* and *Tamarix nilotica* in areas adjacent to river courses. Situation and effects: *P. juliflora* arrived in the area mainly through livestock movements and floods which carry substantial amount of seeds from invaded areas in the north-eastern side bordering Kenya.

title: Experimental Prosopis juliflora Management Practices and Grassland Restoration
text:
Situation and effects: *P. juliflora* arrived in the area mainly through livestock movements and floods which carry substantial amount of seeds from invaded areas in the north-eastern side bordering Kenya. *P. juliflora* has replaced most of the natural vegetation and it is now the dominant tree species in the area. Effects of the invasion: Due to its high densities, *P. juliflora* is already posing management challenges by invading agricultural fields under fallow, making crop production laborious and more expensive. It has also replaced grasslands and thereby reducing the land available for livestock grazing. ### Experimental design ###
The field sites were chosen in areas where the initial *P. juliflora* cover was over 80% and at similar densities. In each country, three 40 × 80 m blocks were established, making nine blocks in total (Fig. 6). Each block was fenced to prevent livestock disturbance and was divided into four plots (40 × 20 m). Each of these four plots was randomly assigned to one of the following four management treatments: basal bark; control (no treatment); cut stump; and mechanical removal. ##### Fig. 6. #####
Schematic representation of treatment allocation per block. *P. juliflora* control treatments in four plots. Half of each plot enclosed in a barbed wire fence to exclude grazers. Colour-coded horizontal subplots indicating which resotoration treatment were assigned to each plot (courtesy of Eschen *et al*., 2023). Half of each plot was enclosed in barbed wire to allow for a controlled grazing component of the investigation. Each plot was divided into four subplots of 10 × 20 m, half in and half outside of the barbed wire enclosure.

title: Experimental Prosopis juliflora Management Practices and Grassland Restoration
text: Half of each plot was enclosed in barbed wire to allow for a controlled grazing component of the investigation. Each plot was divided into four subplots of 10 × 20 m, half in and half outside of the barbed wire enclosure. These subplots were randomly assigned to one of the following four restoration treatments: control; divoting; divoting + mulching; and divoting + sowing + mulching. Divots were shallow hollows of 50 cm and 10–15 cm deep in the ground at a rate of 36 per 10 × 10 m subplot. Mulch consisted of locally sourced grass hay. The seed mixtures used consisted of native grasses and were sown at a density of 2 g/m2. The main grass species in all countries was *Cenchrus ciliaris*, a highly palatable species commonly sown on grassland restoration sites in Eastern Africa.

title: Experimental Prosopis juliflora Management Practices and Grassland Restoration
text:
The main grass species in all countries was *Cenchrus ciliaris*, a highly palatable species commonly sown on grassland restoration sites in Eastern Africa. ### Treatments ###
For control of *P. juliflora*:
* Basal bark treated with the herbicide Triclon (Triclopyr) (BB) (chemical)
* Cut stump treated with herbicide Triclon (Triclopyr) (CS) (physical and chemical)
* Mechanical removal (MR) (physical)
* Control (CO) (no treatment)
Restoration treatments:
* Divoting (DIV)
* Divoting + mulching (DIM)
* Divoting + sowing + mulching (DSM)
* Control (UNR)
Grazing control:
* Half of each subplot was open to grazing and the other half was fenced off
### Data collection ###
The following data were collected:
* Stem base diameter of all *P. juliflora* in each plot prior to treatments in Kenya and Tanzania
* Time taken to conduct the treatments in each plot
* Tree survival at different time intervals – recorded as lack of regrowth from CS treatment or general drying of leaves in BB treatment
* The number of *P. juliflora* seedlings per plot at different time intervals in Kenya and Tanzania
* Species richness in random areas (excluding *P. juliflora*)
* Cover of herbaceous vegetation in randomly selected areas
* Grass biomass
### Statistical analyses ###
Analysis of the univariate parameters was conducted using generalized linear mixed effects models using the glmmTMB function from the glmmtmb package.

title: Experimental Prosopis juliflora Management Practices and Grassland Restoration
text: The time for implementation and effectiveness (mortality) of *P. juliflora* treatment; total vegetation cover and species number of the vegetation were used as response variables, and *P. juliflora* treatment, grazing and restoration interventions as explanatory variables.

title: Experimental Prosopis juliflora Management Practices and Grassland Restoration
text:
### Implementation time ###
Treatment implementation time was highest in the MR treatment and lowest for BB. Time to implement CS was intermediate, possibly due to having to remove cut trees from the plots (Fig. 7). ##### Fig. 7. #####
Prosopis treatment implementation time in three countries (courtesy of Eschen *et al*., 2023). Pale grey bar = basal bark (BB); dark grey bar = cut stump (CS); black bar = manual removal (MR); white bar = control treatment (CO); error bars indicate standard error. ### Mortality ###
All treatments were effective at killing *P. juliflora*, with consistently high mortality rates in CS and MR treatments (Fig. 8). Effectiveness of BB was lower in Kenya than in Tanzania, possibly due to larger stem diameter (Fig. 9). ##### Fig. 8. #####
Mortality (effectiveness) of prosopis treatments in three countries (courtesy of Eschen *et al*., 2023). Pale grey bar = basal bark (BB); dark grey bar = cut stump (CS); black bar = manual removal (MR); white bar = control treatment (CO); error bars indicate standard error. ##### Fig. 9. #####
Stem base diameter (cm) prior to treatment in two countries (courtesy of Eschen *et al*., 2023). BB = basal bark; CO = control treatment; CS = cut stump; MR = manual removal; error bars indicate standard error. Stem base diameter was larger in Kenya than in Tanzania. There were no differences in stem base diameter between the treatments.

text:
BB = basal bark; CO = control treatment; CS = cut stump; MR = manual removal; error bars indicate standard error. Stem base diameter was larger in Kenya than in Tanzania. There were no differences in stem base diameter between the treatments. ### Vegetation biomass ###

text: This study shows that it is possible to kill *P. juliflora* and establish productive grassland in its place. The results demonstrate that the cost (i.e. time investment) and subsequent vegetation development differ among the methods used to kill *P. juliflora*. Both chemical control treatments are far cheaper and quicker than uprooting, with basal bark treatment even quicker than cut stump treatment. The method chosen to control *P. juliflora* depends on the availability of resources, including herbicides, and the need to remove rootstocks if the intention is to plant crops.

### Overview ###
Sugarcane is a worldwide crop providing many products and co-products. However, this crop is infested by many pests and diseases and this case study clearly argues for an effective biosecurity strategy to avoid pest incursions, economic losses and food shortages in Africa. Key management solutions are proposed to curb pest infestation.

title: 'New Invasive and Potential Pests in Sugarcane Agrosystems in Africa: How to
text: Sugarcane, *Saccharum officinarum* Linné, 1753 (Poaceae), is a worldwide crop produced in more than 100 countries and is used to make sugar, ethanol and other by-products. Currently, Brazil and India are the largest producers of sugarcane. Most sugar (80%) comes from sugarcane, while the remaining 20% comes from sugar beet, *Beta vulgaris* L., with production, particularly in developing countries, continuing to increase worldwide (Moore and Botha, 2014). In Africa, even though sugar production is well below that of the leading regions in Asia and South America (more than 80% of the world output), production is projected to increase by 36% to reach 15.1 Mt by the end of 2030. This is due to production expansion in sub-Saharan countries, particularly in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) countries, boosted by national and international investments in the sector, and to suitable conditions for growing sugar crops, including a favourable climate and available land (OECD-FAO, 2021). As with many other crops, sugarcane is infested by a various range of pests (and diseases), some of them being of economic importance, such as the stem borers (e.g., those in the genera *Eldana*, *Chilo*, *Diatraea*, *Sesamia*, etc. ), white grubs (Coleoptera), leaf feeders (e.g., *Spodoptera*, *Mythimna*) and sap feeders (e.g., aphids, thrips, mealybugs, delphacids) which are also vectors of major diseases (Long and Hensley, 1972; Goebel *et al*., 2018).

title: 'New Invasive and Potential Pests in Sugarcane Agrosystems in Africa: How to
text: With global warming and growing world trade in plant products, the risks of agricultural pests and diseases spreading across continents will continue to increase (Kiritani, 2006; Cilas *et al*., 2016; Seebens *et al*., 2017; Skendžić *et al*., 2021). These biological invasions pose a devastating threat to the integrity of natural habitats, the productivity of agricultural commodities and the sustainability of rural economies (Fisher *et al*., 2012). Sugarcane is no exception, and every year, this industrial crop is subjected to the incursion of new insect pests as well as pest outbreaks that are able to threaten the whole sugar industry (Goebel and Sallam, 2011). It is widely recognised, therefore, that all stakeholders in the industry focus not only on pest and disease research of endemic or already present pests but also the risks of new pests and diseases arriving from elsewhere and how to manage those risks and potential impacts (Thompson *et al*., 2010; Goebel and Sallam, 2011; Rott, 2018). This is plant biosecurity which falls under the umbrella of the International Plant Protection Convention (IPPC; Available at: [www.ippc.int](http://www.ippc.int), accessed 1 May 2024). IPPC sets internationally agreed standards for biosecurity and managing biosecurity threats. In this official context, The National Plant Protection Organisations (NPPOs) a member of IPPC presents in all countries/regions of the world can determine import conditions, based on Pest Risk Analysis (PRA). Risk analysis of sugarcane biosecurity is a formal and key step in identifying potential threats with the objective to compare and rank them (Thomson, 2018).

title: 'New Invasive and Potential Pests in Sugarcane Agrosystems in Africa: How to
text: Risk analysis of sugarcane biosecurity is a formal and key step in identifying potential threats with the objective to compare and rank them (Thomson, 2018). PRA is defined as “identifying pests of quarantine concern to an area, determining pathways and the likelihood of introduction and establishment, and selecting optimum effective pest management options for minimising their introduction and establishment potential” (Singh, 1995). The IPPC provides a framework for conducting PRA for insect pests, pathogens, plants, parasitic plants and genetically modified organisms. For instance, invasions of pests and diseases are well known in Australia, where the sugarcane industry is always under threat due to its proximity to other tropical and developing countries such as Indonesia and Papua-New Guinea (Goebel and Sallam, 2011; Magarey *et al*., 2012). Strict quarantine procedures and phytosanitary control occur at ports and airports and huge efforts have been made to prevent numerous alien species from entering in this highly exposed country. In most producing countries in Africa, the incursion of new pests as well as pest resurgence/outbreaks is far less known and documented, except in South Africa and the Indian Ocean islands close to Africa (i.e., Mauritius and Reunion) where government authorities have put in place biosecurity and surveillance at ports of entry. Biosecurity and prevention against new pests and diseases is a part of integrated pest management at the borders and when they are accidentally introduced, there is a need for appropriate action before their rapid expansion (Lovett and Perry, 2014; Paini *et al*., 2016).

text: To illustrate this key component of biosecurity, Australia has recently organised a rapid strategy against the new incursion of *Spodoptera frugiperda* in 2020, a transboundary pest originating from South and Central America (Piggott *et al*., 2021), while the African continent which was severely hit by this pest in 2016, took time to organise an appropriate response and awareness (Goergen *et al*., 2016; Nagoshi *et al*., 2018). After presenting some recent introductions of new pests to the African continent during the last 20 years, we discuss the importance of a biosecurity strategy for the protection of sugar industries in African countries against invasive pests.

section: Incursions of Insect Pests in South Africa: A Warning to Other Sugar Industries
text: Several cases of incursion have recently been described in the South African industry such as the black sugarcane thrip *Fulmekiola serrata* (Kobus, 1892) (Hemiptera: Thripidae) was introduced in 2004 from the Indian Ocean Islands (i.e., Reunion, Madagascar and Mauritius) (Way *et al*., 2006). This pest spread rapidly across the sugarcane areas, particularly in the province of KwaZulu-Natal, where the majority of the crop is cultivated. This expansion was associated with a severe drought and has put the South African Sugarcane Institute (SASRI) on alert and research programmes are currently focused on this pest to find a control strategy (Keeping *et al*., 2008). Experiments on the impact of *F. serrata* on cane yield have revealed that in cases of high infestation, this pest can cause 18–27% losses in cane biomass and 16% and 24% losses in sucrose (Way *et al*., 2010). *F. serrata* is now widespread throughout the sugarcane-growing regions of the country and is listed as a major pest, with infestation that can be exacerbated during periods of long drought. The second threat for the South African sugarcane industry is the spotted stemborer *Chilo sacchariphagus* Bojer (Lepidoptera: Crambidae), which was introduced to Mozambique in 1999. This species is also an imminent biosecurity threat for the Malawian, Tanzanian and Swaziland sugar industries (Benzuidenhout *et al*., 2008). This was unfortunate for South Africa because it already has a stemborer problem caused by the native species *Eldana saccharina* Walker (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae).

section: Incursions of Insect Pests in South Africa: A Warning to Other Sugar Industries
text: This was unfortunate for South Africa because it already has a stemborer problem caused by the native species *Eldana saccharina* Walker (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae). *C. sacchariphagus* is a major pest in many Asian countries, as well as Reunion and Mauritius (Goebel *et al*., 2010) and in Mozambique, where it can cause significant yield losses in terms of sugar (up to 5%) and tonnes of cane per hectare (up to 30%) (Conlong and Goebel, 2002; Goebel and Way, 2009). As a result of the threat to South Africa, the sugarcane industry has implemented a biosecurity strategy based on pest surveillance at the border using a grid of pheromone traps and a planned rapid response (Way *et al*., 2004). The last example in South Africa is the recent incursion of the longhorn beetle *Cacosceles newmannii* Thomson, 1877 (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae) into the sugarcane areas of KwaZulu-Natal, where it was observed for the first time in 2015 in the Entumeni district. *C. newmannii* is thought to be native to Mozambique, but its full host range and distribution are not known (Javal *et al*., 2019). This incursion has necessitated one of the most extensive pest containment exercises ever launched by the industry, with new amendments made to the Sugar Industry Agreement to proclaim the longhorn beetle a hazardous pest (Way *et al*., 2017). The damage caused by the larval stage is extensive since they can grow to a length of 90 mm and burrow in cane stubble attacking the base of the stalk. Larvae then make tunnels of 20–30 cm across several internodes causing severe damage as they hollow out the inside of the stalk (Way *et al*., 2017).

text: Larvae then make tunnels of 20–30 cm across several internodes causing severe damage as they hollow out the inside of the stalk (Way *et al*., 2017). Infested plants turn yellow and suffer poor growth until they ultimately die. In Thailand, yield losses of up to 50% have been reported by another Cerambycidae species *Dorysthenes buqueti* (Guérin-Méneville, 1844), and it can be controlled by entomopathogenic nematods (EPNs) and fungi such as *Metarhizium anisopliae*. In cases of severe infestation of cerambycid species, crops fail to ratoon properly or die completely and ratoon crops usually sustain more damage than plant cane. Efforts are underway to attempt to eradicate the beetle from sugarcane in South Africa by ploughing out all affected sugarcane. The success of these efforts is not clear as yet. In addition, various remedial measures were proposed including the emergency registration of the insecticide Warlock 19.2 EC (Emulsifiable concentrate of emamectin benzoate (active ingredient)) for the treatment of the longhorn beetle on sugarcane, and restrictions on cane movement – in particular the movement and sale of seedcane.

text:
This aphid is today in full expansion across the African continent. *Sipha flava* originates from North America where it was first described in 1884 (Fig. 1). Since then, it has become a well-known pest of sorghum and sugarcane in the USA. In 2006, it was first recorded in African sugarcane in Morocco, and then later on in South Africa (2013) and Zambia in 2014, and more recently in Swaziland and Zimbabwe (Way *et al*., 2015). In Zambia, it caused great concern because of its high population mainly explained by favourable climatic factors in the sugarcane estates (Thomas *et al*., 2018). In Tanzania, *S. flava*, which was first recorded as a pest in 2016, had a rapid expansion into the vast majority of sugarcane areas, particularly in susceptible varieties (Goebel, 2021). Today this aphid can be controlled when pesticides (neonicotinoids) are applied but it continues to be the major pest in two main sugarcane estates, i.e., TPC Limited (North Tanzania) and Illovo (Kilombero, South-east Tanzania). This aphid is currently causing damage and losses in Central Africa, particularly in Gabon (first observations in 2017) and Congo-Brazaville in 2018, in the sugarcane areas belonging to the French sugar company SOMDIAA (Goebel, 2022). ##### Fig. 1. #####

The yellow sugarcane aphid (*S. flava*) (damage, left; apterous individuals) (Photo: F.R. Goebel and CIRAD image). Hosts of *S. flava* include a wide range of cultivated crops (cereals) and wild plants: sorghum (*Sorghum bicolor*), rice (*Oryza sativa*), wheat (*Triticum aestivum*) and other gramineous plants belonging to the genera *Digitaria*, *Panicum*, *Paspalum*, and *Pennisetum*. *Sipha flava* can easily be distinguished from the common sugarcane aphid (*Melanaphis sacchari*) by its longitudinal rows of stout, erect bristles, which are a bit stouter than the others (Nuessly, 2019). The legs are hairy and the ventral segments are also covered with short hairs. *Melanaphis sacchari* is hairless and has bigger and darker cornicles than *S. flava* (Fig. 2). Like other aphid species, *S. flava* is highly responsive to environmental change due to its short generation time, high reproductive rates and efficient dispersal mechanisms (Way *et al*., 2015; Thomas *et al*., 2018). Its life cycle takes approximately 8–15 days to complete at a temperature range of 16–29°C. ##### Fig. 2. #####

text: *S. flava* feeds on the underside of leaves causing yellow to red or purple discoloration of tissues which leads to leaf chlorosis and senescence. In addition, this aphid is able to transmit the sugarcane mosaic virus (SCMV), even though the relationship between the aphid and this virus is not formally established. Apart from chemical insecticides, this aphid has a number of predators and parasitoids that are able to drastically reduce its population. Species of the family Coccinelidae, Syrphidae and Chrysopidae are among the most effective natural enemies. It is expected that *S. flava* will continue its expansion to western African countries.

Armyworms are important pests of cultivated crops in Africa, such as cotton, maize, rice, sorghum, millet and sugarcane. As mentioned above, the fall armyworm (FAW) *S. frugiperda* is an invasive pest and has become a major constraint for maize farmers in many countries in West and Central Africa. Despite severe yield losses recorded in these parts of Africa, FAW is not currently a major pest of sugarcane. However, caution and vigilance are needed as another species, *Spodoptera exempta* has been observed in many sugarcane fields in Cameroon (2021) and Congo causing severe damage to sugarcane leaves. Hence surveillance and warning systems for new pests are needed, particularly in the context of climate change with long periods of drought and heavy rains in most African countries (Fig. 3). ##### Fig. 3. #####

section: What are the Major Pest Threats for the Sugar Industry in Africa?
text: \* SCYLV = Sugarcane yellow leaf virus. \*\* SCMV = Sugarcane mosaic. \*\*\* FDV = Fiji disease virus. Each continent has its own native pest species. For example, in terms of moth borer species, Africa has *Eldana saccharina*, Asia and the Indian Ocean has *Chilo sacchariphagus* (and other *Chilo* species) and the South American continent has *Diatraea saccharalis* (and other *Diatraea* species). However today, the distribution of these pests has changed and will continue to change, with global warming and the intensification of world trade. As an example, *C. sacchariphagus* has been introduced in South Africa via Mozambique (Way *et al*., 2003, 2004) and it is difficult to anticipate what will happen in the near future with these borer species. Additionally, *Telchin* (= *Castnia*) *licus* (Lepidoptera: Castniidae) the giant sugarcane borer also known as the banana stem borer present in Brazil and today in numerous countries in South America (Pabón-Valverde *et al*., 2022) may pose a threat to sugar-producing countries in Africa. Another worrying fact is the change in the status of some important pests. For example, very recently *Rynchophorus ferrugineus* (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) a palm weevil borer was detected in sugarcane plantations in south China and this adaptation of a pest to new crops is well documented (Qin *et al*., 2022). This pest is highly invasive and has recently expanded beyond its natural range from southern and south-east Asia westwards, over vast areas of the Middle East and the Mediterranean basin.

text: This pest is highly invasive and has recently expanded beyond its natural range from southern and south-east Asia westwards, over vast areas of the Middle East and the Mediterranean basin. This type of situation can easily happen in African sugarcane crops, as the pest is also present in countries around the Mediterranean Sea (e.g., Morocco, Libya, Algeria, Egypt). It remains possible that the species will use other countries in Africa as stepping stones for further dispersal, reaching Ghana and other west African countries along the coast. Apart from natural spread, currently, the only major and likely pathway of the introduction of *R. ferrugineus* is through the import of palm trees with a stem diameter >5 cm. Two other weevil borers attacking sugarcane, *Rhabdoscelus obscurus* (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) present in the Pacific islands (e.g., Fiji, French Polynesia, Australia) and native to New Guinea, and *Metamasius hemipterus* (Curculionidae) in Central and South America and the Caribbean Islands, can be considered as potential threats for Africa.
