section: Towards Better Preparedness and Awareness for Pest Incursions in Africa
text: Pests and diseases will continue to threaten agroindustries due to climate change, world trade and pest adaptation to new crops. New pest incursions can occur everywhere because developing countries are more exposed, it is important for them to be well prepared and organised for preparedness, pest risk analysis and implementation of suitable control measures. Plant biosecurity best practices adopted by the Australian plant health agencies can serve as a model to African countries confronted by these new incursions. The strategy includes threat identification, incursion risk analysis, pathway risk analysis, surveillance detection and diagnostic strategies and industry biosecurity planning. Industry biosecurity planning has been adopted not only for risk prioritisation but also for ensuring rapid response through an Emergency Plant Pest Response Deed (EPPRD) process that allows agreement on who will pay for incursion response before the incursion happens based on the scale of the threat. In Africa, one interesting initiative worth mentioning is Cropwatch Africa (Available at: <https://www.cropwatch.africa>, accessed 1 May 2024), which is a specialized Service Provider that focuses on supporting Farmers, Communities, Industries and Governments across Southern Africa, in safeguarding their resources, by ensuring early detection of invasive pests and diseases before they cause significant damage. Efficient monitoring and detection efforts increase the likelihood that new invasive plants, pests and diseases will be noticed rapidly while occurrences are still localized. Cropwatch Africa Platforms include mobile applications to collect data in the field, and in real-time display the data on an online-cloud-based GIS platform. This service provider can also be used in other parts of Africa, particularly the most remote/less developed regions.

The AU-IAPSC is Africa’s Regional Plant Protection Organization (RPPO), serving African countries. AU-IAPSC was established on recommendation of FAO in 1956 in London and became part of the Organization of African Unity (OAU) in 1965. This organisation based in Yaoundé in Cameroon is responsible for coordinating phytosanitary advocacy and capacity-building activities at the continental level and plays a major role in harmonising regulatory and management strategies for emerging plant health and plant pest challenges in Africa. An interesting project (2021–2023) has been coordinated by CABI to support the implementation of the Plant Health Strategy for Africa (Available at: [www.cabi.org/what-we-do/cabiprojects/](http://www.cabi.org/what-we-do/cabiprojects/), accessed 1 May 2024). The sugarcane sector can certainly use this initiative to implement its own biosecurity strategy.

section: Conclusion: Towards a Sustainable and Well-Safeguarded Sugarcane Industry in Sub-Saharan Africa
text: High sugar and biomass-yielding sugarcane already contribute to improving the value and sustainability of the sugarcane industry worldwide, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. Therefore, safeguarding this industry for food and energy security by implementing a concrete biosecurity strategy such as the model developed in Australia will undoubtedly reinforce the capacity of African producing countries to face and combat new pests and diseases. Some interesting initiatives are currently in place across the continent, particularly in Eastern and Southern Africa (SADC countries); however, more effort needs to be done in the least developed countries, which is a big challenge knowing the current political instability of some countries in West Africa. Several Animal and Plant Health organisations have already been created in Africa and it is expected that cooperation with international research organisations such as CGIAR, CABI, CIRAD, FAO and others involved in Africa will be reinforced through dedicated research and training projects. Apart from biotechnology needs (genomics), which requires highly qualified staff, laboratory investments and quarantine facilities, it will be important for African countries to develop sound pest management strategies in the field, based on agroecological crop protection (ACP) principles. It includes containment measures, change or modification of agricultural practices (e.g., fertilisers, varieties), setting up of grid of pheromone traps for early pest detection, enhancement of conservation biological control by introducing companion plants in and around sugarcane fields, use of trash blanketing in sugarcane field which comes with “zero burning practice” (field burning is often used in Africa before harvesting sugarcane) to preserve natural enemies of pests (parasitoids and predators), etc. Insecticide applications generally used as an urgent fix should be avoided as much as possible in this global strategy based on the mobilisation of key ecosystemic services for a sustainable crop production. We thus appeal to a long-term biosecurity and agroecological crop protection plan for the benefit of the sugarcane sector in Africa.

### Overview ###
Sugarcane yellow leaf virus (SCYLV) impacts sugarcane production globally due to its complex aetiology, phylogeny, spread, and effects on yield when infecting different varieties. SCYLV complexity varies in different sugarcane-producing regions, making research on a global scale necessary. Here, we discuss avenues to understand SCYLV impact on sugarcane production better.

title: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus – A Silent Threat?
text:
Yellow leaf disease is caused by sugarcane yellow leaf virus (SCYLV), though it was originally reported under different names, including yellow wilt and yellow leaf syndrome (Fig. 1). The disease was first identified in Tanzania in 1962 as yellow wilt, and later in 1989, it was recognized as yellow leaf disease by researchers in Hawaii. Nearly a decade later, the aetiology of the disease became clearer when it was associated with a previously undescribed luteovirus, which was subsequently named SCYLV. SCYLV has been taxonomically assigned to the species *Polerovirus SCYLV. * While originally being placed in the *Luteoviridae* family*,* it has been reclassified and is now a member of the *Polerovirus* genus and *Solemoviridae* family. SCYLV consists of a positive-sense ssRNA [(+)ssRNA] genome that is approximately 5.8–5.9 kilobases in size with six open reading frames. ORF0 encodes an RNA silencing suppressor, ORF1 encodes a multifunctional protein, ORF2 codes for the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, ORF3 encodes the coat protein, ORF4 codes for the virus movement protein, and ORF5 is hypothesized to encode a protein involved in vector transmission. The genome is packaged in an icosahedral virion with a diameter ranging from 24 to 29 nm. ##### Fig. 1. #####
Characteristic midvein yellowing (white arrow) due to sugarcane yellow leaf virus infection in an experimental field in Houma, Louisiana. SCYLV is transmitted by aphid vectors, with the sugarcane aphid (*Melanaphis sacchari* Zehntner) being the most significant.

title: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus – A Silent Threat?
text: SCYLV is transmitted by aphid vectors, with the sugarcane aphid (*Melanaphis sacchari* Zehntner) being the most significant. Other insect species, such as *Rhopalosiphum maidis* (Fitch), *R. rufiabdominalis* (Sasaki), and *Ceratovacuna lanigera* (Zehntner), can also transmit SCYLV in a circulative, non-propagative manner, though *M. sacchari* remains the principal vector (Figs. 2 and 3). Upon aphid feeding on the phloem of SCYLV-infected sugarcane, the virus moves through the aphid gut tissue, i.e., acquisition and into the haemolymph. Upon movement to the salivary glands, SCYLV can be transmitted to healthy tissue in subsequent feeding. Transmission is also non-propagative in that while crossing these tissue barriers, the virus does not replicate. Transmission experiments in the greenhouse indicate the sugarcane aphid can acquire SCYLV after 4.5 h of continuous feeding on infected sugarcane and transmit it to healthy tissue within two days of feeding (Paray *et al*., 2011). While aphids may acquire SCYLV from infected sugarcane, they could also acquire the virus from non-cultivated host species. For example, this virus was found surviving in Columbus grass, a common weed occurring near sugarcane fields in Florida. Despite continued efforts to understand its aetiology, transmission, and impact on sugarcane production, the disease’s variable symptom expression across different regions, cultivars, and soil types highlights the need for improved detection methods and a deeper understanding of its epidemiology.

title: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus – A Silent Threat?
text:
When the disease was first reported in Hawaii, cultivar H 65-7052 showed the typical yellow leaf disease symptoms – yellowing of the mid rib on the abaxial surface of sugarcane leaves, evolving to leaf tip yellowing and necrosis with an eventual appearance of a reddish colour in the otherwise chlorotic mid ribs. However, even though cultivar H 65-7052 was symptomatic, neighbouring sugarcane fields with different cultivars did not show symptoms. It is noteworthy that the lack of reliable detection methods at the time makes it unclear whether those neighbouring sugarcane fields were infected with the virus. The yellowing of the midrib, the most typical symptom of yellow leaf disease, can be confused with abiotic stresses, underscoring the importance of accurate diagnostic techniques. Moreover, the disease can occur asymptomatically in many sugarcane varieties while still negatively impacting yield, making field surveys and assessments of cultivar resistance or tolerance to SCYLV essential. ##### Fig. 2. #####

title: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus – A Silent Threat?
text:
The impact of SCYLV infection on sugarcane varies significantly depending on the cultivar. Due to the often-asymptomatic nature of virus infection, accurately assessing its effect on yield can be challenging. The most severe yield loss attributed to yellow leaf disease was reported in Brazil with the cultivar SP 71-6163 in 1993, where sugar yields were reduced by 50%, leading to the cultivar’s abandonment by the growers, highlighting the need to understand a cultivar’s susceptibility to SCYLV and virus impacts on yield. In Louisiana, sugar yields were reduced by approximately 11% when comparing SCYLV-infected plants with healthy ones of the cultivar HoCP 96-540, a key variety in the state. In Florida, cultivar CP96-1252 experienced a 27% reduction in sugar yield when comparing a field with 100% SCYLV prevalence to another with only 2% prevalence. Importantly, the above yield losses were often recorded on asymptomatic infections, relying on serological and molecular techniques to detect the virus. Since cultivars vary genetically, they have individual yield characteristics and responses to viral infections, therefore, assessing the impact of SCYLV on popular cultivars in each sugarcane-growing region is crucial to ensure that yields are not being compromised by the disease. ##### Fig. 4. #####

title: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus – A Silent Threat?
text: SCYLV is prevalent across sugarcane-producing regions worldwide, including most countries that grow sugarcane in the Americas, Asia, and Africa, such as Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Cuba, Guatemala, Mexico, China, the Philippines, Senegal, South Africa, and Kenya (Rott *et al. *, 2023). Monitoring yellow leaf disease is challenging due to the variability in symptom expression – symptoms can differ among cultivars, across regions, and between growing seasons. Detection is further complicated by the seasonal nature of symptoms which can appear, disappear, and reappear throughout the growing cycle (Lehrer and Komor, 2008). Following significant outbreaks of yellow leaf disease and the advancement of diagnostic techniques, particularly RT-PCR, SCYLV was detected in numerous sugarcane varieties worldwide, often in asymptomatic plants. Asymptomatic plant material infected with SCYLV was likely propagated by growers unaware of its presence, unintentionally introduced to fields via the planting material, and later exacerbated by aphid-mediated spread (Fig. 4). Vegetative propagation of planting material, and subsequently the virus, likely contributed to the virus’s widespread distribution and its presence in most sugarcane-producing countries today (Fig. 5). With advances in molecular techniques, various SCYLV genotypes have been identified. There are 10 major SCYLV genotypes – BRA, HAW, PER, CHN3, REU, FLA3, CHN1, FLA1/2, IND, and CUB – which have been recently grouped into three phylogroups: G1, G2, and G3.

title: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus – A Silent Threat?
text:
Genotypes BRA, HAW, PER, and CHN3 belong to G1; REU is the sole genotype in G2; and FLA3, CHN1, FLA1/2, IND, and CUB are clustered in G3 (Lu *et al. *, 2021). However, a SCYLV isolate from Guatemala did not fit into any of these major phylogroups, suggesting that SCYLV’s genetic diversity may be even broader than previously assumed (Rott *et al*., 2023). This is especially important considering the global nature of sugarcane may facilitate the sharing of plant material, and subsequently, SCYLV. Regarding the local spread of SCYLV by aphid species, understanding the genotypes present is essential as the sugarcane aphid is reported to transmit different genotypes with different efficiencies (Abu Ahmad *et al*., 2007). This high genetic diversity further complicates SCYLV detection – primers or antisera may be optimized for some genotypes but fail to detect others, making comprehensive monitoring a challenging task. ##### Fig. 5. #####

title: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus – A Silent Threat?
section: Detecting a Barely Visible Threat – A Difficult Challenge
text: Given the potential of SCYLV to significantly reduce yields in susceptible cultivars, substantial efforts have been directed towards developing reliable diagnostic tools. Yield losses from SCYLV infections can occur even in the absence of visible symptoms, making it difficult for researchers to accurately correlate yield declines with traditional visual disease quantification methods, such as disease scales or severity ratings. SCYLV can be detected using various serological and molecular techniques, including tissue-blot immunoassays (TBIA), double-antibody sandwich-enzyme linked immunoassays (DAS-ELISA), RT-PCR, and real-time RT-PCR. The sensitivity of these diagnostic methods is crucial in determining the accuracy of SCYLV detection. While TBIA is a quick, inexpensive, and high-throughput option, it is less sensitive than molecular-based assays and may fail to detect low viral titres in plants, especially during milder infections or periods of natural seasonality. Furthermore, such assays may be unable to detect all SCYLV genotypes, resulting in false negatives. Recently, new assays including reverse transcription-loop mediated isothermal amplification (RT-LAMP), reverse transcription-recombinase polymerase amplification (RT-RPA), and reverse transcription-multienzyme isothermal rapid amplification (RT-MIRA) have been developed. These assays show increased sensitivity compared to RT-PCR, though their sensitivity was assessed using a limited genetic diversity. These assays provide a promising future to detection upon optimization with additional genotypes. In Louisiana, current sampling recommendations suggest collecting the top visible dewlap leaf of the plant in question, since previous studies found that the highest proportion of infected vascular bundles was found in the top leaves based on results from tissue immunoblot assays.

title: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus – A Silent Threat?
section: Detecting a Barely Visible Threat – A Difficult Challenge
text: However, there is limited information on the localization of SCYLV within the host plant throughout the season, although a previous survey indicated that SCYLV incidence tends to rise in late spring to early summer in Louisiana, coinciding with increases in vector populations. This survey, however, did not specifically investigate the seasonal *in planta* distribution of SCYLV within the different parts of the sugarcane plant. A deeper understanding of SCYLV’s movement and localization within the host plant throughout the year is essential for optimizing sampling strategies. Improved knowledge of the virus’s epidemiology in the field and distribution within the host will not only enhance detection accuracy for SCYLV but also support research efforts aimed at assessing the impact of SCYLV on sugarcane yields.

title: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus – A Silent Threat?
section: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Disease (SCYLV): Challenges in Management and Breeding Strategies
text: Like other viral diseases, sugarcane plants cannot be cured of yellow leaf disease using chemical control. Additionally, this virus survives heat treatments effective against other sugarcane diseases, such as ratoon stunting disease. In countries like India, Brazil, and the USA, meristem tissue culture has been employed to produce propagative material free from major sugarcane diseases, including SCYLV. Currently, *M. sacchari* is not a target of pest management programs. In most sugarcane-producing areas, the main pest target is the sugarcane borer, *Diatraea saccharalis* (Fabricius). A previous epidemiological study on SCYLV transmission found that aphid-mediated spread only occurred within short distances, and vector management would not be as effective as the adoption of virus-free seed cane or resistant varieties. No studies measuring the impact of vector management strategies have been performed since then. However, the disease can still spread to multiplication fields from neighbouring areas through vectors, particularly *M. sacchari*. Therefore, varietal resistance is potentially the most impactful management strategy, but breeding SCYLV-resistant varieties is challenging. The inconspicuous nature of SCYLV infections makes it difficult for plant pathologists and breeders to assess varieties for SCYLV resistance. Typically, viral titre quantification is used to evaluate SCYLV resistance. However, recent studies have found that viral titres do not correlate with either symptom expression or yield losses, as some varieties with high viral titres exhibited lower yield losses than those with lower titres (Nithya *et al. *, 2023). To make matters more complicated, the impact of SCYLV on yield can vary significantly among different cultivars, even in asymptomatic epidemics.

Techniques like TBIA have been used to detect differences in disease incidence in biparental tests involving F1 progeny from highly heterozygotic susceptible cultivars. However, the difficulty in accurately rating SCYLV resistance or tolerance, combined with the variable impact on yield, complicates the decision making process for researchers considering resource allocations to tackle this issue. Understanding the incidence of SCYLV and the susceptibility of current cultivars provides three management strategies of interests:
1. *Assess SCYLV incidence in commercial fields*: If the disease is not widespread or is effectively managed with clean propagative material, an extensive breeding effort may not be justified. 2. *Rate current cultivar tolerance/resistance*: Identify valuable genetic resources for future crossings by comparing yield losses between SCYLV-positive and negative plants under identical environmental conditions. Focus on sugar yields, not just biomass, since viral infections affect the carbohydrate composition within plants. Be mindful of mixed viral infections and how they can influence sugar yields. Keep in mind, cultivars that are asymptomatic with minimal yield loss can serve as inoculum sources to more susceptible neighbouring plantings. 3. *Survey for different SCYLV genotypes*: The impact of infections on yield may vary depending on the SCYLV genotype. Conducting a thorough survey in sugarcane-producing regions to identify the dominant SCYLV genotypes can help in challenging varieties against prevalent strains.

### Overview ###
*Brassica napus* (rapeseed in Europe or canola in Canada) is susceptible to a variety of devastating pathogens and fungi. Among these is the clubroot disease caused by a pathogenic, soilborne protist, *Plasmodiophora brassicae*. The disease is emerging not only in rapeseed but also in other brassica crops such as cabbages, broccoli, and cauliflower worldwide with huge yield losses. These are the reasons for intensive research on how it is possible to control clubroot symptoms.

title: Clubroot Disease (Plasmodiophora brassicae) as a Threat to Worldwide Rapeseed
text:
The worldwide cultivation of brassica crops has favoured the spread of the clubroot disease caused by the soilborne protist *Plasmodiophora brassicae* (Kingdom Chromista). This biotrophic organism, as an obligatory parasite, needs its host plant to multiply, yet it is extremely efficient: one original spore can result in millions of progeny spores in the soil from just one infected plant. The first description in the literature was made by Mikhail Woronin, but wrongly: the organism was regarded as a myxomycete, which was corrected only much later. The disease symptoms (Fig. 1) encompass wilting of upper plant parts and the typical root hypertrophy (Box 1) that gives the disease its name. The shoot or leaf symptoms are caused by changes in nutrient distribution that lead to changes in the metabolic sink and draw the nutrients from the leaves to the roots. Therefore, such infected plants are prone to high yield losses. Visible symptoms inside the roots are enlarged cells that are caused by pathogen structures such as plasmodia and the resting spores. (Fig. 1). The impact of clubroot disease on the worldwide economy is enormous since, as a soil-borne pathogen, the problem is intensified in fields where the same crops are grown with only a 1–2-year break in crop rotation, posing a particular threat to sustainable crop production. Geographical distributions of clubroot incidences in recent years have been reviewed by several authors (e.g. Javed *et al. *, 2023). ##### Fig. 1. #####

title: Clubroot Disease (Plasmodiophora brassicae) as a Threat to Worldwide Rapeseed
text: Brassica crops are not only major oil and food crops but also are important key components for the diversity of arable crop rotations, either in the form of break-crops to cereals or as components of bird-friendly greening crops, cover crops and seed mixes. Next to cabbage, radish, mustard, cauliflower, broccoli and other brassica-related crops, rapeseed (in Europe) and canola (in Canada) are the major cash crops to be affected by the disease. The latter are primarily concentrated in industrialised countries, whereas other brassica crops are distributed not only in areas with high consumption and therefore growth, such as China, Russia or Australia but also in Middle or South America and some African regions, where clubroot outbreaks have recently been reported (Javed *et al. *, 2023). Spread can also be attributed to soil contamination, seeds or even fresh produce. Due to this distribution, clubroot does not only spread worldwide, but it also leads to the emergence of new pathotypes for various crops. Therefore, novel strategies for control are needed. European data alone list roughly 70 million hectares of rapeseed for 2018, which constitutes a value of more than 12 billion Euros. In some countries, yield losses can exceed 80% in strongly infected areas, which amount to over one billion Euros of produce at risk for this rapeseed crop. Assuming an evenly distributed annual loss of 10–15% across Europe, nearly 700 kha of OSR are lost which amounts to an equivalent of close to one million football fields! Since these examples are only for Europe, one can estimate that global losses in geographic areas with high rapeseed / canola growth are even higher. In Canada, it was shown that increases in disease severity can result in significant yield losses of canola, namely pods per plant and grain weight (Botero-Ramirez *et al*., 2022).

title: Clubroot Disease (Plasmodiophora brassicae) as a Threat to Worldwide Rapeseed
text: In Canada, it was shown that increases in disease severity can result in significant yield losses of canola, namely pods per plant and grain weight (Botero-Ramirez *et al*., 2022). Despite this danger, efficient and sustainable control strategies are still lacking, and the survival of *P. brassicae* spores in the soil for an extended period of time makes clubroot a substantial, long-lasting threat. Current strategies to control the disease include liming by application of, e.g., calcium-cyanamide, adjusting the soil pH to unfavourable conditions for the pathogen, field hygiene including drainage and cleaning measures, crop rotation, catch crops, choice of fields, fertilisation, as well as changing the growth period (for more detailed explanations see part ‘Is it possible to control clubroot effectively in fields?’). Nowadays, at least in Europe, chemical compounds are only used to a small extent for disease control (Dixon, 2009). Finally, breeding resistant or tolerant plants is a major strategy used to combat the disease in many fields. However, if that is done exhaustively, novel *P. brassicae* spore pathotypes can develop with altered host spectrum and higher virulence. Thus, it seems that the best treatments combine measures against several of the problems outlined above.

section: Phylogeny and Life Cycle of the Biotrophic Pathogen
text: The causal agent of the clubroot disease is the soilborne protist *Plasmodiophora brassicae*. The pathogen is biotrophic (Box 1), meaning that it is completely dependent on its host plant to complete the life cycle. This organism belongs systematically into the group Phytomyxea, supergroup Rhizaria, which contains pathogens on as diverse hosts as plants, diatoms, oomycetes and brown algae (Neuhauser *et al. *, 2014). Together with several other plant pathogens, they form the group of Plasmodiophorida, which also includes the soilborne *Polymyxa betae*, *P. graminis*, and *Spongospora subterranea*. While the two former organisms are not pathogenic themselves, they are transmitters of severe viral diseases, *S. subterranea* can cause small galls on its host potato as well as transmitting a plant pathogenic virus. Interestingly, there is no evidence that *P. brassicae* transmits viruses. The availability of genome sequences for these major groups of pathogens facilitates their study at a molecular level (Schwelm and Ludwig-Müller, 2021). Despite being the subject of extensive studies in the early days of clubroot research (Ingram and Tommerup, 1972), the complex life cycle (Fig. 2) of these organisms still has several question marks, and evidence for some specific parts has been found only lately (Liu *et al. *, 2020). The life cycle starts with resting spores that can survive in plant debris and in the soil. In the vicinity of a suitable host, the spores perceive a signal and germinate into zoospores. These have two flagella and can swim in capillary water towards their host. After finding a susceptible root hair, they will attach and penetrate mechanically.

section: Phylogeny and Life Cycle of the Biotrophic Pathogen
text:
These have two flagella and can swim in capillary water towards their host. After finding a susceptible root hair, they will attach and penetrate mechanically. The root hair is the tissue where the so-called primary infection occurs. The penetration structures have been coined ‘stachel’ and ‘rohr’ since the plasmodia are placed into the root hair using these tools (Aist and Williams, 1971). As such, *P. brassicae* constitutes a ‘real’ intracellular parasite that is only separated from the host cytosol by its own plasmodial membrane. Thus, it resembles an organelle within the host cell. All communication can occur directly between these two host and pathogen compartments. The plasmodia develop into new zoospores, which are called secondary zoospores that can re-infect root hairs of the same or neighbouring plants. This mechanism has already resulted in spore multiplication. ##### Fig. 2. #####
Life cycle featuring points of control to enable breeding for resistant or tolerant cultivars. It could be feasible to overcome the defence suppression by *P. brassicae* via increasing its induction. Also, critical stages of pathogenesis could be targeted. The detailed description of the different stages is given in the text. The zoospores can (most likely after plasmogamy) move into the root cortex as young plasmodia; these structures have been observed to have two nuclei. The young plasmodia might directly infect the cortex from the root hair cells. Movement of the young plasmodia has to occur since they colonise the pericycle of the root and are rapidly found in the vicinity of the host vasculature. Host cell division is induced only shortly later. Observations of such moving plasmodia are very rare events.

Host cell division is induced only shortly later. Observations of such moving plasmodia are very rare events. One hallmark of plasmodia development is the unusual cruciform division of nuclei (Fig. 3), which occurs at the stage of multinucleate plasmodia before karyogamy. Concomitantly to cell division, the plasmodia also seem to divide. The plasmodia-containing cells begin to elongate and both mechanisms lead to the hypertrophied root parts. During this process, a strong metabolic sink is established between host leaves and the infected roots. At the end of the life cycle, the plasmodia develop into resting spores. Millions of such spores can be present in infected roots. The resting spores are liberated into the soil following root tissue senescence. ##### Fig. 3. #####

Especially young, developing plasmodia and resting spore-containing cells can already occur next to each other during earlier phases of pathogenesis. text: The stages of primary (or root hair) infection and the secondary stage (or cortex) infection also differ from each other depending on the host plant and the pathogen isolate. Therefore, they are not included in the life cycle and images for development. Approximations are 4–7 days for the root hair infection, 7–16 days until the first symptoms appear and 16–28 days until symptoms including large resting spore-containing cells are formed. Overall, the secondary stage takes approximately 7–28 days. These stage lengths are typical for greenhouse experiments; in the field, however, the time frames are more variable and may even be significantly longer. Plasmodia and resting spore-forming plasmodia overlap over a large period of time, but the majority of young plasmodia develop during the first 7–14 days after inoculation. When the cells harbouring resting spores mature, then the host root undergoes senescence followed by tissue disruption, which ultimately results in the liberation of the resting spores into the soil. Some researchers call this a third (resting or soil) phase because the resting spores can persist for decades as active propagules in this soil until they again germinate in the vicinity of a suitable host.

title: Clubroot Disease (Plasmodiophora brassicae) as a Threat to Worldwide Rapeseed
text: Although typical clubroot symptoms are unique to members of the crucifer family, *P. brassicae* is capable of infecting the root hairs of noncruciferous hosts such as: redtop (*Agrostis alba* var. *stoloniferae*), orchardgrass (*Dactylis glomerata*), ryegrass (*Lolium perenne*); strawberry (*Fragaria* spp. ); corn poppy (*Papaver rhoeas*); dock (*Rumex* spp. ); mignonette *(Reseda odorata*); red clover (*Trifolium pratense*) and nasturtium (*Tropaeolum majus*) (e.g. Ludwig-Müller *et al. *, 1999). The changes in the host root are attributed to changes in the host plant’s hormone homeostasis. Although the involvement of auxin and cytokinin has long been suspected, evidence for other growth-promoting compounds, such as brassinosteroids, has recently been added to our knowledge of what happens in host roots during club formation (Ludwig-Müller *et al. *, 2009). Cytokinins could play a dual role since they are not only inducers of cell division, they can also induce the metabolic sink that occurs between host leaves and infected roots. While growth-promoting hormones are needed to cause the symptoms, the pathogen also needs to suppress plant defence responses. Many publications have shown that such defence hormones are (unexpectedly) upregulated in some tissues, but they are more upregulated, for example, in resistant vs. susceptible comparisons. The defence hormones seem to be induced during different stages of pathogenesis. While salicylic acid, a player for biotroph defence responses is induced early, the jasmonic acid response is triggered later.

title: Clubroot Disease (Plasmodiophora brassicae) as a Threat to Worldwide Rapeseed
text: The defence hormones seem to be induced during different stages of pathogenesis. While salicylic acid, a player for biotroph defence responses is induced early, the jasmonic acid response is triggered later. Ethylene may play a minor role as a more subtle modulator of the response. Pathogens that rely on their close association with the host interact by secreting, for example, effector proteins, as was also indicated for *P. brassicae* (Javed *et al. *, 2023). One example is a methyltransferase from *P. brassicae* which can convert the defence signal salicylic acid to its methyl ester. Other effectors interact with different molecular targets in the host cell. In several cases, it was found that increasing or decreasing the host target can indeed alter the outcome of the disease.

title: Clubroot Disease (Plasmodiophora brassicae) as a Threat to Worldwide Rapeseed
text:
Resistance against clubroot is cultivar- and pathotype-specific. There are species that are generally considered to be the most susceptible, some medium susceptible, and some only mildly susceptible. Finally, there are also naturally resistant cultivars or species. Finding new sources of resistance is challenging. In order to identify resistances, one could explore genetic backgrounds with either a single gene resistance or a quantitative resistance (Fig. 4). The main sources of clubroot resistance do not originate from *B. napus*, but other *Brassica* species, such as European fodder turnip (*B. rapa*) or *B. oleracea*. Therefore, there is a compelling need to identify new sources of resistance and control strategies that are durable, sustainable and can be scaled up for use across the whole world. The observation that resistance genes often occur in clusters within the genomes of some *Brassica* species may assist this approach. Until now, control of *P. brassicae* has been limited by an over-reliance on a single genetic locus for resistance (‘Mendel’) which is already regionally breaking down as highly virulent *P. brassicae* races have emerged. For example, it was shown that resistance is often broken and that European resistance is not effective against North American isolates (Fredua-Agyeman *et al. *, 2019). Therefore, it is also crucial to know which pathotypes are present in a field, especially since these constitute populations of *P. brassicae*. ##### Fig. 4. #####

text: This starts with the identification of a resistant or tolerant cultivar. Mapping of genes is essential to find the genetic background, single gene (R = resistance) or quantitative resistance (QTL = quantitative trait loci). Either the resistant cultivar is used directly or the genes are crossed into a susceptible background. This is followed by resistance testing and finally bringing the cultivar to the market. Often these are hybrids. It is desirable, but not essential, to identify the mechanism of resistance at the tissue and cellular or molecular level. Single-gene resistance is a specific interaction. As an example of a broader resistance, a phytoalexin of Brassicaceae, Brassinin (Methyl-(1*H*-indol-3-ylmethyl) carbamodithioat), is shown (from Wikipedia <https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brassinin>; accessed 12 June 2024). Some parts are from the trial version of Biorender (Available at: <https://www.biorender.com>; accessed 12 June 2024). For the determination of pathotypes, no real efficient and worldwide accepted method has been established as yet. Some populations can be separated by molecular techniques, but this is not an approach to be used for different geographic regions. The majority of testing is done on host differential sets that consist of resistant and susceptible *Brassica* crop species, and not only *B. napus*. These are first of all laborious to carry out, second depending strongly on the greenhouse conditions performed and third adapted to the different major geographical regions that have to deal with high clubroot loads. So, there are sets for European, Canadian, and recently also Chinese cultivars in the literature in addition to smaller test sets adapted to smaller regions (Schwelm and Ludwig-Müller, 2021; Tso *et al. *, 2021).

text: *, 2021). In the future, clubroot research would benefit from further standardisation of pathotyping systems and the development of molecular tools for pathotype identification (Tso *et al. *, 2021). Both, crop intervals and resistant cultivars can affect the outcome of disease severity in infested fields (Hwang *et al. *, 2019). In the Northern American regions, the original ‘Mendel’-based resistance is therefore now often replaced by other genetic sources or new resistances are placed on top by gene pyramiding. Therefore, novel resistance sources are important to identify. They come from the same species, or related ones, such as cabbages or radish. Some crops that are used as intermediate crops are resistant, i.e., oil radish. One cannot only use resistances from the same species but also from wild species such as oil radish and other brassica crops like cabbages. Single genes can be combined to make resistance more durable, but that process then also takes more time. While it would not be essential to identify the mechanism behind the resistance, it could help to stabilise the resistance or even to identify this mechanism in other species and transfer it back to *B. napus*. Metabolome profiling in a segregating population of rapeseed has led to the identification of compounds that could be associated with the resistance response (Wagner *et al. *, 2019). Other possible broad-spectrum resistance metabolites of rapeseed have been identified as glucosinolate (gluconasturtiin) along with two other metabolites. An example of a phytoalexin from *Brassica* sp. is Brassinin (shown in the lower panel of Fig. 4).

Also, functional analyses of resistance mechanisms can be investigated in the model plant *Arabidopsis thaliana*, which is generally very susceptible to clubroot infection. This has the advantage that testing can be done after a shorter period of time than with the crop plants.

title: Clubroot Disease (Plasmodiophora brassicae) as a Threat to Worldwide Rapeseed
text: Since resistant cultivars are only a partial solution, and few chemicals are available for controlling this disease, an alternative approach that has been discussed for quite some time is biological control. Different microbial biological control products are already on the market for this purpose and some formulations or individual organisms have been already tested against clubroot (Auer and Ludwig-Müller, 2023). While some authors already celebrate the existence of microbes with enthusiastic titles such as "Biocontrol arsenals of bacterial endophyte: An imminent triumph against clubroot disease" (Ahmed *et al. *, 2020), the content of other studies is more of disillusion. Auer and Ludwig-Müller (2023) have compiled the available data in the literature by using the following search terms until November 2022 including the words "biocontrol" and "Plasmodiophora" or "clubroot"/"club root" in various combinations in Web of Science and Google Scholar. The following description is mainly based on compilations from two review articles that have employed different ways to judge the data. The reported results have limitations because they are based on very different experimental conditions and few are already near to practice. Based on the literature, the majority of effects described that are used by the endophytes against clubroot are either antibiosis or induction of defence responses by either ISR or SAR pathways. The effects reported are mainly positive, meaning biocontrol effects between 20 and up to 100%. However, there are also even negative effects, meaning that after application of the biocontrol agent, more symptoms have been observed. Ahmed *et al. * (2020) concentrated on bacterial endophytes, whereas Auer and Ludwig-Müller (2023) also included fungal endophytes in their data review.

title: Clubroot Disease (Plasmodiophora brassicae) as a Threat to Worldwide Rapeseed
text: Ahmed *et al. * (2020) concentrated on bacterial endophytes, whereas Auer and Ludwig-Müller (2023) also included fungal endophytes in their data review. They also compiled the type of experiment (greenhouse, field) and whether a commercial formulation was available and tested. Several bacterial species have been reported independently, including those from the genus *Alcaligenes*, *Bacillus*, *Lysobacter*, and *Streptomyces*; for fungi, *Clonostachys*, *Heteroconium*, *Phoma* and *Trichoderma* species have been primarily studied. Some promising endophytes with biocontrol potential have already been used in commercial or pre-commercial formulations. Two fungal species have been included in biocontrol products, but these are not only on the market against clubroot. The same can be stated for biocontrol bacterial formulations, which are also not used solely against clubroot (see Auer and Ludwig-Müller, 2023). Some commercial biocontrol agents actually contain bacteria and fungi either alone or in mixtures. Since a high percentage of such agents have been investigated in China, their major test plant was therefore not rapeseed, but Chinese cabbage or other cabbages. Approximately 57% of the reported effects were for *B. rapa* (Chinese cabbage), 30% for *B. napus* (rapeseed / canola), the rest for *B. oleracea*, *B. juncea* and *B. campestris* cultivars. In general, the modes of action could be antibiosis, defence pathway induction, hyperparasitism, or competition (Fig. 5).

Against clubroot, the major effects of biocontrol agents seem to be by antibiosis or induction of defence pathways. Both, the salicylic acid (SAR) and the jasmonate-dependent pathway (ISR) have been described in the literature to be activated, but not simultaneously. ##### Fig. 5. #####
Possible treatments with biocontrol agents in the field and questions raised. Some parts are from the trial version of Biorender (Available at: <https://www.biorender.com>; accessed 12 June 2024). The following questions may arise: 1. How long does the effect last; 2. How would sustainable application be possible in the field; 3. Can only symptoms or also pathogen loads be reduced? A possibility could be seed treatments instead of application to the soil as drench or spray. This has been shown to have a better effect on reducing clubroot by commercial agents (Auer and Ludwig-Müller, 2023). However, for non-commercial possibilities, the methods need to be adapted for each microorganism. Furthermore, there has to be permission to release such agents even within seed coats. Animal predators are another potential soil feature that is discussed; hence, it is not just bacteria that may affect the severity of clubroot. (Schwelm *et al. *, 2023). One possibility could be antibiosis since animals in the soil additionally secrete toxic metabolites. These could also lead to changes in the microbiome since a predator could feed on these in the soil, and a third could be direct, namely that predators could feed on *P. brassicae* spores.

title: Clubroot Disease (Plasmodiophora brassicae) as a Threat to Worldwide Rapeseed
section: Is It Possible to Control Clubroot Effectively in Fields?
text: The best management practice examples for mitigating the clubroot disease on rapeseed or canola in the field depend on the geographic origin of the problem (Table 2). While the disease progression in Europe is a problem, the risk of higher incidences is much larger when the fields are also large, like in Canada or the USA (Gossen *et al. *, 2013). Nevertheless, farmers all over the world can implement practices to reduce the likelihood of clubroot in their fields. Such practices include seven main important points identified by the Canola Growers of Canada. To have the best possible control of clubroot, first, one needs to monitor the fields for the disease: that means inspection of suspicious patches. Methods for the detection of resting spores include molecular PCR techniques or testing with strongly susceptible host plants in greenhouse trials. The clubroot pathogen can be introduced to a field by soil movement even in break years and be present at low levels, so the movement of soil in and out of the fields should be minimised. Next to infestation by soil, machines and other means that can lead to contamination, the suspected areas need to be checked and maybe even separated from the rest of the field. This may, of course, not be feasible for small fields. For example, clubroot surveys in Alberta, Canada, have found that many new infestations begin near field access points, which indicates that contaminated equipment with which the farmer moves in and out of the field is the predominant spread mechanism. Another Canadian province, Manitoba, has additional indications for pooling of water that occurs and in which a high risk of contamination with spores can be found. Thus, water can additionally increase the spreading of spores. The labour costs for field hygiene by disinfecting the machinery might be a strong hurdle in reducing spore loads (Canola Council of Canada, accessed September 2024). ##### Table 2.

What are the favourable conditions for infection by the clubroot pathogen? First, low pH (less than 6.5), high soil moisture and also warm soils (20–24°C). Second, the occurrence of susceptible weeds and volunteer crops can help increase spore load even in crop rotation breaks. Third, the development of novel pathotypes in highly infested areas can also break down resistance responses. Knowing that such conditions favour the pathogen, it is advisable to reduce one or more risks from that list. While it is not really possible to change the temperature in a given area, measures against high soil moisture could be to avoid capillary water by improving field drainage. The pathogen has higher infection potential at lower pH, so raising the pH in a field can also help. However, one needs to keep in mind that the disease could be lowered, although the pathogen is still there. Nevertheless, liming of fields has been a method of choice for many decades against clubroot (Dixon, 2009), but it may be most effective under low spore loads. This might be similar to the treatment with calcium cyanamide; this chemical was formerly used as a fertiliser, can bring the pH up as well, and acts also as a fungicide, even though *P. brassicae* is not a fungus, but a protist. In addition, the costs of this chemical may not favour its use, specifically in larger fields. Fumigation has also been used in crops other than rapeseed since it is also economically not feasible for rapeseed.

text: In addition, the costs of this chemical may not favour its use, specifically in larger fields. Fumigation has also been used in crops other than rapeseed since it is also economically not feasible for rapeseed. In addition, fumigants are not always allowed in the different countries that need to deal with high clubroot incidence, since they also destroy the natural microbiome in treated soil. Finally, weeds such as Shepherd’s purse, stinkweed, flixweed, wild mustard, and many others in this family will carry and increase this disease together with volunteer rapeseed or canola plants. Overall, the ultimate goal is to reduce spore load. Crop rotation is one accepted option that is used worldwide. However, in different regions, somewhat different suggestions are given. For example, in different European countries, crop rotation helped to decrease disease incidence (Zamani-Noor *et al. *, 2022). Here, a period of 3 years was favourable, whereas, in Canada, a minimum 2-year break is suggested. However, it is also stated by the Canola Council of Canada that a 3-year break is better and will reduce spore numbers considerably and could even reduce the development of novel pathotypes. In contrast to Europe, crop rotation is suggested to be done in conjunction with resistant varieties and also following in the rotations with different genetic backgrounds.

### Overview ###
*Puccinia triticina* produces orange-brown pustules on wheat leaves lending its name, leaf rust. It occurs worldwide and is controlled by genetic resistance. Surveys of pathogen race structure ensure breeders used effective combinations of race-specific as well as race-nonspecific adult plant resistance (*Lr*) genes to avoid yield loss.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: 1. Understand the host range, life cycle and epidemiology of *Puccinia triticina*. 2. Have knowledge of the genetics behind the boom-and-bust cycles of wheat leaf rust. 3. Know why virulence surveys of wheat leaf rust races are needed. 4. Understand the two different types of leaf rust resistance, and how they are being used in the breeding of new wheat cultivars.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: Wheat leaf rust is caused by *Puccinia triticina* Erikss (formerly known as *Puccinia recondita* f. sp. *tritici*), a fungal pathogen on bread wheat (*Triticum aestivum*), durum wheat (*Triticum turgidum* ssp. *dicoccoides* and *Triticum turgidum* ssp. *durum*) and related grass species. The pathogen reproduces asexually on these species but can also reproduce sexually on the most abundant and principal alternate host meadow rue (*Thalictrum speciosissimum*) and a few other plant species (Anikster *et al*., 1997). However, as the alternate hosts are not present in North America, sexual reproduction is therefore rare on this continent (Levine and Hildreth, 1957). Likewise, in most of the other wheat-growing areas of the world, the alternate host is not present. It is present, however, in Europe and the Middle East which could facilitate sexual recombination in those regions (Fellers *et al*., 2021). The pathogen co-evolved with domestication of wheat species 10,000 years ago in the Middle East which includes modern-day Iraq, Syria, Turkey, Jordan, Lebanon, Israel and Palestine (Anikster and Wahl, 1979). This is the centre of evolutionary origin and domestication of many cereal crop species and is also known as the fertile crescent.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text:
Symptoms of leaf rust infection are initially seen as small circular yellow spots on the upper leaf surface, which over time turn into orange-coloured pustules surrounded by yellow or brown leaf tissue. As the disease progresses the pustules may coalesce to form larger, irregular lesions. The pustules are raised above the leaf surface and contain masses of orange to reddish-brown urediniospores which give the characteristic rust appearance (Fig. 1). The urediniospores can be easily dislodged from the pustules and help to distinguish rust diseases from other leaf diseases, such as common wheat leaf spotting diseases such as *Septoria tritici* blotch, *Stagonospora nodorum* blotch and tan spot. There are three common rust diseases found on wheat leaves, leaf rust, stem rust and stripe rust. Stripe rust symptoms are most distinctive with yellow-orange pustules that are elongated running parallel along the leaf veins. Pustules resembling beads on a string along the leaf vein. Stem rust can be distinguished from leaf rust since stem rust pustules are generally larger than leaf rust, have a diamond shape compared to the circular leaf rust pustules, and the urediniospores of stem rust are brick or dark red compared to the orange leaf rust urediniospores (Fig. 1). ##### Fig. 1. #####
(A) Close view of leaf rust pustules and urediniospores on an infected wheat leaf. (B) Typical symptoms of a heavy wheat leaf rust infection. (C) Stripe rust infection on wheat leaves. (D) Stem rust infection on wheat. Colonization of leaves diverts nutrients from the plant to production of fungal mycelium and spores, and dehydration occurs when the epidermis is ruptured by masses of uredia.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: (D) Stem rust infection on wheat. Colonization of leaves diverts nutrients from the plant to production of fungal mycelium and spores, and dehydration occurs when the epidermis is ruptured by masses of uredia. The affected leaf tissue is unable to photosynthesize leading to stunting of plant growth and reduced grain production. Reports vary considerably on the extent of yield loss caused by leaf rust, but likely range between 5 and 50%, with higher losses in susceptible cultivars, following early on-set of infection, and cool wet weather conditions, with typical losses in the 1 to 10% range in North America (Huerta-Espino *et al*., 2011). Chai *et al*. (2020) estimated that 94.4% of the world’s wheat is vulnerable to leaf rust infection and that global annual yield loss from 2000 to 2050 could reach 8.6–18.3 million tons of grain equivalent to an economic loss of $1.5–$3.3 billion US dollars based on 2016 grain prices. However, their model only attributed an annual crop loss worldwide of 1.2% (baseline scenario) to 2.6% (high-loss scenario) due to leaf rust. Since leaf rust occurs worldwide and spreads by air, it is not a disease that can be controlled by quarantine, particularly between neighbouring countries. Nevertheless, *P. triticina* populations differ significantly among wheat-growing regions. Introduction of races into areas where they do not occur already can cause severe losses to wheat varieties that do not possess appropriate leaf rust resistance. Travellers are therefore advised to avoid accidental long-distance movement of pathogen spores on clothing or footwear for this and other plant and animal diseases.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: Higher precipitation and relative humidity in some areas result in greater yields but also higher incidence of many fungal diseases. Fungicide treatments are common in such areas to control wheat leaf rust. However, fungal species can develop tolerance to fungicides, which then lose their effectiveness, resulting in increasing yield loss over time even in fungicide-treated fields. Several fungicide products effectively control *P. triticina* and decreased sensitivity has not been reported yet. Nonetheless, fungicide tolerance, due to mutations in the gene targeted by the active ingredient, has been identified in a related fungal rust pathogen, *Puccinia striiformis* f. sp. *tritici*, that causes stripe rust of wheat (Cook *et al*., 2021). There can sometimes be a temptation to neglect selection for disease resistance in breeding programs, since some resistance genes may initially be associated with lower yield, which seems unacceptable if the disease is not always present. When fungicides are used in breeding programs, selection for leaf rust resistance is no longer possible. Thus, if breeding for leaf rust resistance is not maintained, wheat cultivars may be highly susceptible when fungicides lose their effectiveness.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: *Puccinia triticina* is an obligate pathogen thus needing living plant tissue of host species to survive and reproduce (Bolton *et al*., 2008). The fungus has evolved molecular mechanisms to evade the plant defence mechanisms and depends on the cellular machinery for nutrients to grow, without killing the plant. The complete life cycle of *P. triticina* has five different spore types (Fig. 1). Urediniospores (dikaryotic; n+n) are produced during successive rounds of infection and sporulation on wheat. The asexual cycle is common in most wheat-producing regions due to the lack of the alternate host. The urediniospores require 100% humidity for germination and temperatures from 2 to 30°C with an optimum of 20°C (Roelfs *et al*., 1992). Germ tubes grow along the leaf surface until they encounter a stoma which they recognize because of the shape of the guard cells (Bolton *et al*., 2008). An appressorium is then formed over the stomatal aperture, a penetration peg originating from the appressorium pushes through the closed stoma to enter the intercellular space, and a substomatal vesicle is formed from which the primary infection hyphae develop (Bolton *et al*., 2008). These infection hyphae grow outwards until they contact a mesophyll cell, at which point a haustorial mother cell is formed (Bolton *et al*., 2008). A penetration peg formed from the haustorial mother cell penetrates the host cell wall, followed by the formation of a specialized feeding structure called a haustorium inside the plant cell wall but tightly adjacent to the plasma membrane (Bolton *et al*., 2008). These haustoria absorb nutrients from plant cells.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text:
These haustoria absorb nutrients from plant cells. Additional hyphae continue to grow extracellularly from the haustorial mother cell, to infect other host cells, the fungus ramifies throughout the infected area and after 7 to 10 days after initial infection, uredinia with thousands of urediniospores erupt through the leaf epidermis (Fig. 2). The new generation of urediniospores is spread by wind over shorter distance to neighbouring wheat plants or over much longer distances by upper wind currents (Huerta-Espino *et al*., 2011), and the pathogen continues to propagate asexually in wheat fields throughout the growing season (Bolton *et al*., 2008; Samborski, 1985). The fungus survives on the host as long as the leaf tissue is alive, and urediniospores can remain viable for weeks without the host as long as they do not encounter high humidity and germinate. ##### Fig. 2. #####
The life cycle of *Puccinia triticina*. Telia with teliospores (A and B) and uredinia with urediniospores (E and F) are produced on the primary wheat host, whereas pycnia with pycniospores (C) and aecia with aeciospore (D) are produced on the upper and lower leaf surfaces on the alternate host, *Thalictrum speciosissimum*. title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: Adapted from Alexopoulos *et al*. (1996) by C. Gubbins Hahn (John Wiley & Sons, reproduced by permission). Photos by T. Eilam and J. Kolmer (reproduced by permission). During times of stress such as senescence of the host plant or extreme temperatures, the fungus can switch to form teliospores which mark the initiation of the sexual cycle (Fig. 2). A thick, black melanized cell wall enables the teliospores to survive months and even years, during hot summers or cold winters and germinate when conditions become more favourable. In teliospores, the two haploid nuclei (n + n) perform karyogamy to produce a diploid state (2n). If conditions are conducive for teliospore germination, a basidium is formed in which meiosis occurs. *Puccinia triticina* has a tetrapolar mating system in which the pheromone/pheromone receptor locus (*a* locus) and the homeodomain mating-type transcription regulators (*b* locus) are on different chromosomes; in a dikaryotic cell, each haploid nucleus has different allelic specificities, e.g., *a1b1* + *a2b2*. Since meiosis takes place in the basidium, the opposite mating types segregate, resulting in haploid (n) basidiospores each with either one of the mating types (*a1b1*;*a2b2*; *a1b2*; *a2b1*).

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: An additional mitotic replication after meiosis produces dikaryotic basidiospores in which the two nuclei are identical (e.g., n(*a1b1*) + n(*a1b1*)) (Anikster, 1983). Basidiospores are shot off and can land on leaves of the alternate host whereupon they infect by direct epidermal cell penetration and ramify in the host tissue (Bolton *et al*., 2008). Pycnia erupts on the upper side of the leaf containing pycniospores and infectious hyphae; each pycnidium represents one mating-type specificity. Insects are attracted to the sweet pycnial fluids and cross-fertilize the fungus by carrying pycniospores from one pycnium to the next. When of different mating-type specificity, fertilization can ensue through cell fusion and one haploid nucleus from a pycniospore combines with another haploid nucleus in the flexious hyphae to produce a new cell type: e.g., n(*a1b2*) + n(*a2b1*). This triggers a new developmental program where the fungus ramifies through the host leaf to produce aecia which erupt on the underside of the leaf, with the production of dikaryotic (n + n) aeciospores. These aeciospores are airborne and can infect wheat which results in the production of uredinia to start the asexual cycle again (Fig. 2).

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: These aeciospores are airborne and can infect wheat which results in the production of uredinia to start the asexual cycle again (Fig. 2). In North America, *P. triticina* overwinters on wheat plants in the southern USA and Mexico, and the initial inoculum, in the form of urediniospores, is spread each year by wind currents into the northern USA and Canada, successively as wheat fields are seeded from south to north (Roelfs, 1985).

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: Populations of *P. triticina* are genetically diverse as a result of natural mutation during cell divisions, facilitated by large numbers of transposable elements and repetitive DNA regions, which may cause chromosomal recombination. Variation may also be caused by vegetative fusion between different genotypes and genetic reassortment without the sexual cycle (Wang and McCallum, 2009). Consequently, new races that are virulent on prevalent wheat varieties have a selective advantage and increase rapidly (Fellers *et al*., 2021; McCallum *et al*., 2021). The rust pathogen produces protein effectors, many of which are recognized by host immune receptors, that often represent the matching leaf rust resistance (*Lr*) genes. This recognition immediately triggers a defence response in the plant, slowing or stopping the pathogen. Mutation and/or deletion of effectors in the pathogen cause it to become virulent on wheat varieties harbouring the matching *Lr* gene which is no longer able to recognize the mutated effector.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: The primary leaf rust management strategy is the growing of wheat cultivars with genetic resistance, which has been practiced for over 100 years (Samborski, 1985). Wheat cultivars were developed to have good genetic resistance to the *P. triticina* population at the time of their release. The pathogen population will often evolve to overcome this genetic resistance, particularly when only virulence to a single *Lr* gene is needed to make a cultivar susceptible. Mutations and genetic recombination often allow for the evolution of virulent races that infect and increase these cultivars. This was documented by Samborski (1985) when wheat cultivar Selkirk, with *Lr10* and *Lr16* genes, was introduced in western Canada in 1954, which resulted in a rapid increase of new races that initially became virulent to *Lr10* and later also to *Lr16*. This phenomenon has been called a boom-and-bust cycle, where a new cultivar with resistance to leaf rust has a few successful years of production (the boom), followed years of increasing yield loss because of the development of new virulent races (the bust). A similar situation developed with resistance gene *Lr21*, which was used extensively for many years in both Canada and the United States but became less effective with the appearance of virulent races in both countries. The general concept is illustrated in Fig. 3, where a pair of leaves of cultivar Thatcher are susceptible to *P. triticina* isolate 198-1 (left), whereas Thatcher with the *Lr2c* resistance gene confer resistance to isolate 198-1 (middle), but not isolate 196-2 (right). It is commonly stated that resistance has broken down by the development of new races.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
section: Types of Leaf Rust Resistance Genes
text:
Genetic analysis of leaf rust resistance has led to identification and genomic mapping of over 80 *Lr* genes, and many more are either unofficial designations or represented by quantitative trait loci (QTL) (Pinto da Silva *et al*., 2018). The known *Lr* genes confer either seedling or adult plant resistance. Seedling resistance is effective throughout all wheat growth stages, whereas adult plant resistance only becomes effective as the plant matures. Most *Lr* genes, whether classified as seedling or adult are race specific, meaning they are effective against specific races but no other races as illustrated for *Lr2c* in Fig. 3. Race non-specific genes have the same level of partial resistance to all races specifically, *Lr34*, *Lr46* and *Lr67*, which are called adult plant slow-rusting genes, since they slow down the development of pustules thereby limiting the spread of the pathogen and damage to the plant (McCallum *et al*., 2016). Figure 4 shows the extent of leaf rust pustules on the wheat cultivar Thatcher with (left) and without (right) the *Lr34* resistance gene. Both *Lr34* and *Lr46* genes have demonstrated durable resistance, since they have been deployed over wide areas for many years without breaking down. The *Lr67* gene is also thought to be durable, although it has yet to be widely deployed. The development of wheat cultivars that combine genes for race-specific resistance with adult plant race non-specific resistance has minimized the negative effect of the boom-and-bust cycles described above. ##### Fig. 4. #####

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
section: Survey of Rust Fungal Races Using Wheat Differentials
text: Tracking of virulence in *P. triticina* populations is essential for alerting plant breeders and growers to new virulent races that might threaten wheat production, and for determining which *Lr* genes would control leaf rust in the next generation of wheat cultivars. To that end, pathogen populations are being systematically assayed annually for the virulence spectrum in many wheat-growing regions of the world. This is done by collecting infected leaf samples from commercial wheat fields or nurseries seeded with leaf rust susceptible lines, during the growing season. Urediniospores are isolated from the leaves and inoculated onto the wheat cultivar Thatcher, which is universally susceptible to all races. A new generation of pustules forms, and urediniospores from a single isolated pustule are collected and stored as a single isolate. A number of isolates are randomly selected, and their urediniospores are inoculated separately onto a set of Thatcher near isogenic lines (NIL), each containing a single different *Lr* resistance gene. When this set of differential plants is rated for rust development, it shows the virulence spectrum of the pathogen population each year (McCallum *et al*., 2016). The proportion of isolates that are virulent on each *Lr* gene changes annually. Figure 5 shows the proportion of isolates virulent on six *Lr* genes in annual surveys from 2002 to 2019 in western Canada. Virulence on *Lr16* has been low and was also low on *Lr21* until 2017 when it was overcome by a higher proportion of virulent isolates, as mentioned earlier. The effectiveness of the other *Lr* genes has fluctuated over the 17-year time period shown here. ##### Fig. 5.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
section: Breeding Wheat Cultivars with Leaf Rust Resistance
text:
Decades of breeding of wheat cultivars with resistance to leaf rust have reduced the severity caused by modern-day *P. triticina* populations. A total of 45 wheat cultivars, released in Canada and the USA between 1880 and 2001, were grown side-by-side in field plots between 2007 and 2010. Under relatively high levels of natural *P. triticina* infection, the older cultivars were more susceptible with higher leaf rust severity ratings than more recent cultivars, some of which appeared to be immune to the disease (Fig. 6; Martens *et al*., 2014). ##### Fig. 6. #####
Average leaf rust rating of 45 wheat cultivars, released in Canada and the USA between 1880 and 2001, measured in two field nurseries with a natural *P. triticina* inoculum. The data clearly demonstrate the value of breeding for genetic resistance to leaf rust.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
section: Elucidating the Genetics of Leaf Rust Resistance
text: Excellent progress has been achieved by breeding wheat cultivars with leaf rust resistance, and many studies have analysed the genetic basis of resistance in cultivars with effective and durable resistance. One recent study focused on the Canadian bread wheat cultivar Carberry (Bokore *et al*., 2022). Carberry (resistant) was crossed with Thatcher (susceptible) and a population of doubled haploid (DH) lines was generated, so that each progeny line was genetically different, but all genes were homozygous in each line. This population was segregated for two race-specific seedling resistance genes, *Lr2a* and *Lr16*, along with two race-nonspecific adult plant genes, *Lr34* and *Lr46*. The presence of these four genes in each DH line was determined using molecular markers linked to each *Lr* gene. The population was also screened for leaf rust severity over multiple field locations and years. These field plots were inoculated with *P. triticina*, by spraying urediniospores onto rows of susceptible wheat included within the nursery to allow spread to all plots by wind, and irrigated to promote disease development. While the *Lr* genes reduced the level of leaf rust severity individually, combinations of genes, particularly those including *Lr34*, showed lower leaf rust infections (Fig. 7). This means that wheat lines carrying *Lr34* together with a race-specific seedling resistance gene were more resistant than lines carrying either gene alone. Carberry has maintained its high level of resistance since its registration in 2009, likely due to stacking of four genes conferring both seedling and adult plant resistance.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host

text:
Carberry has maintained its high level of resistance since its registration in 2009, likely due to stacking of four genes conferring both seedling and adult plant resistance. Other studies have demonstrated that the adult plant resistance genes, *Lr34* and *Lr67*, together with race-specific resistance genes also reduce leaf rust severity in an additive manner (McCallum and Hiebert, 2022). In addition, *Lr34* and *Lr67* confer partial resistance to other diseases of wheat such as Fusarium Head Blight, caused by *Fusarium graminearum*, and resulted in lower levels of the mycotoxin deoxynivalenol (DON) in harvested grain samples (McCallum *et al*., 2024). ##### Fig. 7. #####

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: In wheat, DNA markers linked to a gene of interest can be identified by determining the association of a desired phenotype with a genotypic marker using linkage analysis. Polymorphisms can be identified in the genome either within the actual coding sequence of the gene or in close proximity. Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) are commonly used, while differences in the number of simple sequence repeats (SSRs) in non-coding DNA regions have also been used. Molecular markers are used routinely to genotype large numbers of progeny in wheat breeding programs from which a smaller number of individuals with the appropriate marker can be selected i.e. marker-assisted selection (MAS) (Toth *et al*., 2018). Situations where the *Lr* gene have been identified, along with the actual DNA sequence, provide the most accurate detection of appropriate progenies and vastly improve the selection process. It is very valuable to combine the detailed virulence analyses on differential wheat *Lr* genes described above with a genetic analysis of *P. triticina* populations. Understanding the genetic relatedness among isolates helps explain the evolution of populations through mutations within clonal groups, of potential nuclear exchanges creating novel hybrids, and can reveal unexpected alien introductions of novel races. Though initially using SSRs and related small-scale variants in DNA sequences, over the last few years, Genotyping-By-Sequencing (GBS) using high throughput sequencing technologies and mapping to reference genomes, has generated tens of thousands of SNPs which can reveal the genetic relatedness among such genetic lineages at high resolution (Fellers *et al*., 2021). Such molecular polymorphisms among *P. triticina* isolates can also be exploited to develop markers to quickly identify genetic lineages, and race groups virulent or avirulent against resistance genes deployed in wheat cultivars.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: Tremendous new insights into the molecular basis of plant-pathogen interaction are happening through the assembly of whole genome sequences of *P. triticina* isolates and wheat varieties, and by comprehensive transcriptome studies of genes and proteins during the infection process. This has allowed the identification of ‘susceptibility’ genes in wheat shown to be essential for pathogens to gain a foothold in the host. Removing or mutating one or more of these susceptibility genes through genetic engineering using CRISPR/Cas technologies could deprive the pathogen of tools to manipulate the host resulting in less or no infection (Wang *et al*., 2022). This strategy is believed to lead to more durable resistance, especially if several essential fungal target genes can be engineered without detrimental effects on wheat growth and yield. Large datasets of genomic information from the *P. triticina* – wheat interaction have been used to identify virulence factors and effectors used by the pathogen in the infection process. Inhibition of certain virulence factors through virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) as well as host-induced gene silencing (HIGS) can reduce rust infection (Panwar *et al*., 2018). Research in the use of small interfering siRNAs for spray-induced gene silencing (SIGS) is also advancing fast.

title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host
text: A high level of genetic resistance to *P. triticina* can be achieved, but the development of new cultivars must be continuous and well-informed about the prevalent races of the pathogen. Continuous annual surveillance of *P. triticina* populations in important wheat-growing regions of the world generates important information of race structure and changes in their virulence over time. This informs wheat breeders and growers about the effectiveness of the current leaf rust resistance genes. It also directs the production of inoculum representing the current population, which takes place on universal susceptible wheat lines, since *P. triticina* is an obligate pathogen. A combination of adult plant resistance, such as *Lr34*, *Lr46* and *Lr67*, with race-specific *Lr* genes has shown a high level of durable resistance because the pathogen has more difficulty overcoming the different molecular defence pathways. Molecular markers and genomic-assisted selection are important tools to pyramid *Lr* genes in future wheat cultivars. Indeed, this is among the major goals of the ‘Expert Working Group on Wheat Pathogens’ in the Global Wheat Initiative.

### Overview ###
Cypress Canker Disease affects plants in the cypress family worldwide. This plant health study case describes our current understanding of the disease’s history, biology, symptomatology, and control measures. Finally, we will illustrate future research perspectives about this pathosystem.
