title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
section: Introduction: CCD Causal Agents and Spread
text:
Cypress Canker Disease (CCD) is a lethal infectious plant disease of many *Cupressaceae* that has caused several outbreaks over the last century in all continents excluding the Arctic and Antarctica (Graniti, 1998; Danti *et al.,*
2013; Danti and Della Rocca, 2017). Worldwide CCD is caused by seven ascomycetes fungi belonging to the *Seiridium* genus (class Sordariomycetes, order Amphisphaeriales, family Sporocadaceae): *S. cardinale* (W. Wagener) B. Sutton & I.A.S. Gibson, *S. cupressi* (Guba) Boesew. ; *S. unicorne* (Cooke & Ellis) B. Sutton; *S. neocupressi* (Bonthond, Sandoval-Denis & Crous); *S. cancrinum* (Bonthond, Sandoval-Denis & Crous); *S. pseudocardinale* (Wijayaw., Camporesi, McKenzie & K.D. Hyde); and *S. kenyanum* (Bonthond, Sandoval-Denis & Crous) (Bonthond *et al*., 2018)*. *
Among them, *S. cardinale* is by far the most dangerous and harmful species (at least in the Americas, Europe, and Oceania) and is the most investigated. *S. cardinale* can affect almost all the *Cupressaceae* (*Callitropsis* spp., *Cryptomeria* spp., *Juniperus* spp., *Hesperocyparis* spp., *Cupressus* spp., and *Thuja* spp.).

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
section: Introduction: CCD Causal Agents and Spread
text: It is particularly severe on Monterey cypress (*Hesperocyparis macrocarpa* (Hartw. ex Gordon) Bartel), Italian cypress (*Cupressus sempervirens* L.), and the intergeneric hybrid Leyland cypress (*×Hesperotropsis leylandii* (A.B. Jacks. & Dallim.) Garland & Gerry Moore [*Hesperocyparis macrocarpa* × *Callitropsis nootkatensis*]). The *Cupressus sempervirens*-*Seiridium cardinale* pathosystem is among the most extensively studied forest pathosystems globally, and it is notable for its long-standing research across various regions, particularly in response to epidemic outbreaks. It represents one of the few cases in which it has been possible, through studies of native and invasive population genetics, to trace back the history of the disease, as well as to identify and date the pathways of its spread (Della Rocca *et al*., 2019). The pathogen is likely to be native to California (Della Rocca *et al*., 2011, 2013) where it was first reported in 1928, and where it gave rise to an initial outbreak in *H. macrocarpa* plantations of the Central Valley, well outside the natural coastal range of this species. Within two decades from its first report, the disease had spread to New Zealand (1933), Europe (1944), South America (1947), while reports from North Africa (1973), and South Africa (1988) came later.

section: Introduction: CCD Causal Agents and Spread
text: Within two decades from its first report, the disease had spread to New Zealand (1933), Europe (1944), South America (1947), while reports from North Africa (1973), and South Africa (1988) came later. A comprehensive map of the disease distribution, available in the CABI Digital Library (Available at: <https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/full/10.1079/cabicompendium.49497>), highlights its global reach and impact. CCD is therefore considered a true pandemic as it is present in all regions where cypresses grow. The danger represented by the distribution of the pathogen is due to the fact that infections involve not just planted ornamental trees but also native Cupressaceae hosts. An example of this is the case of native *Widdringtonia* spp. in South Africa that are now getting affected by CCD due to the presence of *Seiridium* species (Wingfield *et al*., 2022). There is now evidence that the introduction of the pathogen into new areas of the planet has been caused by human activity, through the transfer of infected plants that have been routinely traded and transported by ship between continents. Such trades mainly involved *H. macrocarpa* for ornamental use in the Mediterranean, Oceania, and South America for timber production; and *C. sempervirens* from Mediterranean Europe to the Americas, Oceania, and Africa for ornamental purposes. The trades of ornamental cypresses have been ongoing since the late 1800s (Della Rocca *et al*., 2019), and the introduction of *S. cardinale* in Europe is likely to have started sometime in between the two world wars (Della Rocca *et al*., 2013). title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text: The CCD epidemiology has been extensively studied in California. In this region, the disease outbreaks mostly occur in the inland areas where the pathogen is likely native and the main host, *C. macrocarpa,* is planted. Another relevant area where the disease has been extensively studied is the Mediterranean basin, where the main host, *C. sempervirens* is native, but the pathogen is not (Danti and Della Rocca, 2017). The impact of the disease has been devastating at times, especially in areas where epidemic outbreaks have been favored by the density of susceptible hosts, and by cool-wet autumns and springs. These factors were particularly present during the 1930s and 1940s, therefore CCD devastated Monterey cypress plantations intended as windbreakers and grown in nurseries for sale as plant stock in California’s Central Valley. This outbreak severely impacted and limited the economic use of the species ever since. In the Mediterranean area, the situation has been even more severe. Since the 1970s, CCD has caused the death of millions of trees in Southern Europe, the Near and Middle East, and North Africa, leading to heavy economic losses in woods, ornamental plantations and plant nurseries. Beyond the economic impact, the ornamental and cultural loss has been profound. Cypress is an integral part of the Mediterranean cultural and historic heritage, playing an iconic ornamental role, and serving as a distinctive and irreplaceable feature of the landscape. Italy and Greece were the hardest-hit countries in Europe, with disease incidence rates exceeding 50% in several areas. However, North America and the Mediterranean Basin were not the only affected regions. Similar CCD outbreaks have been reported in New Zealand on *H. macrocarpa*, *H. lusitanica*, and *Chamaecyparis lawsoniana*.

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text: Similar CCD outbreaks have been reported in New Zealand on *H. macrocarpa*, *H. lusitanica*, and *Chamaecyparis lawsoniana*. Over the past 20 years, a slowdown in new infections has been observed in Italy, likely due in part to the loss of the most susceptible portion of the host population. Although the disease has reached an endemic phase, it still affects 20% to 25% of cypress trees in regions like Tuscany. In California’s inland valleys, disease incidence is correlated with: (a) density of susceptible hosts growing inland, outside of their natural range, and (b) the presence of Leyland cypress (Danti and Della Rocca, 2017), but large outbreaks are no longer present mostly because CCD prevents the growth of susceptible hosts, which are no longer planted. As aforementioned, Leyland cypress deserves special attention. Although trees of this species are widely used, fast-growing and aesthetically appealing, only a few clonal varieties of Leyland cypress are available on the market and all are highly susceptible to the disease. It is estimated that the extensive and widespread cultivation of this horticulture hybrid may have contributed to the spread of the disease. In Italy, for example, the incidence of CCD in Leyland cypress remains over 55%. The success of *S. cardinale* does not appear to be explained by its high virulence on susceptible hosts, a phenotype or outcome hypothesized for many non-native pathogens. Rather, it appears that intermediate virulence associated with good or high sporulation and a trend to successfully decrease its spore size may be the key to its great invasive potential. Above all, the success of this pathogen is invariably associated with its great demographic plasticity in most traits associated with infection and disease (Garbelotto *et al*., 2015).

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text: Above all, the success of this pathogen is invariably associated with its great demographic plasticity in most traits associated with infection and disease (Garbelotto *et al*., 2015). Although native populations of the pathogen in California include genotypes with a diverse thermal tolerance, in line with the rugged topography of the natural range of the pathogen in the State, including hot desert sites, cold mountain tops and cool coastal shrublands, the restricted thermal tolerance of *S. cardinale* introduced elsewhere may be a factor limiting its distribution. In New Zealand, where at least two genetically distant genotypes were introduced decades apart, novel and significant tree mortality was associated with the second introduction, suggesting that all predictions and trends of disease incidence and severity may need to be reevaluated if new introductions were to occur (Della Rocca *et al*., 2019).

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text: *S. cardinale* is a necrotrophic pathogen that infects, kills, and feeds on host bark tissues, specifically targeting the area from the cribro-vascular cambium outward, including parenchymal tissues and the cork cambium. The pathogen potentially affects every epigeal woody organ of the plant. Although *S. cardinale* can secrete cell wall-degrading enzymes (Graniti, 1998), it is unable to independently penetrate the epidermis or outer bark of the host and is therefore termed a wound pathogen. Notably, *S. cardinale* reproduces exclusively asexually in those regions of the world where it has been introduced. However, the population genetic structure in California suggests that sexual reproduction has occurred historically and thus may be cryptically occurring. We also note that there is a partial description of the sexual stage from California. The pathogen releases airborne conidia serving as the source of inoculum for new infections. Wind and rain are the main means of dispersing conidia, which results in primary infections predominantly occurring on the youngest, most succulent organs located in the highest and most distal parts of the crown. These areas are more exposed to the fungal inoculum and typically have a less thickened periderm making it easier to infect. In contrast, in Leyland cypress, many infections have been observed to occur directly on larger branches or the trunk, possibly due to micro-cracks resulting from the species’ rapid growth. An additional peculiarity of Leyland cypress is that it seems that the impact of the disease is milder in younger plantations, i.e., it is quite difficult to find young symptomatic plants. This is a problematic trait because, based on observations in plantations, one may grossly underestimate both the presence of the pathogen and the susceptibility of the plants.

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text: This is a problematic trait because, based on observations in plantations, one may grossly underestimate both the presence of the pathogen and the susceptibility of the plants. *S. cardinale* is a primary pathogen that infects and thrives in vigorous plants, characterized by living bark tissues well supplied with nutrients. New infections generally start on mechanically damaged host tissues, caused by abiotic factors such as strong winds or frost. Biotic factors, such as damage caused by insects, birds nesting in cypress trees, pruning, and other human-induced damage can also be a source of infection of the disease. As mentioned above, natural cracks in the bark associated with rapid growth or with branching are also susceptible to infection. Although wounds are the primary infection courts, infection can also be caused by conidia vectored by insects in the genera *Phloeosinus* (bark beetles), *Orsillus* (seed bugs), and *Cydia* (moths). A spindle-shaped bark lesion can normally be seen around the infection point and is the result of the necrosis of the living inner bark. As the necrosis progresses within the cambium, noticeable cankers form on the surface of the bark cork tissue, leading to depressions and cracks in the bark, typically accompanied by resin emission. *Seiridium cardinale* generates asexual reproductive structures called acervuli on the surface of the infected tissues, which will release conidia (Fig. 2). Acervuli production is interrupted during hot and dry weather conditions and is halted when the bark tissue is too dry due to further progression of the disease. Cankers can develop further than the area that was originally infected, thus enlarging and girdling the twig, branch, or trunk of the host tree causing diebacks on numerous of the infected shoots or causing general decline.

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text:
Cankers can develop further than the area that was originally infected, thus enlarging and girdling the twig, branch, or trunk of the host tree causing diebacks on numerous of the infected shoots or causing general decline. Cankers developing on the stem or on primary branches eventually lead to the death of the infected plant, however, some plants can survive for decades with dieback limited to the canopy. The growth of *S. cardinale* within the bark parenchyma of the host can occur at varying rates, especially in the longitudinal direction, where it can expand up to 5–10 cm in 6–8 months under favorable conditions and in the presence of susceptible hosts. A twig with an axis of 1–3 cm in diameter can be killed in 6–24 months. However, for branches of larger diameters, the time required for mortality is longer, with adult plants potentially taking anywhere from a few years to even decades to succumb to the infections. In contrast, seedlings infected with CCD have a much shorter survival time, which can be as little as 1 month after infection by *S. cardinale*. ##### Fig. 2. #####

A canker has formed, and the plant tissues appear sunken. Panel B reveals the presence of copious resin exudates leaking from cracks in the bark in advanced stages of the cankers. text:
### Macroscopic symptoms ###
Canopy desiccation levels depend on the affected portion of the plant (twig, branch, trunk). Death on girdled stems occurs due to the destruction of the plants’ phloem and cambium. Symptoms include a gradual change in color of the foliage which initially turns pale green, then straw yellow, light brown, reddish brown, and then ashy grey due to leaf decay, until the leaves fall off completely (Fig. 3). In such cases, the completely bare woody structure of the affected stem or branch remains visible for many years. Moreover, the fungus persists in the bark of the affected portions of the tree and continues to grow downward, leading to continuously enlarging cankers. ##### Fig. 3. #####
Typical sequence of colors assumed by cypress foliage after CCD has girdled the corresponding vegetative axis of the plant (twig or branch). Another macroscopic diagnostic feature is the frequent occurrence of asynchronous infections on the same plant, characterized by multiple infections of varying ages (Fig. 4). It is not uncommon to observe plants, particularly susceptible host genotypes, with portions of crowns of various sizes already dead and others in the dying phase, exhibiting different colors and shades. ##### Fig. 4. #####
This image depicts symptoms displayed by plants affected by multiple infections. The left image illustrates this phenomenon on Leyland cypress, while the right image shows how it can appear on common cypress. In both cases, we can observe that the decline of the canopy is widespread and dieback advanced. Although symptoms can appear simultaneously on plants, a useful diagnostic element is the presence of initial symptoms that lack a directional or homogeneous distribution over the canopy, and which are typically few and never synchronous. As shown in the disease cycle (Fig.

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text:
Although symptoms can appear simultaneously on plants, a useful diagnostic element is the presence of initial symptoms that lack a directional or homogeneous distribution over the canopy, and which are typically few and never synchronous. As shown in the disease cycle (Fig. 2), propagules often spread to other plant organs after the initial infection, typically moving downward and leading to secondary infections. ### Microscopic symptoms ###
Microscopic symptoms refer to the development of the canker lesion, which can be recognized by examining the affected organ. Initially, at the infection point, if the infected organ has not yet developed a thick suberous bark, the epidermis turns red-brown, with a well-defined margin that often assumes a spindle shape, indicating the underlying fungal development in the bark. As the host-pathogen interaction progresses, it leads to the formation of cankers on wooded organs, active lesions that exhibit depressions and cracks in the bark, with resin exudation occurring more frequently on younger trees. Signs of *S. cardinale* can be observed as scattered black pustules, called acervuli, which develops on the surface of the cankers. These acervuli, range from 0.3 to 1.5 mm in diameter, emerge from the bark surface and from openings in the bark during wet weather. When the bark is moist, conidia exude from acervuli in black drop-shaped masses, resembling toothpaste squeezed from a tube (Fig. 5). Conidia are six-celled asexual spores, measuring 18–30 μm by 6–12 μm. The terminal cells are hyaline without appendages, an important diagnostic trait to distinguish them from *S. unicorne* and *S. cupressi*; the four central cells are melanized having an olive-brown to dark-brown coloration (Fig. 5). ##### Fig.

The image on the left illustrates the acervuli of *Seiridium cardinale* produced *in vitro*, growing on 1% Malt Extract Agar amended with cypress seeds. The cypress seeds are colonized by the mycelium of *S. cardinale*, which finds a favorable environment for asexual reproduction. The conidia that form appear as black, globular masses, resulting from an aggregation of individual conidia. The image on the right displays the conidia of *S. cardinale* observed under a light microscope. Notably, one can see the hyaline terminal cells, which appear as the white tips of the conidia located at both ends, as well as the melanized cells positioned at the center of the conidia. Another diagnostic characteristic observable in these conditions is the number of septa, which in *S. cardinale* is five. Gently removing the outer bark at the margins of a canker using a pen knife or scalpel reveals the infected bark tissues. These tissues are easily identifiable thanks to their reddish-brown coloration often referred to as cardinal red, hence the pathogen’s name *S. cardinale*. Additionally, infected tissues often have a pasty, translucent appearance due to the resin impregnating the infected bark (Fig. 6). ##### Fig. 6. #####

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text: To isolate the pathogen, it is essential to collect a branch or twig from a symptomatic tree, ensuring that the entire canker is included in the sample. If the branch or twig is already partially killed by the pathogen, it is important to include at least 10 cm of tissue that is still alive, characterized by white healthy bark tissue and green leaves below the lower limit of the infection (Fig. 6). After sample collection, isolation of the fungus must be conducted in a clean and sterile environment, under a laminar flow hood. A sterile scalpel, 70% ethanol, and Petri dishes with Potato Dextrose Agar (PDA) are all required to isolate the fungus. The isolation procedure begins with exposing the necrotic lesion. While working under the laminar hood, the scalpel must be used to remove the outer bark and reveal the inner bark tissues of the infected branch. It is essential to find the boundary zone of the lesion, marked by the point of contact between infected brownish tissues and still healthy yellowish-white tissues (Fig. 7). At this juncture, small portions of tissue between the necrotized and healthy bark will be excised and plated in Petri dishes containing PDA. These plates must be incubated at 20–25°C for a few days. As the mycelium begins to grow from the plated fragments, the developing mycelium must be transferred individually to new Petri dishes with PDA and stored in the same condition as before. On PDA, the appearance of *S. cardinale* is characterized by a dense, floccose cotton texture with grey-olive green shades in the center and off-white color at the margins of the colony, accompanied by a salmon-orange hue on the reverse side. ##### Fig. 7.

The surface of the mycelium exhibits light-colored outer margins, while the center of the colony takes on a dark, melanized coloration. The underside of the Petri dish reveals the characteristic salmon pink color of *S. cardinale* grown on PDA. To confirm the presence of *Seiridium cardinale*, qPCR or sequencing can be utilized as precise diagnostic tools. Given that the genome of *S. cardinale* has been published (Scali *et al*., 2024), qPCR primers can be designed based on specific genomic regions to detect the pathogen in infected tissues. Additionally, sequencing techniques can be used to confirm pathogen identity at a molecular level, ensuring accurate detection of *S. cardinale*. Such methods offer high sensitivity and specificity, allowing for the detection of the pathogen even in the early stages of infection or in cases where visual symptoms are not yet prominent. Further research is recommended to optimize these techniques for routine diagnostic use, as they could complement traditional isolation methods, improving overall disease management strategies.

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text: Controlling CCD is challenging and complex due to the aggressiveness of the fungus, its ability to spread rapidly, and its development in plant tissues that are not easily accessible. CCD control can be achieved through three approaches: (1) chemical control, (2) sanitation, or (3) genetic improvement of resistant hosts. Biological control of CCD has also been tested. * *Chemical control*: Primarily preventive, chemical control is particularly advisable for young plants in nurseries. However, market restrictions on certain environmentally hazardous pesticides have significantly reduced the possibilities of chemical control against CCD in many world regions. Thiophanate-methyl (70%, contacticide and systemic, at a concentration of 1.5 g L−1) is considered the most effective fungicide; however, it has not been available on the European market for several years. Several new-generation products were tested, among which Boscalid (50%, contacticide and translaminar, at 1.2 g L−1), and Azoxystrobin (22.9%, contacticide and systemic, at 1ml L−1) demonstrated moderate efficacy (Della Rocca *et al*., 2011). * *Sanitation*: This direct control of CCD relies on management strategies aimed at reducing the amount of inoculum. Sanitation involves the careful mechanical removal of infected organs and tissues from affected plants: this method can be effective only if implemented promptly, systematically, and continuously. Given that infected portions of the plant may not always be visible, timely sanitation is crucial. Sanitation is particularly recommended for monumental trees or plants of special significance, where the purpose is preserving the individual specimens. A well-performed pruning allows an affected tree to recover and is the only therapeutic measure available. Interventions can be technically complex and require specialized and trained personnel.

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text:
A well-performed pruning allows an affected tree to recover and is the only therapeutic measure available. Interventions can be technically complex and require specialized and trained personnel. It is imperative to disinfect cutting points and tools such as scissors and chainsaws before moving from one plant to the next to avoid transmitting the disease. * *Genetic improvement*: This strategy involves the planting of host genotypes selected for their resistance to CCD, specifically through the use of plant clones that are vegetatively propagated by grafting or cutting. These agamically reproduced plants have been developed as part of an ongoing genetic improvement program for Italian cypress started in the 1970s at the IPSP-CNR in Italy. They have been patented and six clones are available for purchase on the European market: ‘Bolgheri’, ‘Agrimed No. 1’, ‘Italico’, ‘Mediterraneo’, ‘Le Crete 1’, ‘Le Crete 2’ (Panconesi and Raddi, 1991; Danti *et al.,*
2006, 2013). Resistant cypress expresses resistance to *S. cardinale* infections by forming a ligno-suberized boundary zone in the infection site. This boundary zone is made by four to six layers of cells with suberized walls that are capable of containing the activity of *Seiridium* preventing it from expanding into adjacent healthy tissue (Danti *et al*., 2018). Additional factors contributing to resistance include rapid activation of signal molecules, including hormones, following infection (Scimone *et al*., 2024).

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text: Additional factors contributing to resistance include rapid activation of signal molecules, including hormones, following infection (Scimone *et al*., 2024). Furthermore, there is *ex novo* synthesis of terpenoids as phytoalexins (Achotegui-Castells *et al*., 2015, 2016) in phloem axial resin ducts, which are produced by the host as a defense mechanism against infection, along with other anatomical mechanisms at the phloem level (Della Rocca *et al*., 2021, 2022). Inoculation studies have also shown that resistant clones support significantly less sporulation by the fungus than susceptible clones, hence their use is not likely to increase the overall amount of inoculum present in one area (Della Rocca *et al*., 2018), a concern associated with the use of tolerant genotypes of a host for any pathosystem. * *Biological control*: Promising results have been obtained, both in mesocosm and in the field, with the application of *Pseudomonas chlororaphis* subsp. *aureofaciens* strain M71. The bacterium, through the production of Phenazine-1-carboxylic acid, is apparently able to control the growth of *S. cardinale in vivo* following artificial inoculations and remains viable on cypress phyllosphere for more than 3 months (Raio *et al*., 2011).

title: The Cypress Canker Disease Pandemic
text: This pathosystem provides a unique setting for the investigation of host-pathogen interactions thanks to the presence of genetically identical plant clones that can be easily propagated and have a well-defined level of disease tolerance/susceptibility and also thanks to the mitotic nature and easy *in vitro* growth of the pathogen, with pathogen genotypes also well characterized in terms of virulence. Clonal replication is thus possible for host and pathogen thus providing a wonderful model system to study host-pathogen interactions in a tree disease. Current cutting-edge research efforts involving UC Berkeley and IPSP-CNR in Italy, are focused on understanding the dynamic of host-pathogen interaction (*S. cardinale* vs. *C. sempervirens*) at the molecular level. The dual-RNA seq technique is employed to characterize the genes involved during the infection process and those associated with host resistance. Identifying the molecular pathways and genes linked to resistant plants could facilitate the selection of new resistant clones of cypress that exhibit resistance to a broader range of isolates of the pathogen than that currently present in Europe (Della Rocca *et al*., 2018). Given the current issue of climate change, researchers are further investigating how temperature may modulate disease tolerance, thus greatly increasing our predictive power regarding disease progression of current and future outbreaks. Finally, the comparative analysis of entire genomes will allow us to determine the virulence of various populations growing in different world regions, without necessarily testing such virulence in plants. Findings in these areas might help further understand the disease and interaction between *Seiridium spp. * and their hosts. Furthermore, it might provide essential knowledge for the regulamentation of the worldwide movement of plant materials potentially infected. Besides the molecular interaction between host and pathogen, important coevolutionary investigations might reveal fundamental knowledge for disease management.

The understanding of how coevolutionary dynamics shape resistance and virulence in host and pathogen populations respectively is still an uninvestigated aspect of CCD. Lastly, another relevant research question involves the characterization of different populations of *Seiridum* at the genomic level. Genomes of *Seiridium* species have recently been published (Scali *et al*., *2024*). By comparing the genomes of these different species, important questions regarding why *Seiridum* became such a lethal pathogen upon its introduction to Europe from California might be investigated. In this epidemiological context, the pathogen displayed remarkable adaptability, and genome comparison among different populations will help us understand the evolutionary dynamics that facilitated these ecological successes.

### Overview ###
*Epichloë* spp. are fungal endophytes of cool season grasses often used to increase biotic and abiotic resistances of pasture and turf grasses outside of the United Kingdom. Here we present what is known about *Epichloë* distribution within the UK and discuss the potential use of *Epichloë* technology in UK agriculture.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text: 1. Understand how the life cycle and biology of *Epichloë* are suited to agricultural exploitation. 2. Identify potential benefits and risks of *Epichloë* technology use in UK agriculture. 3. Discuss potential regulation pathways towards the adoption of *Epichloë* technology in UK agriculture.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text: Endophytic microorganisms, or endophytes, exist symbiotically within higher plants. These relationships can range from mutualistic to pathogenic. Endophytes can affect host growth rate, environmental stress resistance, and nutrient uptake (Dubey *et al*., 2020). Within the Poaceae plant family (grasses), there are many species that have coevolved with endophytic fungi in the family Clavicipitaceae. Within this fungal family, species in the genus *Epichloë* form host-specific relationships with grasses from the sub-family Pooideae, a group that includes major cultivated cereals (wheat, barley, oat and rye), as well as pasture and lawn/amenity grass species. While *Epichloë* spp. are not known to associate with domesticated cereal crop species, they are present in many of their wild relatives. Fungal species within the *Epichloë* genus have been associated with positive outcomes for their hosts, such as increased vigour and yield, through a variety of mechanisms such as increasing abiotic and biotic resistances through the production of alkaloid metabolites (Fardella *et al*., 2023, Bastías *et al*., 2024); alkaloids are a diverse class of compounds, some of which have physiological effects on insects and animals. However, some alkaloids produced by *Epichloë* in association with pasture grasses were found to be causing animal health problems in the New World (the United States and New Zealand) where the production of compounds such as ergovaline and lolitrem were causing toxicity to livestock (fescue toxicosis and ryegrass staggers).

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text: Eliminating the *Epichloë* entirely led to poor pasture performance due to insect pest pressure, and the need to reduce toxicity while maintaining pest deterrence using non-toxic strains of *Epichloë* was the beginning of *Epichloë* technology implementation (Johnson *et al*., 2013, 2021). Select *Epichloë* strains are now used extensively in New World agriculture to reduce the instances of *Epichloë*-related toxicity to livestock while providing plant-pest deterrence in pasture settings. It is hypothesised that the vertebrate-toxin-producing ‘wild-type’ asexual *Epichloë* strains that caused such pronounced animal disease symptoms in New Zealand were inadvertently imported from Europe, and likely from the United Kingdom (UK) (van Zijll de Jong *et al*., 2008), where the new environments selected for higher infection rates than occur in European pasture. However, in the UK there are no seed lines intentionally infected with *Epichloë* on the market, and while Plant Breeder’s Rights have been granted for multiple endophyte grass products in Europe (Fernando *et al*., 2021), no obvious examples of these are sold commercially. The UK lacks the pasture toxicity issues mentioned above, as well as the arthropod pest burden found in many areas in the New World that necessitated *Epichloë* product development. Therefore, the justification for deploying *Epichloë*-infected grasses in UK pasture is less obvious. Nevertheless, the biology of *Epichloë* provides an interesting range of possible applications for agriculture within the UK, including cereal production. Specifically, in certain situations *Epichloë* is a compelling candidate for use as a low input biological method of increasing yields through resistance to abiotic and biotic stresses. We also wish to consider the use of *Epichloë* technology in cereal crops.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text: We also wish to consider the use of *Epichloë* technology in cereal crops. Cereal crops are used in a broad range of commodities, including animal feed, bread, beer, and scotch whisky. In 2023, cereals (wheat, barley, and oat) and cereal-derived products accounted for upwards of £4.0 billion in the UK economy (DEFRA, 2023). Pest and disease management represents one of the highest input costs for cereal growers and maintaining land use and high yields for cereal crops is vital for its continued economic value in the UK. The development and implementation of economical integrated pest management strategies, including biological control options such as *Epichloë* technology, offers a new tool to sustain profitability. In this case review, we evaluate the potential application of *Epichloë* to improve UK pasture and cereal crop production, including how its biology is suited for the purpose, benefits and risks of such exploitation, and the potential commercial adoption for use in UK agriculture. There are other potential uses for *Epichloë* grasses in the UK, such as wildlife control in amenity and airport settings, as well as ecological restoration (e.g. through improved plant heavy-metal tolerance), but these will not be considered in the current case review as they are largely relevant outside of agriculture.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text:
### Life cycle ###
Within the family Clavicipitaceae, a variety of agriculturally important fungi exist including the cereal pathogens responsible for ergot (*Claviceps* spp. ), the entomopathogenic fungi (*Metarhizium* spp.) that is used as a bioinsecticide, and phytopathogenic and mutualist species of *Epichloë*. Sexual *Epichloë* spp. establish in the aerial tissues of grasses, particularly the leaves, sheaths, and inflorescences. Asexual species inhabit the apical meristem and migrate to the aerial tissues where some colonise the leaf sheath and even the leaf blade. All *Epichloë* species can be present within the tissue as hyphae within the intercellular space (Fig. 1A) while sexual species can also form a stroma around the tillers of the grass (Fig. 1B). ##### Fig. 1. #####
*Epichloë* spp. in grasses; (A) *Epichloë* sp. mycelia (stained blue) under 20x magnification inhabiting *Festuca rubra* leaf tissue sampled in Glasgow, UK; and (B) *Epichloë* sp. stromata infecting a grass within the Poaceae family and inhibiting further growth of the tillers, a disease known as ‘choke’. Image captured in Cambridge, UK. All images taken by G. Fredell. *Epichloë* spp. fit into three main groups according to their symbioses with host grasses: asexual, sexual, and pleiotropic (Fig. 2). Asexual species are unable to produce hymenium with sexual spores and sparsely produce asexual spores (conidia) depending on the species.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text:
2). Asexual species are unable to produce hymenium with sexual spores and sparsely produce asexual spores (conidia) depending on the species. They are mainly spread through vertical transmission by infecting the seeds of their host. Asexual species are thought to be the result of hybridisation between two different sexual *Epichloë* species (Caradus *et al*., 2021b). Only sexual species can reproduce through horizontal transmission via ascospores. These sexual species produce stroma around the tiller and can inhibit the production of inflorescence and seed, giving rise to the disease known
as ‘choke’. Sexual spores can spread via wind and/or flies within the genus *Botanophila*, which consume the spermatia as larvae and spread spores through their faecal matter as adults, facilitating *Epichloë* spread between infected plants (Saikkonen *et al*., 2016). Pleiotropic species are both able to reproduce sexually and asexually and may do so on different tillers of the same plant. ##### Fig. 2. #####

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text:
### Host specificity ###
Each *Epichloë* species forms specific host-partner interactions with one or a few grass species within Pooideae. The host range of some *Epichloë* can be increased artificially in laboratory settings, but it is unlikely that an *Epichloë* species can establish itself within a host that they do not already inhabit in nature (Schirrmann and Leuchtmann, 2015). This host range is further reduced in asexual species, which often arise through a hybridisation event, creating a strain coevolved into a single or few grass species. These asexual species are housed within and increase the fitness of their specific grass host, creating a mutualistic relationship where both organisms benefit. In pasture grass species that have asexual *Epichloë* associated with them naturally (e.g., *Epichloë festucae* var. *lolii* and perennial ryegrass), the process of infecting these *Epichloë* into new grass cultivars of the same host species is relatively successful, although the stability of the new relationships depends on genotype-genotype interactions. While *Epichloë* species do not naturally occur in modern cultivated cereal grasses, it is still possible to artificially infect cultivated cereal grasses depending on their compatibility with a given *Epichloë* species (Simpson *et al*., 2014). The strong host specificity of asexual *Epichloë* species presents a challenge to infecting non-hosts and achieving stable symbioses, but current research is exploring solutions to this (Simpson *et al*., 2024).

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text:
Different grass-endophyte combinations have been shown to have specific impacts on the host plant as well as unique metabolite profiles, meaning that artificial host switching may not produce the same outcomes in different grass species (Freitas *et al*., 2020). However, current efforts to explore large chromosomal changes that support *Epichloë* symbiosis in modern wheat cultivars are promising for creating new compatible infections in cereals (Simpson *et al*., 2024). Further research addressing this issue of altering host range will allow for broadened symbiosis effects in various asexual *Epichloë-*cereal combinations. ### Distribution and species recorded in the UK ###
There have only been a small number of studies into naturally occurring *Epichloë* presence in the UK, with no systematic surveys for *Epichloë* diversity, alkaloid production, or ecological niches undertaken. The few UK studies reported in the literature are limited in scope, usually focusing on one region or a few aspects of *Epichloë* biology. A British research group that used genomics to determine *Epichloë* presence in dried herbarium samples collected from the UK identified six potential sexual species with one more speculated but not confirmed (Spooner and Kemp, 2005). Those listed as present were *E*. *baconii* (hosts: *Agrostis* spp. ), *E*. *bromicola* (hosts: *Bromus* spp. ), *E*. *clarkii* (hosts: *Holcus* spp. ), *E*. *festucae* (hosts: *Festuca* spp. ), *E*. *sylvatica* (host: *Brachypodium sylvaticum*), and *E*. *typhina* (hosts: multiple).

Older UK studies focused on specific regions or host species. In Wales, stands of common bentgrass (*Agrostis capillaris*) were shown to have as high as a 43% infection frequency, and creeping bentgrass (*A*. *stolonifera*) a 40% infection frequency with pleiotropic *E*. *baconii* (previous *E*. *typhina*, sexual) (Bradshaw, 1959). In 1985, perennial ryegrass (L. *perenne*) meadows from 52 sites across Scotland, Wales, and England were assessed for *Epichloë* infection using microscopy. Plant material with observable endophytes further identified the species as *E*. *festucae* var. *lolii* (asexual) using an ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) technique with an antiserum specific to this species. Endophyte mycelium was found at 14 sites, and 10 of these tested positive for *E*. *festucae* var. *lolii*. Infected swards were from Wales and England but not from Scotland (Lewis and Clements, 1986). However, on the Scottish islands of St. Kilda, Benbecula, and Rum, populations of red fescue (*F*. *rubra*) were tested for endophyte presence, and all populations were infected with *E*. *festucae* (sexual) (Bazely *et al*., 1997).

The authors implicated toxic alkaloid production by *Epichloë* in these grasses to contribute to the sporadic (3–5 year) population crashes of feral sheep in the 1990s. In Berkshire, England, six experimental sites of differing ages were studied for *Epichloë* presence. It was found that in the three oldest sites, Yorkshire fog (*Holcus lanatus*) and creeping soft grass (*H*. *mollis)* had an average of 69% infection frequency with *E*. *typhina* (sexual), with a high proportion of infections asymptomatic at the time of collection (Clay and Brown, 1997). Within tall fescue (*F*. *arundinacea*) populations from across southern and north-central England, presumed to be natural/native stands, 80% were found to have *Epichloë*-infected grasses (assumed to be *E*. *coenophiala*, formerly *Neotyphodium coenophialum*, asexual) (Spyreas *et al*., 2001). A systematic study on populations of *Epichloë* in grass stands of common bentgrass (*A*. *capillaris*), Yorkshire fog (*H*. *lanatus*), and orchard grass (*Dactylis glomerata*) across England described two new sexual species based on ascospore structure. These were *E*. *baconii* and *E*. *clarkii*, with both previously classified as *E*.

text: These were *E*. *baconii* and *E*. *clarkii*, with both previously classified as *E*. *typhina*, and were one of the first instances showing adaptations in sympatric populations of this fungus (White, 1993). More recently, a population genetics study on these sexual *Epichloë* utilising a site at Kew gardens further presented fungal-grass coevolution and adaptation of these species using genome-wide SNP datasets, presenting differences in fungal genetic structure associated with differences in dispersal abilities and overall population structure (Treindl *et al*., 2023). As of 2024, the National Biodiversity Network (NBN) atlas has 906 records of *Epichloë* in the UK and Northern Ireland, with 295 verified as correct by an NBN-appointed independent expert. Of the verified records, 159 are in England, 1 in the Isle of Mann, 9 in Northern Ireland, 114 in Scotland, and 11 in Wales. Species recorded include 63 *E*. *baconii*, 1 *E*. *bromicola*, 5 *E*. *clarkii*, 8 *E*. *festucae*, 3 *E*. *sylvatica*, and 209 *E*. *typhina* (unconfirmed records contain no additional species). The lack of asexual species is not surprising, as most will be identified based on disease (choke) symptoms, while asymptomatic (asexual species) endophytes will only be recorded if specifically surveyed for. While studies into *Epichloë* diversity and biogeography in the UK are lacking, there have been several large studies conducted in parts of mainland Europe, such as that of Cagnano *et al*.

This would suggest that if UK-based surveys were conducted, there is likely to be a range of environmentally adapted species available to exploit in UK agriculture.

text:
### Benefits of mutualistic *Epichloë* in agriculture ###
Microbial biological control agents (MBCAs) are naturally occurring microorganisms that are deployed against pests, including insects, weeds, and diseases. Since MBCAs are based on live microorganisms, with their own set of environmental requirements to be active, it is challenging to achieve consistent pest control. Inconsistent field performance with high costs minimise their attractiveness compared with synthetic chemical alternatives, and MBCAs therefore remain at a relatively low market share (Damalas and Koutroubas, 2018). In contrast, endophyte grass products are commercially successful in countries where their benefits are obvious. For example, they can control insect herbivory that would otherwise substantially impact grass growth and can be considered perhaps the most successful method of biocontrol agent deployment in agriculture to date. The success of *Epichloë* can, in part, be explained by the distinct advantages it has over other MBCAs that are often applied as spore or cell drenches that encounter hostile environmental conditions such as fluctuating temperatures, variable moisture content, and UV exposure. In contrast, asexual *Epichloë* are physically protected as they already occur in the seed when planted, occupy intercellular spaces of the plant cells, and do not require in-season applications. In addition to nutrients provided by the plant, they are also protected from the external environment, and competition from other microorganisms. In effect, infection with *Epichloë* turns the plant into its own chemical factory making it one of the most efficient plant protection products in the market. If precautionary principles are applied, there are likely substantial benefits to employing endophyte-grass products. These include:
1. Quality and yield improvements
2. Reduced herbivory and wildlife deterrence
3. Reduced disease in agriculture and pasture settings

These include:
1. Quality and yield improvements
2. Reduced herbivory and wildlife deterrence
3. Reduced disease in agriculture and pasture settings
4. Environmental stress tolerance
*Epichloë* has been shown to produce a variety of positive effects on the quality and yield of their host plant. In both drunken horse grass (*Achnatherum inebrians*) and barley (*Hordeum vulgare*), *Epichloë*-inoculated plants have shown increased biomass and seed yield (Zhang *et al*., 2015; Liu *et al*., 2022). The mechanisms behind increased yield have yet to be established, but it is likely that this is due to increased biotic and abiotic resistances and/or plant growth promotion. It is noteworthy that if an *Epichloë* isolate were to protect its host against abiotic stress with no claim of pest or pathogen control, then this would potentially see it classified as a biostimulant rather than a Plant Protection Product (as MBCAs are classified under) and have a different regulatory pathway. #### Potential benefits to UK pasture ####
Most data on the benefits of *Epichloë* infection comes from pasture grasses where several commercial options exist overseas, and the symbioses are exploited for increased biotic stress resistance, particularly to insect herbivory. This is most relevant in New World pastures where insect herbivory pressure is high due to the presence of pests like the Argentine Stem Weevil (Ruppert *et al*., 2017). Periods of drought stress (that *Epichloë* can help protect against, potentially directly or indirectly through pest deterrence) have also been more common in some pasture areas overseas (Decunta *et al*., 2021).

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text: Periods of drought stress (that *Epichloë* can help protect against, potentially directly or indirectly through pest deterrence) have also been more common in some pasture areas overseas (Decunta *et al*., 2021). To date, the UK has not possessed the suite of pasture pests that would warrant the use of endophyte-containing grass seed. In the advent of the UK loss of neonicotinoid pesticides and resistance developing to pyrethroids, studies on *Epichloë*-derived biopesticide utility are timely. Evidence of aphid mortality and deterrence has been shown in perennial ryegrass (*L*. *perenne*) (Collinson *et al*., 2024) while developmental delay and lower larval biomass of the armyworm (*Spodoptera frugiperda*) have been associated with *Epichloë*-infected woodland grass (*Poa alsodes*) (Shymanovich *et al*., 2019). *Epichloë* has also been shown to decrease slug (*Deroceras* spp.) herbivory (Pennell *et al*., 2018) as well as reduce populations of root-knot nematodes (*Meloidogyne incognita*) (Meyer *et al*., 2020), a pest absent in the UK, but other parasitic nematodes are. In addition to lacking pasture pests controlled by *Epichloë* overseas, the UK does not appear to suffer the livestock health issues that resulted from high levels of pasture infection with toxic *Epichloë* strains, as has occurred in New World countries. However, this situation has the potential to change if new pasture pests were to invade the UK creating a selective pressure that increases *Epichloë* infection levels in unsown grassland, and if climate change puts additional abiotic stress on pasture productivity.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text:
UK-relevant abiotic stresses such as drought or waterlogging have been shown to be alleviated through *Epichloë* symbioses increasing host resilience (Murphy *et al*., 2015; Saedi *et al*., 2021), in which case the balance may tip in favour of *Epichloë*-infected pasture grass deployment in the future. #### Potential benefits to UK cereals ####
Solutions to mitigate the loss of pesticide actives due both to regulatory changes and pest/pathogen resistance are needed in UK cereal production if plant health, productivity, and product safety are to be maintained (Burnett *et al*., 2021). Antagonism by *Epichloë* spp. has been documented against a variety of plant pathogens that affect UK agricultural production. *Epichloë* has been shown to limit the growth of many common leaf diseases on grasses/cereals, such as rusts (Puccinales), mildews (Erysiphales), and leaf blotch (*Rhynchosporium* sp.) (Card *et al*., 2021). Mechanisms behind producing resistance seem to be varied and multifaceted, including the production of antimicrobial compounds, competitive and vector exclusion, and plant-induced resistance. It has been shown that *Epichloë* inhibits microbial growth *in vitro*, however, rarely has this been studied *in planta* (Xia *et al*., 2018). Further research is therefore needed to determine how this translates to field performance, what mechanisms contribute to pathogen resistance, and how that resistance impacts the yield and quality of cereal crops. Understanding this will allow for a more effective selection of *Epichloë* strains to be used as biological control agents in the cereal context.

Understanding this will allow for a more effective selection of *Epichloë* strains to be used as biological control agents in the cereal context. Abiotic stress resistance as a result of *Epichloë* presence has been demonstrated in various grass systems, suggesting its usefulness in an increasingly unstable climate. In the UK, climate change predictions indicate wetter and warmer winters (MET Office, 2022). *Epichloë* has demonstrated increased waterlogging tolerance for *Hordeum* species (Song *et al*., 2015). Although the interactions and interplay between *Epichloë*, the host, and the environment are complex, with further research into these mechanisms, *Epichloë* is a promising candidate for use in the UK due to its wide range of effects and potential to mitigate the loss of synthetic inputs. ### Risks of mutualistic *Epichloë* in agriculture ###
The lessons learned from the discovery of *Epichloë*-derived livestock toxicity offer perspective on the risks of exploiting such technology. Understanding the possible uncertainties involved with UK-dissemination are important to consider. Some risks include:
1. The *Epichloë* strain is sexual and hybridises with local strains giving unpredictable outcomes. 2. The *Epichloë*-seed combination produces toxins that impact native species, such as arthropods, grazers, and their predators. 3. Toxins enter the human diet at unsafe levels. 4. The improved fitness of the *Epichloë*-seed combination increases its competitiveness, and it becomes invasive in natural or agricultural environments. Currently in New World countries where commercialised *Epichloë*-seed combinations are sold, only asexual species are marketed. It is unlikely that a sexual strain would be marketed as this has intrinsic liabilities, such as horizontal transfer of sexual strains spread through ascospore dissemination.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text:
It is unlikely that a sexual strain would be marketed as this has intrinsic liabilities, such as horizontal transfer of sexual strains spread through ascospore dissemination. This applies primarily to non-native species capable of producing wind-borne spores that could potentially spread to wild hosts, non-infected fields, or pastures resulting in unknown effects on wildlife or livestock. #### Potential risks to UK from *Epichloë*-pasture ####
As mentioned above, the livestock toxicity and specific pasture pest pressures overseas that prompted the development of *Epichloë* products are largely absent from the UK, and so the balance of risk versus benefit is different. Overseas *Epichloë* products have replaced areas with high infection of toxic-type *Epichloë*, whereas in the UK they would replace mainly non-toxic pastures. As a result, there is a burden of proof that these products would have minimal negative impacts prior to commercial introduction. For example, *Epichloë*-infected grasses can reduce invertebrate biodiversity via the ingestion of alkaloids and have been observed to reduce ladybird fitness and prolong pupal stages (Fuchs *et al*., 2013). Similarly, various *Epichloë* species have been documented to impact earthworm populations negatively when feeding on infected grasses (Pennell *et al*., 2018). It is unclear how widespread cultivation of *Epichloë*-infected grasses would influence native invertebrate populations in the UK and is likely dependent on the strains used. As *Epichloë* species naturally exist within UK native grasses, UK wildlife has some level of exposure to *Epichloë* already, however, the environmental risk lies in the potential scale of cultivation and high rates of sward infection.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text:
As *Epichloë* species naturally exist within UK native grasses, UK wildlife has some level of exposure to *Epichloë* already, however, the environmental risk lies in the potential scale of cultivation and high rates of sward infection. There are few studies exploring wider ecological changes resulting from widespread *Epichloë* infection of pasture; one from the United States comparing tall fescue grasslands with or without toxic-type *E*. *coenophiala* found the symbiosis had a transformational effect on ecological systems. Some of these large-scale impacts included herbivore behaviour and infection rates, soil feedback and decomposition rates, as well as plant competition, diversity, productivity, and succession (Rudgers and Clay, 2007). While seed lot testing is currently implemented across the EU and within the UK at cultivar evaluation stages, we note that *Epichloë* has been identified in commercial pasture grass seed within the European market (Krauss *et al*., 2020) yet a lack of negative impacts have been publicly reported. Compared to the evaluation of potential ecological impacts, risk assessing livestock toxicity and the potential of vertebrate-toxic compounds entering the human diet via grazing animals is a mature research area given the history of use overseas. Any novel *Epichloë*-pasture grass associations require re-evaluation of their metabolic profile to assess their safety in this regard, and this is a primary consideration in any commercial endeavour. #### Potential risks to UK from *Epichloë*-cereals ####
*Epichloë* spp. produce multiple potent alkaloids and other bioactive metabolites that can cause toxicity to both invertebrates and vertebrates, so risk assessments must be made when deploying *Epichloë* in an agricultural context, particularly in cereals produced for human consumption.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text: Research on *Epichloë* technology from pasture settings has provided safety data for certain *Epichloë* alkaloids both for grazing animals and for human consumption (e.g. via meat or milk), however different *Epichloë* species producing distinct suits of bioactive compounds are likely to be exploited in cereal cropping. Understanding how *Epichloë* metabolites could affect human health is paramount in adopting this technology in crops. Importantly, asexual *Epichloë* species tend to produce more alkaloids than sexual species, likely due to their dependence on host survival (Panaccione *et al*., 2014), showing genetic capability is an important consideration when choosing the endophyte species. Alkaloid profiles of artificially inoculated *Epichloë*-cereal combinations are beginning to be studied and better understood (Liu *et al*., 2022). The environmental risks of cereal crops infected with *Epichloë* would be similar to those for pasture detailed above, however, many plant-protection products kill non-target organisms so the relative risk of *Epichloë* needs to be evaluated with reference to the application of seed treatments, soil fumigants or foliar pesticides. One of the advantages from an environmental risk angle that *Epichloë* use within cereals has advantages over its use in pasture grasses; the main reason being that cereals are annual crops, and therefore cultivation in the event of unintended consequences can be halted more quickly than with perennial pasture grasses. Additionally, one would also anticipate a lower risk of escape into the wider environment, as cereal crops are more reliant on growers for propagation. Understanding the environmental risks, implementing assessments and regulations for these risks, and communicating them to the public, are critical for adoption of any new management practice.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
section: Pathway to UK Adoption and Regulation of *Epichloë* Products
text: Before an MBCA can be deployed in the UK, it should first receive regulatory approval. If biological control agents are non-native (and for MBCAs, if they are not part of a formulated product), then their release in England/Wales requires a licence by the DEFRA non-native biological control agent (NNBCA) licensing team after an environmental risk assessment. In Scotland, non-native species licencing is the jurisdiction of NatureScot. However, if MBCAs are part of a formulated product then they are the primary responsibility of the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) and require approval through Plant Protection Product Regulation. Arguments could be made either way as to whether *Epichloë* strains implemented within grasses or cereals constitute formulated products, or if they become an inherent property of the plant. If designated a formulated product for use in the Agriculture and Horticulture sectors, they are expected to be augmentative or to not persist in the environment. As mentioned earlier, if an *Epichloë* were to improve abiotic stress tolerance without claim of pest/pathogen control, it may be considered a biostimulant by the HSE, with a different regulatory pathway. There are also considerations to be made with regards to the UK’s DUS (distinct, uniform and stable) and VCU (value for cultivation and use) schemes which are used to assess the utility of a new crop cultivar and to determine if cultivars can be featured on the National Listing (approved for sale). In UK pasture grasses, *Epichloë* products are currently prohibited from entering these schemes, and if the symbiosis impacted uniformity or caused phenotypic instability in cereal crops then these could prevent these seed-endophyte combinations from achieving recognised varietal status. It is unclear if this would be required if an *Epichloë* species was introduced into an already recognised cereal variety.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
section: Pathway to UK Adoption and Regulation of *Epichloë* Products
text: It is unclear if this would be required if an *Epichloë* species was introduced into an already recognised cereal variety. The regulatory pathway for an *Epichloë* product may depend on its origin, the specifics of the plant host, the intended use of the crop, and the claims made on the mechanisms through which *Epichloë* is supporting the plant. We anticipate that all these factors to consider may lead to confusion as to which regulatory umbrella *Epichloë*-infected grasses or cereals fit under. One possible solution to this potential uncertainty would be the formation of a specific body or grouping to oversee endophyte regulation in the UK, to support a pathway for UK adoption and regulation of *Epichloë* products, and potentially other endophytes. There are models of *Epichloë*-specific regulation in other countries. For example, in the New Zealand pasture setting the Endophyte Technical Committee (ETC) is “a cooperative forum to ensure that endophyte strains in commerce or under development are tested uniformly, and to publish industry-agreed descriptions of the animal safety and insect control of commercial endophyte strains each year” (Caradus *et al*., 2021a). It is the role of the ETC to produce industry-agreed endophyte insect control ratings and endophyte animal health and welfare ratings; this entails designing protocols, evaluating results, and approving new endophyte strains. The ETC also acts as a source of expert advice on technical matters relating to endophytes. A similar model of cooperation between industry and government agencies could be implemented in the UK to facilitate the adoption and regulation of *Epichloë* products in agriculture.

title: Distribution, Potential Commercial Adoption, and Possible Impacts of the Endophytic
text: There is uncertainty regarding future biotic and abiotic threats to UK pasture and cereal crops in the coming years and how these stressors could be alleviated by the use of *Epichloë* technology. Climate change could impose more frequent extremes of precipitation causing flooding and subsequent waterlogging of crops. A change in environmental conditions could also see current pest and disease pressures and ranges increase. For example, warmer and wetter winters are forecasted for the UK, increasing the risk of the arrival of new (e.g. blast disease of cereals) or existing pests (e.g. powdery mildew) that thrive in these conditions. Additionally, current changes in policy as well as increasing pest resistance are resulting in the loss of pesticide-active ingredients for crop protection, in turn, limiting effective management strategies for growers. This ushers in and urges alternative crop protection methods such as endophytic associations. It would therefore be prudent for more research to be done on the potential benefits of *Epichloë*-infected grasses/cereals under a changing climate, and the identification of native isolates that help their host perform better under UK-specific environmental extremes and changing pest pressures.

### Overview ###
Fusarium head blight (FHB) affects small grain cereals. Several *Fusarium* species cause FHB and contaminate food and feed with mycotoxins. Biological control uses living microorganisms (biological control agents [BCAs]) that interact with host and/or pathogen to control disease. We focus on the molecular mechanisms underpinning the three-part interactions between host, pathogen and BCA.

title: 'Biological Control of Fusarium Head Blight in Cereals: Insights into Molecular
text:
Fusarium head blight (FHB) and Fusarium crown rot (FCR) affect small grain cereals such as wheat, barley, oat and rye wherever cereals are grown. These crops represent the basis of many populations’ diets; for instance, wheat production ranks third for cereals worldwide, feeding both humans and livestock. In addition, the global human population is increasing rapidly: This presents new challenges to ensure enough and safe food for all while using sustainable production systems (Sustainable Development Goals – United Nations). Diseases reduce the amount of useful biomass produced by the plant (food security) as well as the edibility of grain products (food safety) due to mycotoxin production. *Fusarium* spp. within the Fusarium head blight species complex (FHBSC) produces many specialized metabolites, some of which are toxic compounds that affect both humans and livestock: they are defined as mycotoxins. Typically, these compounds interfere with basal physiological processes of eukaryotic cells. The mycotoxins produced by *Fusarium* spp. are mainly trichothecenes and polyketide compounds (Fig. 1) and they are produced either during interactions with the plant host or in niche competition. Therefore, the impact of Fusarium is the result of both quantity and quality loss. It is particularly difficult to estimate the losses caused by *Fusarium* diseases since the pathogen complex causes both FHB and FCR and the former causes losses affecting both yield and quality. FHB is particularly sensitive to the weather at anthesis (flowering) and therefore losses vary extensively from year to year, and can even exceed 90% (Matny, 2015). ##### Fig. 1. #####

Fossils identified to the fungal genus *Fusarium* date back to 91.3 million years ago (middle Cretaceous) and the genus has expanded and evolved since then. FHB, as a disease, has been reported regularly since the 19th century and has spread aggressively during the 20th and 21st centuries. Current strategies to control FHB disease spread range from agricultural practise (*e*.*g*. crop rotation, tillage, intercropping), fungicides such as demethylation inhibitors (DMIs), partially resistant cultivars, and biological control. Several transgenic plant strategies show great promise in field trials but none are adopted as products to our knowledge (Collinge and Sarrocco, 2022). Biological control of plant disease is a sustainable strategy for food and feed production that is based on the use of living organisms as active ingredients. Biological control has increasingly gained attention both in research and for the development of marketed biological control agent (BCA) products over the last 20 years. This strategy is mainly based on preventive treatments of plants as well as seeds. An advantage of this strategy is a low risk of the development of resistance to the microbial BCA as organisms rather than compounds are used, and these operate through several modes of action (Collinge *et al*., 2022).

title: 'Biological Control of Fusarium Head Blight in Cereals: Insights into Molecular
text: An advantage of this strategy is a low risk of the development of resistance to the microbial BCA as organisms rather than compounds are used, and these operate through several modes of action (Collinge *et al*., 2022). Furthermore, BCA products do not leave toxic residues (as for fungicides). Therefore, many research projects focus on microorganisms capable of controlling plant disease; BCAs are thus studied extensively from lab to field scale worldwide. Nevertheless, relatively few products are available on the market, often due to the complexity of the registration process. Since not all natural products are safe for human, animal, or environment health, these products must undergo the same rigorous assessment risk workflow designed for chemical compounds. Interactions between BCAs, the pathogen and the plant host can vary from antagonism to synergy, and a wide array of tools and strategies are displayed by all three parties. Molecular knowledge and findings about these complex interactions provide a more detailed picture of disease spread and management. In the case of FHB, convincing results are obtained each year from greenhouse and field experiments that demonstrate reductions in disease incidence and pathogen biomass, and hence mycotoxin content (Cesarini *et al*., 2025). A precise and shaped management of FHB is more likely to be achieved by understanding the mechanisms and strategies displayed during the interactions themselves and their effects on microbiomes. For example, using an amplicon sequencing approach, Rojas *et al*. (2020b) showed that *Fusarium* infection modifies the spike microbiome substantially, reducing the diversity of fungal endophytes that could be detected during spike development. This study was followed by the isolation of fungal endophytes from healthy spike tissues under disease pressure, and several of these and other isolates could control FHB in greenhouse trials (Rojas *et al*., 2020a).

However, the geographical distribution of species within the species complex can overlap, leading to interspecific competition. For this purpose, and to penetrate the plant host cells successfully, *Fusarium* species within FHBSC produce a range of specialized metabolites including those we define as mycotoxins. ### Mycotoxins ###
The mycotoxin repertoire of *Fusarium* spp. also includes terpenes, polyketides, alkaloids and non-ribosomal peptides: compounds harmful to human and animal health (Fig. 1). Hence, mycotoxins related to FHB in cereals include type A and B trichothecenes (terpenes), fusaric acid, zearalenone, zearalenol (polyketides) and cyclic peptides (see Fig. 1). Type A trichothecenes include T-2, HT-2 and diacetoxyscirpentriol (DAS) and are produced mainly by *F*. *langsethiae*, *F*. *sporotrichioides*, *F*. *poae* and *F*. *tricinctum*. Type B trichothecenes include deoxynivalenol (DON) and its acetylated forms 3-acetyldeoxynivalenol (3-ADON) and 15-acetyldeoxynivalenol (15-ADON) as well as nivalenol (NIV) and 4-acetylnivalenol (4-ANIV).

text: Type B trichothecenes present a ketone group (=0) at the C-8 position that is lacking in type A trichothecenes. The key enzyme in the terpene synthase pathway is TRI5 (trichodiene synthase) while TRI6 and TRI10 are the major biosynthetic pathway regulators. The type A or type B chemotype is species-specific. In both cases, these compounds inhibit protein synthesis by interfering with peptidyl transferase activity during mRNA translation initiation, polypeptide chain elongation, and chain termination. Ingestion of these compounds is associated with symptoms such as vomiting, abdominal pain and digestive-related disturbances in human and livestock. In severe cases, excessive exposure can lead to death. Fusaric acid and zearalenone (ZEN) are the main polyketide compounds produced during FHB infection. The enzyme PKS21 is responsible for fusaric acid synthesis biosynthesis, whereas PKS4 and PKS13 are responsible for zearalenone biosynthesis. In both humans and animals, fusaric acid is linked to neurotoxicity, immune suppression and gastrointestinal distress, while ZEN exerts estrogenic activity and interferes with the mammalian reproductive system. Some species within the FHB species complex produce non-ribosomal peptides in addition to trichothecenes and polyketides. Notable non-ribosomal peptides include beauvericin (BEA) and enniatins (ENs). The major effects linked to these compounds include cytotoxicity, immune suppression, neurotoxicity, and genotoxicity due to potential DNA damage. *F*. *avenacenum* and *F*.

The major effects linked to these compounds include cytotoxicity, immune suppression, neurotoxicity, and genotoxicity due to potential DNA damage. *F*. *avenacenum* and *F*. *tricinctum* produce moniliformin (MON) a sodium salt known to interfere with the cardiovascular system and energy metabolism in mammals. There are fewer studies with these mycotoxins compared to the trichothecenes. Throughout the infection process and during the colonization of the plant host, additional factors such as chitinases, cell-wall degrading enzymes and killer-toxin proteins are also produced. Environmental conditions and external stimuli modulate mycotoxins production in individual pathogen chemotypes. ### Diseases cycle of FHB ###
By convention, FHB disease cycle (Fig. 2) begins in early spring when rising temperatures and increasing humidity activate the saprophytic stage of the pathogen. Overwintering in crop residues, like straw or corn stubble, *Fusarium* hyphae resume growth, leading to the production of spores that can infect new plants. *Fusarium* spp. commonly produce asexual spores including macroconidia in sporodochia, microconidia on conidiophores, and chlamydospores within the hyphal compartments. *Fusarium graminearum*, with its teleomorph *Giberella zeae*, can also release sexual ascospores, which are produced in perithecia. ##### Fig. 2. #####

Fusarium head blight disease cycle on wheat. (1) Overwintering mycelia and chlamydospores resume saprophytic activity in early spring. (2) Depending on the causal agent, macroconidia, microconidia and ascospores (within perithecia) are produced as infection inoculum. (3) The inoculum reaches the plant host by rain splash or wind dispersal. The main factors for disease success are high temperature, high humidity, and the plant host at anthesis stage (see Fig. 3 for floret morphology). (4) After an initial pathogen growth phase, the interaction with the host begins, and first brownish stains appear at the base of the glumes (see Fig. 4 for molecular interactions between the pathogen and the host). (5) Infected plants are morphologically less vigorous and bleach rapidly. Reddish stains result from sporodochia production (evasion). (6) Infected seeds are contaminated with mycotoxins harmful to mammals. Additionally, they represent a further source of inoculum. (7) Seedling germinated from infected seeds. The inoculum primarily reaches the infection site in flowers through rain splash. The most critical phenological stage for the host is thus flowering, specifically anthesis (Fig. 3). On the host surface, macroconidia germinate within 6–12h post-inoculation. Initially, the pathogen increases mycelial growth and mycotoxin (trichothecene) production to facilitate infection. Initial growth occurs within the plant host’s apoplast, and no symptoms are visible. ##### Fig. 3. #####

*Fusarium* spp. utilize various pathogenicity factors, including fungal enzymes, cell wall-degrading enzymes (CWDEs), secreted effectors (host specific), and toxins (pathogen specific). The pathogenicity mechanisms are regulated by mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPKs) and cyclic adenosine monophosphate (CAMP pathways). The plant host response includes both a general and a more specific repertoire.

However, due to the considerable variation within this protein family, they can also contribute a more tailored response depending on the condition and pathogen involved. Thus, in barley, wheat, and oat, genes regulated by the salicylic acid pathway (SAR), encoding PR1, PR2 (β-1,3-glucanases) and PR3 (chitinases) are up-regulated during interactions with the pathogen. Similarly, WRKY transcription factors, specifically WRKY 23 and WRKY 70, are involved in interactions between the plant hosts (oat and wheat) and the pathogen (*F*. *graminearum*). Plants can also counteract pathogens using more specific tools such as detoxification enzymes. For instance, UDP-glucosyltransferase (UGTs) in wheat, barley, and oats, play a role in this process (Khairullina *et al*., 2022). If the pathogen succeeds, small brown spots appear at the base of the spikelet, and the plant tissues bleach. The pathogen then produces asexual spores and spikes exhibit pinkish to reddish stains. After crop harvest, the pathogen overwinters as residual mycelium or overwintering colonies.

### Biocontrol and molecular interactions between biocontrol agents (BCAs) and plants ###
Biological control (biocontrol) is a strategy used to manage plant and crop diseases. The term “biological” refers to the use of living organisms such as bacteria and fungi (viruses are included), in this approach. We refer to those as biological control (BCAs). The full biocontrol strategy is inextricably linked to three pillars: (1) biological control agents, (2) pests, and (3) human-related advantages (*e*. *g*., crops). This is a three-way interaction where the plant interacts with the BCA, and the pathogen, and all other possible combinations. The interaction between the plant and the pathogen has already been described above. As the plant host interacts with a beneficial organism, the result is either plant growth promotion or the induction of plant defence-related (DR) genes. In addition, the mode of action for BCAs can include competition for nutrients, the production of antimicrobial compounds by the BCA, mycoparasitism and induced resistance; these mechanisms can work in consort (Latz *et al*., 2018; Collinge *et al*., 2022). Here, we discuss only induced resistance, based on the induction of DR genes, as plant growth promotion is considered a sub-group of biostimulants, specifically biofertilizers. In plant growth promotion pillar 2, the pathogen is not involved. Many known and effective BCAs can establish endophytic relationships with the plant host and modulate the expression of genes related to its defence.
