text: In plant growth promotion pillar 2, the pathogen is not involved. Many known and effective BCAs can establish endophytic relationships with the plant host and modulate the expression of genes related to its defence. During the cross-talk between the plant and microorganisms, two kinds of signals are involved to activate plant receptors: microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs also termed as pathogen-associated molecular patterns – PAMPs – for pathogens) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). These molecular structures are recognized by the plant receptors and initiate the plant’s response. MAMPs include pathogen and beneficial microorganism structures, while DAMPs refer to the plant molecular structures resulting from physical damage during the interaction. MAMPs and DAMPs are involved in LAR first, and SAR later, activating the salicylic acid pathway. SAR and LAR are involved primarily during interactions with pathogens. BCAs release MAMPs and enhance the induce systemic resistance (ISR). This defence signalling pathway is based on jasmonic acid and ethylene. Whenever MAMPs are involved, this pathway is referred to as Pattern-Triggered Immunity (PTI) and plant-related receptor genes are pattern recognition receptor (PRR). Often, in three-way interactions, it is not possible to distinguish one response from another. Pathogenesis-related (PR) proteins are involved in all three cases: plant-pathogen, plant-BCA, and plant-pathogen-BCA interactions. Therefore, BCAs enhance a latent defence response, preparing plants to defend themselves when the pathogen eventually attacks. An interesting example concerns *Penicillium olsonii* ML37 on wheat spikes (Rojas *et al*., 2020a, b). *P*.

Among the various types of interaction between organisms, competition and parasitism are the primary strategies used by BCAs in their interactions with plant pathogens (Collinge *et al*., 2022). Competition can be categorized into two main types: exploitation and interference competition. Both result in a winner and a loser, with the difference lying in how victory is achieved. Exploitative competition involves the use of common resources (limiting factors), such as oxygen and carbon, which limits the competitors’ chance to survive. This type of competition does not need to occur simultaneously; two species can consume the same resource at two different times (*e*. *g*., day or night). Resources are reduced, but the competitors do not meet or interact directly. Interference competition, on the other hand, involves a more aggressive approach between the competitors (antibiosis, lytic enzymes, etc.).

Resources are reduced, but the competitors do not meet or interact directly. Interference competition, on the other hand, involves a more aggressive approach between the competitors (antibiosis, lytic enzymes, etc.). *Lactobacillus plantarum* SLG17 and *Bacillus amyloliquefaciens* FLN13 represent successful examples of interference competition. They can reduce the FHB index (in field), on wheat, presumably due to the production of antifungal compounds such as plantaricin (*L*. *plantarum* SLG17), mycosubtilin, fengcin, and surfactin (*B*. *amyloliquefaciens*). Parasitism requires both a predator and a prey (BCA and the pathogen). More specifically, in this case, parasitism is better defined as hyperparasitism because the prey simultaneously parasitizes the primary host. To this end, fungal BCAs produce morphological structures such as coiling, appressoria and papillae as demonstrated by the genera *Trichoderma* and *Clonostachys*. ### Case study *Trichoderma gamsii* T6085 on wheat and *Clonostachys rosea* IK726 on oat ###
At present, numerous lab-scale experiments are being conducted worldwide to identify effective biocontrol agents, with the immediate goal of moving to field trials. Unfortunately, the market does not progress at the same speed as research, mainly due to the lengthy registration process. Currently, Cedemon (*Pseudomonas chlororaphis* MA342) is registered and approved for seed treatment on cereals for Fusarium crown rot (FCR). This product is registered and marketed in several European countries including Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands.

### Overview ###
Yellow rust, caused by the pathogen *Puccinia striiformis*, is a biotrophic basidiomycete responsible for recurring disease outbreaks on wheat globally. This case study describes the epidemiology of yellow rust and the role of *P. striiformis* as a global pathogen. It also discusses the current disease control methods available and outlines future research within the field.

### Life cycle and symptoms ###
*P. striiformis* (causal organism of yellow rust) is an obligate biotroph with a complex life cycle consisting of five different spore stages on two botanically distinct plant hosts. The life cycle of yellow rust can be categorized into two stages: (1) the asexual stage taking place on the primary host (cereals and grasses) and (2) the sexual stage taking place on the alternate host (*Berberis* spp.). The sexual life stage of yellow rust was not discovered until 2010, when Jin *et al*. (2010) found that several *Berberis* species could serve as alternate hosts for yellow rust. Since then, more than 50 species of *Berberis* and *Mahonia aquifolium* (under controlled conditions) have been reported to be susceptible to the pathogen (Jin *et al. *, 2010; Wang, 2013; Mehmood *et al. *, 2020). The initial infection of wheat occurs when asexual, dikaryotic urediniospores are deposited on wheat leaf surfaces by wind or raindrops. The urediniospores germinate on the leaf surface and develop a dikaryotic germ tube that penetrates the wheat stoma and subsequently forms infection hyphae inside the leaf, and develops specialized infection structures called haustoria that take up nutrients from infected host cells (Kang *et al. *, 2017). The infection on adult susceptible wheat leaves will be visible 10–18 days after infection, when the wheat epidermal cells break, revealing yellow to orange urediniospores erupting from uredinia (Fig. 1d–e), which are arranged in characteristic stripes along the veins of the leaves (Fig.

On younger wheat plants and seedlings, uredinia often appear individually or seemingly more at random. On resistant or partially resistant host plants, symptoms will vary from tiny flecks of chlorosis to larger chlorotic/necrotic areas with or without pustules (Fig. 2a). ##### Fig. 1. #####

The asexual cycle of yellow rust is often repeated during the growing season and can lead to wide-scale epidemics in areas with susceptible wheat cultivars. Towards the end of the wheat growing season, when the plants begin to senescence, yellow rust may begin to produce two-celled, diploid teliospores that are dark brown to black (Fig. 2b). When the teliospores germinate, each cell produces a basidium that carries four haploid basidiospores (Fig. 1g) (Liu and Hambleton, 2010). The basidiospores may infect the alternate host, resulting in the production of pycnia, containing haploid pycniospores, on the adaxial side of the leaves. Ultimately, pycniospores will mate with receptive hyphae of another pycnium and develop a mycelium inside the leaf that forms dikaryotic aeciospores capable of infecting the primary host (wheat) and thus complete the life cycle. Direct evidence of sexual reproduction in yellow rust in nature has, so far, only been found in China; however, it is hypothesized that sexual reproduction occurs in the Himalayas (Nepal and Pakistan) or near-Himalaya regions (China), with yellow rust populations in these areas having a high genetic diversity, recombinant population structures and high sexual reproduction abilities (Zhao *et al. *, 2013; Ali *et al. *, 2014; Cheng *et al. *, 2022; Du *et al. *, 2023).

Meanwhile, yellow rust populations in Europe, the Americas and Australia have been characterized previously by their clonal population structures, in which the evolution of virulences is largely shaped by single-step mutations and potentially somatic hybridization (Hovmøller *et al. *, 2016; Ding *et al. *, 2021; Bouvet *et al*., 2022). ### Global dispersion ###
In the past, yellow rust was primarily an issue in cool climates, such as Northern Europe and North America; however, the emergence of new aggressive isolates, adapted to warmer temperatures led to the disease spreading to all wheat-growing areas in the world (Milus *et al. *, 2009; Hovmøller *et al. *, 2023). The pathogen’s international success can be attributed to several factors, one of these being its ability to adapt rapidly via genetic changes, gained through random mutation, selection pressure, sexual recombination or somatic hybridization (Ding *et al*., 2021). Moreover, the capacity for long-distance migration by urediniospores allows the pathogen to spread between countries, overcome plant resistance and cause recurring local disease outbreaks around the world. Urediniospores of the yellow rust pathogen have been found to travel up to 1700 km with prevailing winds, enabling migration between continents (Bouvet *et al*., 2022). While yellow rust has been known in Europe and Asia for hundreds of years, it was not found in North America before the Danish plant pathologist Kølpin Ravn recognized the disease during a visit with the United States Department of Agriculture crop survey team in 1915 (Kang *et al*., 2017).

text: Moreover, yellow rust did not appear in Australia before 1978, where the sudden incursion has been proposed to be the result of an accidental introduction of the disease by travellers carrying urediniospores from Europe to Australia on their clothing (O’Brien *et al. *, 1980). Likewise, yellow rust emerged for the first time ever in South Africa in 1996, causing epidemic outbreaks throughout most of the wheat-producing areas of the country (Pretorius *et al*., 1997). It has since been suggested that the disease spread from West or Central Asia, causing this first ever epidemic in South Africa (Hovmøller *et al. *, 2008; Hovmøller *et al*., 2023). In addition to the colonization of previously unaffected areas of the world, the long-distance migration capabilities of yellow rust spores have enabled the incursion of exotic races into local populations, which further contributes to the shaping of yellow rust populations. A shining example of the role of exotic incursions on the local population dynamics of yellow rust can be seen in the incursions of the PstS1 genetic group into North America and Australia and closely related PstS2 genetic group into Europe in the early 2000s (Hovmøller *et al*., 2023). Further examples can be seen specifically in Europe, where the genetic groups PstS7 and PstS8, first observed in 2011, replaced the pre-existing population of yellow rust in Europe in the course of a few years (Hovmøller *et al*., 2023). These two genetic groups are assumed to have origin in the Himalayan regions (Hovmøller *et al*. 2016), which is considered the centre of diversity and where sexual recombination seems to also be involved in the shaping of yellow rust populations (Ali *et al*., 2014).

### Plant resistance ###
Plant resistance breeding is one of the main disease control methods against yellow rust and the use of resistant cultivars is often considered safer, more compatible with other control strategies and environmentally friendly, compared to the use of fungicides. However, the evolutionary arms race that takes place between newly developed resistant wheat varieties and yellow rust puts pressure on researchers to improve the durability and level of resistance in new varieties. This is largely because of the emergence of new virulent races, that can result in resistant cultivars losing their resistance, leading to large yield losses (Chen, 2020). When it comes to breeding strategies against yellow rust, there are several different types of resistance in wheat used against yellow rust. The two most common types of plant resistance are all-stage resistance (ASR), and adult-plant resistance (APR) (Chen, 2020). ASR can be detected already in the seedling stage and is present through all growth stages, characterized by a hypersensitive response (Wang and Chen, 2017). ASR follows the gene-for-gene hypothesis developed by Flor (1971), which describes that for each R gene present in the host plant, there will be a corresponding avirulence gene in the pathogen. The result of an interaction between the products of the two corresponding genes is a qualitative resistance that is easily recognizable and relatively race-specific, which has made ASR a popular trait for selection in major breeding programs (Bouvet *et al*., 2022). However, the genes involved in ASR are usually race-specific and are easily overcome by new virulent races of yellow rust, examples of which have been seen in ASR genes such as *Yr2*, *Yr9*, *Yr17* and *Yr27* (Bayles *et al.

In the case of APR, on the other hand, plants are susceptible in the seedling stage and are characterized by slow rusting or partial resistance manifesting at the adult plant stages (Wang and Chen, 2017; Bouvet *et al*., 2022). APR genes are generally believed to protect plants from a wide range of pathogen species. Examples of this can be seen in *Yr18/Lr34/Sr67/Pm38* and *Yr46/Lr67/Sr55/Pm46*, whch are effective against yellow rust, leaf rust, stem rust and powdery mildew (Bouvet *et al*., 2022). APR is considered non-race-specific, although exceptions do exist (Sørensen *et al*., 2013; Dinglasan *et al*., 2022). Because APR has a broad-spectrum effect and results in partial resistance, APR genes are considered more durable than ASR genes, since they evoke a lower selection pressure. While the desire to use APR genes in breeding programs has been high, its use has been limited because of the lack of linked molecular markers to support selection, as well as poor knowledge of the gene’s phenotypic effects, gene interactions, environmental stability and genetic background effects (Dinglasan *et al*., 2022). Because of this, efforts are being put into combining ASR and APR to create cultivars with long-lasting and high-level resistance.

Because of this, efforts are being put into combining ASR and APR to create cultivars with long-lasting and high-level resistance. As of now, over 300 quantitative trait loci (QTL) conferring yellow rust resistance have been reported, with around 80 of these being permanently named as yellow rust resistance genes and further 63 designated as temporarily designated resistance genes (Bouvet *et al*., 2022). Most of these are useful in breeding and many have markers developed for marker-assisted selection; however, the continued investigation of resistance genes and QTLs is essential for the future breeding of resistance cultivars control of Pst (Chen, 2020). ### Chemical control ###
Although yellow rust is generally effectively controlled by the use of resistant cultivars, the incursion of new, aggressive strains of yellow rust to various areas globally has overcome many of the long-standing resistance genes and put pressure on farmers, breeders and scientists. Because of this, proper disease monitoring and early warning systems are highly important to alert farmers of new threats. In situations where there is a lack of resistance to wheat cultivars, yellow rust management becomes highly dependent on the use of chemical fungicides. Since the development of systemic fungicides in the 1970s, a wide variety of diverse products with different modes of action have been available for protection against yellow rust on wheat. In general, three classes of fungicides are currently used to control yellow rust on wheat, these being demethylation inhibitors (DMI, FRAC group 3), quinone outside inhibitors (QoI, FRAC code 11) and succinate dehydrogenase inhibitors (SDHI, FRAC code 7) (Carmona *et al. *, 2020; Cook *et al. *, 2021).

(2020) for a list of the most frequently used fungicides to control yellow rust. It has long been the common perception that most species of the Pucciniales have all been well-controlled with fungicides under field conditions, all belonging to the lowest risk category in regard to fungicide resistance development (Brent and Hollomon, 2007). However, mutations conferring resistance to the three fungicidal classes DMI, QoI and SDHI have been discovered in the Asian soybean rust pathogen *Phakopsora pachyrhizi*, which have been linked to the high-intensity use of fungicides in South America (Cook *et al*., 2021). Moreover, a study by Cook *et al*. (2021), which screened 363 isolates of *Puccinia striiformis* f.sp. *tritici,* found mutations with the potential to compromise the efficacy of DMI and SDHI fungicides. This highlights the importance of a diverse management strategy against yellow rust, as well as the application of the precautionary principle in the use of fungicides against yellow rust. ### Cultural practices ###
In addition to the use of resistant cultivars and chemical control, yellow rust can be further controlled by the application of proper cultural practices. Farmers can reduce disease pressure from year to year by reducing volunteer plants on and around the fields, on which the pathogen may survive the winter and provide inoculum for the following year (Chen and Kang, 2017).

text: Farmers can reduce disease pressure from year to year by reducing volunteer plants on and around the fields, on which the pathogen may survive the winter and provide inoculum for the following year (Chen and Kang, 2017). Furthermore, the use of cultivar mixtures to decrease spread of disease and proper management of irrigation to reduce moisture in the field can lead to an overall decrease in the severity of yellow rust epidemics. Moreover, an appropriate timing of sowing is also of importance in the defence against yellow rust. Early sowing of winter wheat can increase the chances of infection during Autumn providing inoculum for further infection in the next season (Chen and Kang, 2017). Therefore, the general recommendation for winter wheat is late planting as far as possible. Meanwhile, the cultivation of spring wheat is highly dependent on the weather conditions and the optimal time for sowing should be determined based on the region and weather conditions. An integrated disease control strategy with a strong cultural practice that is revised on a yearly basis depending on the resources available, the local environment and weather conditions is instrumental in the sustainable disease control of yellow rust.

text: 1. Continued monitoring of yellow rust is of the utmost importance, especially considering the recent tendencies of exotic incursions, in order to increase local preparedness for new disease outbreaks and for the evaluation of evolution of virulence in yellow rust populations around the world. Moreover, a strengthening of global collaboration for early-warning systems would be highly beneficial, especially in areas with limited use of resistant cultivars. 2. Further research in resistance breeding against yellow rust in order to develop more durable and high-level resistant cultivars is needed. The identification and cloning of novel resistance genes, as well as the investigation of the combination and pyramiding of ASR and APR genes, would be highly useful in future breeding programs for the development of long-lasting resistance in new wheat cultivars. 3. Future research into the development of the evolution of fungicide resistance in yellow rust, as well as fungicide resistance monitoring is crucial to ensure the use of current fungicides and their efficacy. Furthermore, research and innovation in fungicide application technology is needed to allow a more timely, accurate and efficient application of fungicides.

title: 'A Global Threat: Epidemiology and Management of Yellow Rust on Wheat'
text: While yellow rust is a long-studied disease, known to mankind for many years, the pathogen remains a threat to the global wheat-growing community due to its capacity for long-distance migration and rapid adaptation to new environmental conditions and host resistance. Continued research in the virulence of yellow rust, novel resistance genes and the development of resistant cultivars, as well as global disease monitoring is important in order to reduce future yellow rust epidemics.

### Overview ###
Crown gall disease causes tumors on plants like stone fruit trees, grapevines, and roses, leading to significant economic losses. Agrobacteria, common soil bacteria, induce tumors after acquiring the Ti plasmid. Climate change influences outbreaks. Effective control requires analyzing pathogenic and non-pathogenic agrobacteria due to Ti plasmid transmission.

title: 'Crown Gall Disease: A Growing Threat to Fruit Tree Health and Productivity
text: Agriculture and food security are highly vulnerable to climate change. Unpredictable variations in weather conditions such as changing rainfall patterns, heat waves, droughts, and floods affect crop yields dramatically. Scientific evidence has particularly identified plant health issues related to climate change. As abiotic conditions undergo changes, pathogens respond with evolutionary adaptation to novel environments that may lead to the emergence of new diseases or recurrent outbreaks of previously controlled ones. Furthermore, variation in weather conditions impacts plant immune system, and therefore, affects host susceptibility to pathogens and pests (Roussin-Léveillée *et al*., 2024). Mediterranean agriculture is not exempt from the impact of climate change. In contrast, agricultural systems in the region are continuously experiencing challenging phytosanitary concerns related to climate change. For instance, *Xylella fastidiosa*, historically known as an endophytic bacterium native to Central America, has been detected recently in Italy, where it was responsible for the rapid decline in olive tree plantations (Morelli *et al*., 2021). Since then, *X fastidiosa* has officially been described as a source of worldwide concern due to global warming (Godefroid *et al*., 2019). Although intensive national and international actions have been undertaken by various organizations, the disease has, at least in part, been prevented from establishing in the Near East and North Africa (NENA) countries—despite favorable weather conditions, frequent trade, and the high prevalence of olive orchards and insect vectors (Bouri *et al*., 2023). Several serious diseases are threatening olive trees and other fruit trees in North Africa. Crown gall is one of the most serious diseases affecting nursery production of fruit trees in the region. Once infected, the plant continues to develop galls although the pathogen is no longer present.

title: 'Crown Gall Disease: A Growing Threat to Fruit Tree Health and Productivity
text: Crown gall is one of the most serious diseases affecting nursery production of fruit trees in the region. Once infected, the plant continues to develop galls although the pathogen is no longer present. Therefore, prophylactic solutions, based mainly on early detection of the disease for pathogen-free nurseries and pathogen-free rootstocks, are highly recommended for successful crown gall control. Efficient diagnosis may require very specific and accurate identification tools at the molecular level. This can be achieved only in the presence of a solid knowledge about the genetic diversity of the pathogen communities in relevant biotopes. The relevance of studying crown gall in North Africa is twofold. First, the disease has shown a troubling recent emergence in this region, especially in crops like grapevines and stone fruit trees. Second, climate change may be altering the distribution and aggressiveness of the pathogen, as warmer temperatures, increased humidity in nurseries, and shifting agricultural zones create more favorable environments for disease establishment. Despite the global significance of crown gall disease, the North African context presents distinct challenges – such as fragmented surveillance systems, underreported outbreaks, and limited region-specific data – that demand focused investigation. This document presents an overview for past and current situation for crown gall in North Africa. Insightful information are collected from several studies that have been conducted in the region over the last few decades in order to discuss the state of the art about this disease in the context of climate change, identify critical knowledge gaps, and highlight urgent research priorities for sustainable disease control.

section: Rootstocks Production Worldwide and Crown Galls
text: Crown gall causes important economic losses both in nurseries and orchards. Therefore, crown gall disease is challenging for both growers and nursery owners worldwide. The disease is of a particular economic importance in pome, stone fruits, and grapes sectors. Global stone fruits production has almost reached 615.7 thousand metric tons in 2022 (Shahbandeh, 2024). The worldwide total value of pome fruit production amounts to more than 83.7 million tons, while the almond production was estimated at 1.45 Million (USDA, 2024). The disease threat to stone and pome fruit trees is particularly observed on their corresponding rootstocks: GF677, Myrobolan and Garnem. Garnem was the most susceptible, Myrobolan was moderately susceptible and GF 677 was the least susceptible to crown gall disease infection (Horuz *et al*., 2018). Global table grape production was estimated at 28.09 million metric tons this year. Among North African countries, Egypt, with 6% of the total production value, is ranked sixth world producer (USDA, 2024). These crops – particularly stone fruits and grapes – play a critical role in the agricultural economies of several North African countries, contributing substantially to export earnings, employment, and rural livelihoods. For instance, grapes are the second largest fruit crop in Egypt, with a volume of 73.67 thousand tons as an average of exportation for the period 2008–2018 (Abd El Menem *et al*., 2022). Consequently, any factor threatening the viability of these sectors, such as crown gall disease, has direct implications for food security, economic stability, and farmer resilience in the region.

title: 'Crown Gall Disease: A Growing Threat to Fruit Tree Health and Productivity
text: Although the isolation of the crown gall disease was first reported from grapevines in Naples, Italy (1897) by Fridiano Cavara and was named *Bacterium tumefaciens* (Bergey *et al*., 1923), the first scientific description of galls on grapevines is attributed to Fabre and Dunal. The origin of the disease is believed to date to biblical times on trees and grapevines galls or nodules (Lacroix and Citovsky, 2013). In 1907, the name was changed to *Phytomonas tumefaciens* (Smith & Townsend). Later on, the crown gall disease has been described on fruit trees (mainly apple and stone fruit trees) and the name of the causal agent was changed to *Agrobacterium tumefaciens* (Smith and Townsend, 1907). Several other names have been applied to this phytopathogen that caused the disease wherever grapevines and woody crops were cultivated. By the late 1940s, the discovery of the tumor-inducing factor (extrachromosomal element termed the Ti plasmid) launched plant genetic engineering with *A. tumefaciens* (Kado, 2014). This inter-kingdom transfer from bacteria to plants occurs via a type IV secretion system (T4SS) (Gelvin, 2010; Lacroix and Citovsky, 2013). Agrobacteria are also using some other genes which are involved in the catabolism of opines, to assist the infection by the T-DNA and bacterium/bacterium conjugation-mediated plasmid transfer (Bhatia and Bera, 2015). Once the T-DNA is integrated into the plant genome, an overproduction of the plant hormones auxin and cytokinin is lunched and overgrowths on the infection site are resulted.

Although artificial inoculations could reproduce galls on at least 643 different plan species (De Cleene and De Ley, 1976), the number of naturally susceptible plants to crown gall agents is still much lower (Fig. 1). ##### Fig. 1. #####

Looking at the chronological history of this disease, from the finding and isolation to the revolutionary research in modern technology of plant transformation, agrobacteria responsible for crown gall are unusual pathogens. They could develop methods enhancing its pathogenicity to overcome host’s defences and microbial competitors along millions years of co-evolutionary process. Although pioneering molecular research has turned crown gall pathogens into a useful tool in plant transformation, the disease continues to be responsible for serious economic losses around the world.

title: 'Crown Gall Disease: A Growing Threat to Fruit Tree Health and Productivity
text:
Crown gall disease, caused primarily by *A. tumefaciens* (now reclassified into several species within the *Rhizobium* genus), follows a unique disease cycle that involves both biological and environmental factors. The cycle includes several key stages (Fig. 2). The cycle begins when the bacterium enters the plant through fresh wounds caused by grafting, pruning, insect feeding, or mechanical injury. Upon entry, the bacterium transfers a segment of its tumor-inducing (Ti) plasmid DNA (T-DNA) into the genome of the plant cell, triggering uncontrolled cell division through the production of auxins and cytokinins (Gelvin, 2010). This results in the formation of characteristic galls, typically at the crown or root zone of the plant. These galls interfere with water and nutrient uptake, reducing plant vigor and productivity. As the gall tissues decay, agrobacteria can be released into the surrounding soil, where it can survive saprophytically for many years, particularly in moist nursery environments (Krimi *et al*., 2002). Dissemination of the pathogen occurs via infected planting material, contaminated tools, soil, irrigation water, or even through insect vectors that cause fresh wounds. The disease is often difficult to eradicate because of the pathogen’s long-term survival in soil and the asymptomatic nature of infected nursery stock, making clean propagation material and resistant rootstocks essential for effective management. ##### Fig. 2. #####
Crown gall disease cycle. Host susceptibility, particularly at the rootstock level, plays a key role in the epidemiology of crown gall. Susceptibility varies widely across genotypes, influencing the severity of outbreaks, especially in nursery settings where infection conditions are optimal.

section: Where Does Crown Gall Disease Occur in North Africa?
text:
Crown gall disease is believed to be particularly serious in Mediterranean countries due mainly to climate conditions. In North Africa, the presence of crown gall disease is reported with restricted distribution according to the EPPO (2024). The most affected crops are stone fruit trees, grapevines and roses. Although tumorigenic agrobacteria were first isolated from grapevine galls in 1897 in Europe (Cavara, 1897a,b), the disease on grapevines was only recently observed in the region; Morocco in 2008 (Habbadi *et al*., 2019); Egypt in 2011 (Tolba and Zaki, 2011) Tunisia in 2011, (Abdellatif *et al*., 2013) (Fig. 3). ##### Fig. 3. #####
Symptoms of Crown gall on grapevine detected in the region of Regueb, Tunisia: A – on young grapevine, B – on old grapevine. This relatively recent emergence suggests a shifting dynamic in disease epidemiology, possibly influenced by climate change and increased trade of propagation material, which may have introduced the pathogen into new environments or amplified its impact in previously low-risk areas. Although the disease is typically detected in vineyards and nurseries, its incidence has been rarely observed in these countries. In fact, culture conditions of temperature and humidity in nurseries are known to be favorable for the development of the pathogen. Moreover, agricultural intensification and high-density nursery production create microenvironments that promote infection and pathogen persistence. Typically, crown gall disease occurs sporadically in every province or state where susceptible crops are grown. Additionally, some soils can facilitate the persistence of tumorigenic agrobacteria for decades and so that they become unsuitable for susceptible cultures (Krimi *et al*., 2002).

title: 'Crown Gall Disease: A Growing Threat to Fruit Tree Health and Productivity
section: Where Does Crown Gall Disease Occur in North Africa?
text: Additionally, some soils can facilitate the persistence of tumorigenic agrobacteria for decades and so that they become unsuitable for susceptible cultures (Krimi *et al*., 2002). For instance, in Morocco, the area of Meknes where the majority of stone fruit nurseries are located, the crown gall disease is considered a serious threat (Boulif, 2016). In Tunisia, nurseries in the region of Ouerdanine were characterized by recurrent attacks of the disease which made the production of the rootstock GF677 impossible (Rhouma *et al*., 2005). While empirical evidence specifically linking climate change to crown gall in North Africa is still limited, studies have shown that climate factors such as temperature and water stress can influence the incidence and severity of various plant diseases. We believe that shifts in rainfall and soil moisture levels may influence the availability of water in the soil, affecting plant susceptibility to crown gall disease and bacterial infection rates. Additionally, changing climatic conditions can lead to the disruption of ecosystems, altering the types of plants that are prevalent in certain regions. This could affect the host range for pathogenic agrobacteria and lead to the emergence of crown gall in new geographic areas. For example, crops that are more tolerant to drought may become more dominant in regions that experience reduced rainfall, potentially creating environments where crown gall is more likely to take hold. Given the sensitivity of the North African climate and the potential for these changes to affect crown gall disease dynamics, further research is needed to fully understand the relationship between climate change and this disease in the region. text:
Although serious initiatives have been conducted in several countries of the region for the control of the disease as an ultimate objective, scientific studies on crown gall are still considered fragmentary and far from reflecting the importance of the disease in North Africa. According to this systematic review, there is a serious lack of data from Libya has been recorded. Except some recent works from Morocco and Tunisia, the current situation of the crown gall disease in North African countries is still far from reporting accurate information related to climate change (Fig. 4). This contrasts with the more extensive literature available from Europe, North America, and parts of Asia. Stone fruits and grapevines are economically critical crops in North Africa, often cultivated in areas already constrained by limited arable land, water scarcity, and energy challenges. In contrast to areas where crown gall has been long-established, well-documented, and effectively managed, the relative lack of regional research and knowledge in North Africa highlights a critical gap. In this context, the economic consequences of crown gall disease may be disproportionately severe compared to regions with more diversified or industrialized agricultural systems. This underscores the urgent need for a focused, locally-informed understanding of the disease to develop prevention and control strategies that are both regionally relevant and responsive to the unique environmental and agricultural constraints of the area. ##### Fig. 4. #####

text: Agrobacteria commonly inhabit soils and in their avirulent form can exhibit beneficial rhizospheric relationship with plants mainly through their capacity to produce phytohormones as noted by Hao *et al*. (2012). However, in the presence of the tumor-inducing (Ti) plasmid, agrobacteria become tumorigenic and can induce tumor growth once they precede successful transfer of their specific DNA fragment (T-DNA) to the host-plant. Crown gall disease occurs worldwide and affects a large number of both woody and herbaceous plants. Infected soils with pathogenic bacteria can rend nurseries inadequate for susceptible plantations. Consequently, maintaining plant stock nurseries free of crown gall-affected plants and prophylactic culturing practices is of ultimate importance. Members of the rose family are considered to be the most susceptible host. Almond, apple, apricot, euonymus, fig, grape, peach, pecan, plum, walnut, and willow are the common woody hosts of this disease. However, almost 140 genera of woody and herbaceous plants belonging to more than 60 families are reported to be susceptible to crown gall disease. Pathogenic agrobacteria are the most interesting gall-inducing disease as they have the widest host range of any phytopathogen. The disease is responsible of important annual losses due to unmarketable symptomatic rootstocks, low productivity of galled trees, and vulnerability of infected plants to biotic and abiotic stresses (Bliss *et al*., 1999). With time, tumors enlarge, become convoluted, and dark brown colored (Agrios, 2005). Therefore, the disease is more fatal on young trees. Severe infection can cause plant death. Poor growth and reduced yield are the main consequences of the disease as galls can obstruct the water and nutrients uptake.

title: 'Crown Gall Disease: A Growing Threat to Fruit Tree Health and Productivity
text: Therefore, the disease is more fatal on young trees. Severe infection can cause plant death. Poor growth and reduced yield are the main consequences of the disease as galls can obstruct the water and nutrients uptake. For instance, infected grape plants show vigor and yield reduction by up to 40% depending on the infection degree (Schroth *et al*., 1988). Crown gall disease is believed to be a growing concern, particularly in the context of nursery production and climate change, in Mediterranean countries and North Africa. Although the disease is still making losses in crop productions, there is a very little information about the real damage caused by the crown gall in the Maghreb region. According to previous studies: in Algeria, symptoms have been detected in 99% of nurseries, whereas in Morocco crown gall affected 15–20% of young plants, with 80% in some regions (Benjama *et al*., 2002), and in Tunisia, the infection rate reached 30% (Boubaker, 1999). Quarantine restrictions have been applied to crown gall disease in North African countries for years. The previously called *A. tumefaciens* and *R. rhizogenes* have figured in the quarantine A2 list before to be removed recently, given the ubiquitous nature of the disease throughout the world (EPPO, 2024).

title: 'Crown Gall Disease: A Growing Threat to Fruit Tree Health and Productivity
text: Although the causal agent of the crown gall is traditionally identified as *A. tumefaciens*, there is a large disagreement about the pathogen name. The nomenclature of *Agrobacterium* species is still controversial even at the genus level. For instance, *A. tumefaciens* (earlier designated Biovar 1) is now recognized as species complex, consisting of several genomospecies. To avoid ambiguity in agrobacteria’s taxonomy, we will refer, in this chapter, to the new genus classification proposed by Lindström and Young (2011) and Mousavi *et al*. (2014, 2015), which excluded both Biovar 2 and Biovar 3 from the genus *Agrobacterium* and delineated them to *Rhizobium rhizogenes* and *Allorhizobium vitis,* respectively. Moreover, we will focus on the most reported species in North Africa, which are: *A. tumefaciens* complex species*, Al. vitis* and *A. rubi* main phytopathogenic agents of stone fruit trees, grapevine and roses, respectively. The tumor inducing plasmid Ti is transferred by pathogenic agrobacteria to plants via a type IV secretion system (T4SS) (Gelvin, 2010; Lacroix and Citovsky, 2013). Plant hormones auxin and cytokinin are overproduced once the T-DNA is integrated into the plant genome. Subsequently, overgrowths on the infection site appear. Additionally, secondary tumors at different distance from the primary tumor can be observed once expanding tissues are infected. Therefore, infected plant tissues are the primarily vectors of crown gall. Crown gall bacteria enter plant roots through wounds. Wounds and injuries are the first infiltration point of pathogenic bacteria to plant tissues.

title: 'Crown Gall Disease: A Growing Threat to Fruit Tree Health and Productivity
text: Therefore, infected plant tissues are the primarily vectors of crown gall. Crown gall bacteria enter plant roots through wounds. Wounds and injuries are the first infiltration point of pathogenic bacteria to plant tissues. Plant tissues damages can be created by biotic factors such as soil insect feeding or by physical factors such as rain splashed. Some cultural practices, like root pruning, grafting and excavation, can also spread the disease. Although root pruning of rootstocks is commonly used prior to transplantation, the resulted wounds from this routine practice facilitate infection with tumorigenic agrobacteria inhabiting the soil (Lacroix and Citovsky, 2013). Bacteria can return to the soil, the main natural reservoir of the disease, from contaminated areal parts by water or equipment. Pathogenic bacteria can survive in soil for years, infect other roots and spread the plasmid Ti into other telluric agrobacteria.

text:
The infection of plants by pathogenic agrobacteria is irreversible. Once the T-DNA is transferred to the plant genome, the gall growth will continue even if agrobacteria are removed. Therefore, prevention is the foundation for crown gall control (Fig. 5). ##### Fig. 5. #####
Crown gall management strategy. ### Detection techniques ###
An early detection of pathogenic agrobacteria in plants or soil of nurseries and fields is very critical to avoid the propagation of the disease and the contamination of new areas. Small galls require careful diagnosis because they may be confused with excessive wound callus. Nonpathogenic Agrobacterium cells are often prevalent in soil and their presence in high population in galls can make diagnosis difficult (Bouri *et al*., 2016). Nowadays, Thanks to new developed molecular methods specific to plasmids and different species of agrobacteria, the detection of crown gall disease is made easier and more reliable even in symptomless samples (Shams *et al*., 2013). ### Cultural practices ###
Good sanitation and cultural practices are very important to prevent the establishment of crown gall disease by avoiding the introduction of pathogenic agrobacteria at all production stages of plantations. In the case of crown gall disease detection, unfortunately the best action is to remove and destroy the infected plants to avoid contaminating healthy ones. Since pathogenic agrobacteria can persist in the soil for years after the plant is gone, it is recommended to avoid planting susceptible species to deprive pathogens from their host plants. Moreover, control of root-attacking insects and nematodes should be performed and, hygiene is needed for pruning equipment, and wounding of plants should be avoided in infected fields.

Even though to be promising, heat therapy soil fumigation and solarization (Fig. 6) are not commonly used due to many difficulties (Pu and Goodman, 1993; Pinkerton *et al*., 1996). ##### Fig. 6. #####
Assay of solarization technique to reduce pathogenic population of agrobacteria in the soil. Experimental station of Olive institute, Sfax, Tunisia (2018). #### Biological control ####
*A. radiobacter* K84 and its genetically engineered strain called K1026 are currently commercialized for the biological control of the disease. These two strains are recognized as very effective agents against crown gall on a number of hosts, with some limitations. In fact, not all strains of tumorigenic agrobacteria are sensitive to agrocin (the toxin of K84). Moreover, transfer of the agrocin plasmid from K48 to pathogenic agrobacteria can make them in turn resistant. Therefore, K1026 strain was engineered to minimize the breakdown of the K84 control. Although K1026 is not able to transfer the agrocin plasmid to other agrobacteria, the use of this genetic modified strain is still rejected by GMO’s (genetically modified organism) protesters. It is very important to note here that biological control can only be used as preventive and not curative alternative, and the timing of the application is critical to efficiently protect wounded plants during harvest or pruning.

text:
It is very important to note here that biological control can only be used as preventive and not curative alternative, and the timing of the application is critical to efficiently protect wounded plants during harvest or pruning. Obviously K84 and K1026 are the most common strains used in the control of the crown gall disease, but many studies reported several *Bacillus* strains that have controlled the disease as effectively as the commercial strains (Rhouma *et al*., 2008; Ben Gharsa *et al*., 2021). Several studies have been reported the efficiency of some biological alternatives for the control of the disease in North Africa (Table 1). Recent studies have explored the use of bacteriophages as a promising biocontrol method against *Rhizobium radiobacter* (formerly *A. tumefaciens*) (Ramadhan *et al*., 2022; Chantapakul *et al*., 2024. These findings highlight bacteriophages as an environmentally friendly and targeted alternative to commercial treatments. #### Chemical control ####
Currently, no chemical that can effectively control crown gall has been registered. #### Rootstocks trade and policies ####
With the increase in commercial exchanges of nursery plant material, the spread of crown gall disease started to take an epidemic aspect. Although tumorigenic agrobacteria are considered as quality pathogens according to the European Union regulations, in some North African countries they are vigorously controlled by national regulations. In Tunisia, the importation of rootstocks is under strict sanitary controls: visible tumors must not exceed 1% in nursery plant material for trading authorization (Anon, 1981). Accordingly, the sanitary status of Tunisian nurseries was likely improved 20 years after the decree (Rhouma *et al*., 2008).

In Morocco, due to recent detection of the crown gall disease in vineyards, the importation of grapevine rootstocks was officially regulated by several phytosanitary requirements; the plant material must (i) show no symptoms, (ii) be produced in crown gall free regions, and (ii) have an analysis certification according to standard methods (Anon, 2018).

section: Future Research Areas to Improve Crown Gall Disease Control
text: An epidemiological survey of crown gall requires a specific determination of the *Agrobacterium* taxonomy. Although the causal agent of the crown gall is traditionally identified as *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*, there is a large disagreement about the pathogen name. The nomenclature of *Agrobacterium* species is still controversial even at the genus level. A set of biochemical and molecular methods has been set up to facilitate the taxonomic assessment of agrobacteria either in pure culture or directly from soils, rhizospheres or/and tumors. The INCO-DC European program ERBIC18CT970198, “Integrated Control of Crown Gall in Mediterranean Countries” presented a simple and efficient identification scheme for agrobacteria based on simple and fast urease and/or esculinase biochemical tests. Nevertheless, the detection of pathogenic *Agrobacterium* in complex environments without prior strain isolation can still be easily done by PCR using primers designed in the conserved vir region. The identification of the agrobacteria’s species and genomospecies present in the soil or galls is also possible directly by specific primers (Shams *et al*., 2012). A better disease management of crown gall can be achieved only with exhaustive investigations to afford large data about the genetic diversity of the agrobacteria populations upon huge variety of soils and plants. Non-pathogenic agrobacteria should not be excluded from any epidemiological study as they can become pathogenic after Ti plasmids transfer and subsequently can induce tumors and participate in the outbreak of the disease.

section: Future Research Areas to Improve Crown Gall Disease Control
text: Non-pathogenic agrobacteria should not be excluded from any epidemiological study as they can become pathogenic after Ti plasmids transfer and subsequently can induce tumors and participate in the outbreak of the disease. Moreover, future research could explore the potential of biotechnological tools such as RNA interference (RNAi), including host-induced gene silencing (HIGS), to suppress key virulence genes in *Agrobacterium*, such as those involved in hormone synthesis or opine catabolism. Early studies have shown promising results using RNAi constructs targeting oncogenes like iaaM and ipt (Escobar *et al*., 2001), offering a potential path toward durable, genetically based resistance strategies. In summary, understanding the interplay between the crown gall disease and shifting climate dynamics is crucial for sustainable crop production in North Africa, especially given the region’s growing agricultural vulnerability and increasingly unpredictable weather patterns. Therefore, it is imperative to expand monitoring and surveillance efforts, and to develop region-specific predictive models that integrate climate and disease data. Strengthening collaboration across the region is essential for integrated disease management. Additionally, investments in the promotion of biocontrol and soil management strategies that enhance microbial diversity antagonistic to *Agrobacterium*, are key to sustainable crown gall control.

### Overview ###
Basal stem rot (BSR) disease, caused by *Ganoderma boninense*, is an important disease in oil palm production worldwide, including in Indonesia. In Indonesia, the incidence of the disease continues to increase year after year; however, there is no a truly effective control for long-term management.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: 1. Summarize the history of oil palm and the occurrence of basal stem rot in Indonesia, and explain the economic impact of BSR disease on the oil palm industry in Indonesia. 2. Recognize the characteristics of major *Ganoderma* species, the causal pathogen of BSR, that infect oil palm trees in Indonesia. 3. Compare and recommend the integrated disease management strategies to reduce the development of BSR disease.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: Basal stem rot (BSR) disease, primarily caused by *Ganoderma boninense*, poses the greatest threat to sustainable oil palm production in South-east Asia, particularly in Indonesia. Early symptoms of BSR are often subtle and easily overlooked, beginning with slight discoloration of older leaves, which gradually fade from green to yellowish, starting at the base of the frond midrib. Over time, plant growth becomes stunted, with young leaves appearing shorter than normal and fewer midribs developing. The plant then exhibits wilting symptoms and irregular patches of chlorosis on the leaf surface, which later progress to necrosis. Older leaves begin to dry from tip to base but do not detach immediately, remaining attached to the stem and forming a distinctive “skirt” around the base. As the disease progresses, more distinctive signs emerge, including unopened spear leaves (Fig. 1A), basal stem decay (Fig. 1B), soft and blackish-brown stem tissue, and eventually the development of basidiocarps at the base of the trunk (Fig. 1C) or around old frond bases, often concealed by vegetation or leaf litter. Basidiocarp formation occurs more frequently during wet seasons or under high humidity, which conditions that favors fungal growth and sporulation. Infection typically begins at the roots, where the fungus penetrates and colonizes vascular tissues, gradually disrupting water and nutrient flow. This systemic invasion causes internal stem decay and structural weakening, ultimately resulting in palm collapse (Fig. 1D), which marks the final stage of *G. boninense* infection. The most severe BSR-related losses have been recorded in Indonesia and Malaysia, with economic damage becoming significant when the infection affects more than 10% of the plantation. ##### Fig. 1.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
section: History of Oil Palm and BSR Disease’s Occurrence in Indonesia and Its Economic Impact
text: Oil palms were first introduced to present-day Indonesia as ornamental plants for botanical gardens. However, by the early 20th century, their commercial benefits became evident, leading to widespread agricultural cultivation, particularly on the islands of Sumatra and Borneo. In 2006, Indonesia became the world’s leading palm oil producer and continues to hold this position. The palm oil sector is a vital component of the Indonesian economy, contributing significantly to the renewable energy, food, and oleochemical industries. Indonesian palm oil represents approximately 25% of global vegetable oil production and 59% of the world’s total palm oil output. In 2023, Indonesia produced 47.08 million tons of palm oil, of which 10.2 million tons were allocated for domestic food needs, 2.3 million tons for the oleochemical industry, 10.6 million tons for biodiesel, and 23.98 million tons for exports. Currently, palm oil accounts for nearly one-third (75.17 million tons) of the world’s total vegetable oils. Despite these achievements, the industry faces serious productivity challenges due to BSR disease. BSR caused by *Ganoderma* was first reported by Thompson in 1931 in the Asia-Oceania region on older palms following replanting in Malaysia. In Indonesia, the disease was first documented by PT Socfin Indonesia, a private oil palm company, in Serdang Badagai, North Sumatra, in 1954. This may represent the earliest recorded occurrence of BSR in Indonesia or the broader South-east Asian region. Initially, the Ganoderma species associated with oil palm was identified as *G. lucidum*. Over the next five decades, around 15 other species names were recorded, including *G. boninense G. chalceum*, *G. miniactocinctum*, *G. tornatum,* and *G. zonatum*.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
section: History of Oil Palm and BSR Disease’s Occurrence in Indonesia and Its Economic Impact
text: While several additional species have suggested as potential pathogens, *G. boninense* is currently recognized as the principle causal agent of BSR in South Asia and Oceania, including Indonesia. Although various diseases threaten the oil palm industry, BSR caused by *G. boninense* has posed the most serious challenge to sustainable cultivation in South-east Asia for over 80 years. It remains the most destructive disease affecting the oil palm industry in Indonesia. While Africa, Papua New Guinea, and Thailand experience comparatively lower incidences of BSR, Indonesia and Malaysia suffer the most severe losses. In Indonesia, BSR disease can reduce oil palm yield per hectare significantly, with plant mortality rates exceeding 50% in heavily infested plantations. The fungus infects and decomposes roots, bole, and trunk tissues, thereby preventing upward transport of water and nutrients. External symptoms include yellowing and wilting of fronds, unopened spear leaves, and eventual plant collapse. In severely impacted plantations, widespread infections can result in palm death and up to 68% reduction in oil palm productivity. Although the disease has long been recognized in coastal regions, a survey of 13-year-old palms in both inland and peat soils revealed a typical disease incidence of approximately 30%. Similar issues are reported across Indonesian plantations. In certain inland areas of North Sumatra, BSR has killed up to 67% of oil palm trees within 25 years of planting. More severe palm losses – up to 25% within seven years – have been observed in fields where oil palm stumps were left in the ground during replanting. Meanwhile, in a peatland oil palm farm in Sumatra, BSR has destroyed between 30% and 54% of the palm stand, with an estimated yield reduction of 0.5 to 0.7 t/ha/yr over 14 years. When the disease affects more than 10% of the stand, financial losses begin to accrue.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
section: History of Oil Palm and BSR Disease’s Occurrence in Indonesia and Its Economic Impact
text: When the disease affects more than 10% of the stand, financial losses begin to accrue. Yield reduction in infected palms may occur either through from two main factors : the total loss of dues to palm death (direct loss), and through decreased weight of fresh fruit bunches (FFB) in still-living but infected palms (indirect loss). For every palm lost, FFB production decreases by an average of 0.16 t/ha. Once the stand is reduced by 50%, the average FFB yield declines by 35%. By the midpoint of the palms’ economic lifespan, BSR can kill up to 80% of a plantation, resulting in cumulative FFB losses ranging from 0.04 t to 4.34 t/ha, depending on the plantation’s age (10–22 years after planting). Recent probabilistic modeling estimates that a single plantation may suffer economic losses due to BSR in Indonesia, potential losses due to BSR are estimated at more than US$256 million for every 1% increase in disease incidence, with an annual regional impact of approximately US$500 million across South-east Asia. Among Indonesia’s major oil palm-growing regions, North Sumatra has the highest infection level, followed by Riau and Jambi provinces, also located in Sumatra (Hendra *et al*., 2024). Environmental factors related to disease incidence are critical to the development of effective strategies. Poor soil nutrients can weaken plant resistance, making them more susceptible to infection. Susanto *et al*. (2013) reported that the incidence and infection rate of *Ganoderma* were higher in sandy-textured soils than in clay-textured soil. This is attributed to the physical properties of loose sandy soils, which have high porosity, fewer microorganisms, and more efficient water circulation, all of which contribute to a higher infection rate compared to clay soil.

text: This is attributed to the physical properties of loose sandy soils, which have high porosity, fewer microorganisms, and more efficient water circulation, all of which contribute to a higher infection rate compared to clay soil. Furthermore, Hendra *et al*. (2024) found that the level of BSR disease infection in various soil types in Sumatra was highest in peat soils (24.79 trees/ha), followed by alluvial (13.41 trees/ha), volcanic (7.25 trees/ha), and inland soils (0.07 trees/ha). The abundance of organic matter and plant debris in peat soil creates a nutrient-rich and conducive environment for *Ganoderma* development. The ideal humidity range for the growth of *G. boninense* mycelial growth is between 50% and 60%, with an optimal temperature range of 25°C to 32°C being optimal (Peng *et al*., 2019). The high infection rate in peat soil is associated with the higher planting density typically used in these areas — 150 to 180 oil palms/ha — compared to mineral soil, which have 136 to 148 oil palms/ha. This denser planting results in shorter distances between trees, increasing root contact and thereby the potential for infection. Dolmat (2005) reported that in deep peatland, a planting density of 200 oil palm trees/ha resulted in an infection rate that was 70 and 36% higher than those densities of 160 and 120 trees/ha, respectively.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
section: Characteristics of *Ganoderma boninense*, the Causal Pathogen that Infects Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: *Ganoderma boninense* is a parasitic fungus with complex life cycle. Although not fully elucidated, its reproductive cycle resembles that of other Basidiomycetes and includes both sexual and vegetative reproduction. It produces sexual spores (basidiospores) and vegetative mycelia. Many researchers consider the basidiospores produced by fruiting bodies to be the primary inoculum, as they are easily dispersed by wind, water, or animals. BSR infection typically originates from an existing inoculum source, such as infected trees, stumps, or trunks left in the field. The fungus forms a fruiting body that releases basidiospores, which may spread via air, insects, or wind. Fruiting bodies have diverse morphological characters, as reported by Gulo *et al*. (2024) (Table 1). Under suitable environmental conditions, basidiospores germinate to produce monokaryotic mycelium (n). When two compatible monokaryotic mycelia meet, they fuse to form dikaryotic mycelium (2n), which is more aggressive and pathogenic. The mycelium then grows and spreads through the soil, facilitating contact between the roots of healthy oil palm roots and infected oil palm trees. Once the mycelium reaches the roots of healthy plants, it invades the root tissue, degrading lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose through extracellular enzymes. This leads to internal decay of root and stem structures, disrupting water and nutrient transport and contributing directly to the physiological symptoms observed in infected palms. At this stage, external symptoms remain invisible, but internal damage has already begun, rendering the plant physiologically unstable.

As the infection advances, external symptoms emerge, beginning with foliar discoloration, stunted growth, and unopened spear leaves – signs of impaired vascular function due to fungal colonization. This is followed by drying of the spear leaves, wilting of leaf sheaths, and the eventual appearance of fungal fruiting bodies on the lower stem surface (Elkhateeb and Daba, 2022). title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: As a soil-borne pathogen, *Ganoderma* employs a survival strategy by forming compact melanin-rich mycelium on infected roots or at the base of the stem. This structure protects the pathogen from chemical and biological agents, allowing it to persist for extended periods. Consequently, the potential for damage from BSR increases annually, presenting ongoing challenges for effective disease control. Several management strategies can be employed to mitigate the impact of *Ganoderma*.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: Infection by *G. boninense* infection often remains undetected in its early stages because symptoms develop internally. Therefore, early detection and systematic monitoring are critical to preventing disease and preserving plantation productivity. Initial detection methods include visual observation of early signs, such as changes in leaf coloration, midrib drying, and failure of spear leaves to open. However, since these symptoms typically appear only after the infection is well advanced, more sensitive techniques are required. Molecular-based diagnostic methods, such as conventional PCR and quantitative PCR (qPCR), enable the detection of *Ganoderma* DNA in root, stem, or soil samples. Additionally, electrochemical and biosensor-based techniques can be used for early identification. Remote sensing tools, such as drone-based aerial imagery, are also effective in detecting changes in canopy structure. Furthermore, metabolite analysis using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) provides an advanced approach to identifying biochemical changes associated with infection. By implementing these early detection and monitoring strategies consistently, disease progression can be curtailed, and control measures can be applied more effectively and promptly (Kurihara *et al*., 2022; Karunarathna *et al*., 2024; Cahyadi *et al*., 2025).

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: The use of pathogen-free planting materials is a crucial first step in preventing the spread of inoculum in the field. Seedlings produced through tissue culture and certified as disease-free have a significantly lower risk of being infected by pathogens. Tissue culture in oil palm is an important technique for vegetative propagation in oil palm, offering several advantages over conventional methods. One key advantage is the potential to propagate plants with resistance to multiple diseases simultaneously. For instance, plants resistant to both *Fusarium* and *Ganoderma* can be selected by initially screening several crosses of clonal plants for resistance to Fusarium wilt. These selected clones are then planted in areas endemic to *Ganoderma* to further identify those resistant to BSR. Tissue culture techniques hold promise for producing pathogen-free planting materials; however, continuous efforts are required to optimize protocols and maintain the necessary systems, infrastructure, and laboratory standards.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: The control of BSR through technical culture practices aims to reduce the rate of infection. In established oil palm plantations, implementing sound culture practices is often recommended as a short-term disease management strategy. These practices are designed to halt disease progression, eliminate or reduce the sources of pathogen inoculum, and provide temporary recovery to affected oil palm plants. Cultural methods include land clearing (clean clearance), sanitation, stem chipping, deboling, soil cultivation, digging large planting holes, and constructing isolation trenches. While these techniques may not completely eradicate the disease, their combined application can reduce the risk of infection and minimize economic losses caused by *Ganoderma*.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: Biological control agents (BCAs) are gaining increasing attention as environmentally friendly alternatives to chemical fungicides in the management of BSR in oil palm plantations. Over recent decades, numerous BCAs have been investigated for their ability to suppress *Ganoderma,* with most studies conducted *in vitro*. These BCAs include actinomycetes, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, *Bacillus* spp., *Diaporthe* spp., mycoparasites, *Penicillium* spp., *Streptomyces* spp., and *Trichoderma* spp. However, *in vitro* results must be validated through nursery and field trials to confirm the agents’ practical efficacy. Lisnawita *et al*. (2025) evaluated six Trichoderma isolates obtained from the rhizosphere of healthy oil palm plants in the Bukit Kijang plantation. *In vitro* tests showed that four isolates effectively inhibited *G. boninense,* with inhibition zone percentages ranging from 64.93 to 78.78%, while the remaining two isolates demonstrated inhibition below 50%. Further testing of these four isolates on 3-month-old Dura × Pisifera oil palm seedlings revealed that two isolates – *T. asperellum* and *T. virens* (as identified through molecular techniques) – significantly suppressed *Ganoderma* development and promoted vegetative growth after 7 months of inoculation. These two isolates are currently undergoing limited-scale field trials on immature oil palm trees. Commercial BCA products already available in the market include Marfu-P and Greemi-G (produced by PPKS), among others. In addition to BCAs, another promising biotechnological approach is the development of genetically resistant oil palm varieties.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: In addition to BCAs, another promising biotechnological approach is the development of genetically resistant oil palm varieties. Several Indonesian plantations have reported success in breeding *Ganoderma*-resistant palm through extensive research. Notable examples include DxP Socfindo Moderate Resistant Gano (MTG) (PT. Socfin Indonesia), DxP 540 NG (PPKS), DxP Spring MR Gano and DxP Themba MR Gano (PT. ASD Bakrie Oil Palm Seed), and DxP Dami Mas IGR (PT. Dami Mas Sejahtera). Offspring from crosses such as Cameroon x Cameroon, Cameroon x AVROS, and Nigeria x Nigeria have shown tolerance to BSR. Furthermore, tolerance genes have been identified in Zaire x Cameroon cultures, while partial resistance genes have been located in Congo x Cameroon cultures.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: In response to many environmental variables, plants produce some primary and secondary metabolites. Plant and other organisms produce and utilize metabolites in their metabolism. Certain specialized metabolites play an important role in the plant defense system against fungi, bacteria, and other pests, depending on their specific metabolite profile. Saragih and Lisnawita (2024) reported that administering *Asystasia gangetica* leaf extract at a concentration of 8 mg/ml to 2-month-old Dura × Pisifera oil palm seedlings infected with *Ganoderma* stimulated vegetative growth, suppressed disease incidence, and reduced disease severity in 8 months after inoculation. These results are supported by research by Saragih *et al. * (2021), who discovered that oil palm seedlings infected with *Ganoderma* contained isothiocyanate compounds (N=C=S), whereas this compound was absent in seedlings treated with specialized metabolites from *Diplazium esculentum* and *Rivina humilis,* both of which possess antifungals properties. Thus, the administration of specialized metabolites from these weed species may enhance the defense of oil palm seedlings against *Ganoderma* attacks and serve as an effective bioprotectant (Collinge *et al*., 2022).

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: Chemical control measures, such as the use of fungicides, have long been employed to manage *Ganoderma-*infected oil palms. For instance, organomercury and potassium hydroxyquinoline sulfate have been injected into diseased trees. More recently, the application of hexaconazole via pressure injection, stem injection, soil drenching, or soil injection has shown effectiveness in reducing the spread of BSR in infected palms. Pyraclostrobin has also proven successful in mitigating BSR in seedlings and has demonstrated beneficial physiological effects, including increased plant height, stem diameter, root mass, photosynthetic rate, PSII quantum efficiency, and relative leaf chlorophyll content. However, its efficacy in mature palms remains underexplored. Despite the availability, several effective fungicides, their use raises concerns about environmental contamination and the development of fungicide resistance. In addition to fungicides, minerals also play an important role in enhancing plant resistance to pathogens through the induction of spesialized metabolites. Disease severity can be reduced through appropriate minerals fertilization, making it a viable strategy for managing calcium has been shown to reduce BSR severity and suppress *G. boninense* growth in infected seedlings. These minerals may also reinforce cell wall and middle lamella, thereby limiting pathogen penetration.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text: Biotechnological innovations are increasingly being explored to complement conventional strategies for BSR management. One promising approach is the genetic transformation of oil palm, although this remains technically challenging due to the crop’s long life cycle and the complexities of tissue culture propagation. Nonetheless, transformation has been achieved using *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*-mediated and biolistic methods. These enable the introduction of resistance-related genes, such as those encoding pathogenesis-related (PR) proteins, chitinases, and antifungal peptides. Another promising strategy is Host-Induced Gene Silencing (HIGS), which involves engineering oil palms to produce double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) that silence specific essential genes in *Ganoderma*. Advances in fungal genomics and transcriptomics have facilitated the identification of virulence-associated genes – particularly those related to lignin degradation and effector secretion – that serve as potential HIGS targets. The integration of HIGS with genomics-based target identification offers a species-specific and environmentally benign approach to suppress fungal pathogenicity.

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
text:
The individual control methods described above have not yet provided fully satisfactory outcomes in limiting the spread of *Ganoderma* infection in the field. Consequently, an integrated control strategy is necessary, combining multiple approaches. While no single method offers completely disease control, integration of these methods can minimize infection risk and reduce economic losses caused by *Ganoderma*. Figure 2 presents an integrated management framework tailored to different growth stages of oil palm: immature palms, mature palms, and replanting areas. The process begins with a Ganoderma census and symptom identification, followed by management interventions based on the age of the palms and severity of infection. The Disease Severity Index (DSI) is employed to assess infection levels and guide treatment decisions. Currently no single control method has been effective for managing BSR disease. Therefore, it is recommended to apply more than one method by either combining the above methods or applying integrated control. Furthermore, collaborative efforts involving scientists, breeders, and farmers are essential for developing and implementing sustainable strategies against this destructive plant pathogen. Through rigorous scientific investigation and evidence-based practices, it is possible to safeguard global plant health and mitigate the severe economic consequences of *Ganoderma* infections (Fig. 3). ##### Fig 3. #####

title: Basal Stem Rot Disease of Oil Palm in Indonesia
section: Future Research Areas to Improve BSR Management
text: Emerging microbiome engineering approaches focus on utilizing Plant Growth Promoting Microorganisms (PGPMs) – including biofertilizers, biostimulants, bioprotectants, and biological control agents – to preserve microbial diversity for oil palm sustainability. These efforts must be aligned with ongoing climate change research. Innovative genetic and detection systems are needed to enhance disease resistance and improve management precision. This includes the application of genome editing technologies, the identification and tracking of *Ganoderma* resistance genes, and the integration of molecular diagnostics into precision agriculture frameworks. Spray-Induced Gene Silencing (SIGS) presents a non-transgenic, RNA-based approach to silencing key pathogenicity genes in *G. boninense*. SIGS involves the external application of synthetic double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs), and its effectiveness can be significantly enhanced through nanocarrier-based delivery systems that improve dsRNA stability and uptake. CRISPR/Cas genome editing offers a promising avenue for engineering disease-resistant oil palm varieties and modulating plant-microbe interactions. Functional genomics and transcriptomic analyses of both host and pathogen will be critical to identifying novel molecular targets, thereby enabling the development of durable, precise, and environmentally sustainable BSR management strategies.

### Overview ###
Banana is cultivated in Ghana at commercial and smallholder scales. Production is threatened by banana bunchy top disease (BBTD), a destructive viral disease spread by aphids. We discuss measures to prevent BBTD from entering Ghana and to mitigate its effects and eradicate it, if it enters the country.
