title: 'The Banana Aphid and Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Potential Threats to Banana
text: Banana bunchy top disease (BBTD) is the most destructive viral disease affecting banana (*Musa* spp.) and plantain (*Musa* × *paradisiaca* L.) cultivation (Bouwmeester *et al*., 2023). These monocotyledonous crop plants are grown across about 150 countries, where they are extremely important for food security and national income. The dessert (Cavendish) banana is the world’s most important fruit in terms of export value (*c*. US$11 billion in 2017). This export trade is dominated by Asian and South American countries. However, in Africa, *c*. 70 million people generate revenue from banana and plantain, which are widely grown for local consumption. Three countries, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana and Cameroon, are the most significant African exporters. In Ghana, the income from banana has been increasing for farmers and value chain participants, with annual exports to the UK and EU valued at approximately US$53 million (2015 figures: Ghana Export Promotion Authority, 2017). Banana grows well in the temperature range of 15–35°C at a relative humidity of 75–85%, which is characteristic of southern Ghana, where cultivation of the crop is expanding. In this case study, we discuss the potential threat of BBTD to banana and plantain production in Ghana and what measures can be applied to detect the disease and mitigate its effects. The issue is important since BBTD can cause losses of up to 100%, and if not controlled it can cause significant financial losses to smallholder and commercial farmers and threaten food security. Furthermore, BBTD is highly invasive, having spread from Fiji, where it was first observed in the late 19th century, to South-east Asia, South Pacific, India, and to Africa, where it was first reported in Egypt in 1900.

title: 'The Banana Aphid and Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Potential Threats to Banana
text:
Furthermore, BBTD is highly invasive, having spread from Fiji, where it was first observed in the late 19th century, to South-east Asia, South Pacific, India, and to Africa, where it was first reported in Egypt in 1900. BBTD has spread to at least 19 African countries, and although at the time of writing this case study the disease has not reached Ghana, there is a high risk of introduction (Bouwmeester *et al*., 2023; Gaitu *et al*., 2024). ### The causal agent of banana bunchy top disease ###
BBTD is caused by banana bunchy top virus (BBTV). BBTV was at one time thought to be a luteovirus, i.e., a phloem-limited RNA virus transmitted by aphids in the persistent mode (see next section on transmission). However, following the successful purification of BBTV particles (virions) in the 1990s, it was found that they contained single-stranded circular DNA. In the latest release from the International Committee on Viral Taxonomy, BBTV is classified as the viral species *Babuvirus musae* in the Genus *Babuvirus* in the Family *Nanoviridae*. The DNA genome of BBTV is hexapartite, with each of the six circular ssDNA genomic components (DNA-R, DNA-U3, DNA-S, DNA-M, DNA-C, and DNA-N), ranging in length from 1 to 1.1 kb. Each genomic DNA molecule is encapsidated separately in a non-enveloped T = 1 icosahedral particle, assembled from 60 coat protein subunits, that is 18–19 nm in diameter.

title: 'The Banana Aphid and Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Potential Threats to Banana
text: Each genomic DNA molecule is encapsidated separately in a non-enveloped T = 1 icosahedral particle, assembled from 60 coat protein subunits, that is 18–19 nm in diameter. DNA-C encodes a protein that initiates host cell division by interaction with the banana retinoblastoma-Rb protein orthologue, the DNA-M component encodes the BBTV cell-to-cell movement protein, DNA-N encodes a protein that shuttles viral DNA between the host cell nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments and is implicated in aphid transmission, while the viral coat protein is encoded by DNA-S. DNA-U3 encodes a factor with no currently known function. Nanoviruses and other small single-stranded DNA viruses encode Rep (replication initiator) proteins that facilitate rolling circle DNA replication, which occurs in the nucleus utilising the host’s DNA synthesis machinery. In the case of BBTV, the Rep protein is encoded by DNA-R (Guyot *et al*., 2024). Within the nucleus, the viral mRNAs are transcribed from the BBTV genomic DNAs by host RNA polymerase II. Some BBTV isolates are associated with alphasatellite DNAs. Alphasatellites are hyperparasitic single stranded circular DNA molecules that depend upon a ‘helper’ virus (in this case BBTV) for packaging into particles made of the helper virus coat protein, for movement through the plant, and for vector-mediated transmission. Alphasatellites encode their own Rep proteins and initiate replication by host DNA polymerase activity independently of the helper virus (Guyot *et al*., 2024). BBTV replication occurs in phloem tissues, where it induces hyperplasia. Cells surrounding the phloem have increased numbers of chloroplasts, giving rise to symptoms of dark green streaks.

title: 'The Banana Aphid and Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Potential Threats to Banana
text:
BBTV replication occurs in phloem tissues, where it induces hyperplasia. Cells surrounding the phloem have increased numbers of chloroplasts, giving rise to symptoms of dark green streaks. BBTV can travel down the phloem to the vicinity of the meristem, allowing viral spread into developing tissues. Systemic infection with BBTV induces the major symptoms of BBTD, i.e., plant dwarfing, leaf narrowing, leaf margin chlorosis, and induction of dark green discontinuous streaks on the leaves, petioles and pseudotrunks. Additionally, infected plants are unlikely to yield fruit (Halbert and Baker, 2015) (Fig. 1). Interestingly, coinfection of plants by BBTV and an alphasatellite may ameliorate symptoms, decrease the titres and dysregulate the ratios of the BBTV DNA components, and inhibit aphid-mediated BBTV transmission. This was recently observed with an alphasatellite associated with BBTV in the Democratic Republic of Congo (Guyot *et al*., 2022). ##### Fig. 1. #####

title: 'The Banana Aphid and Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Potential Threats to Banana
section: Banana Bunchy Top Virus is Vectored by Aphids but Can also Be Disseminated Vegetatively
text: BBTV is vectored by the banana aphid *Pentalonia nigronervosa* Coquerel (Hemiptera: Aphididae) (Halbert and Baker, 2015). Aphids feed predominantly on pseudostems, unfurled immature leaves and leaf sheaths. Vegetative transmission of BBTV also occurs via infected suckers and planting material, which can act as an inoculum source for other plants if the vector is present (Bouwmeester *et al*., 2023). *P*. *nigronervosa* vectors BBTV in a persistent, circulative and non-propagative manner. That is, virus particles enter the body of the aphid and circulate but without virus replication occurring. When BBTV particles reach the salivary glands, the aphid becomes competent to transmit the virus, and the insect remains viruliferous and infectious for life. Both acquisition of viral inoculum and infection require sustained feeding (15 min to 4 h) by aphids from phloem vessels (Halbert and Baker, 2015). Interestingly, BBTV infection modifies host biochemistry, resulting in the emission of a blend of volatile organic compounds that attract *P*. *nigronervosa*. However, it was found that once the aphids have acquired BBTV they are less attracted by infected banana plants and will be more likely to migrate to uninfected hosts. It is thought that this apparent manipulation of aphid host selection behaviour will accelerate transmission of BBTV, profound effects on epidemic development and important implications for formulating disease control methods (Murhububa *et al*., 2024).

title: 'The Banana Aphid and Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Potential Threats to Banana
section: Banana Bunchy Top Virus is Vectored by Aphids but Can also Be Disseminated Vegetatively
text: It is thought that this apparent manipulation of aphid host selection behaviour will accelerate transmission of BBTV, profound effects on epidemic development and important implications for formulating disease control methods (Murhububa *et al*., 2024). BBTV also induces changes in the chemical composition and/or nutritional quality of plant tissue so that aphids reared on infected plants grew less well and show morphological differences to those propagated on healthy plants, indicating that infected banana plants are poor hosts for *P*. *nigronervosa* (Murhububa *et al*., 2024). *P*. *nigronervosa* was first described in 1859 on the Island of Reunion but is widespread across the world’s tropical and subtropical regions (Robson *et al*., 2007). Although this aphid is a plantain and banana specialist, *P*. *nigronervosa* can accept a few other host plants, notably *Heliconia*, which is also a host for BBTV. The wide distribution of *P*. *nigronervosa* means that once BBTV has been introduced into a new territory, the pre-existing vector population will ensure the rapid spread of the virus.

title: 'The Banana Aphid and Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Potential Threats to Banana
section: Direct Damage Caused by the Banana Aphid
text: *P*. *nigronervosa* does the greatest harm by vectoring BBTV. Direct damage by the aphid is generally negligible, but heavy infestation weakens the plant, which impedes plant growth and development (CABI, 2021). Additionally, heavy infestations of the fruits will reduce their market value due to the growth of sooty mould fungi fed by honeydew secreted by the aphids (CABI, 2021).

title: 'The Banana Aphid and Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Potential Threats to Banana
text: The initial symptoms of BBTD on banana consist of dark green streaks and J-shaped hooks in the veins of lower portions of the leaf midrib and the leaf stem (Fig. 1a and b). As the disease progresses, emerging leaves are progressively stunted and malformed with a more upright bearing than usual and appear to be ‘bunched’ at the top of the plant; hence, the disease name ‘bunchy top’ (Hapsari and Masrum, 2012) (Fig. 1c–e). Other symptoms include crinkling and mottling of the petioles and overall stunting of infected plants (Fig. 1c–e). Banana plants that show BBTD symptoms rarely bear fruit, but when it is produced it is edible, although deformed and decreased in size (Fig. 1i and g). Figure 1f, h and j represents a healthy plant, inflorescence and fruit.

section: Disease and Vector Research and Management
text:
### Detection of BBTV and identification of *P*. *nigronervosa* ###
In addition to the recognition of BBTD or BBTD-like symptoms it is important to be able to definitively identify the causative agent. Serological detection of BBTV with antibodies raised against the coat protein has been possible for many decades and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits are commercially available for BBTV and other viruses affecting banana. Sequence-specific detection of BBTV DNA based on polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and isothermal DNA amplification methods are also well established. DNA amplification methods are generally more sensitive than serological approaches and have the additional benefit that the amplicons can be sequenced, which allows for specific BBTV strains and lineages to be identified. This can be useful in tracking the potential source of an outbreak and the evolution of BBTV as epidemics develop (Wickramaarachchi *et al*., 2016; Barros *et al*., 2024). PCR-based DNA detection methods are sufficiently sensitive to identify aphids carrying BBTV (Chen and Hu, 2013) and newer high-throughput sequencing methods allow for simultaneous indexing of plant and insect samples for the presence of BBTV and other banana-infecting pathogens (Rong *et al*., 2023). Generally, the DNA amplification methods described above could be used to detect BBTV from infected plants and from the viruliferous aphids. However, based on the study by Chen and Hu (2013), high-throughput sequencing using TaqMan®PCR detect rapidly and accurately BBTV in banana plants, whole aphids, aphid honeydew and aphid haemolymph, and requires only a minute initial amount of sample for analysis without virus purification.

section: Disease and Vector Research and Management
text:
Identification of the aphid *P*. *nigronervosa* is aided by its distinctive morphological features, most notably the alates’ black wing venation, which gives the insect its taxonomic name (Fig. 2) (CABI, 2021). However, unambiguous identification may be challenging for insects recovered from water or sticky traps, in which case PCR-based ‘DNA barcoding’ using primers specific for insect genes such as *cytochrome oxidase subunit I* (*CO I*), followed by amplicon sequencing becomes essential (Fening *et al*., 2020). Indeed, *CO I*-based DNA barcoding is vital in unambiguously distinguishing between *P*. *nigronervosa* Coquerel (which most typically feeds on banana and plantain and only occasionally on other hosts) and the related *P*. *caladii* van der Goot that is found only very occasionally on *Musa* spp. (Foottit *et al*., 2010). ##### Fig. 2. #####
(a) A colony of banana aphids (*Pentalonia nigronervosa*) on a banana petiole. Individual winged (alate) (b) and non-winged (apterous) morphs (c). Adults range between 1.2 and 1.8 mm in length. Image credits Scot Nelson (University of Hawaii), public domain (Available at: <https://www.influentialpoints.com/Gallery/Pentalonia_nigronervosa_banana_aphid.htm>, accessed 10 August 2025). Training personnel in the routine use of these serological and molecular BBTV detection methods and in the trapping and identification of the *P*.

section: Disease and Vector Research and Management
text:
Training personnel in the routine use of these serological and molecular BBTV detection methods and in the trapping and identification of the *P*. *nigronervosa* vector will be essential to support surveillance, quarantine, phytosanitary and eradication efforts for BBTD, which are discussed in the following sections. In Ghana, banana and plantain plants in both households and farms are randomly examined for BBTV symptoms and the presence of the aphid vector. Monitoring of the vector is done by inspecting banana and plantain plants, especially the undersides of leaves, leaf bases, and pseudostems, for the presence of small, reddish-brown to almost black, oval-shaped aphids or using yellow sticky card traps or water bowl traps. Alternative host plants found are also inspected for the presence of the vector. This monitoring is done by Ghana’s National Plant Protection Organisation (NPPO), with the support of Academia, and the National Research Institutions and Development Partners (mainly by the Centre for Agriculture and Biosciences International, CABI) as and when resources are available. Leaf samples of suspected (symptomatic) and healthy looking (asymptomatic) plants and aphids are collected into separate vials containing 95% ethanol for identification. ### Preventive and active measures ###
BBTV is persistently transmitted from plant to plant by *P*. *nigronervosa* and by transporting infected planting materials (Hapsari and Masrum, 2012). It can, however, be limited by culling diseased plants, chemical control of the vector and by using virus-free planting material obtained through *in vitro* meristem tip culture (Ferreira *et al*., 1997; INIBAP, 2001).

### Quarantine measures ###
If practicable, constant monitoring of national or regional borders to prevent BBTD from being introduced through planting material is an important preventive strategy (Gaitu *et al*., 2024); where national quarantine measures are less practicable, it is important to discourage farmers from importing planting materials from neighbouring countries where BBTV is present. However, to obtain the cooperation of farmers, it is important to provide training on how to multiply their own healthy and clean planting materials. ### Alternative hosts ###
The broad range of alternative hosts of BBTV seems to be congruent with the host ranges of its oligophagous vectors, *P*. *nigronervosa* and the taro aphid *P*. *caladii*, including mainly members of the Musaceae, Cannaceae, Araceae, Zingiberaceae, and Heliconiaceae (Foottit *et al*., 2010; Bagariang *et al*., 2019) (Table 1). Usually, *P*. *nigronervosa* favours *Musa* hosts, while *P*. *caladii* prefers non-*Musa* hosts though there is some overlap in host range (Foottit *et al*., 2010; Bagariang *et al*., 2019). Alternative hosts for BBTV may act as reservoirs for infection and could potentially frustrate control programmes, although several listed in Table 1 do not occur outside of specific geographic locales, and would not occur as infection reservoirs in Ghana. ##### Table 1. #####

Since *P*. *nigronervosa* is BBTV’s only effective vector, prompt detection and destruction of this pest should prevent the spread of BBTD. Although BBTV has not yet been reported in Ghana, continual monitoring for its presence is essential. If the virus is detected, an immediate and realistic measure that can be put in place to prevent further spread is prohibition of movement of planting materials from infected areas to other parts of the country. Additionally, the identification, collection and destruction of infected plants (culling, rogueing) has a strong possibility of eradicating it, as was demonstrated in Togo (see below). The success of such a programme pivots on effective legislation and its efficient enforcement at local and national levels. ### Host plant resistance to the virus ###
Until recently, it was thought that all banana cultivars were susceptible to BBTV. However, work in Australia suggested that the wild species *Musa coccinea* and the banana cultivar Kluai Teparot (ABBB/ABB) possess some degree of resistance. Studies undertaken to evaluate *Musa* genotypes for BBTV resistance found genotypes with tolerance (no symptoms and near normal performance of virus infected plants, e.g., Gros Michel), delayed expression of symptoms (e.g., cv. Dwarf Apple, also known as Santa Catarina) or decreased susceptibility (e.g. cv. Fugamou) (Espino *et al*., 1993; Niyongere *et al*., 2011).

While wild *Musa* species are known to be resistant to BBTV, and some banana varieties are more readily infected with the virus, no variety of banana is considered truly resistant (Ferreira *et al*., 1997). A study in East Java in Indonesia indicated that susceptibility is related to genotype. Thus, cultivars in AAB, ABB and BBB genome groups tend to be more tolerant to BBTV than cultivars of AA and AAA, i.e., possession of one or two B genomes enhances tolerance (Hapsari and Masrum, 2012). These genotypes should be evaluated by farmers and consumers in case it becomes necessary to transition to acceptance of these genotypes, to replace current BBTV-susceptible varieties (Gaitu *et al*., 2024). ### Biological control of the vector ###
In Tonga, the polyphagous aphid parasitoid *Aphidius colemani* Viereck (Hymenoptera: Braconidae) was released in an attempt at biological control of *P*. *nigronervosa*, but its effects on BBTD incidence were disappointing (Wellings *et al*., 1994). Another attempt at biological control of *P*. *nigronervosa* was undertaken in Western Samoa using two coccinellid species, but neither agent could establish breeding populations (Waterhouse and Norris, 1987; Stechmann and Völkl, 1988). In Ghana, biological control options for *P*. *nigronervosa* have received little attention. Thus, current efforts to document the range of natural enemies (predators and parasitoids) attacking *P*.

Thus, current efforts to document the range of natural enemies (predators and parasitoids) attacking *P*. *nigronervosa* on banana, plantain and alternative hosts (e.g. *Heliconia*) are important to support development of biological control options for integrated pest management of BBTD (K. O. Fening, unpublished data). ### Cultural and chemical control of BBTD ###
Banana plantations can last for several years in Ghana, but the lifespan of individual plants within a plantation is shorter, ranging from 12 to 16 months, from planting to harvest, depending on the variety and local growing conditions. After a banana plant flowers and fruits, the ‘mother’ plant dies, and a new ‘daughter’ plant from the same corm takes over. A plantation can be maintained for many years by cycling through these mother-daughter plants, potentially for 7–10 years or more, depending on the management practices and the lifespans of individual plants. This might result in older plants becoming disease reservoirs. If this occurs, BBTD can be effectively controlled by culling diseased plants and replacing them with virus-free planting material. Before culling, diseased plants should be sprayed with an appropriate insecticide to kill all potentially viruliferous aphids. To prevent vegetative transmission, the whole stool, including the corm and all associated suckers, must be destroyed by uprooting and chopping into small pieces or by herbicide treatment, as BBTV will ultimately spread to all parts of the mat. Control must be practised across whole production areas to avoid re-infection of planting material (Kumar, 2017). Insecticides have been used in some countries to control *P*.

text: Control must be practised across whole production areas to avoid re-infection of planting material (Kumar, 2017). Insecticides have been used in some countries to control *P*. *nigronervosa*, and consequent decreases in BBTD incidence have been reported. A 2017–2018 field study in Pakistan evaluated the efficacy of various insecticides and concluded that the highest reduction percentage of *P*. *nigronervosa* was observed with Spinetoram followed by Methoxyfenozide, a repeat Spinosad treatment, Chlorantraniliprole and Flubendamide on the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th days, respectively (Baloch *et al*., 2023). Injecting plants with herbicides combined with systemic insecticide spraying can kill infected plants and the viruliferous aphids infesting them. However, this is labour intensive, costly for many farmers, and of questionable effectiveness in smallholder farming systems, where it may be difficult to adopt common practices between farms. In addition to prohibitive costs, the development of resistance in the aphids, and concerns with the effects of chemical residues on farmer health and on the environment make it unlikely that vector control using pesticides will gain wide use in Ghana. Amsavalli *et al*. (2022) applied the entomopathogenic fungi *Lecanicillium lecanii* (at 109 colony-forming units/ml), *Metarhizium anisopliae* (108 cfu/ml) and *Beauveria bassiana* (108 cfu/ml) to banana plants infested with *P*. *nigronervosa*, resulting in 63–76% aphid mortality.

However, in the same study, two botanical insecticidal preparations, Neem oil (1% effective concentration) and Pongamia oil (2% EC), killed 80–83% and 80–81% aphids, respectively. These higher mortality rates are close in efficacy to the synthetic neonicotinoid insecticides Acetamiprid (82–84%) and Imidacloprid (89–91%) (Amsavalli *et al*., 2022). Research in Ghana showed that homemade aqueous Neem kernel extract (applied at 50g/L of water) or a commercial Neem-based formulation (0.3–1% azadirachtin applied at 30–60 ml/15L of water, respectively) were very effective in controlling the aphids *Lipaphis erysimi pseudobrassicae* Davis (Hemiptera: Aphididae) and *Myzus persicae* Sulzer (Hemiptera: Aphididae) on cabbage (Forchibe *et al*., 2017; Adenka *et al*., 2021). Taken together, these finding indicate that treatments using homemade Neem extracts or Neem-based products can readily be adapted to control *P*. *nigronervosa* on banana and plantain in Ghana. The efficacy of these treatments in decreasing *P*. *nigronervosa* populations can be monitored by sampling alates using yellow water bowl and sticky traps placed near the crop and monitoring the plants for apterous aphids. RNA silencing [also known as RNA interference (RNAi) and post-transcriptional gene silencing (PTGS)] is a highly effective means of protecting plants against both RNA and DNA viruses (Jekayinoluwa *et al*., 2020). RNA silencing is a potent natural antiviral system that is elicited during virus infection by the presence of RNA molecules containing substantial stretches of double-stranded structure, which leads to the generation of small (21–26 nucleotide long) RNAs. These small RNAs direct Argonaute endonucleases to ‘slice’ homologous sequences in viral RNA. RNA silencing can target the genomic RNAs of RNA viruses and mRNAs produced by RNA and DNA viruses. RNA silencing can be stimulated artificially using double-stranded RNA molecules either through expression in transgenic plants (Cillo and Palukaitis, 2014), or by application of synthetic RNA molecules by spraying leaves of non-transgenic plants (Fletcher *et al*., 2020). Since RNA silencing in transgenic plants works well against geminiviruses, which like BBTV have single stranded circular DNA genomes, it has been suggested that the approach would be a feasible strategy for control of BBTD (Jekayinoluwa *et al*., 2020). In other plant systems, both transgenic expression and topical application of double-stranded RNAs with sequence homology to insect transcripts can provide protection against aphids (Fletcher *et al*., 2020), suggesting a means of controlling BBTV transmission. Gene editing is a method of introducing targeted mutations into DNA sequences.

title: 'The Banana Aphid and Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Potential Threats to Banana
section: Disease and Vector Research and Management
text: Gene editing is a method of introducing targeted mutations into DNA sequences. The most used approaches use adaptations of the prokaryotic antiviral defence system (‘CRISPR’) comprising a DNA endonuclease, such as Cas9, that can be directed to a specific site in DNA by a guide RNA with homology to the target sequence. CRISPR has been used to generate non-transgenic plants rendered resistant to specific viruses by mutation of plants genes conditioning susceptibility (Chandrasekaran *et al*., 2016; Pyott *et al*., 2016). CRISPR has also been shown to be effective when used directly against DNA viruses, including several geminivirus, especially if guide RNAs target the non-coding intergenic regions of the viral genomes (Ali *et al*., 2016). RNA silencing (especially using topical double-stranded RNA application) and gene editing have significant potential for control of BBTV. However, the deployment in Ghana of these technologies would depend on regulatory regime, the attitudes of growers, and consumer preferences both within Ghana and in export markets.

text: BBTV occurs in countries neighbouring Ghana such as Benin (localised) (Lokossou *et al*., 2012) and Nigeria (localised) (CABI, 2021), and was present in Togo, where it has been eradicated (Kolombia *et al*., 2021). Since *P*. *nigronervosa* is widely distributed in Ghana (CABI, 2021; PPRSD, 2024), there is a very high risk of BBTD introduction. Thus, continuous monitoring for BBTV and vector abundance in banana and plantain plantations is essential to support informed and rapid decision making in the event of an outbreak. Increased surveillance at the borders of Ghana for import of banana and plantain suckers from neighbouring countries (Togo, Burkina Faso and Ivory Coast) will be crucial for interception of infected planting material. Integrating BBTV survey data and reports from neighbouring countries, could also be used for parameterisation of epidemiological models to aid in assessment of the probability of entry of the virus into Ghana and provide an additional means of alerting stakeholders (Retkute and Gilligan, 2025). Early detection of BBTV introduction will allow for its immediate containment and possible eradication. In contrast, failure to detect BBTV introduction early will make containment and eradication difficult since *P*. *nigronervosa* is widespread. It is, therefore, recommended that Ghana’s National Plant Protection Organisation (i.e., the Plant Protection and Regulatory Services Directorate, PPRSD, of the Ministry of Food and Agriculture) should partner with other border agencies through awareness creation to prevent the entry and spread of this devastating banana and plantain disease. ### Overview ###
*Luteovirus glycinis* is a plant RNA virus that exerts various effects on legume crops, depending on the strain, geographical region, and environmental conditions. It has been responsible for significant yield reductions in soybean production in Japan and is also known to impact other legume crops.

title: Soybean Dwarf Virus
text: 1. Understand the mechanisms of virus transmission to crops and identify the primary vectors of plant viruses on a global scale. 2. Understand the various strains of virus that have been described and how they differ. 3. Appreciation of current research directions in this field. 4. Understand the importance of viral reservoir’s role in influencing the incidence of viruses in crops. 5. List pest control methods currently in use.

title: Soybean Dwarf Virus
text: The novel viral disease responsible for dwarfing in soybean was first documented in Japan in 1952 (Tamada *et al*., 1969). The pathogenic agent responsible for the disease was characterised in 1969 (Tamada *et al*., 1969) and has since been identified in various countries and across different hosts (Stone *et al*., 2024). The virus infects many legume species: beans, peas, lentils and clovers, but is symptomless in some of its hosts, for example white clover (Tamada, 1970). Although the virus is globally distributed, its impact on crops is variable, leading to significant yield losses in soybean in Japan, while not being regarded as a threat to soybean in the United States (Hill and Whitham, 2014). Its relevance extends beyond soybean, as it also induces disease in legume crops in other regions worldwide, for example in the Middle East or in Australia (Makkouk *et al*., 1997; Congdon *et al*., 2023). Effective pest management requires an understanding of its local hosts, including potential viral reservoirs, and vectors. Development of commercially available resistant varieties of soybean is ongoing.

title: Soybean Dwarf Virus
text:
The virions of *L. glycinis* comprise linear, positive sense single-stranded RNA of 5.8 kB, which encodes five open reading frames (ORFs). Like many other plant viruses, *L. glycinis* is transmitted by insect vectors. The mode of transmission is circulative and non-propagative (Tamada, 1970): upon acquisition from an infected plant during phloem feeding, the virus circulates within the insect’s body, including accessory salivary glands, without entering the cells or replicating within the insect. Despite the absence of replication within the insect’s body, the virus retains its infectivity within the vector. As a result, when the insect feeds on a new plant, the virus is released through its saliva (Fig. 1). ##### Fig. 1. #####
Plant virus circulative route in insects. Courtesy of SwissBioPics (Available at: [https://viralzone.expasy.org/3738, accessed 19 February 2025](https://viralzone.expasy.org/3738)). The main aphid species serving as vectors worldwide are *Aulacorthum solani* and *Acyrthosiphum pisum* (Terauchi *et al*., 2001). Other potential vectors have been identified, including *Nearctaphis bakeri* and *Myzus persicae* (Damsteegt *et al*., 2011; Congdon *et al*., 2023).

title: Soybean Dwarf Virus
text:
Other potential vectors have been identified, including *Nearctaphis bakeri* and *Myzus persicae* (Damsteegt *et al*., 2011; Congdon *et al*., 2023). Several strains of the virus have been described:
* – Based on the symptoms caused in the soybean: Yellowing (Y) and Dwarfing (D) strain
* – Based on the transmission vector – *A. pisum* (P) or *A. solani* (S), with P strain being transmitted also by *N. bakeri*
This classification results in four commonly recognised strains: YP, YS, DP and DS; with natural occurrences of mixed strain infections confirmed. The main strains – Y and D – are distributed worldwide, and subclades of both strains can lead to significant crop diseases. Recent phylogenetic studies have confirmed that yellowing and dwarfing genotypes are separated in distinctive clades, each containing several subclades (Stone *et al*., 2024). These subclades differ in the severity of disease they cause in soybean. However, there is insufficient information about the strains responsible for diseases in other crops (Fig. 2). ##### Fig. 2. #####
Phylogenetic tree of complete and near-complete *Luteovirus glycinis* genomes. Courtesy of Stone *et al*. (2024). The vectors exhibit differing levels of transmission efficiency, with *N. bakeri* demonstrating lower efficacy in transmitting *L. glycinis* from clover to soybean compared to *A. solani*, while *Acyrthosiphon kondoi* is regarded as an inefficient vector (Harrison *et al*., 2005; Congdon *et al*., 2023).

title: Soybean Dwarf Virus
text: Furthermore, even within the same vector species, factors such as host preferences, morphological variations and feeding locations on the soybean can contribute to regional differences in the viral transmission efficiency and the perceived threat to crops (Damsteegt and Voegtlin, 1990). For example, *A. solani* populations are limited and do not typically colonise soybean in the USA, unlike the Japanese *A. solani* biotypes.

title: Soybean Dwarf Virus
text: *L. glycinis* is distributed worldwide. Since its discovery in Japan in 1952 (Tamada *et al*., 1969), the presence of the virus has been confirmed in Australia, New Zealand, the USA, Syria and several European countries, including Czech Republic, Germany, UK and Ireland (Harrison *et al*., 2005; Gaafar and Ziebell, 2020; Luoto *et al*., 2021; Fowkes *et al*., 2021; Niedzicka *et al*., 2025). The presence of *L. glycinis* has been confirmed in a wide range of legumes – soybean, multiple species of beans, peas, chickpeas, lentils and lupins, and a number of clover species – as well as a few other species, such as *Chenopodium* spp. (Tamada, 1970; Congdon *et al*., 2023). Although all these species may host the virus, its deleterious effects vary significantly, ranging from severe symptoms, as described in soybean crops in Japan, to an absence of symptoms, commonly noted in white clover (Tamada, 1970). Even within soybean crops, the severity of infection is influenced by regional characteristics: the virus causes significant disease of soybean in Japan, whereas only mild infections are reported in the USA (Damsteegt *et al*., 2011). In many regions, clover species and other legume species can act as viral reservoirs, facilitating the transmission of the virus to crops. Clovers from perennial pastures can serve as a primary source of viral infection in nearby crops, making the presence of non-crop legume species a critical factor in risk assessment.

title: Soybean Dwarf Virus
text: There are several documented diseases in legume crops caused by *L. glycinis*. 1. Soybean yellowing disease was first documented in Japan during the 1960s. The virus causes severe stunting or yellowing, and yield losses can reach up to 80%. The main symptoms are yellowing of leaves, stunted growth, and reduced seed yield. Mixed infections involving yellowing and dwarfing strains result in more severe symptoms (Hill and Whitham, 2014). 2. Read leaf disease in subterranean clover has been observed in Australia, where the virus causes sporadic outbreaks. Symptoms include reddening of leaves, stunted growth, and in some cases, premature plant death. High virus incidence leads to reduced herbage and growth, losses in seed yield and decreased hay production (Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development, 2018). The virus causes symptoms in other pulse crops, like pea, lentils, common beans and faba beans. Field experiments have clearly demonstrated that the virus can cause up to 56% yield loss in faba beans (Makkouk and Kumari, 2001). However, its economic impact in pulse crops others than soybean and subterranean clover remains largely unexplored. The significance of this threat depends on the region, distribution of legume species in arable margins and pastures, and the presence of vectors. While the soybean dwarfing disease caused significant yield losses in Japan, with all cultivars susceptible to the disease, the same virus found in the USA is not considered a major threat, as plants only exhibit low to moderate symptoms. That discrepancy is likely attributable to variations in the virus strains and transmission vectors, i.e. the main aphid species and its biotype characteristics, such as host preference, transmission efficiency and specificity (Hill and Whitham, 2014).

This underscores the importance of monitoring potential threats in the future, as the introduction of efficient transmission vectors could precipitate a disease outbreak.

title: Soybean Dwarf Virus
text: The main diagnostic methods of *L. glycinis* are ELISA and RT-PCR (Hill and Whitham, 2014). The monoclonal antibodies have been in use since 1989 (D’Arcy *et al*., 1989), and accurate virus-specific ELISA tests from plant tissues are commercially available and can be used on material from plants or aphids. Developed and tested RT-PCR primers are either species or strain specific (Abraham *et al*., 2007; Damsteegt *et al*., 2011). For example, strain-specific multiplex PCR assay has been developed by Schneider *et al*. (2011) and is used by other researchers. Additionally, multiple sequences of virus were assembled via both Sanger and high throughput sequencing and were deposited in GenBank.

title: Soybean Dwarf Virus
text: To establish management practices, it is essential to understand the interactions between virus strains, vectors and potential viral reservoirs. Viral reservoirs, often asymptomatic and found in pastures or wild legume species, serve as the main sources of infection for crops, as infected vectors spread the virus from these reservoirs. One management practice is to avoid planting soybean next to clover pastures. However, in regions where white and/or red clovers are widespread, preventing the infection of *L. glycinis* in the main crop becomes challenging. The main management approach focuses on early-season insecticides applications, eliminating the vectors (aphids) – for example, in the case of subterranean clover pastures, the insecticide application is recommended at 2 and 6 weeks after seedling emergence. Pest management includes further spraying during the season, aligned with the migration pattern of winged aphids, to prevent the later onset of the disease. Additionally, adjusting planting date may also be considered as a potential management tool, soybean crops planted later in the season, after the main migration of winged aphids, are less likely to be severely impacted (Hill and Whitham, 2014; Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development, 2018). At the same time, the virus-resistance Indonesian soybean cultivar “Willis” has been developed, and two different resistance traits are reported and studied. The ongoing soybean breeding program in Japan focuses on introducing the resistance not only in soybean but also common bean (Yamashita *et al*., 2014). The resistance trait has to be introduced to cultivars that are adapted to specific environmental conditions. However, these solutions are not yet commercially available.

title: Red spider mite on tomato-Kenya
text: * Avoid planting new crop next to an infested field. * Avoid continuous cropping of tomato & Solanaceae plants (potato, eggplant, nightshades). * Intercrop tomato with repellent crops e.g. garlic, basil or onion. * Clean & disinfect stakes & twines with chlorine-based products. * Remove residues of previous susceptible plants and destroy them. * Minimize application of broadspectrum pesticides to conserve natural enemies (particularly predatory mites). * Avoid dusty conditions and water stress (irrigate crops regularly & apply mulch to reduce water evaporation). * Avoid high levels of nitrogen which will encourage spider mite reproduction. * Keep the field weed-free especially those that are alternative hosts such as *Solanum nigrum*.

* Start scouting for presence of pest 2-3 weeks after germination by inspecting the leaves and stem base for symptoms
* Look out for:
- swelling and cracking on the base of the stem
- stunted growth of older plants
- wilting and death of seedlings
- oviposition marks on the leaves
- larvae and pupae in the stem base (root collar)
* Institute control measures when 5-10% of the plant population has been infested

title: Bean stem maggot / bean fly-Kenya
text:
* Use botanical insecticides such as neem:
- 100 g of dried leaves in 1 litre warm water (30°C) Kept for 12 hours then filter and spray
* Uproot infested plants and destroy by burning

title: Bacterial wilt on tomatoes-Kenya
text: Bacterial wilt on tomatoes-Kenya

title: Bacterial wilt on tomatoes-Kenya
text: * Carry out soil testing to determine the presence of bacterial wilt before planting. * If irrigating, test the water before planting. * Plant tolerant and certified varieties from reliable nurseries if available, e.g. Ansal F1, Kilele F1 or Zara F1. * Avoid planting crops in infected soil. * Solarise soils by covering them with clear polythene in hot weather for 1 month. * Rotate with maize, beans, garden peas, cabbage, and sweet potatoes to reduce the bacterial inoculum for 3 seasons. * Avoid planting in low-lying, wet areas that are prone to run-off. Prevent surface run off from infected areas to clean areas. * Analyse for the presence of the pathogen in organic manure before use. * Destroy alternative hosts of Solanaceae family near the tomato crop, such as nightshades and Irish potato. * Clean all farm implements with 1% sodium hypochlorite for 10 minutes before use. * Disinfect all farm tools after they have been used in fields with bacterial wilt. Dip farm tools in a Jik solution (500ml for every 10L of water) for at least 5 minutes.

title: Bacterial wilt on tomatoes-Kenya
text: * Begin scouting for the presence of bacterial wilt symptoms throughout the growing crop cycle. * Look out for rapid wilting of the entire plant without yellowing. * Look for drooping of vegetative parts of the entire plant. Infected plants are still green but have lost turbidity even after watering. * Cut the affected stem, place it in a glass of water, and check for a milky, slimy ooze to confirm the presence of bacterial wilt. * Initiate disease control immediately after one plant is affected.

title: Bacterial wilt on tomatoes-Kenya
text: * Uproot and destroy by burning and burying all infected plants. * Diseased plants should be carried away in a container to avoid spilling any affected soil. * Apply wood ash in the affected holes after uprooting plants. * Drench the plant using *Trichoderma* based products. * Apply biopesticides with Chrysophanol 12g/L (e.g. KOBE 1.2 SL or KHITO 1.2 SL).

title: Bacterial wilt on tomatoes-Kenya

Do not empty into drains. * Always consult a recent list of registered pesticides (PCPB).

title: Late blight on tomato-Kenya
text: Late blight on tomato-Kenya

title: Late blight on tomato-Kenya
text: * Avoid planting sites previously planted with tomatoes, potatoes or peppers. * Plant tolerant varieties. * Plant using certified seeds or disease- free seedlings. * Rotate tomatoes with non-solanaceae family crops like bean, maize, cowpea, onion, sweet potato, and carrot. * Do not plant tomatoes next to an already infected field including peppers and potatoes. * Plant tomato seedlings at the recommended spacing for good aeration. * Clean and disinfect all farm implements and equipment with approved products for 10 minutes before and after use. * Stake and prune tall varieties for aeration to reduce chances of disease development. * Avoid planting during wet and cool periods because they favour disease development. * Remove old crop residues and infected plants and destroy them by burying them.

title: Late blight on tomato-Kenya
text:
* Look for symptoms at least three times a week in wet weather. And twice a week in dry weather. Symptoms include:
* Leaf lesions begin as water-soaked spots and later enlarge to black-brown lesions. * In advanced stages, the entire plant is affected and it emits a foul smell. * In high humidity, white fluffy growth may be observed on the leaf surface. * Stems that turn black, dry up and die. * Take action immediately when one plant shows symptoms of the disease.

title: Late blight on tomato-Kenya
text: * It's very difficult to control once the disease is in the crop. Chemical control will almost certainly be required. * Use dry mulch to avoid the spread of disease from splashing.

title: Banana weevil-Kenya
text: * Set up pit fall traps to collect adult weevils in the field before planting. * Use certified, pest-free planting material, preferably tissue cultured plantlets. * Avoid planting banana on old banana fields. * Remove weeds, trash & debris to reduce breeding sites. * Maintain good soil health, e.g. use mulch and apply balanced crop nutrition. * Cut-off old pseudostem, stumps & wind-damaged plants at ground level; burn to destroy.

title: Banana weevil-Kenya
text: * Look out for reddish-brown to black weevils (10-13 mm) with a long, curved snout & hard shells. * Check for grubs/larvae that are creamy white, stout, fleshy, legless, wrinkled & spindle shaped, with a red head. * Check for young infested suckers that are withered & fail to develop. * Check for weak plants with dull yellow green & floppy leaves, easily blown away by wind. * Check your crop for holes in the corm & plant base, extensive root damage, plant breaking at base.

title: Banana weevil-Kenya
text: * Set up weevil traps made of banana stem pieces placed around a stool, turn them over daily & kill weevils hiding underneath. * Put dry, powdered neem seed kernels @ 50g per plant on leaf axis to kill/repel weevils. * Apply 60-100g neem seed powder or neem cake on suckers at planting, repeat at 4 month intervals. * Dip suckers in 20% neem seed solution at planting to repel egg laying adult weevils. * Apply products based on the entomopathogenic fungi *Metarhizium anisopliae var. anisopliae, Beauveria bassiana* or *Paecilomyces lilacinus*. * Apply neem based products (Azadirachtin 0.03%).

title: Banana weevil-Kenya

title: Red spider mite on papaya-Kenya

title: Anthracnose of sorghum-Ethiopia
text: * Resistant hybrids may be available, information is available from research centres and suppliers. * Use certified or clean seed from disease-free plants; this is important as this disease can be transmitted by the seeds. * Remove other susceptable host plants such as grasses which may harbour the disease. * Burn plant residues after harvesting and immediately deep plough the field as the fungus can survive on crop residues. * Rotate sorghum on a 2 year basis with crops other than cereals such as chickpeas or beans. * In poorly rotated fields, plough under infested residues where soil erosion is not a problem.

title: Anthracnose of sorghum-Ethiopia
text: * Monitor the crop from the seedling stage to maturity weekly for signs of disease on the leaves, stalks and the seed panicles. * Look for small circular red/orange lesions with distinct margins on the upper portion of the stalks, leaves and seeds. The lesions can measure 2mm-2cm and can contain dark brown fungal structures. Brown sunken areas can also appear on the stems. * When the first symptoms of the disease are seen, take direct action and remove infected plants.

title: Mango scale on mango-Ethiopia
text:
* Use seedlings that are free of scales
* Use recommended spacing and size of planting holes
* Avoid movement of farm tools, animals, seedlings and fruits from infested areas to the orchard because they can spread the scales
* Use recommended fertilizer rates and irrigation schedules for the mango orchard because healthy plants are less susceptible
* Remove weeds and other plant residues from the orchard

title: Mango scale on mango-Ethiopia
text:
* Scout the orchard fortinightly and inspect the whole plant particularly leaves, branches, twigs and growing points
* Look for soft bodied white scales (1.5-3 mm in diameter) on upper side of the leaves and twigs. Lift the white transparent scale covering to check for live females, crawlers and eggs under the scales
* The females white scale changes to a pink colour when eggs are laid under the scale
* Infested leaves turn pale green to yellow and leaves and branches can eventually die
* Check fruits for external feeding conspicuous pink lessions can be seen around the feeding sites

title: Mango scale on mango-Ethiopia
text:
* Prune to remove infested twigs, leaves and fruits and burn or burry more than 20cm deep
* Remove unnecessary branches before flower setting and after harvesting of the fruit
* Conserve natural enemies by not spraying during high peaks of natural enemies
* Intercrop with sesame, soyabeans or haricot beans to improve the field diversity and to encourage natural enemies
* Application of a liquid soap solution can reduce the problem. Apply at a rate of 1-2 ml per 1 litre of water

text: Maize Stem Borer-Ethiopia

title: Maize Stem Borer-Ethiopia
text:
* Remove crop residues after harvest to kill larvae and pupae left in old stems to prevent carry over to next season crop. These can be used immediately for animal feed or fuel
* Plough (20cm deep) to kill larvae and pupae by burying stems and exposing pupae to natural enemies and heat
* Remove alternative host such as wild sorghums and thick stemmed grasses such as Napier grass
* Intercrop with legumes such as cowpeas, soya, haricot or faba bean
* Rotate with crop such crops as soya and faba bean or field pea
* Use push pull technology with napier grass for pulling and desmodium for pushing the moths from the maize
* Synchronize planting time with low pest occurrence

title: Maize Stem Borer-Ethiopia
text:
* Check the field weekly staring from 2 weeks after emergence
* Look for leaf windowing, holes and tunnelling in the stems and cover of the maize cob
* Look for caterpillars of different stages of development inside the growing shoot and stem
* Look for deadhearts in maize whorls

title: Onion thrips-Ethiopia
text:
* Destroy crop residues and plow fields after harvesting to eliminate the resting sites of the pest
* Avoid planting onion crops in the same field continously to avoid thrip re-infestation
* Prepare the soil well before transplanting onions so encourage fast and healthy growth
* Use pest free seedlings
* Intercropping onion with vegetables such as carrot and cabbage minimize thrips infestation and damage. It also helps to increase the number and activity of predatory thrips (*Aelothrips* spp.) * Remove weeds that may harbour thrips within and around the field
* Use recommended spacing and fertiliser rates
* Maintenance of clean fallow after cropping may be of value as the practice eliminates weeds and volunteer plants in the heads of which adult *T.tabaci* over season

title: Onion thrips-Ethiopia
text:
* Scout regularly starting when plants are at the 4-5 leave stage, check spaces between newly emerged leaves, stem and inner neck of the onions for signs of the pest
* Look for feeding signs such as white or silvery leaf spots, streaks or patches on the leaves
* Use yellow, blue or white sticky trap to monitor and sample pale yellow immature and brown adults
* Scout at least five plants in 10 different parts of the field and the edges of the field where adults infest first
* Take action when thrips number reaches 5 to 10 per plant

title: Onion thrips-Ethiopia
text:
* Mulch with straw to provide shelter for thrip predators, thereby reducing thrip populations
* Use sprinkler irrigation to reduce thrips population if possible
* Spray with neem seed preparation at a rate of 30 kg/ha
* Or commercial product Nimbecidine EC (contains 0.03% Azadirachtin) at lml/Litre of water (or 2.5-3 L/ha). Apply 3 to 4 times fortnightly after a threshold of 5 to 10 thrips per plant are observed

title: Tomato leaf miner-Ethiopia
text:
* Use pest free seedlings and clean transportation boxes
* Uproot and burn crop residues soon after harvest and plough the field to kill the larvae and pupae
* Cover soil with transparent plastic mulch to prevent the insect pupae from transforming to adult
* Rotate tomato with non solanaceous crops such as maize and wheat
* Avoid planting tomatoes near alternative hosts such as pepper, egg plant and wild hosts (eg. *Datura* and *solanum*)
* For greenhouse production use double doors covered with black polythene sheets at the entrance to prevent moth entry

title: Tomato leaf miner-Ethiopia
text:
* Scout the field twice a week from transplanting to harvest
* Check seedlings for presence of eggs and larvae
* Check plants for leaf mining, stem tunneling, borings in buds and fruits
* Look for dark frass inside the mines and rotting fruits
* Use Delta pheremone traps (10 per ha) to trap and monitor adult moths (keep the trap on the ground or crop surface)
* Take action when 100 males per trap per day are captured

title: Tomato leaf miner-Ethiopia
text:
* Selectively remove and burn or bury infested plant materials including fruits
* Infested fruit should be sorted as unmarketable and should be removed from the farm. They should be disposed of in tied polythene bags
* Mass trap male moths using 0.5 mg pheromone lure by depolying 20 to 40 water tray traps per ha depending on the level of infestation (keep the trap on ground level or crop surface and replace the lure monthly)
* Use neem seed preparations (30 kg per ha)
* Plant bottle (calabash) gourd around tomato fields to increase the natural enemy population

title: Yellow rust on wheat (Stripe rust)-Ethiopia
text:
* Remove residues from the previous rust infected crop before planting
* Crop rotation with pulses or other horticultural crops. Remove alternative hosts (e.g. volunteer wheat, barley and wild species)
* Use rust resistance wheat varieties e.g. Mendoyu, Gelan, Sinja and Sanate
* Take care in working in the field the field to not transmit the disease spore
* Prevent movement of infected plants across the field across the fields
* Continuous wheat field monitoring and surveillance that aid to take immediate measures

title: Yellow rust on wheat (Stripe rust)-Ethiopia
text:
* Check fields regularly in early growing season especially during the rainy season when the temperature is cool (10-16ºC)
* Look for rows of tiny yellow, light brownish powdery pustules that form in rows on the leaves and leaf sheathes
* Examine a number of plants throughout the field and take action when the rust symptom are noticed on a single plant. Because with rust diseases the threshold level is zero tolerance
* Action is too late if you find many plants with long rows of yellow coloured powdery pustules, lesions and necrosis across many leaves per plant

title: Yellow rust on wheat (Stripe rust)-Ethiopia
text: * Remove and bury or burn infected plants at the early stage of infection before its expansion to the rest of the field to reduce the initial inoculum source

title: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing)-Ethiopia
text: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing)-Ethiopia

title: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing)-Ethiopia
text:
* This disease is transmitted by the psyllid vector *Trioza
erytreae*
* Avoid planting citrus in monoculture
* Use disease-free material for replanting
* Remove alternative hosts (eg. wild plants, other citrus spp) from around the field
* Encourage natural enemy populations in the orchard (e.g., spiders, lacewings, predatory mites, ladybird beetles, hover flies) by reducing pesticide use in the general area
* Citrus greening symptoms can be confused with zinc deficiency. So use appropriate fertilizers containing zinc micronutrient to avoid confusion
* Enforce phytosanitary measures: it is difficult to ensure plants are free from eggs and nymphs so importation of planting material from affected areas should be prohibited
* Only clean and healthy plants, without any insects on them, should be transported & transplanted into new plantations

title: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing)-Ethiopia
text:
* Monitor regularly the whole year for presence of psyllids and disease symptoms to avoid it spreading
* Monitoring psyllids (vectors): 1) Adults feeding on leaves resemble winged aphids 2) Orange/yellow eggs appearing on the edges of tender young leaves 3) Raised bumps on the underside of leaves hide nymphs, which are small green/yellow scale-like insects
* Disease symptoms: 1) Leaves: pale-yellow, yellow veins and blotchy mottling 2) Whole tree: sparsely foliated, extensive branch dieback and reduced size 3) Fruits: small, lopsided and poorly colored with aborted seeds, severe fruit drop
* Act quickly as soon as symptoms of the disease are seen or when the vector is detected

title: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing)-Ethiopia
text:
* If only a few branches are affected, prune them immediately and bury them more than 60cm deep
* It is important to destroy only very severely infected trees not producing economical yield
* Disinfect tools after pruning each tree with bleach
* Remove any young citrus trees that become infected, as they will never produce fruits and replace with disease free planting material

title: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing)-Ethiopia
text: * There are no registered insecticides in Ethiopia for the management of psyllids on citrus.

title: African bollworm on French beans and snow peas-Kenya

title: African bollworm on French beans and snow peas-Kenya
text: * Avoid rotation with host crops e.g. maize, beans, pepper, eggplants, wheat, barley or sorghum. * Rotate peas with crops like rice and crops from the onion family. * Apply chemicals judiciously to conserve natural enemies (predatory ants, spiders, damselflies, robber flies, parasitic wasps, parasitic flies). * Plough the field after harvest to expose pupae to the sun's heat & natural enemies.

title: African bollworm on French beans and snow peas-Kenya
text: * Look out for caterpillars (larvae) with short hairs along their backs regularly. * Look out for circular holes through pods, bored holes near the fruit stalk or frass. * Take action after observing 1 larvae per row-meter of crop.

title: African bollworm on French beans and snow peas-Kenya
text: * Handpick and destroy caterpillars found. * Spray *Bacillus thuringiensis* based products. * Spray Azadirachtin-based (Neem) products. * Cover the crop using agronets from KALRO to reduce pest spread & infestation.

title: African bollworm on French beans and snow peas-Kenya

title: Leaf miner of black nightshade-Kenya
text: Leaf miner of black nightshade-Kenya

title: Leaf miner of black nightshade-Kenya
text: * Practice crop rotation with non-host plants like maize, sorghum or millet. * Destroy weeds and crop residues by deep ploughing. * Use a Tephrosia hedge to repel leaf miners from the crop. * Avoid high levels of nitrogen fertilization. * Conserve natural enemies (parasitic wasps and ladybird beetles) by providing hedge rows of flowering plants around the farm.

title: Leaf miner of black nightshade-Kenya
text:
* Additional relevant crops: tomato, French beans, soybeans, eggplant, pumpkin. * Look out for:
* Thin, white, winding lines/tunnels on the leaves of plants. * Small yellow and black flies hovering around the crop. * The larva (maggots) that are often pale green or yellow in colour and can grow up to 3 mm long. * White puncture marks on leaves caused by adult laying eggs and they drop early. * Tunnels/irregular mines on the upper/lower surface of leaves both in the nursery and field. * Use direct control when you spot 7 larvae/plant or on 3 leaflets.

title: Leaf miner of black nightshade-Kenya
text: * Rogue the affected seedling in nursery or defoliate the affected leaves. Dispose by burying 30 cm deep or burn to kill larvae. * Destroy leaf miner pupae and crop residue by deep tilling. * Use 1 to 4 yellow sticky cards per 300 square metre field area to capture adult flies. * Spray azadirachtin at a rate of 50 ml in 20 litres of water (neemroc EC). * Hand-pick and destroy mined leaves especially in low infestation and those with the larvae still in the tunnel.

title: Leaf miner of black nightshade-Kenya
text: * When using a pesticide always wear personal protective equipment. * Follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, max number of sprays, restricted re-entry interval. * Always consult recent list of registered pesticides (PCPB). * Chemical control should target the larvae. Spray when larvae are actively feeding on the leaves (in the tunnels).

title: Damping off of tomatoes-Kenya
text: Damping off of tomatoes-Kenya

title: Damping off of tomatoes-Kenya
text: * Plant using certified seeds or clean seedlings from reliable nurseries. * Use sterile well-drained soil, cocopeat or peatmoss media. * Plant seeds in soil treated by solarization or fumigation. * Burn dry trash on a wet seedbed to sterilise it. * Raise nursery beds at least 1m above ground level to improve drainage. Mix topsoil with a thin coating of sand and gravel to improve drainage. * Avoid crowding of seedlings to ensure air circulation. * Don't overwater seedlings or leave them standing in water. * Avoid working with the plants when the soil is too wet. * Avoid planting in previously affected areas. * Sterilize pots, trays, and tools for 30mins by soaking in 1% sodium hypochlorite.

title: Damping off of tomatoes-Kenya
text:
* Look for symptoms daily during first 3 weeks after sowing. * Look out for:
* Sunken necrotic lesion girdling of the stem near the soil line, eventually leading to the collapse and death of the plant. * Thin twisted and discoloured stems (wirestem). * Look for emerged seedlings that are severely stunted and do not recover. * Fuzzy white substance on the surface of the damp soil. * Take action after one to three seedlings are affected.

title: Damping off of tomatoes-Kenya
text: * Remove and bury any infected seedlings immediately. * Drench with *Trichoderma* based products.

title: Damping off of tomatoes-Kenya
text: * When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing. * Follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre-harvest interval, max number of sprays, and restricted re-entry intervals. Do not empty into drains. * Always consult a recent list of registered pesticides (PCPB).

title: Leaf miners on kale-Kenya
text: Leaf miners on kale-Kenya

title: Leaf miners on kale-Kenya
text: * Plough early in the season to expose pupae in the soil. * Destroy crop debris at the end of cropping season to prevent build up of the leafminers. * Cover the soil with a transparent polythene for 1-2 months before planting to kill pupae in the soil. * Plant pest-free seedlings. * Remove weeds as they serve as a reservoir for leafminers. * Practice crop rotation with maize and other cereals.

title: Leaf miners on kale-Kenya
text:
* Additional relevant crop: cabbage. * Look out for:
* Small dark flies on the leaves. * Irregularly shaped mines on the leaves caused by the larvae. * Black frass within the mines. * Wilting of the leaves in severe infestations. * Transparent/yellowish maggots at the broad end of the mines/tunnels. * Use yellow sticky traps for monitoring adults. * Take appropriate control measures when 5% of leaves are affected by the mines.

title: Leaf miners on kale-Kenya

* Cover with plastic mulch -use colored polythene. * Use yellow sticky traps to control of adults.

title: Red spider mites on black nightshade-Kenya
text: Red spider mites on black nightshade-Kenya

title: Red spider mites on black nightshade-Kenya
text: * Remove and destroy the old crop, infested residue and weeds by burning or burying after harvesting. * Plant new crops away from infested fields. * Avoid movement of tools and people from infested fields. * Plant perennial hedges such as pigeon peas that host predatory mites and other natural enemies.

title: Red spider mites on black nightshade-Kenya
text:
* Additional relevant crops: Amaranth, beans, cucumber, eggplant, okra, peas, peppers, pigeon pea, tomato, watermelon. * Look out for:
* Clusters of yellow spots on the upper surface of leaves giving the leaf a speckled or mottled appearance. * Tiny red or yellow-greenish mites on the underside of leaves with whitish particles and webbings. * Mites seen on white paper when leaf is tapped on it. * Take action when 5-7 spider mites seen on three leaves per plant.

title: Red spider mites on black nightshade-Kenya
text: * Use preditory mites e.g. *Phytoseiulus persimilis* and *Amblyseius californicus* from Dudutec in infested crop. * Intercrop with garlic or onion to repel the pest. * Spray a mixture of 1 teaspoon of liquid soap in 4L of water or quarter bar soap in 20L of water. * Spray neem based insecticides- Azadirachtin e.g. Nimbecidine EC or Achook 0.15% at 20-50ml in 20L of water 3-4 times per season. * Use overhead irrigation.

title: Red spider mites on black nightshade-Kenya
text: * When using a pesticide always wear protective equipment. * Follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, max number of sprays, restricted re-entry interval. * Always consult recent list of registered pesticides (PCPB). * None of the below pesticides have been registered in Kenya for use on the blacknight shade crop to control the target pest but they have been registered for use on the target pest on related crops in the same family as black nightshade crop. However, biocontrol agents usually, even when not registered, pose no danger to the crop and user and can be recommended with no cause of alarm.

title: Red spider mites in Irish potato-Kenya
text: Red spider mites in Irish potato-Kenya

title: Red spider mites in Irish potato-Kenya
text: * Avoid dusty conditions around potato crop; they predispose crop to mite infestation. * Avoid planting on the windward side of infested field. Mites can be transmitted by wind. * Keep field free of weeds. * Perform farm operations starting from the non-infested areas to minimize spread. * Apply mulch and incorporate organic matter to increase soil moisture. * Uproot and burn infested plants soon after harvest. * Encourage natural enemies such as *Phytoseiulus persimilis*, predatory mites, ladybird beetles and lacewings by planting flowering strips or hedgerows.

title: Red spider mites in Irish potato-Kenya
text:
* Additional relevant crops: tomato, eggplant, pepper and many common weeds. * Look out for:
* Small red mites barely visible to the naked eye on the underside of leaves. * White to yellow speckling of leaves which later turn pale or bronze with increasing infestation. * Withering and browning of leaves leading to leaf fall. * Take action when 10 mites are seen on 1 plant.

title: Red spider mites in Irish potato-Kenya
text: * Spray a strong jet of water to dislodge mites and destroy their webs. * Apply Azadirachtin (Achook® or Nimbecidine®) at the rate of 40ml in 20L of water) - PHI 1 day. * Soap sprays can also be used. Test on one or two plants to be sure they don’t burn leaves before spraying whole field.

title: Sweet potato weevil-Kenya
text: Sweet potato weevil-Kenya

title: Sweet potato weevil-Kenya
text: * Plant certified pest-free vines. * Try to keep distance to other sweet potato fields and to sweet potato storage facilities. * Crop rotate with cereal crops e.g. maize. * Plant barrier crops (cassava, maize, banana, sorghum) to restrict movement of weevils between fields. * Use pesticides judiciously to conserve natural enemies (predatory ants, earwigs, spiders, ground beetles). * Hill or mulch to avoid exposure of roots to weevils. * Maintain moist soil with irrigation to reduce pest infestation. * Harvest the crop immediately after maturity and remove and destroy crop residues immediately.

title: Sweet potato weevil-Kenya
text: * Look out for: Legless white coloured grub with a comparatively large brown or pale yellow head inside infested tubers or vines. * Thickened & malformed brownish to blackish vines. * Discoloration, cracking, or wilting of damaged vines. * Beetles of 6-8 mm length with a long pointed snout.

title: Sweet potato weevil-Kenya

text: Thrips on tomatoes-Kenya

title: Thrips on tomatoes-Kenya
text: * Use only thrips-free seedlings from certified nurseries. * Control weeds in and around the fields to reduce thrips population. * Use UV-reflective mulches to disrupt host location by the thrips. * Plant early so that crops are well established and able to withstand thrips infestation. * Avoid intercropping tomato with host crops of thrips, e.g. capsicum, onion, nightshade, egg plant, irish potato etc. * Preserve natural enemies e.g. predatory mites, bugs, lacewings and ladybirds by planting flowering plants along borders and by avoiding broad-spectrum pesticides in the crop. * Apply balanced crop nutrition and avoid overuse of nitrogen.

title: Thrips on tomatoes-Kenya
text: * Use blue or yellow sticky traps (one per acre) to check for presence of thrips in your field. * Look for tiny slender brownish insects on leaves & flowers by shaking them on a white piece of paper. * Look for deformation, speckling, or small necrotic patches on the surface of the attacked fruit. * Flowers and bud abortion may occur in heavy infestations. * Take action when 4-6 adults are seen per flower.

title: Thrips on tomatoes-Kenya
text: * Uproot and destroy heavily infested plant/plant parts. * Spray with Azadirachtin based (Neem) products. * Spray *Beauveria bassiana* based products. * Introduce predatory mites (*Amblyseius cucumeris*) when infestation is high.

title: Thrips on tomatoes-Kenya
text: * Use appropriate personal protective equipment. * Follow the instructions on the product label (Dosage, PHI, REI). Dispose chemical waste appropriately. * Consult PCPB list of registered pesticides (https://www.pcpb.go.ke/)

text:
