text: * Plant crop in high densities, as sparce planting increases aphid infestation (80 kg/Ha seed rate). * Prior to planting, remove all weeds to reduce aphid hosts in field area. * Remove nearby host plants and weeds to reduce spread of aphid infestations from other areas into fields. * Plant winter crops early (May-June). * Intercropping with maize to reduce aphid infestation. * Use appropriate irrigation in fields, but avoid excessive nitrogen levels in the soil.

title: Aphids on beans.
text: * Monitor crops once or twice a week during dry periods and before plant flowering. * Observe for colonies of small green/black insects, notably around the stems, growing points and the underside of leaves. * Sooty mould is a characteristic feature of aphid infestation, it grows on sticky honeydew produced by aphids. * Leaf distortion and curling is a sign of aphid feeding. * Ants are commonly associated with aphid infestation as they are attracted to the honeydew. * Use yellow sticky and water pan traps to monitor for aphids. * Undertake direct control methods 15-20% plants are found to be infested.

title: Aphids on beans.
text: * Prune leaves showing infestation symptoms. * Plant flowering plants as a border to attract natural enemies (e.g. wasps and syriphids). * Spray crops with strong jets of water to remove aphids from plants. * Spray plants with insecticidal soap mixed with water (ratio of 1:9) once a week. * Spray with neem oil products once a week for 4 weeks (4.5 ml/10 m2). Contact your local agro-input supplier to organise access of such products.

title: Late blight on tomato.
text: CABI: Late blight on tomato.

title: Late blight on tomato.
text:
* Late blight is a fungi-like mould disease which can affect the leaves, stems and fruits
* Plant resistant varieties if available
* Transplant disease-free seedlings (seedlings without symptoms and not from an infected crop)
* Keep wide plant spacing (80cm X 50cm) to reduce the spread of disease by improving aeration and plant-to-plant contact
* Support the plants with sticks and prune for better aeration. Do not do this when conditions are wet since the disease can be spread by people and tools
* Disinfect hands and tools after working on the infected plants to prevent the spread of the disease to healthy plants. Use household bleach or 5% sodium hypochlorite
* Water in the morning so the leaves can dry in the sun
* Avoid planting during wet and cool periods
* Use dry mulch to reduce water splash and therefore avoid spread of disease
* Apply recommended rates of nitrogen fertilizer as high rates increase likelihood of disease
* Remove and burn debris from tomatoes and other solanaceous crops (potato, peppers and eggplant) after harvest
* Do not plant solanaceous crops (e.g. tomato, Irish potato, pepper, eggplant, nightshade) on land that suffered from the disease in the previous season or near land that currently suffers from the disease
* Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops such as beans, sweet potato, maize, cowpea, soybean, groundnuts, onion, carrots for 2 growing seasons

title: Late blight on tomato.
text:
* Monitor at least twice per week for symptoms and on a daily basis during the raining season since wet and humid conditions favour the disease
* Look for irregular greasy greyish patches on the leaves which expand rapdily under damp/humid conditions. These patches are an early symptom of the disease
* Look for brown elongated lesions on the stems and brown-green blotches or spots on the tomato fruits. These are symptoms of the later stages of the disease
* Look for white downy moulds at the margin of affected areas on the lower leaf surface
* When dry weather is expected, some infection symptoms might be tolerated and infected plant parts can be removed. When wet, cool weather (< 24°C) is expected, 2-4 plants with symptoms per ¼ acre are enough to consider quick action.

title: Late blight on tomato.
text:
* If plant parts show early symptoms, remove the infected plant parts in dry conditions. Carry the diseased materials away in a closed container to prevent spreading the disease. Burn the planting material or bury to at least 1 m deep. Do not compost
* Neem has a slight anti-fungal effect. Spray 50 ml of neem oil with some soap per 10 litres of water within 8 hours of mixing, and every 7-14 days until no more fungal infection appears. Ask your local input suppliers to organise such products if neem trees do not grow in your area. * If the plants are badly infected/show later symptoms then remove the entire plants in dry conditions. Carry the diseased materials away in a closed container to prevent spreading the disease. Burn the planting material or bury to at least 1 m deep. Do not compost.

title: Aphids on tea.
text: CABI: Aphids on tea.

title: Aphids on tea.
text: * Actively remove weeds and alternate hosts from the field and surrounding area (including mango, cocoa, coffee and magnolia). * Maintain sufficient nutrient levels in the soil to ensure promoted plant development to withstand potential aphid infestations. * Avoid the use of broad spectrum insecticides to conserve natural enemies such as spiders, parasitic wasps, lacewings and ladybugs). * Plant resistant varieties if locally available. * Encourage the presence of natural enemies such as predatory ladybug beetles by planting flowing plants such as marigold as a border crop. Marigold can also act as a trap crop for aphid control.

title: Aphids on tea.
text: * Monitor crops roughly one week from the seedling stage, observe the underside of leaves and plant stems for aphid presence. * Adult aphids are roughly 1-2 mm long, with black-brown/red/green bodies. * Nymphs are roughly 1-1.5 mm long, with lighter black/brown bodies. Both the adults and nymphs are commonly found on the underside of leaves or on stems. * Symptoms of aphid infestation include distored leaf development, wilting, yellowing and rolling/folding. * Ants are commonly associated with aphid infestation due to the secretion of honeydew. Black sooty mould may also develop on the honeydew. * Consider direct control actions when 30% or more of crops show signs of infestations of are found with aphids.

title: Aphids on tea.
text: * Collect and destroy infested plant parts by burning. * Use of soap spray solution (1 teaspoon of liquid soap per litre of water) to spray the leaves to remove aphids from the plant. * Control ant populations using ant bait stations or with tape on the plant stems, this will expose aphids to natural predators.

title: Aphids on watermelon.
text: CABI: Aphids on watermelon.

title: Aphids on watermelon.
text: * Remove weeds and alternate hosts (such as citrus and other solonaceous crops) from the field and surrounding area. * Intercropping with onion or garlic to reduce aphid populations on your crop. * Separate early and late planting areas to minise the risk of aphids spreading from one field to another. * Avoid the use of broad spectrum insecticides to conserve natural enemies such as parasitic wasps, spiders and ladybugs. * Use of resistant varieties to aphid infestations if locally available. * Use of row covers to prevent early infestation and potential virus transmission, covers can be left on crops until flowering stage to protect from pest activity.

title: Aphids on watermelon.
text: * Monitor for aphids weekly or a week after crops are planted, observe the underside of leaves of runners for insect presence. * Adult aphids are light/dark green, pear-shaped, grow up to 1-1.5 mm long and are commonly found on the underside of leaves and on stems. * Symptoms of aphid infestation include yellowing of leaves, stunted growth and leaf curling. * Sooty black mould may also be observed during aphid infestations due to the secretion of honeydew. * If 20% or more of runners are infested then consider direct control actions.

title: Aphids on watermelon.
text: * Use of parasitic wasps as biocontrol (such as *Lysiphlebus testaceipes*). * Prune heavily infested plant parts and destroy by burning. * Use of soap spray (1 tablespoon of liquid soap with 1 litre of water) on all leaf surfaces to kill aphids. * Use of garlic spray (one garlic bulb, 1 litre of water, 1 tablespoon of liquid soap and 1 teaspoon of cayenne pepper powder). This solution will last for a week in the refrigerator. * Use of stinging nettle spray (fill a quarter of a container with nettle and cover in water, leave to ferment for 3-4 weeks. Mix 1 part of the fermented solution with 7 parts water) to repel aphids.

title: Citrus blackfly.
text: CABI: Citrus blackfly.

title: Citrus blackfly.
text: * Remove weeds and alternate hosts of blackfly (e.g. guava and pomegranate) from neighbouring areas to reduce the presence of blackfly populations. * Improve spacing and air circulation within citrus orchards by pruning infested plant areas to reduce suitable habitat for blackflies and population spread. * Avoid the use of wide spectrum pesticides so to conserve the natural enemies of blackfly such as parasitoids, ladybird and lacewing.

title: Citrus blackfly.
text: * Monitor citrus trees for symptoms of blackfly infestation, also observe trees for distored leaves and ant presence. * Symptoms of blackfly infestation include sticky honeydew accumlating on leaves and stems and the appearance of sooty black mould. Ants are commonly associated with the presence of blackflies due to the honeydew deposits. * Adults are 1-1.7 mm long, black/grey insects. Young adults are initially orange bodied which darkens over time. The wings have pale markings in a band, with the legs having pale-yellow markings. * Larvae and pupal stages can be observed as sedintary, small black scales attached to the underside of leaves. * Eggs are found on the underside of leaves, they are golden brown and darken prior to hatching.

title: Citrus blackfly.
text: * Control ant populations to reduce their ability to protect blackflies from natural enemies. * Use of parasitic wasps (e.g. *Encarsia perplexa* and *Amitus hesperidum* to reduce blackfly populations. * Use of fungi *Ascgersoni aleurodis* or *Aegerita webberi* to control larvae and pupae. * Use of neem seed extract spray (4%) to reduce blackfly populations and not harm natural enemies.

title: False codling moth on citrus.
text: CABI: False codling moth on citrus.

title: False codling moth on citrus.
text: * Remove weeds and alternate hosts from the orchard and surrounding areas (such as mango, cotton, guava etc.). * Use appropriate levels of irrigation, as overwatering has been noted to increase infestation levels. * Remove residual plant material leftover from the previous harvest to reduce potential spread of infestation into new crops. * Avoid the use of broad spectrum insecticides to conserve natural enemies such as ants, spiders and parasitic wasps.

title: False codling moth on citrus.
text: * Actively monitor for false codling moth from seedling stage through to the fruiting stage. * Symptoms of infestation are difficult to identify to the pest activity occuring internally within plant parts. * Eggs are less than 1 mm long, oval and flattened. They can be found laid in rows or individually. * Larvae are yellow/white with dark spots. Colouration changed during development to bright red/pink with a yellow/brown head (15 mm long). Young larvae are commonly found burrowed into leaves and fruit. * Open fallen citrus fruit and observe for larval presence. Be sure to destroy fruit after inspection by burning or burying 60-90 cm deep. * Use pheromone bait traps to catch adult moths (1 trap per 5 acres), inspect every week. If more than 5 moths are caught in a trap then consider direct control actions for immediate use.

title: False codling moth on citrus.
text: * During low infestation, handpick and destory larvae by burning or burying. Do this during the early morning or late afternoon when the caterpillars are most likely to be outside of the fruit. * Collect fallen and infested fruit and place in a clear, plastic bag and leave in the sun to kill any larvae. * If available, release Trichogrammoidea spp. Parasitoids or other pest enemies to control existing populations. * Use of specialised pheromone traps (1 trap per 5 acres) using anti-mating chemicals to disrupt mating behaviour between male and female moths.

title: Fruit flies on banana.
text: CABI: Fruit flies on banana.

title: Fruit flies on banana.
text: * Undertake appropriate phytosanitary procedures. Only use planting materials from approved sources and do not use from areas known to be threatened by fruit fly infestations. * Cover immature banana with polythene or paper bags within one month of flowering to prevent fruit fly accessibility. * Removal and destruction of plant residue from previous harvests and fallen fruit to kill any larvae present. * Collect fallen fruit in a black polythene bag. Tie up and leave in the sun to kill any larvae. * Rake and disturb the soil below banana trees to expose pupae to the environment, leading to dessication or predation. * Harvest fruit at physiological maturity before they ripen to reduce the ability of the flies to lay eggs.

title: Fruit flies on banana.
text: * Monitor plantations regularly for fruit fly presence and symptoms, especially during fruiting stage of crops. * Adults are small flies, roughly 5-8 mm long with black and yellow colourations. Larvae are roughly 10 mm long, white maggots which develop into brown pupae. * Observe fruit for signs of egg-laying, this will be small holes in the surface of the fruit. * Collect fallen fruit and check inside for the presence of maggots. * Use 10 pheromone traps within the plantation. If 2-3 adult fruit flies are caught per trap every week then consider direct control actions.

title: Fruit flies on banana.
text: * Use of heat treatment on fallen fruit to destroy larvae. * Use of cold treatment (below 15 degrees celsius) on stored fruit for 5 days to kill any fruit flies and/or larvae/pupae living inside fruit. * Use of neem oil or seed extract (4%) spray on foliage to kill pupating larvae and deter oviposition.

title: Fruit fly on cucurbits.
text: CABI: Fruit fly on cucurbits.

title: Fruit fly on cucurbits.
text: * Deep plough the field during winter to expose and damage any overwintering pupae. * Undertake appropriate phytosanitary procedures. Only use planting materials from approved sources and do not use from areas known to be threatened by fruit fly infestations. * Cover immature vegetables with polythene or paper bags within one month of flowering to prevent flruit fly accessibility. * Removal and destruction of plant residue from previous harvests to kill any larvae present. * Collect fallen vegetables in a black polythene bag. Tie up and leave in the sun to kill any larvae.

title: Fruit fly on cucurbits.
text: * Monitor fields regularly for fruit fly presence and symptoms, especially during fruiting stage of crops. * Adults are small flies, roughly 5-8 mm long with black and yellow colourations. Larvae are roughly 10 mm long, white maggots which develop into brown pupae. * Observe crops for signs of egg-laying, this will be small holes in the surface of the vegetables. * Collect fallen crops and check inside for the presence of maggots. * Use 3-4 pheromone traps (contact local extension officer for advice on what pheromone to use) within the field. If 2-3 adult fruit flies are caught per trap every week then consider direct control actions.

title: Fruit fly on cucurbits.
text: * Collect infested and damaged fruit and destroy by burning or burying deep in the ground. * Use of heat treatment on fallen fruit to destroy larvae. * Use of cold treatment (below 15 degrees celcius) on stored crops for 5 days to kill any fruit flies and/or larvae/pupae living inside fruit. * Use of bait pheromone traps to attract fruit flies and reduce populations within field.

title: Black cutworm on cotton.
text: UK, CABI: Black cutworm on cotton.

title: Black cutworm on cotton.
text: * Avoid planting cotton in fields previously used to grow alternate host crops, such as chickpea, groundnut and onion. * Avoid planting cotton in areas which were previously meadow or pasture land. * Use certified, disinfected seeds to avoid introduction of the pest into your field. * Remove weeds to reduce egg presence during the growing season. * Flood the field for 6 hours during the seeding stage (after germination) to drown any caterpillars, wait 2-4 days before soil preparation when the soil has dried. Subsequent irrigation (3-6 hours) will vary based on soil type and climate. * Kill and burn post-harvest plant material and wait at least 2 months before further use to kill any pupae or other insect stages. * Avoid intercropping/growing near to host crops such as maize. * Plough in the Autumn and use shallow tillage to reduce late autumn/early spring plant growth. * Avoid use of broad spectrum insecticides to conserve natural enemies such as spiders, minute pirate bugs, damselflies and lacewing larvae. * Consult and follow local dates for sowing, killing/burning, phytosanitary control and weed control.

title: Black cutworm on cotton.
text: * Cutworms are small (1-2 cm long), grey caterpillars which primarily feed on seedlings and young plants during the night. In the day they are found burrowed in the soil or plant stems. * Observe seedlings for shotholes caused by young larvae. * Later stage instars become active only at night. Observe the base of plants and surrounding soil for cutworm presence. * During plant growth stages, note that cutworm larvae can burrow into stems, so observe for boreholes. * Cutworm caterpillars are light/dark grey with no other markings and can grow up to 1-2 cm long. * Adult moths have a black dagger shape on the outer margins of the wings. * If 5-10 caterpillars are identified per 10 plants then consider undertaking direct control actions.

title: Black cutworm on cotton.
text: * Actively remove weeds in fields to reduce available space for egg laying. Destroy by burning. * Irrigate land for short periods (3-6 hours) to kill pupae and reduce cutworm larvae feeding activity. * Search the undergrowth of fields and soil around the base of seedlings. Actively remove and destroy larvae. * Use of *Bacillus thuringiensis* to reduce populations of larvae. * Use yellow blacklight traps (during summer) and pheromone traps to control adult populations.

title: Chironomus on rice.
text: UK, CABI: Chironomus on rice.

title: Chironomus on rice.
text: * Reduce the slope of paddocks to create uniform, shallow water to reduce potential infestations of bloodworm larvae. * Undertake appropriate tillage of land prior to planting to expose any larvae in the soil to natural enemies. * Soil management practices such as crushing and removing plant material by a tractor with paddle wheels. * Flooding and sowing of smaller paddock areas are suggested to reduce bloodworm infestation and crop damage. * Use pre-germinated seeds to reduce the risk period of seed attacks by larvae as the pest doesn't damage secondary root systems. * Use independent irrigation in nurseries to prevent the spread of pest.

title: Chironomus on rice.
text: * Bloodworm larvae have distinct dark heads and can grow up to 18 mm long. Larvae are commonly red but can also be variations of brown and black. * Aquatic earthworms are commonly misidentified as bloodworms. However, they are much larger, growing up to 75 mm long and lack a distinct head capsule. * Larvae can burrow into seeds and consume the endosperm, feed on shoots and seedlings, and attach the root system (causing stunted growth). * High infestation levels of larvae can destabilize soil surfaces, resulting in poor plant anchorage. * Adults are pale green/brown midges (up to 15 mm long) with long antennae. * To monitor larval populations, take a soil sample using a core sampler or a kitchen ladle. Take 3 core samples, if the number of larvae in 2 of the 3 samples are greater than 10 (serious infestation) then consider direct control actions immediately.

title: Chironomus on rice.
text: * Periodic applications of irrigation and dry conditions throughout the vegetative stage of crop after transplanting. * Contact your local agro-dealer or agriculture agency for approved treatments of the pest in your area. * Undertake fangueo post-harvest to reduce the likelihood of larvae surviving into the following season.

title: Rice thrips.
text: UK, CABI: Rice thrips.

title: Rice thrips.
text: * Remove plant residue from previous harvest to reduce suitable habitat for pest overwintering. * Use certified, resistant seed varieties. * Plough soil 2-3 times before planting to control weed populations which could host thrip populations. * Flood rice field to submerge rice seedlings and young plants for 2 days to control thrip populations. * Optimum seed rate (74 kg/Ha) should be used to avoid dense vegetation. Seed rates vary according to seedbed preparation method. * Avoid water stress conditions, maintain the optimum level of water in the nursery and field. * Avoid use of broad spectrum insecticides to conserve natural enemies (e.g. dragonflies, spiders, waterbugs, predatory thrips, and ladybugs).

title: Rice thrips.
text: * Regularly monitor fields 3 times per week for the first 30 days after transplanting. * Observe crops for damage on leaves and stems and leaf rolling, which are signs of thrip activity. * Typical symptoms also include stunted plant growth, wilted leaves with fine yellow lines or/and silver streaks and seedling death (in severe infestations). * Young plants (1-2 weeks after transplanting) are most affected by thrip infestations. * Using wet hands, brush hands across the top of plants. Any thrips present will stick to your hand. * If 10-20 thrips are observed on your hand, then consider direct control actions.

title: Rice thrips.
text: * Under high levels of thrip infestation, flood the field for 2 days (especially when rice plants are young as they are most at risk from damage at this stage). * Flood the nursery and drain after 15 minutes.

title: Sheath blight on rice.
text: UK, CABI: Sheath blight on rice.

title: Sheath blight on rice.
text: * Increase plant spacing (25x25 cm) to increase aeration and reduce humidity which is favourable for fungal spread. * Practise appropriate use of fertiliser to promote plant growth, and reduce impacts of fungal infections. Overuse of nitrogenous fertilizers may damage crops and make them more susceptible to pest damage. * Remove weeds from fields and neighbouring areas to reduce availability of hosts for fungal spread. * Appropriate land management (i.e. deep ploughing and levelling) to promote fungus-free soil. * Avoid high seeding rates.

title: Sheath blight on rice.
text: * Monitoring should start from panicle differentiation until heading. Scout crops 3 times a week for signs of fungi, especially during warm wet periods. * Symptoms of sheath rice blight include round lesions (1-3 cm long) on leaf sheaths or dark green spots located at the bottom of rice plants. The centers of the spots turn yellow/grey/white before turning brown. * If fungal infection is identified throughout the field then consider taking direct control measures.

title: Sheath blight on rice.
text: * Remove infected plant material and destroy by burning. * In heavily infected areas, drain the field and allow to dry. Increase circulation between plants and allow good sun coverage to suppress further fungal development and spread.

title: Cotton aphid.
text: UK, CABI: Cotton aphid.

title: Cotton aphid.
text: * Rotate planting of cotton with onion or maize. Be sure not to plant alternate hosts such as cucumber or tomato. * Use of resistant varieties. Contact local extension officer of agro-dealer for locally available varieties. * Avoid the use of broad spectrum insecticides to conserve natural pest species such as ladybird beetles, lacewings and parasitoids. * Top the plants following boll opening to remove the upper leaves where aphids primarily feed. This reduces infestation on lower areas of the plant.

title: Cotton aphid.
text: * Actively monitor crops for symptoms of infestation and aphid presence by eye and using a hand lens. * Symptoms of aphid infestation include yellowing and curling of leaves. Stunted growth and distortion of plant stems. * A characteristic feature of infestation is the presence of black sooty mould growing on the honeydew secretion from aphids. * Adults are 2 mm long, with black heads and yellow/green bodied. * Nymphs are pale yellow/green, roughly 1-1.5 mm long. * Consider direct control actions if more than 5 aphids are found per plant when 20 are surveyed.

title: Cotton aphid.
text: * Using a strong jet of water, wash aphids off the underside of leaves during early and low infestations roughly once a week. * Prune heavily infested plant parts and destroy by burning. * Control ant populations, as ants are associated with aphids due to their honeydew secretions and protect aphids from natural enemies. Use a band of sticky tape around the base of plants to trap ants. * Use of neem extract (50 g neem seed cake per litre of water and 2 tablespoons of liquid soap). Spray no more than twice per season. * Use of liquid soap solution (10 ml liquid soap, 85 g chopped/ground garlic, 1 litre of water and 50 ml of vegetable oil). Add 2 litres of water to the solution before use then spray.

title: Cotton seed bug.
text: UK, CABI: Cotton seed bug.

title: Cotton seed bug.
text: * Remove alternate hosts from the field, these include apple, avocado, grapes and pomegranate. * Avoid the use of broad spectrum insecticides to conserve natural enemies, including parasitic wasps and lacewings. * Use okra as a border trap crop to help prevent pests from entering the crop field. * Harvest cotton as soon as possible so to reduce the period for heavy infestations to occur.

title: Cotton seed bug.
text: * Actively monitor for infestation during growth periods, inspect seeds and internal areas of plants by hand for adults and nymphs. * Eggs are oval shaped (0.25-0.1 mm), pale yellow/pink and found laid close to seeds in clutches of 2-4 or individually. * Nymphs have pink/orange abdomens and brown heads. Brown colouration darkens during development (14-20 day period). Primarily found on seeds as this is their food source. * Adults are 3.8-4.3 mm long, with brown/black colourations across the body. Males have rounded abdomens and females have elongated, trunk-shaped abdomens. Notably the adult has pale green/yellow striped on the legs and antennae. * As the pest feeds on seeds, seed germination may be reduced by up to 88% in high infestations. * Common symptoms of infestation are pink lint as insects are crushed in cotton plants, large numbers of the insect on neighbouring buildings, foul odour emitting from insects.

title: Cotton seed bug.
text: * In the early morning, walk through the field and brush off any adults found on the plants, crush any fallen adults to kill. * Remove heavily infested plant parts and destroy by burning away from the field. * Use of biocontrol agents such as the entomopathogenic fungi *Beauverua bassiana* and *Metarhizium anisopliae*. Contact your local extension officer for further advice on control options available in your area.

title: Cutworms on tea.
text: UK, CABI: Cutworms on tea.

title: Cutworms on tea.
text: * Avoid planting crops in or near fields with a known history of cutworm infestations. * Prior to planting, plough the field to expose any cutworm larvae to the sun and natural enemies. * Remove weeds from the plantation and neighbouring areas to reduce host plant availability. * Avoid the use of broad spectrum insecticides to conserve natural enemies such as parasitic wasps, ants, spiders and lacewings. * Plant sunflowers as a border around tea plantations as a trap crop.

title: Cutworms on tea.
text: * Monitor for cutworm activity during the early morning and late evening as this is when larvae are most active above ground. * Symptoms of cutworm infestation include feeding activity on leaves, stalks and stems by larvae which can result if heavy defoliation. Larvae can also feed on roots and tubers, leaving small holes. * Damage is more severe under dry conditions, deeper below the soil surface. * Eggs are found stuck to plant material and on soil, pale red/pink in colour and roughly 0.5 mm in diameter. * Larvae are 2-4 cm long, with dark brown/grey heads and cream/brown bodies. * Pupa are 20-30 mm long, yellow/brown which darkens during development. * Adult moths have a wingspan of 4-45 mm with grey/brown wings. Females have grey hind wings and males have silver/white hind wings. * Consider direct control actions as soon as larval activity is identified.

title: Cutworms on tea.
text: * Handpick larvae during the early morning and late evening during low infestations. * Use biological control measures such as the release of *Trichogramma* spp. Release weekly for 3 weeks as soon as adult moths are identified. * Apply a paste solution of molasses, sawdust and eggshells around the base of plant stems to kill larvae before they can climb up and eat away at the crops.

title: Helopeltis bugs on cotton.
text: UK, CABI: Helopeltis bugs on cotton.

title: Helopeltis bugs on cotton.
text: * Remove alternative host plants from the field and surrounding area (such as coffee, mango, avocado and cocoa). * Prior to planting, remove all weeds from the field to prevent spread of pests via host weeds. * Apply a band of grease or petroleum jelly along the base of plant stems, 15 cm above the ground. * Avoid the use of broad spectrum insecticides as these may kill natural enemies of pests, such as parasitic wasps.

title: Helopeltis bugs on cotton.
text: * Actively monitor crops for feeding punctures and lesions, seedling and shoot damage, and necrotic areas on plants due to feeding activity. * Eggs are banana-shaped (1.8-2 mm long) with two air-tubes protruding from the upper exposed end. * Nymphs are found in various sizes and colours depending on their specific developmental stage. However, the majority have a similar dorsal spine to the adult. Commonly found with red spots. * Adults are red (female) or orange (male) with dark brown antennae. Adults have characteristic legs similar to that of mosquitoes. Size varies between the sex, ranging between 6-8 mm long. * Survey fields using sweep nets (collect insects caught after 10 sweeps and monitor for helopeltis) and by hand. * Nymphs are notably found on younger cotton leaves towards the top of plants. Hold the plant stem towards light to help locate eggs.

title: Helopeltis bugs on cotton.
text: * Hand pick and destroy (by burning) any pest insects found during inspection of crops. * Prune heavily infested plant parts and destroy by burning away from the field. * Use of biocontrol such as *Trichogramma*. Control your local extension officer for advice on specific release information for your crop.

title: Red spider mite on coffee.
text: UK, CABI: Red spider mite on coffee.

title: Red spider mite on coffee.
text: * Use resistant crop varieties, contact local extension officer for advice on locally available varieties. * Plant nurseries away from areas of known infestation. * Apply mulch to improve health of crops and reduce impact from potential infestations. * Plant perennial hedges (e.g. pigeon pea) to attract predatory mites to kill *O. coffeae*. * Actively remove weeds form plantations to reduce suitable habitat for mite infestations. * Undertale suitable phytosanitary practices, wash clothing and tools used in infested areas before entering new ones. * Avoid the use of broad spectrum insecticides to conserve natural predators such as predatory mites, spiders, lacewings, and ladybird beetles.

title: Red spider mite on coffee.
text: * Actively monitor crops for mite activity, note that it may be hard to distinguish between mite infestation symptoms and nutrient deficiency. If so, observe 10 random leaves per 20 plants for small red mites. * Mite colonies are commonly found on the supper surface of old leaves, but may move to either surface of young leaves under drought conditions and heavy infestations. * Mites are around 360µm long, with dark red, oval bodies. Males may appear to have a slightly elongated dorsal end. * Symptoms of infestation include yellow spots on leaves, turning brown and necrotic under heavy infestations. * Defoliation may occur in heavily infested plants. * When mites are identified or symptoms first appear, consider undertaking direct control actions.

title: Red spider mite on coffee.
text: * Remove infested plant parts and destroy by burning. * Use of a soap spray (3 tablespoons of liquid soap with 4 litres of water). Apply during the early morning or late afternoon. * Use of neem seed kernel extract spray (grind 500 g of neem seed kernels and mix with 10 litres of water). Spray during dry periods as rainfall will wash off the solution. * Use of flour solution spray (2 cups of flour with 5-10 litres of water). Apply to the underside of leaves, when the solution dries during the day any mites present will be encrusted in flour and die.

title: Root-knot nematodes in coffee.
text: UK, CABI: Root-knot nematodes in coffee.

title: Root-knot nematodes in coffee.
text: * Use of healthy, certified seeds to prevent the use of infested seeds in fields. * Use of resistant varieties such as Nemaya or hybrids (contact local extension office for advice on locally available options). * Undertake suitable phytosanitary actions, clean machines and tool after use in a field. * Avoid the use of surface irrigation from infested fields to healthy ones. * Use of border trap plants such as marigold to attract nematodes away from coffee crop. * Use of border trap plants such as marigold to attract nematodes away from coffee crop.

title: Root-knot nematodes in coffee.
text: * Actively monitor plantation and nurseries for symptoms of nematode infestation. * Characteristic symptoms of nematode infestations are root knots on the roots, therefore focus monitoring primarily on seedlings and young plants. * In mature plants, symptoms include stunted growth, wilting and yellowing of leaves. Severe infestation may cause plants to turn brown and die. * Consider direct control actions as soon as symptoms are observed.

title: Root-knot nematodes in coffee.
text: * Uproot and destroy heavily infected plants and destroy by burning. * Add compost to the soil to reduce the impact of nematode infestations. * Actively remove weeds and infested crop material to reduce the likelihood of infestation spread. * Deep plough soil to expose any nematodes to the environment (e.g. the sun) to kill pests. * Use of neem cake in the soil to reduce the reproductive ability of nematodes. * Use of basil leaf extract spray (grind 50 g of basil leaves, soak overnight in 2-3 litres of water. Strain solution and add 10 ml of liquid soap).

title: Cotton boll worm in chickpea-Ethiopia.
text: Cotton boll worm in chickpea-Ethiopia.

title: Cotton boll worm in chickpea-Ethiopia.
text: * Remove crop residues from the field, because the pupal stage hibernates inside. * Plough 2-3 times in the dry season to expose bollworm caterpillars and pupae to predators and sun. * Soil solarisation with plastic mulch 3-4 days ahead of sowing. * Plant at the end of rainy season (late August). * Closely space plants (10cm \* 40cm intra and inter row space instead of 20cm \* 60 cm). * Apply Di Ammonium Phosphate (DAP) at a rate 25kg/ha to reduce succulent vegetative growth attractive to bollworms. * Remove alternative hosts and off type crops such as Abutilum indicum. * Intercrop with repellent crops, e.g. chickpea with sorghum. * Plant Marigold round the field 6 days after sowing of chickpea to trap boll worm moth. * Trap crop with less important crops (cotton). * Rotate chickpea with wheat or sorghum. Do not rotate with other leguminous crops.

title: Cotton boll worm in chickpea-Ethiopia.
text: * Inspect chickpea fields from two weeks after seedling emergence, via vegetative to flowering stage. * Look for eggs and caterpillars on the lower blade leaves, blossoms and pods. The caterpillar has white-yellowish to reddish brown body with a dark brown to black head capsule. * Action should be taken when 2-4 caterpillars are observed in one-meter planting row. * Urgent action should be taken when 3 to 4 caterpillars are observed in one-meter planting row. * Look skeletonized leaves and bored pods of chickpea, but then action is often too late.

title: Cotton boll worm in chickpea-Ethiopia.
text: * Beat bollworm caterpillars off the plant onto a below sheet using a stick or by hand. Pick and kill early onset of caterpillars, remove affected plant pods. * Apply botanicals such as Neem seed oil (mix 0.075 litre of Neem oil with 15 litre of water), Neem seed kernel extract (0.75 litres of Neem seed kernel extract in 15 litres of water). * Spray biopesticide Nuclear polyhydrosis virus (HaNPV products). * Release chickens and crows to bollworm infested fields.

title: Cotton boll worm in chickpea-Ethiopia.
text: * Good coverage of sprays is needed because the insecticides must get into contact with the caterpillars to kill. * When using a pesticide or botanical, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre-harvest interval, max number of sprays, restricted re-entry interval. Do not empty into drains and water sources. * Always consult recent list of registered pesticides of Ethopia.

title: Cotton boll worm in chickpea-Ethiopia.
text:
### Spray 1-2 times Spinosad (such as 5% WP). Contact pesticides ###
WHO toxicity class III (Slightly acute hazardous to humans) Restricted entry interval = 4 days after spray. Pre-harvest interval PHI= 7 days
Risks to pollinators and parasitoids. Thus, spray after sunset or before flowering to protect bees. Slightly hazardous to parasitoids. ### Datura stromanium botanical pesticide (called መስተናገር ጣልያን) leaf extract (0.75 litre Datura in 15 litre water) ###
Do not use higher doses, because it’s toxic to non-target organisms and even humans. Do not spray without personal protective equipment. Mix with adjuvants and stickers such as soap to increase it’s efficacy
### Spray Fenitrothin (such as 50%EC) 1-2 times. ###
WHO toxicity class-II (Moderately acute hazardous to humans) Extremely harmful to most beneficial organisms including bees. Thus, do not spay onto flowering chickpea or spray after sunset. REI= 24 hours, PHI= 5 days
### Spray Deltametrin (such as 2.8%EC) 1-2 times. ###
WHO class-II (Moderately acute hazardous to humans) Harmless to birds, spiders and hoverflies, but harmful to bees and many other natural enemies. PHI 3 days, REI 14 days

title: Black armyworm on maize-Ethiopia.
text: Black armyworm on maize-Ethiopia.

title: Black armyworm on maize-Ethiopia.
text:
* Remove weeds such as Amaranthus and grassy weeds since they are food for young armyworm caterpillars
* Plough and harrow field thoroughly after harvest or before planting to expose pupae from the soil to natural enemies and desiccation Note that ploughing reduces water retention of soil and destroys soil structure. * Crop rotation has little effect on the pest because the adult moths are mobile and can immigrate to new maize fields. You may rotate maize with non-cereals such as legumes (haricot and soya bean, cow and pigeon peas). * Avoid nearby planting or rotation with hosts such as teff, barely, oat, millet, sorghum, wheat

title: Black armyworm on maize-Ethiopia.
text:
* Monitor from germination till late vegetative maize
* Armyworm moth: stout-bodied, 1 ½ to 2 cm long, wing 3 cm. Forewings dark brown with grey-dark markings. Hind wings white with dark edges
* Place 1 sex pheromone trap / 100 m around maize. When more than 30 moths a trapped / week and rainfall is >5mm on any day / week and maize is < knee high, then the main armyworm period may start. * Get armyworm forecasts from trained farmers. * Check weekly for caterpillars and feeding on leaves. * Check for caterpillars late evening/early morning; as they feed at night and hide under debris or at the base of plants during the day.2
* Young caterpillars are green. yellow and brown with longitudinal stripes. Length is ½ cm They sometimes hang threads below the leaves. * Young caterpillars feed by scraping the surface of young leaves leaving a thin layer known as windows
* Older caterpillars (1 to 2.5 cm) are velvety-black on the upper body with green, black, yellow, and white lateral stripes. Inverted V-shaped mark on head. * Fall armyworm looks similar has four dark spots forming a square at the end of the back. * Older armyworms bite and cut through leaves Look for chewed leaves making the crop look ragged
* Consider green control when 5 – 10% leaf damage on about half of plants at young caterpillars. But at older caterpillars, direct control maybe more urgent. * When 15 – 25 % of leaf damage per plant consider chemical control
* At >30 % damage and old caterpillar stage, action may be too late

title: Black armyworm on maize-Ethiopia.
text: * Hand pick caterpillars, destroy them by crushing or feed to chickens or ducks. * Dig a 30 cm deep trench with vertical sides around the field to trap marching caterpillars. Collect and destroy them. * Put a handful of sand (mixed with lime or ash), sawdust or soil in the whorl of the attacked plants to repel the caterpilars. * Encourage natural enemies such as birds, toads, lizards and spiders by planting trees and shrubs.

title: Black armyworm on maize-Ethiopia.
text: * Yearly check lists of registered pesticides of Ethiopia for less dangerous pesticides against armyworm than Malathion. * When using a pesticide always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre-harvest interval, restricted re-interval. * Always consult recent list of registered pesticides from Ministry of Agriculture (Plant health regulatory directorate of Ethopia)

title: Black armyworm on maize-Ethiopia.
text:
### Foliar sprays of Malathion – based products (Fyfanon 50 % E.C) Organophosphate. Double check product label for right dosage. Contact insecticide. Pre – harvest interval (PHI) – 7 days; Restricted re-entry interval (REI) 1 d. Maximum 1 treatment per growing season. ###

title: Oxalis weed in onion - Kenya.
text: Oxalis weed in onion - Kenya.

title: Oxalis weed in onion - Kenya.
text:
* Oxalis latifolia is a multi-year invasive weed that spreads vegetative below-ground by bulbs, and less often by seeds. The weed occurs on a wide range of soils and causes problems to many field crops. * Onion crop is not good in competing with weeds because slow-growing, shallow-rooted and narrow leaves6. 4. Use onion seeds certified free of weed seeds
* Prepare the seed bed and leave it for14 moist for weed to grow. Remove the initial weed flush mechanically by shallow hoeing (to reduce subsequent weed flushes and also prevent bringing up weed seed and bulbs from deeper soil)
* Apply mulch from plant residues or polythene sheets to prevent Oxalis germinating
* Deep plough and desiccate the rhizomes/ bulbs – do not plough when the soils are moist as this will initiate Oxalis germination
* Remove, where possible, all the bulbs on ploughed field by hand when the soil is slightly moist (tiny brownish to white bulbs easy to spot on moist ploughed soils)
* Do not place the weed in compost bins/heaps for re-use as this will re-introduce the weeds to the fields
* Rotate onion with broad-leaved crops as cover crops such as legumes and pumpkin to suppress the Oxalis weed.

title: Oxalis weed in onion - Kenya.
text:
* Monitor once a week at seed bed and continue after transplanting until up to 3 months after transplanting (time for the onion to form bulbs )
* Look for small low, creeping plants with three heart-shaped or fish-tail shaped leaflets, at the tip of about 10 cm weak thin stems. * Leaves are green to purple about 4cm wide. They fold at the midrib at night
* The flowers have five flower-leaves which fuse at the base. They are greenish on outside and purple on the inside but pale towards the base
* Look for small whitish to brown bulbs (short carrot shaped, 1-2 cm) when the soil is moist before sowing
* Oxalis weeds grow in clusters of >15 plants per cluster. Control measures should be initiated when there are 3 – 6 clusters/ m

title: Oxalis weed in onion - Kenya.
text:
* Emphasize reducing weed pressure before planting (see preventive column)
* Apply organic or dry grass/plant residue mulch 15-20cm thick around the onion plants to limit the number of germinating oxalis and suffocate any germinated
* Uproot or hand hoe in the germination nursery before the oxalis starts to flower. Growth span of oxalis from germination to seed production is 8-10 weeks

title: Oxalis weed in onion - Kenya.
text:
* When using a pesticide or botanical, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre-harvest interval, max number of sprays, restricted re-entry interval. * Many herbicides fail to control Oxalis and even favour re-grow
* Always consult the most recent list of registered pesticides of Kenya.

title: Oxalis weed in onion - Kenya.
text:
### You may consider oxyfluorfen – based products (Galigan 240EC, Predator 340EC and others) pre-emergence and post-emergence herbicides used for controlling a wide range of broad-leaf weeds in onion. ###
WHO toxicity class U (unlikely to present acute hazard to humans). Apply to soil surface prior to crop emergence after field preparation/tillage. Apply once during the cropping season and combine with other mechanical weed control methods. Restricted re-entry interval (r.e.i) is ½ day. Degradation time in soil 14 days
### Glyphosate – based herbicides (Glycel 480SL, Burnwid 48% SL and others). Applied against germinating weeds pre-emergence of crop. Requires 2 days of no rain. Dosage as indicated on label It will only clear surface growth but not the Oxalis bulbs. The bulbs will re-grow ###
WHO toxicity class II (moderately acute hazardous to humans). Apply 3 days before planting and without rain/watering if no/minimum tillage is practised. R.e.i. 24 hours. Do not spray glyphosate after planting because it will kill the onion. Glyphosate is moderately harmful to water, observe the required distance from water bodies. It is moderately harmful to bees and other pollinators

title: Tea aphid-Kenya.
text:
* Transplant aphid free tea seedlings from Tea Research Institute

title: Tea aphid-Kenya.

* Look out for mottled leaves, yellowed leaves, stunted growth, browning, wilting, low yields and death of plants

title: Tea aphid-Kenya.

title: Armillaria root rot in tea-Kenya.
text:

title: Armillaria root rot in tea-Kenya.

* Expose the base of the newly infected plants for up to 3 to 4 inches deeper for aeration. * To reduce the inoculum build up, remove the stumps of all infected tea bushes and burn down. * Ring incise the trunks for 6 to 12 months before uprooting the infected tea bushes
* Uproot infected tea stems and roots if possible.

title: Barley-yellow dwarf virus-Kenya.
text:
* Barley yellow dwarf virus is transmitted from plant to plant by different species of aphids
* Select small grain cultivars eg kenya sunbird, kenya hawk 12, with documented resistance or tolerance to the virus from certified dealers, i.e. simlaws
* Plough deeply affected post harvested areas to ensure complete decomposition of all plant material
* Practice crop rotation with non host plants such as green grams, kales and spinach
* Proper spacing of the plants at 80-120 plants/square metre apart to optimize aeration
* Early planting to avoid aphid population build up

title: Barley-yellow dwarf virus-Kenya.
text:
* Look out for small pale green insect (aphids) with an elongated, spindle-shaped body under the leaf one week after crop emergence
* Check for chlorotic to reddened leaves in young plants. Upright stiff leaves with serrated edges, stunted plants
* Take action when 50% of cereal tillers have 15 or more aphids three weeks after emergence

title: Barley-yellow dwarf virus-Kenya.
text:
* Remove and destroy affected plant parts by burying them 1m deeply in the ground or burning
* Destroy and remove volunteer cereals to help reduce or delay pest build-up
* Add a layer of organic manure mixed deeper into the soil up to 20 cm at a rate of (2 tones/acre) and irrigate the farm to prevent water stress to the plants

text: Black spot of papaya-Kenya.

title: Black spot of papaya-Kenya.
text:
* *A. caricae* is a fungus that cause black spot on fruits and leaves of papaya. It is spread from tree to tree by wind and wind-driven rains
* Initiate orchards hygienically using seedlings that are free from pathogens from KALRO, JKUAT
* Prune the trees to reduce humidity and improve air circulation in the orchard
* Avoid overhead irrigation which spreads the spores through splash
* Ensure crop vigor and good health through fertilizer and manure application
* Keep the orchard free of weeds to minimize alternative hosts to the pathogen
* Avoid working in fields when plants are wet and work on infected areas last

title: Black spot of papaya-Kenya.
text:
* Scout the farm regularly for initial small, black spots on fruits and underside of leaves. Spots are sunken yellow on the upper leaf surface
* The black spot pathogen is hyperparasitized by another fungus (*Cephalosporium* sp.) showing a white fungal growth around affected spots in the later stages
* Take action once spots are observed on plants since the disease spreads fast through dispersion of spores, by air and splash and compromise fruit quality

title: Black spot of papaya-Kenya.
text:
* Practice field sanitation by removing and destroying (by burning) severely infected plant parts and plant debris to reduce disease inoculum on the farm
* Disinfect farm tools between plants and farms (Use 50 ml JIK in 1 litre of water), to prevent spread of the fungus
* Spray the plants by using Trianum-P (*Trichoderma harzianum*) at a rate of 15g in 5L or Trichotech (*Trichoderma asperellum*) at a rate of 2.5g in 20L of water

title: Black spot of papaya-Kenya.
text:

* Follow instructions on the product label
* Disinfect all farm tools by dipping in 10% jik solution at 50ml/ L of water for atleast 5 minutes
* Always consult recent list of registered pesticides (PCPB)

title: Botrytis gray mold on strawberries-Kenya.

* Look for fruit that are completely rotten dry, tough and mummified. * Take action when 3% of the crop is affected.

title: Lesser grain weevil in barley-Kenya.
text: Lesser grain weevil in barley-Kenya.

title: Lesser grain weevil in barley-Kenya.
text:
* Store properly dried, non-infested grains (at 12% moisture content) in hermetic bags
* Remove previous years grains, debris, contaminants and thoroughly clean the storage facilities
* Inspect all grains and storage containers thoroughly before use
* Never mix infested with non-infested grains
* Dry barley grains in the sun to achieve 13% of moisture content
* Before storing new grains, remove infested residues from the previous harvest, sweep floors and inspect walls for holes and cracks to amend

title: Lesser grain weevil in barley-Kenya.
text:
* Look out for small (3-5mm long) brownish to blackish adult insects with an elongated snout on stored grains
* Check grains for adult emergence holes with irregular edges
* Disturb stored grains to check for weevils migrating upwards to the surface
* Monitor regularly and thoroughly for weevil reappearance – it may take a while to get rid of them completely
* When 5-10 weevils are detected, take action to control them

title: Lesser grain weevil in barley-Kenya.
text:
* Store grains in tightly sealed glass, metal, sturdy plastic containers, or hermetic bags (not normal bags)
* Place black pepper around the grain stores to repel weevils
* Apply neem seed powder into grain storage at 20g/kg of barley. Alternatively, finely spray the grains with need oil or neem leaf extract. Spray the grain in shade and wait for the grains to dry well and put them back into storage. * Coating of wood ash, edible oils or inert clay to prevent further development of the weevils
* Sun dry bags of infected grains for 48 hours using either tarpaulin sheets or drying floors
* Sieve infested grains and dry again in the sun to kill the remaining eggs and adults

* Plant early and avoid planting the crop very close to each other

* Take action when damage holes are seen on 2-4 plants

title: Green gram pod borer-Kenya.

* Remove and destroy by burning or burying in a 30 cm pit all affected plants
* Install pheromone traps 50 m apart @5 traps/ha, install bird perches @50/ha from the beginning of pod maturity
* Create a conducive environment for natural enemies (e.g lady bird beetles, spiders, praying mantis etc.) to multiply by growing hedges of flowering plants

title: Cotton bollworm on sorghum-Ethiopia.
text: Cotton bollworm on sorghum-Ethiopia.

title: Cotton bollworm on sorghum-Ethiopia.
text: * Select and plant loose or open head sorghum varieties because they are rarely attacked by the bollworm. * Deep ploughing in off-season to expose the pupae of bollworm in the soil to sunlight and natural enemies.

title: Cotton bollworm on sorghum-Ethiopia.
text: * The larvae feed on the sorghum head, monitor for bollworm larvae from head emergence to grain fill once in a week. * Look for larvae ranging from about 1 cm (small size) to about 4 cm (fully grown larvae) on the sorghum head. * Choose five different points in ¼ hectare, check 6-10 sorghum heads by beating heads to dislodge the larvae onto a sheet or onto the ground. Count them. * In addition, look for sheared developing grain, and frass in leaf axils and into tight compacted head. * Consider control measures when larvae are seen on 5 to 10 % of the sampled plant heads. * The crop is considered heavily damaged when the larvae reach older stage (35-40 mm) and if the infestation is high.

title: Cotton bollworm on sorghum-Ethiopia.
text: * Shaking the plants to induce the larvae to drop into a bucket or other appropriate materials; handpick and kill/crush larvae, in small fields. * Larvae on open panicles are exposed to predaceous insects and birds.

title: Faba bean gall on faba bean-Ethiopia.
text: Faba bean gall on faba bean-Ethiopia.

title: Faba bean gall on faba bean-Ethiopia.
text: * The faba bean gall is a fungal disease, the disease survives in crop debris/residues and in the soil. * Use of tolerant varieties like Degaga, NC-58 and Tumsa varieties. * Practice crop rotation for at least two seasons with cereals like wheat and barley or Gomenzar (Brassica carinata) to reduce or eliminate the disease in the soil. * Remove crop debris of the previously diseased pulse crops. But do not remove debris and residues if no major pest problem is in the field, to help to improve soils. * Avoid or remove excess surface water to prevent the spread of the disease.

title: Faba bean gall on faba bean-Ethiopia.
text: * Look for Faba bean gall symptoms on leaves and stems from seedlings to pod setting stage every week. * Look for small chlorotic spots, and that then progressively enlarge to become light brown, circular or elliptical rough spots. * Act Immediately when first symptoms are seen. * Action is too late when small tumor like galls are formed and adjacent galls form huge galls, resulting in rolling up and abnormal growth of leaves. * At the later stage, the galls turn black or brown and a few galls break to form necrotic areas, but action is far too late.

title: Faba bean gall on faba bean-Ethiopia.
text: * Immediate removal of infected faba bean plant.

title: Faba bean gall on faba bean-Ethiopia.
text: * No fungicides are registered against this disease yet. Check the updated list of registered pesticides by Ministry of Agriculture of Ethiopia

title: Leaf hoppers in rice-Kenya.
text: Leaf hoppers in rice-Kenya.

title: Leaf hoppers in rice-Kenya.
text: * Protect natural enemies such as Spiders, Dragon flies, Ladybird beetles, Predatory wasps and Parasitic wasps through conservation of patches of natural vegetation. * Plant early in the season at the onset of rains.Plant companion crops such as marigold and geraniums around the rice field. * Control weeds in the field to remove the preferred grassy hosts of GLH and promote crop vigor. * Rotate rice with non-grass crops like potatoes, cabbages, soya beans, beans etc. * Avoid overlap/relay planting of rice crop. Reduce the number of rice crops to two per year and synchronize crop establishment across farms to reduce leafhoppers infestations. * Avoid planting during the peak of leafhopper activity (shown by historical records) to avoid infestation. * Transplant older seedlings (>3 weeks) to reduce susceptibility to viral diseases transmitted by leafhoppers.

title: Leaf hoppers in rice-Kenya.
text: * Inspect regularly for slender, wedge-shaped insects with varying body colors of green, yellow, brown and are often mottled, mostly matching the colour of the host plant. * Look for light-colored speckling on plant leaves that gradually lead to browning of the leaves. * Inspect young plants or new growth for stunted growth and/or deformations. * Inspect shoots for curls and/or dying while the tips of infested leaves develop diamond- shape yellowing, may also appear stippled, pale or brown. * Use light traps to show leafhopper presence. * Take action when 3-5 nymphs per hill are seen.

title: Leaf hoppers in rice-Kenya.
text: * Uproot infected plants and feed livestock or burn. * Control the leafhoppers by digging a trench between rice fields and planting grass on the bands.

title: Leaf hoppers in rice-Kenya.
text: * When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label. * Do not use chemicals with the same mode of action year after year as this can lead to resistance. * Always consult the most recent list of registered pesticides (PCPB).

title: Rice gall midge-Kenya.
text: Rice gall midge-Kenya.

title: Rice gall midge-Kenya.
text:
* Keep fallow land free of seasonal host plants
* Synchronize early planting so that the insect does not find and infect young plants to build up its population
* Remove all alternate hosts (grass family) and wild rice from the field and field boundaries
* Apply proper fertilizer doses to avoid over-dose as this would cause profuse leaf formation

title: Rice gall midge-Kenya.
text:
* Check for elongate-tubular eggs (laid singly) and maggot-like larva feeding inside developing buds. Adult looks like a mosquito
* Look for stunted plants with deformed, wilted, and rolled leaves
* Look for elongated leaf sheaths, also called onion leaf or silvershoot
* Monitor affected tillers which inhibits growth of leaves and fails to produce panicles
* Take action when 30% of plants have typical symptom or 5-10 adult flies are seen on the crop

title: Rice gall midge-Kenya.
text:
* Handpick and destroy egg masses at the nursery and at transplanting
* Remove and destroy the onion/silvery shoots
* Apply pesticides judiciously to conserve pteromalid wasps (that parasitize the larvae), phytoseiid mites (feed on eggs), spiders (feed on adults)

title: Rice stem borer-Kenya.

title: Strawberry aphid in strawberry-Kenya.
text: * Do not apply more than recommended nitrogen fertilizer as this will increase leave growth which favours aphid egg laying (Not more than 45kgN per hectare at planting. * Plant and/or maintain habitats that support beneficial insects such as flowers or grass strips. Such beneficial insects can largely reduce aphid populations. * Dust with ash other plants growing near the strawberries if they are hosting aphids before they enter the strawberry field. * Plant strawberry varieties resistant to viruses transmitted by aphids such as San Andreas which is moderately tolerant to most viral diseases.

title: Strawberry aphid in strawberry-Kenya.
text: * Inspect strawberry fields especially when young and during flowering, every 3 to 4 days. * Look under the leaves, especially along main veins particularly at the base of leaves of every 10th plant. * Look for clusters of tiny light-green soft-bodied pear-shaped insects (about 1 to 3 mm long). Most are wingless, few have wings. * Take action when aphids reach 5 to 10 per leaf on the inspected plants. * It’s too late if the aphids have started attacking the fruits. * Look for sticky honeydew or blackish sooty moulds on fruits and leaves. If on leaves, action may still be possible. * If many natural enemies, are near the aphid colonies, such as lady beetle adults and their larvae, no action may be needed.

title: Strawberry aphid in strawberry-Kenya.
text: * Mix 1 tablespoon of soap (non-perfumed) with 4L of water and spray the crop early in the morning or late afternoon. * Dust ash evenly onto the infested parts of the crop. * Soak green leaves and seeds of castor oil plant for 24 hours in water, filter, dilute and spray. * Use Ervipar (*Aphidius ervi*), a parasitic wasp that parasitizes aphids. Available in major agrochemical shops. Read the label for directions for use. Release when temperatures are below 30° C.

title: Strawberry aphid in strawberry-Kenya.
text: * When using a pesticide or botanical, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre-harvest interval, max number of sprays, restricted re-entry interval. Do not empty into drains and water sources. * WHO toxicity class II products may not be allowed in local IPM schemes. * Always consult recent list of registered pesticides from Pests Control Products Board of Kenya. * In most cases, no application of synthetic insecticides is needed against aphids in strawberries, because they only do damage in high numbers (see thresholds), and are often controlled by natural enemies. text: * Avoid intercropping or growing cotton, tomato, okra, eggplant, pepper or sweet potato near the orchard because they are alternative hosts to false codling moth pest

title: False codling moth in citrus-Kenya.
text:
* Check every fifth tree in an orchard
* Check trees at flowering and fruit set for 1 cm big brown moths with a dark coppery brown band at the tip of the wings
* Look for the moths early in the morning as they are inactive during the day
* Control the insect when you see at least 10-20 moths on 30% of the trees inspected
* Use pheromone traps for effective long-term monitoring. Check the traps once weekly during the fruiting period. Control pest at 60-80 moth catches per trap per week
* Look for 1 mm diameter holes/ burrows and frass on the rind of the fruit. This is the larvae entry hole
* Look for 1 to 1 ½ cm long light pink larvae with a dark brown head inside the fruit
* Look for above signs especially during early fruit development and entire fruiting stage
* When larvae have entered the fruits, action is too late this season, but may warrant action next season

title: False codling moth in citrus-Kenya.
text:

* Release egg parasitoid *Trichogrammatoidea cryptophlebiae* (from Dudutech company outlets) several times while the fruits are susceptible to the pest. Up to about 125,000 are per hectare. * Pick all infested fruits (both on trees and those fallen on the ground) and destroy by burying at least 50cm deep twice every week during fruiting stage. * Apply Azadirachtin 0.03% based products like Nimbicidine EC at the rate of 20 - 25ml/20l of water to reduce infestation

title: Citrus greening disease in oranges-Kenya.
text:
* Citrus greening is a serious disease of citrus caused by a bacterium and transmitted by citrus psyllid *Trioza eritreae* (insect vector)
* Source certified healthy seedlings from a certified nursery
* Leave flower strips along the edges of the farm/ intercrop with beans, black night shade or similar flowering plants to encourage natural enemies (parasitic wasp) that feed on psyllid nymphs

title: Citrus greening disease in oranges-Kenya.
text:
* Check for leaves that look yellowed or mottled with green midribs on the trees in neighbouring farms to confirm if disease is in the area. It is important for neighbouring farmers to take collective action to control the disease vectors, if the disease is present. * Yellowing process of leaves due to citrus greening disease does not follow any defined pattern while the nutrient deficiency yellowing is symmetric between left and right leaf side next to the green midrib
* Look for brown psyllid insects with a light brown head, with a head down and tail up posture as it feeds (citrus psyllids). They jump and fly off when branches are shaken
* Look for the psyllids on new leaf growth as they like feeding on young leaves
* Look for the psyllids early in the morning as they are inactive during this time
* Consider action when the disease is in your area, and be quick if it is in neighbouring fields
* Control for the disease is too late once it has been introduced into the orchard
* Citrus greening can be confused with other diseases such as citrus stubborn and tristeza which also cause yellowing of the leaves. Uneven ripening (greening) and uneven shaped fruits are diagnostic. Diseased trees also show poor growth and dieback.

title: Citrus greening disease in oranges-Kenya.
text: * Remove and destroy young infested trees by burning at a safe place outside the orchard. Uproot and replace diseased seedlings and young trees as they will never bear fruits. Destroy the diseased uprooted trees by drying in sun or burning. This is needed to prevent further disease spread. * Use biopesticides such as neem oil to control the citrus psyllids that transmit the disease. Neem oil kills psyllids by suffocation and is a repellent for psyllids

text:

* Always consult recent Pest Control Products Board (PCPB) list of registered pesticides of Kenya. * There is no synthetic bactericide against the greening disease. * To control the bacteria vectoring psyllid insects, some insecticides can be foliar applied, also reaching underside of leaves.

title: Phytophthora root rot in avocado-Kenya.
text: * Avoid soils with poor drainage. Avoid salty soils. * Plant on slightly elevated spots. * Plough the land deep (92-152cm) to improve drainage and aeration before planting. * Soil solarization with black polythene sheets before planting. * Apply organic mulches and inorganic gypsum to the soil to prevent rot disease. * Plant disease free seedlings from certified nurseries. * Do not move soil from diseased orchards 3 Do not work in infested ochards when the soil is wet as phytophthora is readily spread by walking or driving on infested soil. * Disinfect tools with 2.5%JIK after working on each tree. * Begin harvesting and other activities in healthy parts of the orchard, work in diseased areas last to minimize disease movement.

title: Phytophthora root rot in avocado-Kenya.
text: * This is a water mould disease spread by infected seedlings, soil, water runoff and infected tools. * Do regular visits in the orchard especially when the trees are young (fortnightly). * Check the tips of leaves and shoots, check for small pale green or yellowish leaves which often wilt and have necrotic tips. * Look under the trees, there may be prematurely dropped leaves under infected trees. * If above symptoms are found on young trees showing early symptoms early action with *Trichoderma* may be needed. * Look for branches with sparse foliage and little new growth. Look for small branches with die back on the tree exposing other branches and fruits to sunburn. action however is too late. * Remove a bit of soil and check for roots that are small, black, brittle and dead at an advanced stage of the disease. * It’s too late for chemical control when several avocado trees are infected.

title: Phytophthora root rot in avocado-Kenya.

text: Fruit flies in citrus-Kenya.

title: Fruit flies in citrus-Kenya.
text: * Protect natural enemies such as spiders, dragon flies, ladybird beetles, predatory wasps and parasitic wasps through conservation of patches of natural vegetation. * Choose a site far away (>1 Km) from other orchards that may be infested to prevent the flies crossing over. * Encourage fellow farmers to control fruit flies (area wide approach to fruit flies). * Remove neglected (unmanaged) host plants like guava, chillies, citrus, melons, coffee, mangoes, wild fruits to reduce pest population. * Use mulch and do not destroy long flowering weeds to attract natural enemies. * Harvest early when crop is mature and green because over-ripened fruits attract fruit flies.

title: Fruit flies in citrus-Kenya.
text: * Set pheromone traps to detect adult fruit flies presence. * Look for oviposition marks especially on immature fallen fruits. * Dissect the fruits with symptoms and examine them for larvae presence and fruit rot. * Look on fruit surfaces for small holes, punctured fruit, black lesions, soft spots, rotting, maggots and discolouration. * Look for pupae 2-5 cm beneath soil under host plant and take action to control as soon as fruit flies and damage symptoms are observed.

title: Fruit flies in citrus-Kenya.
text: * Increase pheromone traps density to 2-4 traps per acre depending on fruit flies infestation levels. Trap flies using commercial pheromone traps - Methyl Euginol (Bactrolure liquid) at 20 traps per acre. * Collect fallen fruits and bury more than 40 cm deep, drop in a pool of water or put in black plastic containers and cover tightly and leave for a few days in the sun to kill the insect. * Apply *Metarhizium anisopliae* in the pheromone trap which causes plague on the fruit flies. * Spray neem based botanical products as protection, to prevent egg laying at a rate of 5g/1L of water sprayed after 3 to 5 days intervals. * Spray neem extracts e.g Achook 0.15% EC at 20 ml in 20L of water.

text: Citrus mealybug-Kenya.

title: Citrus mealybug-Kenya.
text: * Apply banding materials like grease or tangle foot to prevent ants from climbing to the canopy to introduce the mealybugs. * Construct slippery bands of alkathene or plastic sheets around the tree trunk at about one meter above the ground level. * Use clean planting materials from certified nurseries such as KALRO Mutuga, JKUAT to reduce spread of infestation into new fields. * Conserve natural enemies; lacewings, pirate bugs, lady beetles and parasitoids by maintaining natural habitat. * Avoid the use of infested plant materials. Before planting, seedlings can be treated by immersing them in heated water (mix equal volumes of boiling and cold water) for 5 to 10 minutes to kill the pest. * Plant early in the rainy season to allow citrus to grow well, before the dry season, as strong plants are more likely to withstand pest attack. * Use soil amendments and mulch to avoid moisture stress in sandy or poor soils. Mealybug numbers are higher in poor soil, and may cause damage in spite of the presence of natural enemies. * Restrict movement of infested planting materials across to mealybug-free areas.

title: Citrus mealybug-Kenya.
text: * Inspect regularly for dark sticky covering on affected part (sooty mold). * Check for ants climbing to the plant canopy. * Check for white immobile oval and flattened insects with body covered with a white mealy powder on the leaves, stems, fruit stalks and growing tips. * Symptoms on the plant include stunting, wilting, leaf distortion, leaf fall, rosetting of the stem, bunchy top and dieback. * Ants may also be present as they protect the mealybugs from natural enemies and feed on the honeydew they produce. * Black sooty mould may grow on the leaves and stem in the presence of honeydew. * Take action when you notice white waxy material on shoot tips, leaves and stems or any signs of mealybugs.

title: Citrus mealybug-Kenya.
text:
* Prune and burn the highly infested plant parts. * Spray the affected plant part with a mild solution of water with dish washing detergent at rate of 1 tea spoonful of detergent in 1 litre of water. * Collect fallen fruit and leaves and destroy by burning or bury more than 50m deep. * Spray using Beauvitech® WP (250g/1500-200water in 1 acre depending on crop canopy) or Lecatech® WP from Dudutech. Spray every 5-7 days and repeat 2-4 applications
* Destroy egg masses by digging around the tree trunk. * Mix 5 g of soap + 5 g of powdered pepper in 1 litre of water and leave it for about 30 minutes. Pour the mixture into knapsack and apply in 15 litres of water. * Apply neem oil. Add 10 ml soap to 1 litre of water and stir to mix. Add 50 ml neem oil to the 1 litre water-soap solution and mix thouroughly. Add the oil-water-soap solution to 14 litres water in the knapsack and apply within 8 hrs. Ensure thorough coverage
* Control ants as these will reduce the amount of natural predators.

text: * When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label. * Do not use chemicals with the same mode of action year after year as this can lead to resistance. * Always consult the most recent list of registered pesticides (PCPB).

text: * Keep the farm weed free as they can act as alternative hosts, such as solanum family crops. * Observe correct planting spacing of 1 m by 1 m to avoid over crowding of plants. * Conserve natural habitats to enhance indigenous natural enemies. * Avoid planting gooseberries next to infested field or crops. * When moving through the gooseberry orchard, start with the non-infested area before moving to infested area.

title: Red spider mites in gooseberries-Kenya.

title: Rust in greengram-Kenya.

title: Stem rust of wheat-Kenya.
text: * Symptoms include: Reddish brown, powdery, elongated, blister-like pustules on leaves, glumes and awns. * On leaves the rust develops mostly on the underside but may penetrate to the upperside. * Black spores are produced firmly attached on leaves and stems towards end of season. * Inspect all plant parts every 7-10 days from flag leaf emergence to early grain development. * Consider direct control when orange pustules are observed on leaves of 4-5 plants.

title: Wheat head blight-Kenya.
text: Wheat head blight-Kenya.

title: Wheat head blight-Kenya.
text: * Plant certified clean seeds from reputable seed companys and avoid recycling seeds from infected fields. * Plant tolerant varieties such as Njoro BW1, Njoro BW2. * Practice crop rotatation using legume based crops. * Select sites with good drainage and a good soil profile to avoid water logging. * Deeply plough the soils to expose the innoculum to harsh conditions 3 to 4 months before planting. * Avoid use of overhead irrigation, especially during cool and wet conditions. * Avoid reuse of water for irrigation. * Sow seeds in well prepared nursery and fertilized soils for good root growth and vigorous development.

title: Wheat head blight-Kenya.
text: * Scout wheat farms during the flowering stage and high humidity levels for disease incidences. * Check for light-straw and bleached spikelets. * Look out for white/light brown color on wheat spikes. * Look out for shrivelling and discolouration of kernels on the infected spikes. * Towards the end of the season look for dark purple-black fruiting bodies on the infected spike. * Consider direct control actions when symptoms are observed on 1-3 plants.

title: Wheat head blight-Kenya.
text: * Uproot or prune infected plants and destroy by burning the infected debris. * Sterilize farm tools with 10% sodium hypochloride or Jik while working in the wheat farm. * Drain soggy or water logged soils to reduce humidity that enhance spread of the disease. * Use Trichotech WP at 1.25 g/L water every 2 weeks to one month depending on disease pressure. * Apply leaf extract of neem (Achook, Nembecidine) at 20 ml/20 L of water (maximum 3 times).

title: Wheat head blight-Kenya.

title: Septoria leaf blotch of wheat-Kenya.

Consider taking action when 2 of the 5 have more than 25% incidence.

text: * Use disease-free seed material. * Undertake crop rotation with rice, maize, sorghum and pearl millet. * Early sowing before 30-45 days before normal date of sowing. * Follow good field sanitation practices such as sufficient irrigation, as over-irrigating can increase the risk of spreading the bacteria.

title: Early shoot borer in sugarcane-India.

title: Fall armyworm (FAW) in sorghum-Uganda.
text:
* Protect natural enemies such as spiders, dragon flies, ladybird beetles, predatory wasps and parasitic wasps through conservation of patches of natural vegetation of flowering plants such as lantana
* Plant early and adhere to regional planting calendar as well as avoiding off season crop
* Plough land, especially before onset of rains, to expose pupae to predators and solar heat
* Regularly weed to remove alternate hosts
* Plant at correct spacing and ensure optimum use of fertilizer of Nitrogen fertilizer, 100kg CAN/acre
* Do not move infested sorghum materials from one area to another to reduce spread of the pest instead graze livestock on them or make silage
* Avoid planting new crop near infested plants

title: Fall armyworm (FAW) in sorghum-Uganda.
text:
* Look for green, brown or black caterpillars inside the growing tip of sorghum
* Look for feeding marks on leaves appearing like “scratch” on young plants but 'ragged' leaves as caterpillars grow older
* Scout for egg mass (large numbers) 50-200 covered by a mass of whitish sheath
* Look for saw dust/pellet like feacal material from young and older caterpillars respectively, on the growing tips/whorl
* Set pheromone traps to attract and trap male moths to determine FAW presence
* Take action when 10-30% of plant have typical symptoms or if eggs are found on greater than 5% of plants

title: Fall armyworm (FAW) in sorghum-Uganda.
text:
* Handpick and squash or drop caterpillar in hot water. Killing one caterpillar prevents more than 1500 new caterpillars after a period of 4 weeks. * Apply a pinch from a mixture of 50g ground hot pepper + 2kg wood ash into plant funnel at knee-high stage
* Set more pheromone traps to control FAW at densities of 2 traps per Ha but this should be before populations are high
* Put a half handful of sand/sawdust or soil in the whorl of the attacked plants to kill the larvae
* Release egg parasitoid *Trichogramma* spp at a rate of 50,000 to 100,000 eggs per acre
